title: The Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treason | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Politicians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidence
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Politicians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidence
Content: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham face being stripped of their citizenship for treason.Photograph: Maria Laura Antonelli/AGF/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham face being stripped of their citizenship for treason.Photograph: Maria Laura Antonelli/AGF/ShutterstockOpinionNAZAThe Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treasonEditorialPoliticians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidenceFri 18 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTShareAcross Israel, politicians, military leaders and much of the media are trying to discredit a documentary that almost none of them have seen. Produced by the Guardian, NAZA examines theAI-powered targeting systemsused by the Israel Defense Forces to bombard Gaza after Hamas’s brutal 7 October 2023 attacks. Named after the Israeli military acronym euphemistically usedfor “collateral damage”, NAZA features interviews with 24 anonymous insiders who reflect on their role in the death-dealing. Israeli leaders have branded the film a “blood libel” and “fiction”. Its Oscar-winning directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, face beingstrippedof their citizenship for treason.This is absurd. NAZAshowshow bureaucratic distance and routine can turn extreme violence into ordinary work. More than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 20,000 children, have been killed in the campaign by Israel’s military. A democracy that values life would at least investigate the film’s claims. Instead Israel’s government, which says it is committed to democratic accountability, is attacking journalists.The allegations in NAZA come from military insiders. For many, it does not appear to be remorse that drives them to speak out. Some are proud of what they have done. One recalls the“insane fun”of planning airstrikes in Gaza. Crucially, Israeli soldiers describe the military accepting large numbers of Palestinian casualties as the price for killing a single Hamas operative. When civilian fatalities rise to as many as hundreds for one enemy combatant, proportionality looks less like a military assessment and more like a licence for mass death.NAZA’sstoryis not only about death and destruction but also some of the people behind it: polite, educated members of Israel’s liberal middle class, much like the directors themselves. They built and operated a system that told them women and children would die in large numbers. Yet they told themselves that responsibility for the deaths of innocent Palestinians lay elsewhere. The acronym, NAZA, turns possible fatalities into a number per target. By the time an operator approves a strike, morality has disappeared up the chain of command.An election campaign has seen Israeli politicians shamefully weaponise controversy to outflank each other on the right. If such leaders are saying that the conduct of the Israeli military is beyond independent review, that can hardly be consistent with the commitment to the rule of law. Israel’s government might invoke national security to defend its actions. But the film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Ominously, Israel’s domestic intelligence service may be involved in a leak investigation. By turning the army on the documentary’s directors, Israel is making anexampleof them. Far-right activists target their families by making threats. If the filmmakers were to return to Israel now, their lives might well be indanger.TheCommittee to Protect Journalistsand 10 other press-freedom groups have warned that Israel must protect its journalists and filmmakers – not brand them traitors and paint targets on their backs. Yet the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has seized on the controversy to threaten anyone who “defames” Israeli soldiers with loss of citizenship. Rather than investigate alleged crimes, he would punish those who expose them. Israel’s leaders ought to be protecting those who scrutinise power, not pointing a mob towards them.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Tech billionaires trying to live for ever? That’s a waste of time, says physicist | Physics | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Prof Jim Al-Khalili says he will offer solution to ‘arrow of time’ problem in Royal Institution lectures
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Exclusive: Prof Jim Al-Khalili says he will offer solution to ‘arrow of time’ problem in Royal Institution lectures
Content: Prof Jim Al-Khalili will explore some of the paradoxes of theoretical time travel in his Christmas lectures.Photograph: Paul SteadView image in fullscreenProf Jim Al-Khalili will explore some of the paradoxes of theoretical time travel in his Christmas lectures.Photograph: Paul SteadPhysicsTech billionaires trying to live for ever? That’s a waste of time, says physicistExclusive: Prof Jim Al-Khalili says he will offer solution to ‘arrow of time’ problem in Royal Institution lecturesNicola DavisScience correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTech billionaires attempting to live for ever are, quite literally, wasting their time, a leading physicist has said.While some normal people are turning tounregulated peptide injections, cold plunges and supplements in an effort to defy ageing, the ultra-rich are aiming for immortality with even more drastic interventions: the tech chief executive Bryan Johnson has even triedinjecting plasma from his 17-year-old son– although he later said he saw no benefit from it.View image in fullscreenBryan Johnson  (and son Talmage) is the world's most measured human.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaProf Jim Al-Khalili, who will be giving this year’sRoyal InstitutionChristmas lectures on the topic of time, has said people expending their energy on trying to live for ever may be missing out on the here and now.“We have a finite interval of time in which we exist in the universe. And the more I study the nature of time, the more I think about it, the more I realise that I just want to make the most of the time that I have,” he said.“We’re [here for] a blink of an eye compared with the age of the universe. If I spend that blink of an eye trying to extend it to two blinks of an eye, I’m not sure if that is actually a worthwhile thing to be spending my life doing.”View image in fullscreen‘I just want to make the most of the time that I have’: Jim Al-Khalili prefers temporal quality over quantity.Al-Khalili has long been fascinated by time. As a child he was baffled when his father, an engineer, said no one really understood what time was. “I had no idea what he was talking about,” he said. “It was only after training as a physicist you realise that, actually, the notion of time – our commonsense view of time – somehow it is very far removed from the way we think about time in physics in particular.”Among other examples, Al-Khalili points out that the renowned theoretical physicist Albert Einstein revealed time does not run at the same rate for everyone. “What I might call a second would be longer than a second for you if I was flying past you with my clock in a rocket,” he said. “I’ll say, look, it’s ticking by one second. And you’ll say, no, actually, five seconds have gone by. You’re doing everything in slow motion.”Gravity, he added, had an effect too. “That for me is the most spine-tingling aspect to it, that time runs at different rates depending on how strong gravity is.”Einstein’s work may also shed light on a Christmas conundrum: how the ghosts of past, present and future could turn up on the same night to spook Ebenezer Scrooge in Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol.View image in fullscreenAlbert Einstein, seen here circa 1933, theorised that the past, present and future all coexist.Photograph: Harold M Lambert/Hulton Archive/ Getty ImagesAl-Khalili says that according to Einstein all times coexist – past, present and future – in the same way as all points in space exist. “The problem, of course, is that we only ever experience the present moment,” Al-Khalili said. “So, the idea of the Christmas Carol is a wonderful one that highlights this notion that times maybe aren’t all separate. That maybe we can join with people, someone from the past, someone from the future. But of course, in relativity, that means time travel.”Time travel is another topic Al-Khalili plans to explore in theChristmas lectures. “Mathematically, it is possible to travel back in time,” he says. The reality, however, is a little more complicated – akin to travelling a rollercoaster’s loop-the-loop.“You’re travelling forward along the rollercoaster, but what’s happening is you’re doubling back on yourself and arriving back at your starting point. It’s the same sort of thing [with time travel]. What’s called a closed time-like curve in relativity, is somewhere in space-time which is so warped and curved by gravity that you’re travelling what you regard as forward in time, but in fact you’re looping back through space-time to a moment before you started,” he said.“But the problem, of course, is most physicists think ‘surely that is impossible’, because time travel into the past leads to all sorts of paradoxes.’”‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western biasRead moreTravelling into the future is, at least in theory, easier. “The way you do it is by slowing time down, either by travelling close to the speed of light or doing what Matthew McConaughey does in Interstellar – you go and orbit around a supermassive black hole whose gravitational field is so strong that, I think in the movie, every hour they spend near this black hole, seven years go by on Earth.”Al-Khalili will also tackle a conundrum that has bothered scientists for centuries: why time only seems to flow in one direction.“Things decay, batteries run out, balls roll downhill, we grow older, your children’s bedroom gets more messy, not more tidy – unless you intervene,” he said. “All those things point to a directionality to time, and yet fundamentally our equations say there is no preferred direction in time.”The problem has kept Al-Khalili up at night for months, if not years. But now he thinks he has the answer: for those who tune in.“In the lectures, I’m going to give an explanation for how to solve that problem,” he said. “I won’t give any spoilers, that’s for the Christmas lecture. I have solved the problem of the arrow of time.”The Christmaslectures from theRoyal Institutionsupported by CGI will be broadcast on the BBC and iPlayer in late DecemberExplore more on these topicsPhysicsRoyal InstitutionAgeingnewsShareReuse this content

title: This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during a Likud party campaign rally in Tel Aviv on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during a Likud party campaign rally in Tel Aviv on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelThis Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myselfJonathan FreedlandSpend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alikeFri 18 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareCandidates always say it, but this time it’s true. When Israel goes to the pollson 27 October, it really will be the most important election in the country’s history – and not just for Israelis. I saw that for myself this last week, in a visit that served as a sharp reminder of both what is at stake – and the role of those watching from afar.More than one voter I spoke to voiced the fear that, if the coalition headed byBenjamin Netanyahuis returned to power next month, 27 October will not merely be Israel’s most important election: it will be its last. They were not referring to the absence of democracy in theoccupied territory of the West Bank – which we’ll come to – but rather to Israel’s internationally recognised, pre-1967 borders: what you might call Israel-proper. There, the last four years have seen a sustained assault on the machinery of liberaldemocracy by the most rightwing government since Israel’s establishment in 1948 – a committed, focused attempt to remove the checks and restraints on its own power, installing instead a kind of elective dictatorship.Democratic norms are breaking down all the time. While I was there, Netanyahu joined calls tostrip two Israeli film-makers of their citizenship, as a livid mob surrounded the home ofthe parents of one of the two directors. The film in question isNAZA, produced by the Guardian, which features interviews with two dozen Israeli military insiders, their identities disguised, and which is named for the acronym euphemistically used by the Israeli military when calculating the number of civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. Unlike everyone protesting against it, I have actually seen the film: I have some misgivings about specific choices it makes, but that is irrelevant. A country true to its self-designation as the only democracy in the Middle East would not threaten with expulsion or violence those who say what its rulers do not want to hear.But such egregious behaviour is becoming commonplace. Last month, Netanyahu’s wife, Sara,implied, without evidence, that Yair Golan, leader of the left-leaning Democrats party, had inside knowledge of the 7 October 2023 attacks that saw the massacre of 1,200 Israelis and the abduction of 251 hostages – the trauma of which still touches every aspect of Israeli life and looms over this election campaign. It’s part of a baseless conspiracy theory pushed by Netanyahu and his “poison machine” of acolytes and media allies to shift the blame for the PM’s own 7 October failures, but it’s especially despicable when directed against Golan. A former general, he leapt into his car on 7 October, drove south andpersonally rescued six of those who had come under fire. He is a hero of that dark day – and has threatened to sue Sara Netanyahu. As it happens, soon after her intervention, it was reported thatsomeone high upin Israel had indeed been explicitly warned before 7 October that a devastating Hamas attack was on the way. That someone was Benjamin Netanyahu and the warning came from the president of the United Arab Emirates. Netanyahu vehemently denied the allegation.It is a dirty campaign, filled with disinformation and lies, utterly in keeping with the degraded state of Israeli politics in the age of late-stage Netanyahu. Thanks to Israel’s unwritten constitution, there now remains only one serious obstacle in his way: the courts. He has had the judiciary in his sights since he returned to office nearly four years ago, not least because he wants to halt the ongoing corruption trial that could send him to jail. He tried to gut the supreme court once already,in early 2023, and, if he wins next month, most observers are clear: the court will be gone.That matters for Israelis, who will find themselves in a Turkey- or Russia-style autocracy poorly disguised as a democracy. But it also matters for Palestinians. Yehuda Shaul, an Israeli anti-occupation activist fully aware of the court’s inadequate record as a defender of Palestinian rights, told me thatIsraelhas been on the wrong road for a long time: “But so long as the courts and basic democratic institutions are standing, we can still turn back. If they’re gone, we’re heading off a cliff.”View image in fullscreenMahmoud Eshaq and his family prepare to leave their home in Ras ‘Ein al ‘Auja after continued harassment from Israeli rightwing settlers, 11 January 2026.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianI was with Shaul driving around the West Bank, seeing the changing reality there up close. I stood in the burnt-out and broken mosque of what had been the small Bedouin village of Mu’arrajat, its population chased out by settler terrorists – to use the formulationfavoured, remarkably, by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee. Through harassment and violence, they made the lives of the inhabitants there so unbearable that the villagers could hold on no longer. It was the same story inRas ‘Ein al ‘Auja, where I stood among similar ruins, including a small, abandoned school, and where a herd of settler-owned goats now grazes. Shaul points out the vast swathe of land, more than 100 sq miles, in the east of the West Bank, close enough to see Jordan, where now next to no Palestinians live. Small wonder that former Israeli prime ministerEhud Olmert speaks of ethnic cleansing, or that UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband does the same.I saw, too, in what the settlers call northern Samaria, the four settlements that Ariel Sharon dismantled in 2005, now returned and rebuilt along with 14 others either built or approved for construction. Their arrival sees roadside buildings demolished and olive trees uprooted, in the name of safety for settlers as they travel. And dotted, seemingly on every ridge and hilltop, the distinct, bright white caravans that mark a new officially “unauthorised” outpost, popping up with such frequency that Shaul can barely name them all – he estimates 250 new settlements and outposts have gone up since 2023 – and which are steadily encircling the major Palestinian cities, reducing them to isolated enclaves, thereby preventing the territorial contiguity that would be essential for a viable Palestinian state.Netanyahu’s coalition, with radical settler Bezalel Smotrich in de facto charge of theWest Bank, has directed this settlement expansion and turned a blind eye to the pogroms staged by the movement’s most aggressive wing. The best chance to stop it going farther and further comes on 27 October.Those outside the country appalled by what they see in Gaza or the West Bank sometimes struggle to know what they can do to help. The temptation is to rally around, say, the rapper Macklemore, calling out “Free Palestine” from Ed Sheeran’s stage – but that temptation fades a little when you see that the same Macklemore once performed dressed up as what looked unmistakably likean antisemitic caricature of a Jew, complete with a false, giant nose. He later apologised, saying a “Jewish stereotype” had never crossed his mind.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOr you might want to get fully behindMiliband’s sanctions package, which at long last signals that the settlement enterprise will not be allowed to continue with impunity – until you hear from those involved who say that the immediate impact will fall not on settlers but on Palestinians. That’s because the Netanyahu government’s predictable and predicted response – which includedthe closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem– has robbed Britain of its main mechanism to aid Palestinians through delivering development programmes and the like.The truth is that, for those desperate to see change, the best hope is the ejection from office of what has been a vile, cruel, bigoted and lethally dangerous government. Be under no illusion: even if Netanyahu is toppled, he will not be replaced by a peacenik who will instantly lead the country in the opposite direction. It doesn’t work like that. But there is a bloc, unofficially led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, which is defined by its opposition to the man who has ruled Israel on and off for much of the last 30 years and there are campaigners and activists, such as Shaul, who are fighting every hour of every day to avert further disaster. They are branded as traitors at home and shunned simply for being Israeli by too many supposed progressives abroad. They need allies and friends, because right now they are all that stands between this moment and the abyss.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Talk less, listen more and six other top tips on giving good advice | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Are you someone who thinks they have all the answers? Is your experience relevant here? Experts on the questions to ask yourself before giving advice
Author: Amelia Abraham
Headline: Are you someone who thinks they have all the answers? Is your experience relevant here? Experts on the questions to ask yourself before giving advice
Content: Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Getty ImagesLife and styleTalk less, listen more and six other top tips on giving good adviceAre you someone who thinks they have all the answers? Is your experience relevant here? Experts on the questions to ask yourself before giving adviceAmelia AbrahamFri 18 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo they actually want my advice?“Often, when people approach you for advice, they just want to talk about how they feel,” says Annalisa Barbieri, advice columnist for the Guardian for almost 20 years. For example, you might vent to a friend about your awful boss, and if they’re shocked it could confirm you’re being treated badly. “I also think people can have a lot of shame when things aren’t working out, and we like to share shame because it’s a hot potato of a feeling.” In other words, not every situation warrants advice. Sometimes, the person just wants to gauge a reaction or to share.In his Ted Talk How to Tame Your Advice Monster, Michael Bungay Stanier, the author of bestselling book The Coaching Habit, highlights the part of all of us that thinks we can solve people’s problems. “The advice monster looms up when someone starts talking, and you think: ‘Right, I’m about to add value to the conversation,’” he explains. “You think: ‘I have all the answers, and I want to have control and manage uncertainty.’ These are human drivers that are often useful, but can turn into patterns that are less helpful.”It may sound simple, but ask before giving advice, says Bungay Stanier. Barbieri suggests a phrase she uses, albeit gently, with her children: “Do you want advice, or do you just want to vent?”Am I jumping in too quickly?As Bungay Stanier puts it in his book The Advice Trap, giving advice is not bad; it’s when advice is your default response to every situation or arrives too quickly that it can become a problem.The solution? “Understanding that people aren’t looking for a silver bullet, but to be seen, heard and encouraged,” he says. When we move into advice mode too fast, we can send out the message that we think we’re smarter, better, faster. This sets up a power imbalance that makes people resistant to the advice they came for in the first place.If you’re questioning whether you’re rushing to advice too quickly, do an audit, he suggests. “People don’t realise how fast they move to advice-giving. Even coaches who have been trained to slow down on giving advice can be very trigger-happy, because they want to be helpful. You have to unlearn that.”Try it: can you let the conversation play out for more than two or three minutes before jumping in?What’s the ‘real’ problem?Listening is important because people are more likely to act on advice they feel they’ve come up with themselves, says psychologist Dr Lee Valls from the London Clinic. But also because, with time and space, they may discover that the presenting problem is not therealproblem. “One problem may be masking a bigger, more existential one.”One way to dig deeper into the real problem is to “stay curious”, says Bungay Stanier. You can ask questions such as: “What’s hard about this for you?” “What’s really going on?” “What have you already figured out?” He explains that “these kinds of questions can encourage agency, but also ensure you’re not giving them stuff they’ve already thought of.”Barbieri has found that often when people are struggling it’s because their expectations do not match their experience: “Over the last 10 years, I think people’s expectations have become more divorced from reality, particularly with comparing ourselves to others over social media.” With this in mind, if someone says: “My partner is treating me like this,” you might say: “Is that how you want to feel?” rather than “That’s awful, you should do this.” This avoids putting more responsibility on the person when they’re already feeling burdened.View image in fullscreenComposite: Getty ImagesShould I encourage them to ‘commit’ or ‘decommit’?Yitong Zhao of the University of Toronto researches how people help loved ones feel better during stress. In two recent studies, her team examined romantic relationships and friendships, exploring which approaches to advice led to better reported results for the relationship and advice seekers’ mental health.They studied two approaches. Commitment to the problem involves staying with the person’s feelings rather than dismissing them, and suggesting new ideas, goals or perspectives, such as: “OK, this is hard, but is it also something you can learn from?” Decommitment involved responses such as “It’s not as bad as it seems,” or “It’s out of your hands.”In highlighting their ability to take control of the situation, commitment led to the loved one feeling more supported and less judged. Decommitment, on the other hand, while an attempt at de-escalation, was riskier. “It can be invalidating – the person may assume you think they’re overreacting, or that they should feel less.”The key takeaway: how people help is as important aswhetherthey try to help. “When you try to help, it’s not about taking away how someone is feeling; it’s more about expanding what they’re feeling and adding new perspectives,” says Zhao.Is my experience relevant here?We’ve all been there. We’re seeking advice, and the person starts talking about their problems; worse yet, projecting. “We’re all biased,” explains Valls. “Whether we’re a friend or a sibling, the advice we give is shaped by our past experiences, alone or shared. Bias means you feel you know what’s best for the person. Sometimes that’s in their best interest; sometimes it isn’t.”Valls’ advice: be wary of hijacking the conversation and making it about you. While sharing your own similar situation can be comforting, it’s better to try to hold the space, listen, then maybe share. “But it’s not necessary, and if you do share your experience, always bring it back to them,” says Valls. The dynamic should be like a dance or a game of tennis, where there’s a symbiosis, a back and forth, informing not dictating.One way to focus the conversation on the person seeking advice is to ask them what their options are. When they go through the options, encourage them to listen to their body, their gut, their instincts, and see where that leads them. This is an approach that therapists and psychologists use. It can help improve the connection between the mind and the body, marrying thought with feeling. “The more there’s a connection there, the more we’re able to make good decisions.”Are we both emotionally regulating?Child psychologist Dr Margot Sunderland has written several books, including What Every Parent Needs to Know and Conversations That Matter. According to her, the most important thing for parents to know when giving advice to children and teenagers is not to shame. “If they come to you and you get angry or say: ‘That’s a terrible thing you did,’ you will be disqualified as someone to go to for help. Children very quickly decide: ‘Am I going to others for problem-solving or am I going to self-help?’” Self-help may sound positive, but can result in internalising problems and finding coping mechanisms that involve self-harm.Regulation is important for both parties. “You’re in pain because your child is in pain, so we rush to fix it, rather than wait until you’re both calmer and can think together.” That might mean taking your shock elsewhere by talking to someone else before the difficult conversation. For your child, it might mean letting them run out of the room. “When there’s a problem or distress, we go into survival mode: they might slam a door (fight mode) or hide under the table (flight mode). Allow this to happen first, or they won’t hear your advice anyway.”A term she comes back to is “hurry slowly”. Sunderland suggests something she did with her own small children: find two nearby toys and suggest that when the child needs help with their feelings, they can let you know by putting the toy cat on top of the Lego house, for example. “They can’t always tell you when they are ready to talk – that would be an adult thing to do – but they can show you.” Another tool for thinking together is drawing out the problem and possible solutions on paper. “It can take the pressure off a face-to-face conversation.”Last, she reminds us, if a child or teenager comes to you with a problem, you have a child who is help-seeking, not going into self-help. “You should applaud yourself, that means you’ve done something right.”Have I really got theanswer?When Barbieri agreed to become an advice columnist, it was on the condition that she could also consult experts: “I don’t have a problem with saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I like finding out. I often send people to books or websites, or I go away and speak to a psychotherapist.”When we don’t have the answers, it’s OK to support a friend in finding them – that’s not the same as saying we don’t want to help. Is there a podcast that might be useful? A way to seek third-party input? Or is it appropriate to ask: “Could therapy or counselling help?”Often, says Valls, we go to a particular person for advice because they will validate us; what can be more helpful is an objective approach. Besides, there’s no one way to do life “right” – meaning there may not be one right answer either.What’s the best way to follow up?Zhao’s research suggests that sharing advice can improve our interpersonal relationships, if approached in a considered way. Other research suggests that responsive, empathetic advice is more likely to increase trust (as opposed to prescriptive advice, which can undermine it).Today, people can always ask a chatbot for advice, but it doesn’t know us like we know one another. In the 10th anniversary edition of The Coaching Habit, Bungay Stanier reflects on what has changed since he first wrote the book. “ChatGPT can give good advice, with references and extra reading, faster than a person, and without personal entanglement. But the unintended effect of AI getting good at this stuff is people getting more isolated, and that’s a heavy price to pay as a society.”What AI is also less good at than humans is following up with care. “Advice should not be a one-off conversation,” says Sunderland. Come back to the advice-seeker with: “I’ve been thinking of our conversation the other day – how have things been?”And crucially, ask for feedback, to become a better advice-giver, advises Bungay Stanier. “Ask: ‘Was any of my advice useful?’ Usually, it’s the thing you least expected to help that has value.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleFriendshipRelationshipsFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Eating is my superpower’: Nigella turns up the heat on Bake Off | The Great British Bake Off | The Guardian
description: The domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty Gang
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: The domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty Gang
Content: Sweet and sour … Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood in the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Patch Dolan / Channel 4View image in fullscreenSweet and sour … Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood in the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Patch Dolan / Channel 4The Great British Bake OffInterview‘Eating is my superpower’: Nigella turns up the heat on Bake OffMichael HoganThe domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty GangFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike the Cleopatra of cake, new Great British Bake Off judge Nigella Lawson reclines on a chaise longue throughout our interview, gently fanning herself. Fellow judgePaul Hollywoodchuckles from a nearby armchair. “She’d sit like this between takes in the tent,” he says indulgently. “Reading a book and sipping a coffee while someone fed her grapes.” “Peeled grapes,” specifies Lawson with a grin.After Prue Leith stepped down from soggy bottom-spotting duties in January – on the unarguable basis that “I’m 86, for goodness sake!” – there was widespread jubilation when Lawson was announced as her replacement. The arrival of the domestic goddess has created serious buzz around Bake Off’s upcoming series. A contest that was at risk of growing stale has become essential viewing again, thanks to the velvet-voiced, spatula-licking doyenne of culinary TV.“It was lovely to see Nigella come into the tent,” says Hollywood. “We’ve only had two changes to the judging team in 16 years but it’s worked really well. I’ve always been a big fan and she fitted in beautifully – not just with me but with the whole team. She picked up the Bake Off vibe straight away. It was pretty seamless, actually.”View image in fullscreen‘Even Paul got the giggles!’ … Paul Hollywood and Nigella Lawson in the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch DolanHer TV career was launched with Nigella Bites way back in 1999. Why Bake Off, and why now? “I wanted to do something a bit different,” says Lawson. “I’ve written many books, which I adore, but it means spending a lot of time alone. I was keen to be part of something bigger, part of a team. When I was approached about Bake Off, I instinctively thought: ‘That would be lovely.’ It almost feels too good to be true that you can enjoy something this much and call it work.”Predictably, there have been tabloid rumours that the judgely duo have been butting heads. Lawson allegedly said that Hollywood arriving on set at Welford Park in a helicopter was “cringe”, which is all the evidence gossipmongers need. Yet there’s no sign of tension on screen, let alone today. Their conversation is full of good-natured ribbing and punctuated by peals of laughter. Hollywood seems enchanted by his new partner-in-cake, while Lawson is endearingly self-effacing, all too aware that she’s joining a long-running hit and simply doesn’t want to “stuff it up”.Before her appointment was confirmed, the pair had an unofficial chemistry test at a Channel 4 event. “We chatted for 10 minutes and had a great time, didn’t we?” recalls Lawson. “I knew instantly it was going to work. It surprised even us, I think, how well we hit it off. It was lucky that we did get on. Can you imagine if we didn’t? I bet Paul would have said so!”What does she like about the marquee’s resident master baker? “One of the many lovely things about Paul is that he’s good at being teased. I called him ‘Professor Precision’, then he teased me back and suddenly it all relaxed. He’s much more playful than he looks on camera. He often acts bad cop and does that laser stare but he’s always himself, which encourages other people to be themselves, too. We complement each other. He gets straight to the point and, as you can tell, I’m a witterer. I love talking about food and sometimes can’t stop. When I wittered on in the tent, I did see him go like this once …” She mimes pretending to nod off. He shrugs unrepentantly.Once she was officially onboard, Lawson hosted separate bonding sessions with her co-stars. “I decided to meet everyone properly before we started,” she says. “I didn’t want the first time we hung out together to be on set.” Hollywood came first. “I went for drinks at Nigella’s house,” he remembers. Oh, to be a fly on the wall. Was there food? “Salami, olives, that kind of thing,” says Lawson. “I wasn’t going to bake for him. That would be madness.” “I was disappointed,” deadpans Hollywood. “I was hoping for a cake on a gingham altar.”View image in fullscreenOven ready … (from left) Paul Hollywood, Alison Hammond, Nigella Lawson and Noel FieldingPhotograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4“Play your cards right and you never know,” she shoots back. “No, I wanted it to be as relaxed as possible. Paul brought a bottle of red wine and said: ‘Do you want a glass?’ I said, ‘You’ll have to open it yourself. I’m wearing a white suit!’ And we went from there.” Next came co-hosts Noel Fielding andAlison Hammond. “Noel came round for tea and I did make him a cake,” Lawson confesses. “Oh, thanks very much,” says Hollywood.“I love Noel,” she continues. “He and I look like two ghouls first thing in the morning.” “Two goths, climbing out of your coffins,” laughs Hollywood. Lawson puts her pale forearm next to his teak-tanned one. “Look! I have to be painted a bit brown, otherwise it’d cause issues for the camera.” And Hammond? “I met Alison at This Morning and we went out to lunch. I hitched a ride to the restaurant in her car and we were practically married by the time we arrived. We have a real laugh together and talked about everything.”The love affair seems to be mutual. Fielding has compared her to “an Italian film star”, while Hammond says: “We’re obsessed.” As they pose for photos, Hammond whispers: “Doesn’t Nigella look beautiful? She’s a vision!” “Stop it,” scoffs Lawson modestly.When the casting call came, it wasn’t an immediate yes. “I was apprehensive at first,” she admits. “I wasn’t sure whether I was even qualified and mindful that it was a risk, both for me and the show. So I had a big meeting with the producers and said: ‘Look, these are the things I can’t do.’ They said: ‘That’s OK, that’s what Paul does.’ I didn’t want them to go to the wrong shop, as it were. I’m not a scientist, a technician or a professional baker but what I can do is talk about food, its taste, texture and why I like it. I said: ‘If you now decide you don’t want me after all, I promise I won’t be offended.’ Happily they still did.”Hollywood previously formed partnerships with Dame Mary Berry and Dame Prue Leith. He refers to their successor in regal terms: “I’ve gone dame, dame, queen. I loved working with Mary. She’s got a lot of bantz, has Bez. We made a good team with Mel and Sue. We’d watch Eurovision, all sitting on the bed in dressing gowns. Prue and I would open a bottle of wine and put the world to rights. Nigella and I have done a very similar thing – not with wine but with a couple of dirty martinis or spicy margaritas.”Lawson describes her judging style as “pretty direct”. “I assumed I was going to be good cop but realised I just have to be honest. I can’t pretend if I don’t like something. Honesty can feel a bit brutal but you’re not critiquing the person, you’re critiquing the bake. It’s not personal. We’ve all got our own palate and can only speak subjectively.” This double act have their own areas of expertise. “I talk about flavour because eating is my superpower. I’m learning from Paul, though. I’ll start stealing all his lines, going: ‘This needs another three minutes, turn the oven up 20 degrees.’ But on the whole, I talk taste and he talks technique. You’ve got to play to your strengths.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs an avowed Bake Off superfan – she reels off a list of her favourite alumni, from series one winner Edd Kimber through to last year’s Jasmine Mitchell – how was walking into the fabled tent for the first time? “Oh god, a bit overwhelming,” she confesses. “But I held hands with Alison, which helped. It felt daunting but became cosy within about two minutes.”This year, the climate crisis came for Bake Off. We’re meeting on one of summer’s most sweltering days, with temperatures hitting 35 degrees. Was it this hot in the tent during filming? “Hotter, like a greenhouse” grimaces Lawson. “Plus you’ve got a mic pack on, which is like wearing a mini radiator. The bakers coped well, considering.” Were there melting chocolate disasters? “It was more caramel that was the issue,” says Hollywood. “There were some sticky moments.” “And that was just Paul,” quips Lawson.Don’t expect mention of microwaves. Lawsonwent viralin 2020 when she jokingly referred to her “meecro-wah-vay” – a clip shortlisted as one of Bafta’s TV moments of the year. It was a family in-joke and she’s determined to resist saying it again, instead calling it “the you-know-what”. Bake Off viewers, however, should listen out for a reference to “desecrated coconut”.View image in fullscreenLine-up … (from left) Gabe, Nikki, Shannon, Danni, Mo, Clara, Tom, Molly, Yannis, Gary, Moyin, and Connie are the new contestants on the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Love Productions/Channel 4Her predecessor Leith had a penchant for boozy bakes. Does Lawson have a similar sweet spot? “It’s not a sweet one, actually,” says Hollywood. “Nigella loves salt.” “I don’t mean over-salty,” she says. “Just that a pinch of salt can balance the sweetness. Similarly, I love anything citrus. A tang of sharp and bitter, rather than unadulterated sweetness. That’s why having raspberries in a vanilla cake is nice. They all tease me, saying: ‘Just add a tablespoon of salt and she’ll like it.’ I’m landed with that now.” “So much so that our WhatsApp group is called Salty Gang,” says Hollywood. Who’s the most active? “Not us,” says Lawson. “It’s mostly Noel and Alison sending funny stuff. We just reply with laughing emojis, like old people.”The Nigella factor is likely to give Britain’s biggest cookery show a ratings boost. “She’s a breath of fresh air, for sure,” says Hollywood. “Certainly for my male mates. They’ve told me they’ll be tuning in for the first time in 16 bloody years!”Lawson demurs. “Not trying to be humble but it’s not about me. I’m joining a long-established, deeply loved show. Bake Off is a national treasure with a fabulous audience. It’s been part of people’s lives over many years. I wouldn’t blame them if they thought: ‘Oi, why is she coming on my programme?’ As long as I don’t actively drive people away, I’ll be happy.” Will the viewing figures include the new judge herself? “I don’t like watching myself but I do want to see it because there’s an awful lot of action that we’re not around for. I’ll fast-forward through my bits and watch the bakers.”During her first time in the tent, the new recruit had a hoot. “We sometimes did a bit too much rabbiting and got told to shush,” says Lawson. “We had so much fun. Even Paul got the giggles. Alison once sent us out of the tent in disgrace. Paul’s very good at remaining poker-faced and then when nobody else is looking, he makes faces at you.” Has Hammond succeeded in her mission to get them all dancing? “I cannot dance on camera, I told her that,” says Lawson. “As judges, we need to retain a modicum of decorum and dignity … we try, anyway.”Salty and sassy, it sounds like La Lawson is in the tent to stay. “Bake Off’s like Hotel California,” says Hollywood. “You can check out any time you like but you can never leave. And I think Nigella’s here for good.”The Great British Bake Off returns on Tuesday22 Septemberat 8pm on Channel 4.Explore more on these topicsThe Great British Bake OffTelevisionReality TVNigella LawsonPaul HollywoodAlison HammondNoel FieldingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The definitive guide to men’s shirts: 19 of the best for every occasion | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Is an Oxford shirt the ultimate wardrobe staple? Are skin-tight fits ever a good idea? And what’s the perfect fabric for autumn and winter? Our menswear expert has all the answers
Author: Peter Bevan
Headline: Is an Oxford shirt the ultimate wardrobe staple? Are skin-tight fits ever a good idea? And what’s the perfect fabric for autumn and winter? Our menswear expert has all the answers
Content: Leading by example: Harry Styles makes a case for the relaxed white shirt.Photograph: XNY/Star Max/GC Images/GettyView image in fullscreenLeading by example: Harry Styles makes a case for the relaxed white shirt.Photograph: XNY/Star Max/GC Images/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterMen's fashionReviewThe definitive guide to men’s shirts: 19 of the best for every occasionIs an Oxford shirt the ultimate wardrobe staple? Are skin-tight fits ever a good idea? And what’s the perfect fabric for autumn and winter? Our menswear expert has all the answersThe best white T-shirts for menPeter BevanFri 18 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe photo above stopped me mid-scroll: Harry Styles, before his 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden, dressed in a big white shirt and smart tailored trousers. After a summer spent parked in front of three fans with ice packs on rotation, when wearing actual clothes felt like punishment, here was proof that normal service had resumed.So, now the rain’s back and autumn’s creeping in, it’s time to follow Harry’s lead and reintroduce some structure to your wardrobe: coats, knitwear, tailoring, all the pieces that make you look forward to getting dressed in the morning. One staple that’s long overdue a comeback? Shirts.The classic button-up is the shirting equivalent of awhite tee– an all-rounder that will hold its own in almost any setting (and it’s perfect for the time of year when a coat’s overkill but a T-shirt’s optimistic). But that’s just one option. You’ve also got the French workwear shirt – the way I’ve seen guys wearing it lately, thrown over a shirt and tie, might be my favourite styling trick of the season – as well as flannels, corduroy, denim and preppy Oxfords.Before you buy anything new, though, it’s worth raiding your own wardrobe. Shirts never really date, so there’s a good chance you’ve got some solid pieces already. If you do want something new, keep scrolling for the best shirts to buy this season – I’ve broken these down into 10 categories, with a few styling tips for each.The best men’s shirtsThe white shirtYou can’t go wrong with a white shirt. Keep it feeling laid back – poplin, relaxed fit, nothing too formal – and you’ll be able to wear it with almost anything. My go-to combination is blue jeans and black loafers.View image in fullscreenCospima cotton poplin shirt£55 at CosView image in fullscreenMujimen’swashedcottonlong-sleeveshirt£29.95 at MujiThe blue striped shirtMy personal favourite (I own nine): this is the white shirt’s more relaxed sibling that feels a touch more “weekend”. Same rules apply: avoid anything tight or dressy and wear it relaxed.View image in fullscreenUniqlooversized Oxfordshirt£34.90 at UniqloView image in fullscreenReisslyocellstripebutton-throughovershirt£36 at ReissThe corduroy shirtLightweight needlecord is the gold standard here – anything thicker tends to look stiff and bulky. With that in mind, it’s worth sticking to independent labels like Sunspel or Sirplus that put real thought into their choice of fabric. As this is the kind of low-key wardrobe investment you’ll wear for years, if you can, it’s worth spending a little extra to get it right.View image in fullscreenSunspelfinecordshirt£185 at SunspelView image in fullscreenSirplusoliveneedlecordcollaredshirt£135 at SirplusThe denim shirtView image in fullscreenDouble denim, done differently: Drew Starkey mixes his washes in New York.Photograph: Raymond Hall/GC ImagesDouble denim is still going strong this year – and Drew Starkey’s recent look in NYC is all the proof you need that it doesn’t need to match. Sure, his look is by Dior, but the pieces themselves look like an elevated version of what you’d find at the vintage shop. If you’d rather go matching – a proper Canadian tuxedo – take your jeans with you when you shop to coordinate the shade.Rokitis a good place to start.View image in fullscreenArket regulardenimshirt£65 at ArketView image in fullscreenCharles Tyrwhittdenimshirt,oceanblue£64.95 at Charles TyrwhittThe flannel shirtView image in fullscreenFlannel in flight: Steve Martin at Los Angeles international airport in 1994.Photograph: Ron Galella Ltd/Ron Galella Collection/GettyFlannel is the ultimate autumn fabric: it’s cosy, but it won’t make you immediately start sweating the moment you step on public transport. You could go for a check, but it’s not compulsory – a plain, brushed version does the same job without the lumberjack affiliations. See Steve Martin making flannel look cool in the 90s. Just add a cap.View image in fullscreenUniversal Worksbrownbrushedflannelsquarepocketshirt£130 at Universal WorksView image in fullscreenEtoncheckflannelshirt£210 at Eton ShirtsThe boxy shirtPaul Mescal’s never met a boxy fit he didn’t like – and, actually, neither have I. Nothing bunches, nothing rides up – it’s just a clean, straight,slightlycropped hemline that looks sharper than any tucked-in shirt could. The brand to know is Percival, which has a huge selection to choose from, but Asos or Weekday are your best bets for this style on the high street.View image in fullscreenPercival Hinsleycheckedboxyshirt, blueskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£140 at PercivalView image in fullscreenWeekdayboxylong-sleevedcottonpoplinshirt£39.99 at WeekdayThe evening shirtWhenever you’ve got a dinner reservation at a restaurant with a dress code, this is the kind of shirt you’ll want in your wardrobe. Go for something silkier than your usual cotton – lyocell or viscose – which will drape nicely when it’s tucked in. The key is feeling louche rather than stiff: one button more undone than feels natural, plus a great aftershave.View image in fullscreenSelectedrelaxedfitlong-sleeved shirt£55 at SelectedView image in fullscreenA Day’s Marchclean-cutlyocellshirt£130 at A Day’s MarchThe preppy OxfordView image in fullscreenOff-duty polish: JFK Jr in New York.Photograph: Lawrence SchwartzwaldJFK Jr-coded preppy menswear is still going strong and the Oxford shirt is the piece that does the heavy lifting. Look for one with an embroidered logo from one of the OGs – Gant, Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger – and you’re already on the right track. Keep the fit loose: anything too tight loses the whole off-duty Ivy League aesthetic.View image in fullscreenTommy Hilfigerregularfitbutton-down Oxfordshirt£85 at Tommy HilfigerThe work shirtVintage is the natural home for this one, though Service Works has the silhouette nailed down, too. Call it what you like – chore jacket, shacket, overshirt – the vibe you’re looking for is old-school French workwear. That means a soft, worn-in fabric with patch pockets low on the hem. Stains, paint splatters or distressed details are welcome.View image in fullscreenServiceworksclassicchoreshirt£85 at Service WorksView image in fullscreenFrench Chorejacketmen’svintageworkwearcanvasshirtShop French Chore jackets on eBayThe check shirtChecks were a big part of Jonathan Anderson’sautumn/winter 2026 collection for Dior, so it’s no wonder they’re everywhere right now. The trick is keeping it refined: a microcheck (a small-scale check, rather than anything bold or tartan-y) is usually a safe bet; try to keep the colours to two or three, max.View image in fullscreenNN07 Deoncasualflannelshirt£110 at NN07View image in fullscreenCotton On Richmondlong-sleeveshirt£35 at AsosHow should my shirt fit?View image in fullscreenPreppy blueprint: Paul Newman keeps it relaxed.Photograph: Silver Screen Collection/GettyIt depends on the occasion, but there’s one golden rule: never go for anything super-tight. Your shirt should always look comfortable and never pull; it’s better to hint at your physique rather than shout it, so skip the “muscle fit”. I think a relaxed fit looks way more stylish too, though if you’re wearing a dress shirt with a suit, it should sit closer to the body. If it’s too loose, it starts to look sloppy.What is the staple shirt every guy should own?An Oxford – it’s the most versatile one. Bar formal occasions, it’s an easy fallback that feels smart but never stiff – and it works all year round. Layer it up when it’s cold. Wear it loose when it’s warm. Buttoned up, it’s office-ready but thrown over a vest, it’s sorted for a date. If you want to lean casual, go for a shirt that’s oversized with a low-key embroidered logo – vintage Ralph Lauren is a great place to start. For style cues, check how Paul Newman wore his: relaxed and undone with a preppy edge.Which other shirts should every guy have in his wardrobe?Beyond a classic Oxford, a poplin shirt (white or striped) is your next everyday go-to, followed by denim, flannel and a fine corduroy once autumn properly sets in. For anything dressier – a dinner reservation or party, for instance – try something more flowy: viscose, silk or lyocell.How do you choose fabrics that look and feel good?On the whole, stick to natural fibres – cotton, linen, wool or silk. They come in different weaves and finishes (a cotton could be poplin, twill, Oxford or flannel, for instance) but natural fabrics tend to feel more expensive than synthetics like polyester or nylon. They breathe better, too (although silk is slightly less breathable than other natural fibres).How do I make my shirts last longer?As with most clothes, the number one rule is washing them as little as possible – most shirts can handle two to three wears before they need a cycle. In between, a spritz of fabric freshener (such as The Lab Co’sSignature fabric mist) and a good airing go a long way. When you dowash them, skip the tumble dryer and hang them up instead – it helps reduce creases and keeps their shape. Deal with stains the moment they happen. Once they’ve set in, it’s hard to shift them.For more, read our guide to thebest white T-shirts for menandhow to buy secondhand clothes online that you’ll actually wearPeter Bevan is a stylist and fashion journalist covering menswear, womenswear and beautyExplore more on these topicsMen's fashionThe FilterMen's topsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sensitive UK police data vulnerable to ‘compromise’ by US government and foreign actors | Police | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackers
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Exclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackers
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyPoliceSensitive UK police data vulnerable to ‘compromise’ by US government and foreign actorsExclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackersAisha DownFri 18 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVast troves of highly sensitive police data are lying onMicrosoftcloud platforms which an oﬃcial UK security assessment deemed to be vulnerable to “compromise” by foreign actors and the US government, a Guardian investigation can reveal.The files include criminal records, victim statements, internal emails and sensitive information held by more than 40 police forces across the UK.Some files exceed “oﬃcial” classification, according to a policedocument seen by the Guardian, raising the possibility the information could be classed as “secret” or “top secret”.The cloud platform is Microsoft Azure, one of the main commercial offerings of the US tech company. It is used by businesses and governments globally and rests on a web of IT infrastructure – datacentres, networking gear, fibre optic cables – that spans more than 100 countries.In recent years, doubts have surfaced about how cloud platforms store data and whether they are truly secure.British police decided to put some of their most sensitive data on the Microsoft platform in a 2017 meeting, a record of which was examined by the Guardian.In doing so, officers accepted that “US government insiders” would be able to see the data, and that it could be “transmitted worldwide”, with “the extent of this … unknown”.According to five specialists who reviewed the Guardian’s findings, the risks identified in that document persist today. Almost every UK police forcenow depends onMicrosoft Azure, and the UK government spends at least £1.9bn on Microsoft software each year.“There’s no evidence that this has been properly understood,” said one source who has held senior roles in UK policing. The data is “some of the most sensitive that exists”, he added. “You’re talking about information that, if it gets into the wrong hands, or if the information is incorrect, [means] people can get hurt or may die.”When the Guardian approached the police about the possibility that sensitive information was not secure, they appeared to wave aside these risks, saying Britain’s contracts with Microsoft meant US authorities could not view data without express permission and that the data it stored on Microsoft remained in the UK.These statements appeared to contradict public admissions by Microsoft, which said in a disclosure toPoliceScotland in 2023 that data “can go outside the UK” and that it “cannot guarantee data sovereignty”.Microsoft said it “does not provide any government with direct or unfettered access to customer data”, and that it had not provided UK data in response to a US government request. It added that, like all US-based tech companies, it responded to US government requests made through valid legal processes.The threat of ‘US government insider attackers’In 2017, a senior police oﬃcer, Ian Dyson, chaired a meeting in which stakeholders considered15 risks the UK would face if police forces decided to transfer their data to Microsoft’s global cloud.View image in fullscreenIan Dyson, pictured in 2016.Photograph: Jamie SmithThat meeting considered both the police’s use of Microsoft’s software, such as Office 365, and the reliance on the cloud that underpins these services, Azure. Those risks, and the resulting police decisions, were set out in a summary document seen by the Guardian and signed off by Dyson.This was four years after the advent of a policy called “cloud first”. Introduced by the Cabinet Office in 2013, it became a government-wide effort to push almost all departments to migrate their data on to the “public cloud” – commercial offerings by tech companies, often based in the US. Departments that did not want to do this had to jump through burdensome administrative hoops.Dyson was the police commissioner of the City of London at the time, but he held another title: senior information risk owner for all of Britain, or the SIRO. It was his job to set the norms for how British police could safely handle their data.In their assessment, officers came to startling conclusions about what would happen if they put police data on Azure. Firstly, they considered it would be vulnerable to hackers: Microsoft’s software “carries vulnerabilities which will be exploited by cybercriminals and other threat actors in due course”.Separately, it added: “Police forces cannot be certain where their data will be processed or stored.“The hyper-scale and global nature of the Microsoft cloud means that police data, and metadata relating to police data could be transmitted and stored worldwide by Microsoft, and the extent of this will be unknown.”The document specifically identified the potential risk from what it described as “US government insiders”. It said: “There is a risk of compromise of sensitive data shared by, or taken from, Microsoft by the US government being released by US government insider attackers.”The document explained that the data intended for migration was sensitive. In fact, “a significant volume” of it exceeded the classification “oﬃcial”. In the UK, this suggests it was either “oﬃcial sensitive”, “secret”, or “top secret”.The assessment also suggested Microsoft’s platform was unable to guarantee this data would be secure. “This places sensitive data, inadequately protected in an environment which then becomes a significantly more attractive target for attackers,” it said.double quotation markWe really don’t know if the data has been breached or notFormer senior policing sourceAs well as risks, the report also listed mitigations. On the problem of cyber-attacks, it mandated that police servers should be repaired promptly, kept up to date and have antivirus software.To address the risk of “US government insiders” and the concern that Microsoft might store UK policing data “worldwide” it suggested “applying Microsoft’s ‘out-of-the-box’ native encryption” and leaving the final decision about using Microsoft up to individual police chiefs.Several experts interviewed by the Guardian, including cloud computing specialists and engineers working for Microsoft, suggested these mitigations were inadequate. Microsoft’s internal encryption does not prevent its employees accessing UK police data; nor would it stop the US government obtaining British policing files.The National Police Chief’s Council (NPCC) said access to data stored on the cloud is limited to those with a genuine need to access it and that this is subject to strict controls. Despite that claim, a Microsoft engineer who reviewed the Guardian’s findings said the information “could be viewed by hundreds of people around the world, some of them not vetted, many of them not directly employed by Microsoft”.Despite the risks identified by the assessment, every police force in the UK put its data, wholly or in part, on Microsoft’s cloud. Some began migrating their information in 2017. A few forces, such as Police Scotland, are still finalising their adoption of the technology.The files cover the “full gamut of data: intelligence, body-worn video, digital evidence and case files, as well as the non-law enforcement data any organisation has”, said the source who held senior roles in UK policing.‘We do not expect any sharing … without permission’The UK government spends billions each year on services oﬀered by three US tech companies: Amazon, Google and Microsoft.Up to 60% of its IT infrastructure ishosted on cloud platforms. Britain’s intelligence data is hosted on Amazon’s cloud services, as is its customs data. The Ministry of Defence uses Azure. There is “a deep dependency on US hyperscalers”, said Dave Michels, a researcher with the Cloud Legal Project, at Queen Mary University of London.This is the result of 13 years of decisions like Dyson’s. It is unclear if the potential consequences are broadly understood.When the Guardian approached the NPCC over the document signed by Dyson, it said: “UK policing as standard requires the use of UK-only datacentres,” but added that “on occasion” Microsoft employees could access the data “to provide support”.Asked whether the US government could access the data, a police spokesperson said they could not comment on the phrase “US government insiders”, because “terminology … changes continuously” and the document was “outdated”.“In line with the contract signed with Microsoft, we do not expect any sharing with the US government without the express permission of the UK government,” they added.Microsoft said: “The suggestion that use of Microsoft cloud services means customer data is inherently insecure or automatically exposed to foreign governments is inaccurate.” It said it had “never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”.Two legal experts, as well as several Microsoft engineers who spoke anonymously to the Guardian, suggested these assertions did not give an accurate picture of the potential risks.double quotation markThe risk is obvious, even though the providers of the cloud and the government both have an interest in talking it downDouwe Korff, professor of international lawBy default, Microsoft’s cloud was “a global network of datacentres”, said Michels. It had facilities on every continent and this meant, generally, that data stored on it was stored everywhere: pieces of a single file could be held across multiple countries, from Sweden to Ethiopia.In recent years, Michels said, Microsoft had begun to offer clients in Europe greater assurances about where their data was stored, including assuring some customers that their data would remain within EU borders. But “the focus on data location is a bit of a red herring”, he said.This was because thousands of engineers from more than 100 countries maintained Microsoft’s systems. Some were directly employed by Microsoft, others worked for subcontractors in countries potentially hostile to the UK, from Israel to Egypt, China and Kazakhstan. “You’ve seen the list of their sub-processors of people who have access to customer data,” said Michels. “It’s a long list.”Some of the engineers could access data, such as UK police data, directly as part of customer support. Many more could see key features of what the data included.View image in fullscreenA Microsoft datacentre in the Netherlands.Photograph: Ramon van Flymen/EPAMicrosoft said it had “strong guardrails” around data access by engineers.Douwe Korff, a professor of international law at London Metropolitan University, said the police statement that “we do not expect any sharing [of our data] with the US government” was “typical lawyers’ wriggling”.“The risk is obvious, even though the providers of the cloud and the government both have an interest in talking it down,” he said.Michels said: “As a cloud customer, if you’re relying on a contractual commitment from a cloud provider not to hand over data when forced to under foreign law, that is not worth much more than the piece of paper it’s written on.”US law, including the Cloud Act, allows US authorities to access any data held by US cloud companies, including data held abroad. US authorities do not need a warrant to do this, and they can require US companies to not disclose such access to cloud customers.Microsoft, Amazon and Google have insisted they would fight such requests, said Korff. But there is “nothing that is legally binding” that would prevent them from sharing other governments’ data if US authorities demanded it.In response to a query from the Guardian, Microsoft said it “has never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”. It added in a follow-up that it was bound by its “contractual commitments”.“If UK law prohibits us from turning over data to another government, that is a binding law that would govern our response to any hypothetical demand,” it said.‘The security guys expected a big breach by now’The Guardian spoke to six people who have closely followed the country’s data storage arrangements over the past decade. Several of them said that senior leaders did not view dependence on US tech companies as a concern, and trusted them not to give data to US authorities.“Government security departments are painfully aware of all the risks,” said Mark Butcher, a cloud expert who acts as a strategic adviser across government. “But the way that most senior leaders talk about it is: ‘Well, we’ve been reassured by Microsoft that it would never happen.’”But the source who has held senior policing roles said: “All the security guys I worked with when this policy came in expected a big breach by now, and we know it will take that to change the police’s position.“The truth is, however, the level of logging and information in the cloud systems would not necessarily tell us if there was a problem. We really don’t know if the data has been breached or not.”Explore more on these topicsPoliceCloud computingMicrosoftComputingInternetData protectionData and computer securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Earl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s death | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Buckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Buckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’
Content: Spencer stood firm in his recollection after the palace suggested his memory had been clouded by ‘fraternal grief’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenSpencer stood firm in his recollection after the palace suggested his memory had been clouded by ‘fraternal grief’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAMonarchyEarl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s deathBuckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’Sammy GecsoylerFri 18 Sep 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said ofDiana, Princess of Wales, “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her death, saying he is telling the truth.The alleged comments, revealed in Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, prompted Buckingham Palace to issue an extraordinary statement suggesting Diana’s brother had misremembered events, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise”.In an interview with the BBC, Spencer stood firm in his recollection, telling Laura Kuenssberg:“I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”Responding to the palace’s statement, Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious, or is he embarrassed?” When asked about the inference that his memory was coloured, Spencer said: “They’ve sort of smudged that one, haven’t they?They’ve said that recollections may vary.”View image in fullscreenDiana died in a car crash in 1997, at the age of 36.Photograph: Simon Kreitem/ReutersSpencer said the call was one of two he had with Charles in his lifetime and said he told his friends and family members at the time about the comment “because it was so monstrous”.The alleged comment was revealed on Wednesday in an extract from the memoir published in the Daily Mail. The comment by the then prince was allegedly made during a heated argument over funeral arrangements. Spencer says it reflected Charles’s“pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, the Daily Mail reported.Charles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after Diana’s death, claims Earl SpencerRead moreAmong other claims in the book are that Diana told a friend on the eve of her wedding to Charles that he said he was happy to marry her, but was not actually in love with her.On Friday, the second extract from the memoir was published. Spencer writes Charles was “polite and formal” on the day of Diana’s funeral and says Prince Philip told him to look ahead while walking in unison alongside his nephews and former brother-in-law.“It was hellish, entering that tunnel of grief, particularly because we were unable to put a face to it by looking at the individuals in the crowd,” said Spencer of the procession.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Prince Philip, Prince William, Charles Spencer, Prince Harry and King Charles, then a prince, walking in Diana’s funeral procession.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/APIn the extract released on Wednesday, Spencer says he insisted to Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, to walk in her funeral procession. In the end, her sons walked behind her coffin, which William later called “one of the hardest things I’ve ever done”.Spencer wrote that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer writing: “‘Rest assured,’” he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”Spencer wrote that he was stunned and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”Spencer also claimed that Diana “never would have wanted” her sons to walk behind her coffin, to which Charles allegedly replied: “That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty.”Swan Song is due to be published globally next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.Four copies of the Dutch-language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.Buckingham Palace did not issue a statement responding to the BBC interview, but on Wednesday a spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”Explore more on these topicsMonarchyDiana, Princess of WalesKing Charles IIInewsShareReuse this content

title: Latvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine | Europe | The Guardian
description: Edgars Rinkēvičs says drone warfare in Ukraine is moving at ‘lightning speed’ and efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by next year
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Edgars Rinkēvičs says drone warfare in Ukraine is moving at ‘lightning speed’ and efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by next year
Content: Edgars Rinkēvičs: ‘It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company. We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEdgars Rinkēvičs: ‘It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company. We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEuropeLatvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in UkraineEdgars Rinkēvičs says drone warfare in Ukraine is moving at ‘lightning speed’ and efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by next yearAndrew Rothin WashingtonFri 18 Sep 2026 18.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLatvia’s president has warned that Europe is not keeping up with developments of drone and aerial warfare inUkraineand that most countries in Nato could not repulse an attack by Russian missiles if the conflict expands.The remarks came during a Guardian interview in Washington DC in which Edgars Rinkēvičs said that the technological developments in drone warfare in Ukraine are moving at “lightning speed” and that current efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by the middle of next year.“What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” he said. “And let’s be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole ofEuropeand Nato has it.“Because ifRussiadecides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added.Ukraine and European allies are now facing a delay in supplies of crucial Patriot and other air-defence missiles. The US has expended nearly two-thirds of its stocks of critical interceptors in the war in Iran, according to analysis of a Congressional Budget Office assessment, and it could take at least five years to replenish stocks.The US has considered outsourcing Patriot production to Ukraine and Europe but so far an agreement has not been made.“It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company,” Rinkēvičs said, noting that discussions were continuing and acknowledging the difficulties of some technical issues with licensing. “We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.”At next week’s United Nations general assembly in New York City, Donald Trump is expected to hold meetings with senior European leaders, and asNatoallies have stepped up their warnings about the risk of Russia escalating the war in Ukraine.Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned in a speech on Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against Nato countries supporting Ukraine in the coming months in an effort to test the alliance’s commitment to collective defence under article 5 of its charter.Tusk said that Russia would seek to “weaken Nato’s integrity” and show that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”, adding that Russia would seek to play off the incidents as accidents.Asked about Tusk’s concerns about Russia attacking Ukrainian allies in Europe, Trump said: “I think they already have attacked Ukrainian allies.
