They’ve been attacking Ukrainian allies for approximately five years.”He then pivoted to throw his support behind the Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, who is supported by the conservative Law and Justice party, saying: “You have a great president, he was a big Trump fan … he’s doing a fantastic job, and he’s got it under control.”The Baltic nations, which are also on Russia’s eastern flank, have tempered their warnings, saying that there was no indication that Moscow sought to launch a conventional war to retake territory that it once held under the Soviet Union.But Russia would increase mobilisation in the coming months after local elections, Rinkēvičs said, then use the winter to “push” in Ukraine, and also to “do whatever it takes to dissuade nations that are supportive of Ukraine to continue”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionActs of sabotage, cyber-attacks and drone and missile incidents all indicated Russia testing European resolve to support Ukraine, he said.“I would rule out a conventional military incursion but we should be very vigilant when it comes to all kinds of other possibilities,” he said.A Nato jet shot down a Russian drone over Lithuania on Tuesday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and closed Lublin and Rzeszów-Jasionka airports on Thursday due to a Russian strike on western Ukraine.Rinkēvičs also expressed concern about whether European allies were on track to hit a goal of spending 5% of GDP on defence that has become a White House benchmark for the Trump administration’s continued support for Nato.He also said that discussions over Europe bearing a great burden for its own defence were growing “more constructive”, but added that when it comes to “real capabilities … you need time”.“Our message is also to do that, we need time,” he said. “It cannot happen in a month, or in a year.”Explore more on these topicsEuropeLatviaUkraineRussiaDrones (military)NatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second term
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: President has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second term
Content: Trump speaks to the press onboard Air Force One in August.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump speaks to the press onboard Air Force One in August.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White HousePresident has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second termUS politics live – latest updatesLucy CampbellandRobert MackeyFri 18 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his latest attack on the US constitution’s first amendment and the press,Donald Trumpabruptly announced that he is banning outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage.In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the US president said he was expelling the news outlets “effective immediately” over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and threatened that bans for others outlets could follow.He went on: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”Trump defended the ban at an Oval Office event to promote his administration’s healthcare policies.“I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump told reporters, referring to friendly media outlets. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.”Reminded by one reporter that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, Trump said: “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.”He added: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.”Towards the end of a chaotic news conference, when a reporter asked Trump to explain how his ban on the three outlets would work, the president expressed confusion. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” Trump asked, seeming confused.After another correspondent rephrased the question, asking, “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?”Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?”On Friday, the Washington Postreportedthat more American service members have died in the war on Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed; CNNrevealedthat an “entirely false” intelligence report about a Chinese ship in the Middle East generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) had “almost started a war”; while a Politico reportuncovereda Hill investigation after sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology unexpectedly made its way to Hong Kong, possibly giving China access to them.Trump said his decision to ban the three outlets was unrelated to the stories. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said, beforethreatening more media prohibitions could follow.“There may be others to join them,” Trump said.In a statement, a spokesperson forCNNsaid the network “stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting”.“We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right,” the spokesperson said.Politico said its reporters would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones”.“We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” it added.Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), said the organization “stands in defense” of the banned reporters “who are being singled out for doing their jobs”.“This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Henrich wrote in a statement. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”A spokesperson forMS Nowdeclined to comment.Trump’s move drew swift condemnation from Democrats and free speech groups. Chris Coons, a Democratic senator, wrote on social media: “Trump is once again trying to use the power of the presidency to punish a free press, now banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. That is the behavior of an authoritarian, and we must defend the press’ right to hold those in power accountable.”The White House press pool is a “public forum” under the first amendment, so the president cannot expel journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director at Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. To do so, would be “doubly unconstitutional”.“The first amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent,” said Jaffer. “With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now.”Similarly, Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the first amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the ‘People’s House’ for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move.“The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”Since returning to office, Trump has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media at the White House, including the Associated Press, which wasbanned from press pool eventsin the Oval Office and on Air Force One after it continued to use Gulf of Mexico instead of Gulf of America in its coverage. The APsued, and that case remains in litigation.Trump’s White House also seized control over the organization of the presidentialpress pool, a rotation that determines which news organizations and reporters are allowed to follow – and question – the president in places such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One. The WHCA, an independent association made up of members of the media, traditionally coordinated rotating pool coverage of more than a dozen journalists allowed access to the president in smaller settings.The Pentagon also attempted to introduce a new press policy to restrict the ability of journalists to gather and report on sensitive information, which culminated in a mass walkout of news media outlets who refused to sign the pledge. A federal judge later ruled the policy was unconstitutional.The president has also launched high-profile legal battles with major outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and the BBC.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsUS press and publishingMS NowCNNNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Polanski request to postpone Greens’ conference to focus on byelection refused by party | Green party | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against plan
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Exclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against plan
Content: Zack Polanski is standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyView image in fullscreenZack Polanski is standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyGreen partyPolanski request to postpone Greens’ conference to focus on byelection refused by partyExclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against planPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski requested that the Greens’ ruling executive committee postpone the party’s imminent annual conference so they could focus on theHolborn and St Pancras byelectionbut was refused.While party officials say the formal request came from staffers worried about diluting resources by staging a conference a week before Polanski tries to win Keir Starmer’s former Commons seat, the Guardian understands the party leader wanted this to happen.In the end, the executive committee of the Greens in England and Wales, which has about 25 voting members including Polanski, voted against the plan on Thursday.The party expects about 3,000 people to attend what would be its biggest gathering, beginning in Brighton on 2 October.Calling off the event at such short notice would have cost the party a significant sum given it has rented a conference venue, and risked annoying members who have taken time off work and booked travel and hotels.The byelection, in which Polanski hopes to challenge for a traditionally safe Labour seat, takes place on 8 October, just four days after the conference finishes.The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly ToynbeeRead moreThe end of a byelection campaign is traditionally marked by parties trying to canvass as many voters as possible. Having thousands of the Greens’ most active members gathered somewhere else for the final weekend greatly complicates their operation.Some Greens have also speculated that Polanski would have preferred to fight the byelection before the party votes on a contentious policy motion at its conference, which sets out a motion on Zionism.Polanskiis under pressureto take a stance on the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference, and is thus almost certain to feature.The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state in Palestine – with racism and would call for a single Palestinian state. Members who support Zionism would risk being disciplined for racism.A number of Greens fear passing the motion could alienate Jewish supporters. Polanski, who is Jewish, has not given a public opinion on the issue, but is understood to support a pair of amendments that would tone down the motion.A Green party spokesperson said: “The party was exploring different ways of allocating our resources effectively while fighting theHolborn and St Pancras byelection. One possible option was to postpone our conference.“After discussion we remain committed to running an incredibly ambitious Holborn and St Pancras byelection campaign and holding what will be our biggest ever party conference.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brentford blitz Chelsea as Fábio Carvalho caps stunning second-half display | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Brentford won 3-0 against Chelsea via second-half goals from Jaidon Anthony, Igor Thiago and Fábio Carvalho
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Brentford won 3-0 against Chelsea via second-half goals from Jaidon Anthony, Igor Thiago and Fábio Carvalho
Content: Jaidon Anthony (left) and Igor Thiago – two of Brentford goalscorers – after the opener against Chelsea.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersView image in fullscreenJaidon Anthony (left) and Igor Thiago – two of Brentford goalscorers – after the opener against Chelsea.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersPremier LeagueBrentford blitz Chelsea as Fábio Carvalho caps stunning second-half displayJonathan Wilsonat the Gtech Community StadiumFri 18 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose early-season thoughts thatChelseamight be the team best-placed to challenge Arsenal are beginning to look extremely over-optimistic. The two chaotic wins with which they began were always difficult to read: they might have been useful points picked up on the way to a more solid structure, or they might have represented evidence of significant problems. After three games without a win, and 12 goals conceded in five games this season, it’s beginning to look like the latter.At the final whistle, Keith Andrews tipped his head back and roared at the sky, celebrating Brentford’s first home win over Chelsea since 1938. They remain unbeaten, coherent and disciplined, and moved up to third in the table. The comparison is impossible not to draw: as one side flail in an orgy of structured spending, their far less wealthy neighbours thrive with a clear plan and sense of direction. “It was a performance I felt was bubbling,” said Andrews. “I could see it in the players’ eyes over the last two days. They were very focused, very determined.”Brentford v Chelsea: Premier League – liveRead moreSuch is the state of perpetual flux at Chelsea that the usual homilies about the benefits of stability always seem a little redundant when applied to them. With 11 new signings this summer maintaining the sense of the club as a trading hub, learning the names of everybody in the dressing room has probably been a greater priority than worrying too much about boardroom wrangling. But, still, their first game since Todd Boehly and Mark Walteragreed to sell their 12.8% stakein the club to the major shareholder Clearlake Capital felt significant. At the very least, a more harmonious boardroom should be beneficial.Boehly, the great disruptor, who arrived blithely telling English football it was doing everything wrong, has departed having achieved very little other than splurging £300m on players who didn’t fit and giving Raheem Sterling a £325,000-a-week contract in his shambolic spell as de facto sporting director. Four years on, after 60 arrivals, do Chelsea look any more like title challengers than they did then? It was, in truth, very hard to say what this looked like, other than a team that is every much still under construction. Jordan Henderson made his full Chelsea debut at his former club, while Danny Welbeck, Pep Chavarría and Valentín Barco made their first league starts.Barco, whose overenthusiastic celebrations after Argentina’s winner against England at the World Cup earned him a post-match slap from Jude Bellingham, was booed with impressive consistency from the home fans. The lesson was clear: if you’re going to be a major irritant while in possession of a distinctive shock of hair the colour of burnished copper, there will be consequences. Emí Martínez was jeered as well for the crime of being Argentinian. Henderson, by contrast, was treated relatively gently, his booing as a returnee more sporadic and muted, tending to the perfunctory.View image in fullscreenJaidon Anthony rises to head Brentford in front.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersThe pattern for Chelsea was a familiar one: a fast start, fading to something a little scratchier. The opening, for the second successive game, did not produce an early goal, although Pedro Neto would have given them a ninth-minute lead had it not been for a sharp save from Caoimhín Kelleher.“We have dropped our consistency, our competitive mentality in the second half,” said Xabi Alonso. “We have not been able to keep our level. When you lose shape you are out of control. To be able to understand and know what it takes to be competing to the end, it’s a process and it takes time.”The longer the game went on, the less assured Chelsea looked and a Brentford opener arrived just after the hour. Perhaps inevitably, it came from a dead ball; the stats had suggested that Brentford this season had been creating significantly more chances from set plays than they had converted. As modern corner routines go it seemed very straightforward, Jannik Schuster climbing above the diminutive Barco to head Mikkel Damsgaard’s corner back across goal, where Jaidon Anthony nodded in from close range, his first goal since his summer move from Burnley.View image in fullscreenFábio Carvalho fires Brentford into a three-goal lead in injury time.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersChelsea belatedly applied some pressure but, although the final minutes were played largely in the Brentford half, they created little beyond corners, as Brentford maintained their composure and structure.The second goal arrived seven minutes from time. Damsgaard, perhaps the tidiest player in the league, led the break, playing in Kevin Schade. Martínez saved his side-footed effort but Igor Thiago guided an awkwardly bouncing ball inside the post for his first goal of the season. Fábio Carvalho made it 3-0 in added time, slamming in a cross from Schade, who had been left inexplicably unmarked on the left after a long throw was half-cleared.As Brentford begin to consider that European qualification is a real possibility, Chelsea remain what they have been since the takeover: a work in progress – and, particularly at the back, it feels that progress has a long way to run.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBrentfordChelseamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Oxford United apologise for launching ‘United 93’ clothing range around 9/11 anniversary | Oxford United | The Guardian
description: Oxford United have been forced to abandon a new range of American sports-influenced merchandise given its jarring association with one of the aircraft hijacked on 11 September
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Oxford United have been forced to abandon a new range of American sports-influenced merchandise given its jarring association with one of the aircraft hijacked on 11 September
Content: The club published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of ‘the historical context and associations’ related to the branding.Photograph: Oxford UnitedView image in fullscreenThe club published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of ‘the historical context and associations’ related to the branding.Photograph: Oxford UnitedOxford UnitedOxford United apologise for launching ‘United 93’ clothing range around 9/11 anniversary‘Campus Collection’ aimed to mark 1893 club foundingRange pulled from website two hours after launchPaul MacInnesFri 18 Sep 2026 10.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOxford United have abandoned a new range of American style-sportswear after it inadvertently referenced the tragedy of September 11.The League One club launched their new “Campus Collection” on Friday morning but had removed it from sale by lunchtime, after clothing designs were revealed to bear the slogan “United 93”. The U’s immediately published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of “the historical context and associations” related to the branding and made “sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused”.“Inspired by the style and culture of American sports,” the club originally trailed the Campus Collection as launching on 11 September of this year, the 25th anniversary of the atrocity that killed nearly 3,000 people. Concerns over sensitivity saw the launch then delayed, but when the online collection was finally made available for sale on Friday, images showed models wearing an NFL-style shirt with “United 93” on the chest, in recognition of Oxford being founded in 1893.United 93 wasone of four domestic passenger jetsseized by al-Qaida terrorists on 11 September 2001. A mutiny by passengers prevented hijackers from using the plane to destroy a government building in Washington DC, and it ultimately crashed into a field, killing all 44 people on board. A film titled “United 93”was also madeabout the tragedy.The Campus Collection was live for approximately two hours on Friday before the webpage was deleted by the club after they realised the meaning of the phrase. “The range was released without understanding of the historical context and associations,” the club statement read. “It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence.“We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again. Once again, we would like to put on record our sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpinion was mixed among Oxford fans, with many outraged but others inclined to forgive the error. One user of the Yellows Forum called it a “monumental cock-up that I would expect to be sacked for if I’d signed off on it”. Another wrote: “Whilst not ideal … everyone who sees this realises there’s no malicious intent. Ultimately there was just no consideration to it at all.”Explore more on these topicsOxford UnitedUS sportsSeptember 11 2001newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias | Geography | The Guardian
description: Equal Earth projection, adopted by the UN last week, provides an alternative to 16th-century Mercator display
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Equal Earth projection, adopted by the UN last week, provides an alternative to 16th-century Mercator display
Content: Geography‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western biasEqual Earth projection, adopted by the UN last week, provides an alternative to 16th-century Mercator displayOliver Holmes,Ana Lucía González PazandPablo GutiérrezFri 18 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTShareThree cartographers have spoken of their astonishment at the UN’snear-universal adoptionof a map they created to more accurately show the sizes of Africa and Europe, even though they have received a few complaints from some disgruntled diplomats.The creators of the Equal Earth projection aimed to provide an alternative to the dominant 16th-century Mercator display, which critics have long faulted for giving the impression that northern hemisphere nations are larger than they are – and therefore subtly reinforcing perceptions of where global strength lies.“It has been a very busy week for me,” said Tom Patterson, a renowned US national parks cartographer who has had to virtually come out of retirement after being inundated with questions from governments on details of the new projection.The UN general assemblyvoted this month to adopt the new map, which more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa. It is hoped the projection will gradually replace Mercator on school walls and government websites.Put forward by Togo,the proposalwas hugely successful, with 164 countries voting in favour. The only “no” vote came from the US, whose UN representative, Yaryna Ferencevych, said resolutions such as the “correct the map” effortwere “barnacles on our work here”. The US is one of the countries that appears smaller on the new projection. It also makes Greenland – a territorial prize Donald Trump has openly coveted as a “big beautiful piece of ice” – seem significantly less dominant.Map showing how Greenland and Europe seem bigger in size than Africa in the Mercator projection, while looking smaller in comparison in the Equal Earth projectionSix other nations abstained from the vote, and Patterson said he had been contacted by diplomats from government embassies in Washington DC looking for clarification.Japan asked for a revision because it said the map made the disputed Kuril Islandsappear to belong to Russiaby putting them in the same shade of yellow. Ukraine also abstained, as Russian-occupied Crimea was a different colour to the rest of the country. Ukraine’s representatives at the UN said thisopened a “Pandora’s box” and violated international law.The cartographers see these objections as stemming from something of a misunderstanding. The map voted on at the UN is simply a mathematical projection of the land and sea, without human-made borders or shading. The confusion arose due toa websiterun by Patterson that offers free Equal Earth projections. He had annotated these with geopolitical lines and the names of countries, and has been rushing this week to update them, including switching colours and changing spellings, such as Turkey to Türkiye.“I view the Equal Earth maps as living documents and am grateful for the many helpful suggestions that I have received,” he said.Pattersondeveloped the new projection in 2018with a California-based software engineer, Bojan Šavrič, the “maths wizard” of the trio, and Bernhard Jenny, an associate professor at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.Jenny said people generally believed maps were accurate representations of the Earth, but that logic breaks down because we live on a curved surface. This creates a problem, as a sphere cannot easily be transformed into a flat rectangle.“It’s like the orange peel analogy,” said Jenny. “You have to tear it and stretch it, and it’s not possible to flatten it out … so you have to make compromises.”One global map, called the Goode homolosine projection, looks strikingly like a ripped-up orange peel. Its main problems are that it is not very pleasing to the human eye and not very easy to use for navigation – something the flawed Mercator excels at, because north is always up.View image in fullscreenThe Goode homolosine projectionPhotograph: Tobias JungFor Jenny, cartography is about aesthetics as well as science. “We cartographers say cartography is the art and science of making maps. So it’s kind of the combination of the two.”Equal Earth is not the first attempt to address Mercator’s shortcomings. Several other projections were developed in the past century, includingthe Gall-Peters model, which shows the true relative sizes of land masses, but which often appears oddly elongated, almost like the continents are drooping. Jenny said: “There was a lot of backlash from cartographers who said: ‘Well, it looks like clothes are hung up to dry.’”There are always compromises when making maps. Spend any amount of time with a cartographer and what might seem like fundamental truths quickly break down. “Which way is up?” or “Where is the centre” are not simple questions for cartographers – ancient Islamic maps had a south-up orientation, which put the holy city of Mecca in the eyeline. A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented, with Greenwich in the centre.View image in fullscreenA copy of a south-up map originally made by the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi.Photograph: UniversalImagesGroup/Getty Images“You have to make compromises,” said Jenny. The Equal Earth map, for example, would not be useful for getting around, as countries on the edges are squeezed. In fact, if any country had a claim to be upset, it could be New Zealand, which is stretched and distorted, and on the edge of the map.“A map is never neutral,” said Jenny. “So you cannot please everyone.”Šavrič, who worked on the mathematical formula, said he never imagined eight years ago that the trio’s research would be discussed at the highest levels.“What pleases me more is that this creates a valuable opportunity to strengthen map literacy and raise awareness that there is no single map projection capable of providing a completely ‘true’ representation of the world,” he said. “Every map projection involves trade-offs. I particularly appreciate that the [UN] resolution does not completely ban the Mercator projection or mandate a single replacement for all maps.”View image in fullscreenThe Chinese mapmaker Hao Xiaoguang’s vertical world map, which he created in 2021.Photograph: TPG/Getty ImagesJenny was also thrilled, watching on from Australia. “It’s kind of a cartographer’s dream, right?” he said. “The fact that the UN is debating map projections for an entire hour is already totally thrilling for cartographers, and then it wasourmap projection. I mean, what else can you ask for?”He does, however, have a hunch that another factor helped the Equal Earth map: the power of a good name. “I think, definitely, that you know what it is immediately,” said Jenny. If they had called it the “Šavrič-Patterson-Jenny projection”, he joked, maybe it would not have done so well.Header image is A Correct Sea Chart of the Whole World, According to Wright’s Commonly Called Mercator’s Projection, made in 1728. Courtesy of theDavid Rumsey Map Collection

title: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate | Technology | The Guardian
description: Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear
Content: Christine Lagarde asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.Photograph: Bryan Meade/EPAView image in fullscreenChristine Lagarde asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.Photograph: Bryan Meade/EPATechnologyAnalysisWhy Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debateDan MilmoandAisha DownThough Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bearFri 18 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.19 EDTShareEurope’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank,Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear –and experts have differing views on this– then the technology will impact the continent regardless.Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’Read moreEurope has largely been absent from the highest levels of that debate, a result of the continent’slongstanding inabilityto produce a Silicon Valley-scale titan like Apple, Google or newcomer OpenAI. While it is a powerhouse in regulation, much to the White House’s chagrin, its lack of an Anthropic or Nvidia-sized frontrunner in the AI race has diminished its voice in the safety debate.Ursula von der Leyen, a powerful political figure on the continent as president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, addressed the issue this week by saying she will “invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.Her remarks gained nowhere as much traction as Donald Trump and China’s dismissal of a slowdown. Without the support of Washington or Beijing, any sort of pacing is impossible – with our without Europe’s input.Lagarde’s speech on Monday underlined the continent’s relative weakness. She asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force.” Self-sufficiency would also give Europe a chance to develop its own answer to the AI safety crisis.Margrethe Vestager, who clashed with the US tech industry as the EU’s former competition commissioner, co-authored a report this week – A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe – that echoed Lagarde’s warning. AI threatens to accelerate a development already affecting Europe, where citizens “are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere”, she says.Solutions to this, according to the report, include building more datacentres – the central nervous systems of AI – and also to ensure the continent is resilient enough to withstand “AI crises” like a powerful model slipping out of control.Vestager said that Europe does have a voice in the safety debate through its EU AI Act, the rare piece of AI legislation that sets out requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems to report safety incidents and address risks like a cutting-edge model evading control.But she adds: “Europe must … build its own AI to strengthen the ecosystem, retain talent, and inspire innovation.”Vestager acknowledges that if there is an existential threat, it requires a global solution; one that does not hand power to the US and China. And that requires a different kind of supranational body.“As for existential threats to humanity, we must first assess the actual level of threat – then act with urgency. The UN general assembly is an opportunity to address this. It is vital to move beyond the US-China rivalry narrative. There must be space for humanity between the egos of leaders like President Xi and President Trump.”Frederike Kaltheuner, an adviser to the AI Now Institute, a research body, says that Europe is dependent on US technology in ways that will be hard to undo, from search engines to chips to datacentres. But thenarrative that Europe is grievously behind in the racedepends on a particular view of artificial intelligence aggressively promoted by American tech bosses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBecause of their doomsday warnings, “we are exclusively talking about AI in a very narrow, specific kind of way – namely, the idea that there is such a thing as the AI frontier, which is getting better and better, and that access to the frontier is the most important thing that Europe needs for its security and economy.”The reality of the market points at something else, she says: many companies are not adopting so-called “frontier models” – like ChatGPT and Anthropic – because of high costs and fears over what might happen to their data.If this trend continues, Europe may not be so terribly positioned: the EU AI Act has a number of pragmatic measures which address how consumers might encounter AI on a day-to-day basis, legislating over matters such as labelling AI content, and the use of AI in medicine and hiring.“Europe has a competitiveness problem, that’s true,” says Itxaso Dominguez de Olazabal, a policy adviser at EDRI, a European digital rights organisation. But US tech boosters are “blaming it on laws and protections, and have promised that deregulation will make European companies more competitive … in a race to the bottom to see if we can catch big tech”.Nonetheless, the EU AI act is not viewed as model legislation for other countries or a vehicle for a global slowdown. Georgina Kon, a partner at law firm Linklaters, says the act is unlikely to be adopted as a global benchmark for several reasons, including criticisms of the heavy compliance burden, which has led to delays in parts of the act becoming active, and a narrow territorial focus on Europe. Those criticisms have also meant that lawmakers elsewhere have looked to differentiate their approach to AI legislation from the EU’s.“The EU AI Act is not something that everybody else in the world feels constrained by, although many tech companies will of course want to sell to the EU,” she says.Big tech still has a vast customer base in Europe. Kaltheuner worries that the doomsday narratives will push Europe towards dependency, encouraging it to adopt US AI models across the economy out of ill-defined fears over being left behind.“There’s a vision of the future where Europe’s economy, its public sector, its education system runs on models and on infrastructure that is controlled by a very small number of companies that happen to be also in the US. This would be a sovereignty problem.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)EuropeEuropean UnionChristine LagardenewsShareReuse this content

title: Marks and Spencer’s first LFW catwalk gamble pays off with compelling looks at affordable prices | Marks & Spencer | The Guardian
description: Retailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway show
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Retailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway show
Content: All of the clothes went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces priced under £50.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersView image in fullscreenAll of the clothes went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces priced under £50.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersMarks & SpencerMarks and Spencer’s first LFW catwalk gamble pays off with compelling looks at affordable pricesRetailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway showJess Cartner-MorleyFri 18 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoan Collins declared the coats “very chic”, and has her eye on a graceful ivory evening dress with caped shoulders. Kemi Badenoch plans to snap up the classic black tuxedo jacket. If the British public are as enthusiastic as the celebrity front row, Marks & Spencer’s first everLondon fashion weekcatwalk looks like a hit.The show, held at the Design Museum for 310 guests including Ian Wright and Jamie Carragher, was a gamble on both sides. Would snobby fashionistas be traumatised by elasticated waistbands and practical rainwear? Would M&S customers be alienated by a world of £2,000 handbags and shoes you can’t walk in?The style message was “fashion with a small f, not a capital F”, said the M&S womenswear director, Maddy Evans. The look was new enough to be compelling (sharp kilts instead of flouncy tiered skirts, low-rise slouchy denim replacing mom jeans), but pitched at a before-the-watershed comfort level. A judicious amount of catwalk theatre was added with some sauce (a very short skirt, the odd semi-visible nipple) and a little zeitgeisty styling (faux fur stoles, Charli xcx-adjacent sunglasses).The real stunner is the price. All the clothes in this collection went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces under £50. The most expensive, a leather coat, will retail for £450. The message – that catwalk style is for everyone – is a win for London fashion week, which has struggled to feel relevant to real lives as designer prices have soared during a cost of living crisis.View image in fullscreenThe show featured Lennon Gallagher modelling a classic grey office suit.Photograph: Ian West/PAAs a vision of where our wardrobes are going next, the collection will not give Phoebe Philo or Jonathan Anderson any sleepless nights. M&S is not seeking to define the next vibe shift. Instead, they picked up on the currents that make a wardrobe look contemporary: a colour palette of neutrals with pops of red (for men, as well as women) and a shift toward outfits built from separates over dresses. Menswear featured a classic grey office suit – worn, in a witty casting touch, by scowling nepo-rocker Lennon Gallagher – and centrist-dad chore jackets.M&S are now ranked in second place in style perception, behind Zara. “That’s exactly where we want to be”, said Evans. “Zara are the cutting edge of fashion, and we are fashion for everybody.”Many pieces felt intentionally familiar, with nods to the archives to celebrate the centenary of fashion being sold at M&S. There was a twinset, reworked as a cardigan over a knitted camisole, and a sage-green lace two-piece set which nodded to the proud history of M&S lingerie. Models of a broad range of ages and body sizes “were chosen to reflect our 23 million customers”, said Evans.After the show, Wright caught up with Carragher as a fashion week version of an M&S “picky tea” was served: smoked salmon finger sandwiches and champagne on silver trays.The show was a bold statement about how M&S sees itself, reflecting resurgent style confidence after fashion hits that have included suede loafers that could pass for Saint Laurent and a sellout collaboration with Bella Freud.M&S is not the only big name giving the London schedule fresh momentum and a renewed sense of occasion this season. McQueen is returning to London after showing in Paris, while Christopher Kane – one of the city’s most beloved and influential designers – is making a keenly anticipated return to the catwalk with a new job at Mulberry.Fashion editor’s top picksDouble-breasted tuxedo jacket, £85Modern party-dressing made simple. Double-breasted shape and satin peak labels bring just enough drama. Machine washable!View image in fullscreenTuxedo jacket, £85.Photograph: M&SIvory satin party dress, £89Crepe-back satin (one side matt, one side glossy) is the kind of high-end fabric you do not often find on the high street. Kimono sleeves and a train for real wow factor. Also comes in black.View image in fullscreenSatin mini dress, £89Photograph: M&SSequin fringe skirt, £50Swishy! The personality skirt is big in fashion and with gold sequins and silk fringing, this has main character energy.View image in fullscreenSequin fringe skirt, £50.Photograph: M&SRed half zip sweater, £40From tech bros to pop stars, everyone is in a half zip. The ketchup red is fun.View image in fullscreenHalf zip jumper, £40.Photograph: M&SLeather jacket with borg collar, £250Vintage style pilot’s jacket in tobacco leather with a cream shawl collar and waist tabs.View image in fullscreenPer Una vintage borg leather jacket, £250.Photograph: M&SExplore more on these topicsMarks & SpencerLondon fashion weekFashion weeksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Letter to Brezhnev review – terrific return for Merseysiders’ romance with Russian sailors | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Ellie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, passionate yet still tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 film
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Ellie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, passionate yet still tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 film
Content: Hello, sailor! … Thomas Cotran and Ellie Clayton in Letter to Brezhnev.Photograph: AB PhotographyView image in fullscreenHello, sailor! … Thomas Cotran and Ellie Clayton in Letter to Brezhnev.Photograph: AB PhotographyTheatreReviewLetter to Brezhnev review – terrific return for Merseysiders’ romance with Russian sailorsRoyal Court, LiverpoolEllie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 filmMark FisherFri 18 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy some quirk of marketing,Letter to Brezhnevis always associated with Margi Clarke. In the 1985 movie, she was the actor who played Teresa, the sharp-talking chicken-factory worker out for a good time in post-industrial Liverpool. The film, though, rightly belongs to Alexandra Pigg as Elaine, Teresa’s best friend, who trades a dead-end life of unemployment for a fantasy fling with a Russian sailor.A few years before the collapse of the Soviet Union – and a year before Willy Russell’s similarly themedShirley Valentine– Elaine dared to believe in escape and in border-defying love. On stage, she is played just as winningly by Ellie Clayton and with much the same combination of wit and wonder. She is the Kirkby girl who has a night on the town with a wallet of stolen cash and finds the world unexpectedly opening up to her. Elaine can be naive, petulant and cynical, but she never lets you stop rooting for her.As Teresa, Angela Simms is the necessary corrective to Elaine’s dreamy romanticism: she lives for the moment and gives as good as she gets. Only in her quieter moments will she admit her rebelliousness is skin deep. They make a terrific pair.View image in fullscreenOut for a good time … Leona Sinama-Pongolle, Angela Sims and Ellie Clayton in Letter to Brezhnev.Photograph: AB PhotographyFrank Clarke’s if-it-ain’t-broke adaptation hugs closely to his original screenplay, adding the odd joke but sticking to the same sequence of taxi rides, club nights and ferry crossings. You might expect that to constrain the director – but no, Nicole Behan injects her production with tremendous energy, exchanging the movie’s subtle charm for ribald theatrical flair, drawing out the humour and the passion without diminishing the tender emotional heart.Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaRead moreThe show takes shape around a multi-level set by Mark Walters, inventively lit by Ian Scott, with gangplanks, bedrooms and barbed wire neatly emerging from a towering frontage of wooden cupboards. In lesser hands it could dwarf the performers, but it is too cleverly conceived for that: something also true of Rob Green’s musical direction. At choice moments, he elevates the soundtrack of 70s and 80s hits by mixing in live vocals, whether it’s You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real) orLips Like Sugar, showcasing an excellent ensemble.Say what you like about movie adaptations, but with cast members from the film in the first-night audience, this one is joyfully at home on the stage.AtRoyal Court theatre, Liverpool, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreLiverpoolreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Singapore is paying people to read books – can it fix the reading crisis? | Books | The Guardian
description: A government scheme is giving citizens cash for spending time with a good book. We ask behavioural scientists, along with The Anxious Generation author and psychologist Jonathan Haidt, whether it’ll help make the habit stick
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: A government scheme is giving citizens cash for spending time with a good book. We ask behavioural scientists, along with The Anxious Generation author and psychologist Jonathan Haidt, whether it’ll help make the habit stick
Content: ‘A tiny immediate reward can help bridge the gap between intention and action’ … A man browses books in Singapore.Photograph: Jackyenjoyphotography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A tiny immediate reward can help bridge the gap between intention and action’ … A man browses books in Singapore.Photograph: Jackyenjoyphotography/Getty ImagesBooksSingapore is paying people to read books – can it fix the reading crisis?A government scheme is giving citizens cash for spending time with a good book. We ask behavioural scientists, along with The Anxious Generation author and psychologist Jonathan Haidt, whether it’ll help make the habit stickElla CreamerFri 18 Sep 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCould the solution to thereading crisislie in paying people to put down their phones and pick up a book? That’s what one government, at least, is resorting to: this month, Singaporelaunched a schemepromising actual cash to citizens as a reward for logging reading time on a government website.It’s unlikely to make you megabucks – you have to rack up 50 reading sessions of at least 15 minutes to earn oneSingaporedollar (£0.59), with only one logged session allowed per day. But behavioural scientists and psychologists told the Guardian such a scheme could still help boost a habit in precipitous decline.Singapore pays people to pick up a book in battle against doomscrollingRead moreJonathan Haidt, a psychologist and the author of the bestselling bookThe Anxious Generation, about the impact of social media on young people’s mental health, says that some children are highly motivated by money, and “all kids respond to rewards to some degree” – so for young people, the scheme is “likely to have some beneficial effect in setting up a habit of reading”. Lory Barile, associate professor in economics at the University of Warwick, adds that “there is good evidence that repeating a behaviour consistently can help it become more automatic over time”.If participants find reading “pleasurable in itself”, then the habit may stick, says Haidt. Yet, for some, the monetary reward “will convey to them that they are reading only for the extrinsic reward”, and so when the money stops, the reading will, too. Barile agrees that the most interesting question isn’t whether people read more while they’re being rewarded, but whether the scheme “helps people establish a reading habit that persists once the reward is no longer present”.While the earning potential of the Singapore scheme is low, this doesn’t necessarily mean it won’t be effective, says Ivo Vlaev, a professor of behavioural psychology at the National University of Singapore. “One of the interesting findings from behavioural science is that incentives do not always work in proportion to their monetary value.”double quotation markThe question is whether it helps people establish a reading habit that persists once the reward is no longer presentLory BarileThe scheme shouldn’t be thought of as “paying people to read” in a conventional economic sense – a dollar every few weeks is obviously not enough to compensate participants for the time they’ve invested. Instead, the payment “may be acting more as a trigger than as a wage”, says Vlaev. Logging reading time and accumulating points means participants “receive an immediate signal that the behaviour has been recognised, your streak continues and you make progress towards a goal”. And once someone has actually started reading, “the intrinsic rewards of the activity can take over”, he adds.We all know reading has long-term benefits, but a key element of the Singapore scheme hinges on introducing a short-term reward for the activity, mimicking the immediate dopamine hit of scrolling. In fact, the “gamified” element may be “smarter” than the financial reward offered, says Patrick Taylor, director of education at the Behavioural Insights Team (which originated in David Cameron’s Cabinet Office, also known as the “nudge unit”). “Having a manageable 15-minute daily goal, built around existing routines like commuting or bedtime, with streaks and tracking to keep progress visible” are the aspects that could make the scheme a success, he says.View image in fullscreenOnce a habit is started, the intrinsic rewards of the activity can take over.Photograph: Luis Alvarez/Getty ImagesSuch a scheme may be particularly effective for lapsed readers. “If people are already intrinsically motivated to read, this may be enough to tip them over the edge to read a bit more,” says Katy Milkman, a professor at Wharton business school, University of Pennsylvania. Vlaev adds that “if somebody already intends to read but repeatedly fails to get started, a tiny immediate reward can help bridge the gap between intention and action”.double quotation markIncentives do not always work in proportion to their monetary valueIvo VlaevIn the UK, non-monetary reward schemes for reading and other types of learning have long been in place, such as the primary school rainbow certificate scheme, through which “the value comes primarily from recognition and a sense of achievement”, says Barile. The Reading Agency’sSummer Reading Challengeallows children to receive badges and certificates for reading, too.A UK pilot of the Singapore-style scheme could therefore “compare small financial rewards with symbolic rewards such as certificates or badges, as well as gamification, goal-setting and progress feedback”, says Barile. Others agree that such schemes should be run as trials, “so we find out what works and why”, says Taylor. Haidt suggests a few variations to test: some children could be randomly assigned to be paid in cash, others could be paid in free books of their choice (“so that they see books as a reward, not money as a reward for reading”), and others “are simply urged to read to get points in a competition, no money”. A fourth group “would be a true control, nothing is done, other than measuring how many books they read”.But the question remains: should governments financially reward what has been traditionally considered something you do for fun? Milkman sees it differently: “We subsidise, and even require, many other forms of education.” So why not reward reading, too?Explore more on these topicsBooksSingaporeLiteracyPsychologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Quentin Bell and Olivia Sterling review – two artists with a magic touch | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Bell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and power
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Bell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and power
Content: A brilliant young painter … Olivia Sterling, Our General Aims, 2022.Photograph: Hendrik Zeitler/Olivia SterlingView image in fullscreenA brilliant young painter … Olivia Sterling, Our General Aims, 2022.Photograph: Hendrik Zeitler/Olivia SterlingArt and designReviewQuentin Bell and Olivia Sterling review – two artists with a magic touchCharleston, LewesBell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and powerEddy FrankelFri 18 Sep 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQuentin Bell was not a great artist, but that didn’t stop him. He saw the world as a magical place. The ceramicist (son of the Bloomsbury group’sVanessa Bell; biographer of his auntVirginia Woolf) spent his life lost in a world of magic, myth, newts in ponds, levitating women and knights on horseback. He died in 1996, leaving behind decades of pots, plates, figurines and drawings filled with wonder and amazement.It all started when Bell was nine years old. Taken to a magic show by some relatives, he saw a jaw-dropping spectacle: a beautiful woman seeming to float in the air. It stayed with him throughout his life.Five sculptures here show bodies caught in mid-air, raised off the ground, stiff as a board. There are rough messy works in wire and wood and plaster from the 1960s, bronze from the 80s and painted ceramics from the 90s; from modern and stark to gaudy and bright, it’s levitation that set him on his creative path and never left his side.View image in fullscreenA spectacle he couldn’t forget … Quentin Bell with Levitating Figure at Cobbe House, Sussex.Photograph: The Charleston TrustMost of the work hereis ceramic: plates, pots and figurines. They’re humorous, brightly coloured, shiny objects. They’re like messy, rough takes on chintzy 18th-century European decorative art, rococo porcelain with its depictions of reclining ladies in voluminous dresses. The figurines aren’t great: they’re basic and poorly rendered, often malformed and pretty unremarkable, if quite funny in places.View image in fullscreenNo minimalism … Quentin Bell, Platter: Playing Card.Photograph: Lee RobbinsHis plates and teapots fare better, especially the later cups and jugs, which are colourful and decorative. But his drawings and illustrations are where it really falls apart. He paints Greek myths and biblical scenes, he illustrates the story of Cinderella and his own imagined history of Sussex, but none of it is well executed or particularly interesting. They feel like fun creative projects meant to entertain his kids, which some of them were.What makes it compelling is that everything here is at odds with the aesthetic trends of his era. There’s none of the austere minimalism of influential contemporary potters such as the amazing Bernard Leach, none of the abstraction or surrealism that was coursing through Europe, none of the grim interwar realism that defined so much English modernism. Instead, there’s something way more anachronistic. This is strange, charming, incredibly English, totally eccentric creativity being expressed on its own terms.The main takeaway from this exhibition isn’t that Quentin Bell is good at art; he’s not even the best Bell. The main takeaway is that there’s something powerful, even beautiful about dedicating your life to creativity.Way better is thedisplay of new works next doorby the brilliant young English painter Olivia Sterling. She’s taken the magical obsessions of Bell and pushed them to bawdier, weirder, funnier, more critical extremes. Her whole shtick is about using the language of old cartoons and comics, the symbolism of food, the representation of the human body, and twisting it all into biting critiques of race and power dynamics. This is her at her strangest, darkest and filthiest.View image in fullscreenMenacing … Olivia Sterling, Emotionally True, 2026.Photograph: Olivia SterlingYou walk into a room-sized painting of vast bodies squeezed into corsets and girdles or flopping about in dressing gowns, like you’ve stumbled into the backstage of some burlesque show. And then the performance starts. A woman has become a dirty dining table in one menacingly red painting, plates of half-eaten cake and glasses of milk strewn across her body. In another work, a pink corpse is littered with ice-creams, a magician’s rabbit scampers over her belly and milk spurts from her nipple. Smaller works show white liquid being squeezed and pulled out of teats and orifices. A huge triptych depicts a white body lying in a magician’s sword box, one black woman pressing down on top of it, another plunging a sword in.Sterling is drawing a line between magic and power; she’s saying they’re both fundamentally the same thing: an illusion, a world maintained through artifice. It’s clever, political, incisive narrative painting. But, crucially, it’s also fun, ridiculously colourful and totally overblown. If it was miserable, serious and dour, you’d feel like you were getting lectured. Instead, you feel like you’re watching a Tom and Jerry episode about greed and racism, with all the violence and slapstick intact. Now that’s a good magic trick.AtCharleston, Lewes, until 7 MarchExplore more on these topicsArt and designBloomsbury groupPaintingArtCeramicsDrawingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trent Alexander-Arnold recalled by England but with a warning from Thomas Tuchel | England | The Guardian
description: Thomas Tuchel has told Trent ­Alexander-Arnold he must bring defensive solidity to the England squad after giving him a surprise recall for the upcoming Nations League matches
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Thomas Tuchel has told Trent ­Alexander-Arnold he must bring defensive solidity to the England squad after giving him a surprise recall for the upcoming Nations League matches
Content: Trent Alexander-Arnold is back in the England fold.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTrent Alexander-Arnold is back in the England fold.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockEnglandTrent Alexander-Arnold recalled by England but with a warning from Thomas TuchelReal Madrid player must help improve defensive solidityScott, Hall, Lewis-Skelly and Calvert-Lewin selectedDavid HytnerFri 18 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 05.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel has toldTrent Alexander-Arnoldhe must bring defensive solidity to the England squad after giving him a surprise recall for the upcoming Nations League matches.The head coach has selected the Real Madrid right-back only once before – for the games against Andorra and Senegal in June last year. Tuchel made headlines when he did so by urging Alexander-Arnold to focus on the defensive side of his game or risk a slip that could undermine the team’s World Cup campaign.‘Embrace the chaos’: Tuchel aims to harness England’s football cultureRead moreTuchel used him as a 64th-minute substitute against Andorra and Alexander-Arnold was out of the picture by the timeEnglandwent to North America for the tournament. He is now back, despite starting only three of Madrid’s seven matches this season and largely going under the radar with his performances. Tuchel’s message to him has not changed.“He has to, it’s necessary,” Tuchel said when asked whether Alexander-Arnold offered enough defensively. “My conviction is that he will but he has no choice.”Tuchel continues to see Alexander-Arnold, who is famed for the range of his passing, as a right-back rather than a midfielder. The head coach has previously said he has Tino Livramento and Jarell Quansah ahead of Alexander-Arnold in the right-back pecking order. He has named both of them in the squad for the games against Spain (home), Czechia (home and away) and Croatia (away).Quick GuideEngland's squadShowGoalkeepers:Jordan Pickford, James Trafford, Jason Steele.Defenders:Trent Alexander-Arnold, Jarrod Branthwaite, Trevoh Chalobah, Marc Guéhi, Lewis Hall, Ezri Konsa, Tino Livramento, Nico O’Reilly, Jarell Quansah.Midfielders:Elliot Anderson, Jude Bellingham, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Kobbie Mainoo, Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Alex Scott.Forwards:Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Eberechi Eze, Anthony Gordon, Harry Kane, Rio Ngumoha, Marcus Rashford, Morgan Rogers, Bukayo Saka.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Tuchel has been unable to include his first-choice right-back, Reece James, or Djed Spence, who can operate in either full-back position, because of injuries. Ben White is also injured; Tuchel said he would have considered him. The centre-half Ezri Konsa, who is in the squad, has played at right-back.Tuchel said he had spoken to Alexander-Arnold to tell him he would not go to the World Cup but had not called him this time. “He heard the good news over the nomination,” he said. “I am not sure a lot of things have changed. I know what he is capable of. I know about his talent. I know what he is saying: that he is desperate to play for England and he will fight for his shirt. It’s a long camp and it’s a good moment to show up. It’s a chance for Trent to claim what he feels is his – his place on the right side. So here we go.”Graphic showing minutes played for England under Thomas Tuchel by members of this squadAlexander-Arnold was the headline selection on a day when Tuchel gave further recalls to Jarrad Branthwaite, Lewis Hall, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Alex Scott, Cole Palmer and Dominic Calvert-Lewin. He also included Rio Ngumoha. Dean Henderson, John Stones, Dan Burn and Jordan Henderson miss out because of injury. Noni Madueke, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney have been dropped.Tuchel overlooked Levi Colwill, Adam Wharton, Phil Foden and Morgan Gibbs-White. Nor was there a recall for Harry Maguire. Tuchel gave the defender hope of involvement at the World Cup when he selected him against Uruguay and Japan in March before he ignored him for the tournament. It drew an outspoken response, Maguire using social media to pronounce himself “shocked and gutted”. His mother, Zoe, said she was “disgusted” by the decision.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Of Maguire’s reaction, Tuchel said: “I will not hold it against him for the rest of his life because I’m not that type of person. I can forget easily and quickly. But I didn’t like it and it doesn’t help.”Tuchel said he had not spoken to Maguire since.Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelTrent Alexander-ArnoldNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: We wanted to let Max Dowman bloom in the shadows but he has become hard to ignore | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: This most modern and well-honed of footballers will not be able to escape the spotlight in an age of constant scrutiny but looks equipped to handle it
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: This most modern and well-honed of footballers will not be able to escape the spotlight in an age of constant scrutiny but looks equipped to handle it
Content: Max Dowman’s excellence seems comfortable with itself.Illustration: Nathan DanielsView image in fullscreenMax Dowman’s excellence seems comfortable with itself.Illustration: Nathan DanielsArsenalWe wanted to let Max Dowman bloom in the shadows but he has become hard to ignoreBarney RonayThis most modern and well-honed of footballers will not be able to escape the spotlight in an age of constant scrutiny but looks equipped to handle itFri 18 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTShareThe poet Jorge Luis Borges wrote a famous short story about a society that had become so good at making maps, so obsessed with capturing every detail, that its rulers decided the only way to do the job right was to make a lifesize map of its entire empire, which could then be laid out across the actual land from coast to coast. Imagine a map of Britain the exact same size as Britain, showing every branch of Greggs, every nail bar, every vape shop in perfect detail. Only then can we really see what Britain looks like, by standing on a fake Britain laid over the top of actual Britain.Borges was writing in the 1940s, at a time when people were fascinated by the mechanised future, with its new forms of measuring out the world: the wireless, the 30mph motorcar, the rise of Big Tape Measure. And to be fair, the mega-map is a pretty accurate vision of our own fully networked present, a place where you can snoop around a village in Mozambique from your laptop in Egham, where no one ever stops committing acts of minute self-surveillance, even if they think they’re just searching “What is beetroot?” on the internet.‘They are very similar’: Arsenal’s Dowman reminds Merino of Lamine YamalRead moreBorges also hated football. “Soccer is popular because stupidity is popular,” he wrote, which probably seemed a bold statement at the time. But then Borges also didn’t live to see an episode of Wow Sports Premier League Breakfast at Breakfast with Roger McRoger and a puzzled Lee Trundle. After which, perhaps less of a surprise. But the process he describes is also a good description of what football is doing to itself. Endless data, endless analysis, no spaces or free air, matches that are just schematised movement. At times it can feel like football is out there laying a lifesize real-time map on top of itself.In Borges’s story, the land soon begins to decay beneath the massive map – which is reassessed by later generations as insane, pointless and stupid – and left to rot in the desert. We haven’t reached this point. Nobody is de-mapping football. But it does perhaps explain why everyone gets so excited when a talent emerges that seems to be playful and human, to exist outside the grid. And also why it has felt wrong to gush too soon about Max Dowman, to fear placing the hex on him. We know how this works. Here is a fluffy new thing. Let us break him. Let us heap pressure on his shoulders. Don’t talk about Max Dowman. Let Max Dowman exist, breathe, bloom in the shadows.So, Max Dowman then. It has become quite hard to ignore him. He was brilliantagainst Ipswich in midweek, and brilliant in a way that seems solid and real and comfortable with itself. Most obviously there were the two goals, both a perfect snapshot of why Dowman seems equipped to survive, more state‑of‑the‑art than some other young players we’ve burdened with expectation.The second goal is particularly good, five perfect little actions packed into six seconds of football.Arsenalhave the ball on the edge of the Ipswich box. Dowman shows for a pass, sees it’s going elsewhere, changes his mind, and makes a three-yard sprint to create space. Finally he has the physical capacity to control a bouncing ball in that sliver of space, to move his feet so much quicker than the nearest defender it looks like a glitch in the machine, and to finish in a way that involves sifting the options and timing the shot, all without breaking stride.View image in fullscreenMax Dowman leaves Cédric Kipré floundering to score his brilliant second, and Arsenal’s third, goal at Ipswich.Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Every Second Media/ShutterstockThe first goal is on his other side, and involves a more classical piece of one-on-one deception. This is the same defender: Cédric Kipré, 29 years old, came through Paris Saint-Germain’s youth system. Dowman walks through him with a micro-feint and a switch of feet, then reels off another hilariously understated finish, doing it all while a second defender is still gathering himself to lunge, like a man operating in a different time signature to everyone around him.This is the key point of difference, the ability to make everything stop, the fly-vision that means he sees what’s about to happen while everyone else is whirling about trying to read the charts, in the same way Lionel Messi (yes, sorry, sorry) always seems to have time to pass the ball into the net, like this is all a kickabout in a pair of sliders.Our way ofunderstanding young creative playershas often seemed to lag behind where the game actually is, to be driven by nostalgia for what this thing used to look like. I remember the excitement over the 18-year-old Jack Rodwell’s physicality at the exact moment physicality was no longer going to be a thing, like proudly unveiling the latest horse‑drawn train just as the Ford Model T rolls off the production line.Michael Owen was brilliant at 17, but he was mainly brilliant at running very fast in a straight line and smashing the ball into the net. Plus of course there was Wayne Rooney, who emerged a pale, unformed teenager composed entirely from energy drinks and white bread, out there making the game up on the fly, as though some urban foundling had come barrelling over the advert boards with a string of sausages still dangling from his mouth.The narrative around Rooney is that he lost this vital native quality. But Rooney adapted and survived, and clearly understood what he had to be a lot better than those of us watching. And even now creative players have to exist against this. Cole Palmer is exciting because he does surprising things that seem to be striking a blow for freedom, beauty and older people who struggle to make their email work. But his real challenge is to retain just enough of this while fitting the world around him.Dowman is a bit different. The things that make him stand out seem to speak very easily to how football is now. Being a modern creative footballer is not jinking runs, rasping drives or dribbling across a cabbage field in a pair of cowboy boots. It’s targeted energy, high-intensity semi-freedom. Lamine Yamal and Désiré Doué have the same fast-twitch foot and brain speed, the ability to operate in micro-moments, to see patterns just ahead of time. Dowman is 6ft tall and getting stronger. He won’t be kicked to pieces. He can repeat this without taking bites out of himself.There is still the issue of his youth. But maybe this doesn’t matter so much either. The world has changed. In the age of Rooney and Owen there was no care, no data, no softness. This is where the structures of modern football are an advantage. Dowman will be GPS’d to the last decimal point. Endless physical scientists will have a say on his output and stress levels.View image in fullscreenWayne Rooney and Michael Owen broke through as teenagers in an age of less data and less care.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyThe money is too big. The talent is too valuable. It also comes ready to plug and play. You don’t get to this level unless you can ingest systems and briefings. You’ve already been pressure-cooked and stress-tested. What you’re being asked to do in the orderly spaces of professional football is the same thing you were asked to do in the orderly spaces of academy football, just five levels up and with more people watching.Borges was anti-football because he saw it as inauthentic, the players no longer sports people but “actors in jerseys before the TV cameras”. And this is also fine, further evidence that boomer-dad nostalgia is one of the key archetypes of human behaviour.Life is also different now; not harder or easier, but more instant, a series of moments, the creation of rapid-fire energy. Dowman has grown up inside this. He can parcel his time out, disappear for a bit, maybe make a show of things in the spring.And yes, this is another way of fitting him to a model, laying a lifesize map of future Max Dowman across the present. But I strongly suspect he will be fine, and that unlike so many other things out there he’s pretty well adapted to whatever the future is supposed to look like.Explore more on these topicsArsenalcommentShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League: Lauren Hemp hits double as Manchester City see off lively Liverpool | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Manchester City maintained their 100% start with the England star scoring twice but Liverpool threatened a shock before a 4-2 win for hosts
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Manchester City maintained their 100% start with the England star scoring twice but Liverpool threatened a shock before a 4-2 win for hosts
Content: Manchester City’s Lauren Hemp celebrates scoring their fourth goal as Khiara Keating looks to the ground.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City’s Lauren Hemp celebrates scoring their fourth goal as Khiara Keating looks to the ground.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Super LeagueWomen’s Super League: Lauren Hemp hits double as Manchester City see off lively LiverpoolTom GarryFri 18 Sep 2026 16.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City continued their winning start to the new Women’s Super League season but the defending champions needed a 90th-minute own goal from Grace Fisk to help them edge past an ever-improving Liverpool side after an entertaining game in which Lauren Hemp scored twice.Fisk inadvertently turned Grace Clinton’s dangerous cross into her own net to put City 3-2 up and then – with Liverpool searching for an equaliser and committing players forward deep in stoppage time – Hemp added another on the counterattack to make it 4-2 and widen the margin of victory, but that slightly masked how well the visitors had played.Gareth Taylor – against his former side – will have taken significant encouragement from his Liverpool team’s performance, on a night when they made the league leaders dig deep.Laura Kaminski relishing trophy hunt at Brann after Crystal Palace ‘crash course’Read more“Playing that way, we believe we’ll win a lot of games this season,” Taylor told Sky Sports, as he praised his team’s effort. “What you saw was a more improved version of what we were towards the end of last season.”That certainly seemed the case. Nevertheless, the result ensured that City, who had already been the only WSL side who held a 100% winning record after the opening two rounds of games and now will certainly stay top of the table for at least another week, have still not dropped any points in home league fixtures since Andrée Jeglertz took charge in the summer of 2025.It had looked as though Jeglertz’s City were set for a routine evening when Hemp met Carlotta Wamser’s incisive inside ball and sent a controlled, low finish into the far bottom corner. It was Hemp’s first goal sincescoring for Englandin a victory over Spain in April, her first club goal since scoring in the FA Cup in February and her first WSL goal since last November’s Manchester derby.Moments after Hemp’s opening goal, with 13 minutes on the clock, the entire crowd rose to applaudthe late Matt Beard, the former Liverpool manager, in reference to the year 2013, when he won the first of two consecutive WSL titles with Liverpool.Supporters of clubs across the WSL and WSL2 have been invited to applaud at the same time in games across this weekend, to mark a year since Beard’s death on 20 September 2025.
