He was a much-loved character and hugely successful coach at Liverpool, whose performance – particularly in the remainder of the first half – would have done him proud.View image in fullscreenVivien Endemann puts Liverpool 2-1 up against Manchester City.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAThe away side deservedly struck back and found themselves 2-1 up before the half-hour mark, as their pressing gave the defending champions a headache. First a misunderstanding between Wamser and Alex Greenwood allowed Vivien Endemann to set up Alice Bergström for the equaliser, which she calmly tucked past Ayaka Yamashita.Soon afterwards, after City failed to clear a cross, Endemann – who had opened her Liverpool account with a debut goal at Charlton on the opening weekend – fired in a shot that Yamashita got a hand to but could only help into the net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom Segura to Maltby: six breakout stars from the Women’s Under-20 World CupRead moreKhadija Shaw struck a post from a difficult angle after rounding Khiara Keating, but Shaw eventually did equalise after a goalkeeping error shortly before half-time. Keating – returning to face her former club after her summer move to Liverpool – did well to block Hemp’s strike but was unable to prevent the ball trickling into the path of the onrushing Shaw, who gratefully poked home.Keating impressed in the second half with a fine reaction save, keeping out a Shaw effort that had looked destined for the top corner at her near post. But the hosts began to build pressure and the introduction of the lively Clinton inside the final 15 minutes boosted their attacking threat.Her near-post cross proved too difficult for Fisk to clear and – just as they did on countless occasions last term – City lived up to Jeglertz’s mantra of “we will find a way to win”, a message that has been imprinted on the walls of their training base.Jeglertz hinted at that again as he told Sky Sports: “I’m very pleased with the mentality of the group. They never stop believing, they keep on going and – in the end – we are winners.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueManchester City WomenLiverpool FC WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Wakefield reach Super League playoff semi-finals after eliminator win against Leigh | Super League | The Guardian
description: Second-half tries from Isaiah Vagana and Caius Faatili sealed 12-man Wakefield’s 26-16 win against Leigh and a last-four clash with Wigan or Leeds
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Second-half tries from Isaiah Vagana and Caius Faatili sealed 12-man Wakefield’s 26-16 win against Leigh and a last-four clash with Wigan or Leeds
Content: Caius Faatili powers over to score Wakefield’s fourth try against Leigh.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCaius Faatili powers over to score Wakefield’s fourth try against Leigh.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueWakefield reach Super League playoff semi-finals after eliminator win against LeighWakefield 26-16 LeighVagana and Faatili’s second-half tries seal victoryAaron Bowerat DIY Kitchens StadiumFri 18 Sep 2026 17.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese are the nights Matt Ellis dreamed of bringing to Belle Vue when hetook control of his boyhood clubthree years ago: but not even he could have imagined all of this could be happening quite so quickly.For the first time in their history,Wakefield Trinityare 80 minutes away from the Super League Grand Final. It may sound quite trivial in the scheme of things but this is a club who have spent the majority of the summer era residing in the competition’s lower reaches, which finally culminated with relegation to the Championship in 2023.Wigan dominate the present but NRL cash is key to Super League futureRead moreThat coincided with Ellis’s purchase of the club and some bold promises about where Wakefield would go in a short space of time. His claims that he would turn Trinity into aSuper Leagueforce were largely met with laughter: but very few people are laughing right now – except for Ellis of course, who delivered his traditional fist pumps on the pitch after his club created history.After storming through the Championship in 2024, Trinity surprised everyone last year by reaching the playoffs in their first season back in Super League. This year was supposed to be trickier; no longer an unfancied side, some expected Wakefield and Daryl Powell to be found out. But this club, under Ellis and Powell, are making a mockery of the predictions once again.Their route through to a first Super League playoff semi-final was ultimately straightforward. Even the sending off of their prop Emre Guler for a moment of madness when he lashed out at a Leigh player couldn’t derail Wakefield. They had far too much class, quality and physicality for a Leigh side who beat Trinity at this stage last year, but couldn’t repeat it here.This was Wakefield’s night. Led by an outstanding effort from the forwards including Tyson Smoothy and Caius Faatili, Trinity now advance to the final four – where they will face Wigan or Leeds for a place at Old Trafford. They will be underdogs but they have been underdogs before. Nobody can write off Super League’s newest force now, surely.“We’re in such a good place, the team and the club is in a good place,” Powell said. “It’s all happened quicker than we might have thought, to do what we did in getting the playoffs the first year back in Super League and now in the semis.” They dominated almost the entire evening, but led by just six points at the break in West Yorkshire.Tries for Smoothy and Tom Johnstone put them in control but when Leigh responded on the stroke of half-time through David Armstrong, you wondered if that would spur the Leopards into life. However, they failed to do anything of significance when it mattered most, and their season ended with a whimper.View image in fullscreenIsaiah Vagana, scorer of Wakefield’s third try, glides through the Leigh defence.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/Shutterstock“It was very frustrating to watch and certainly not the performance we planned for,” their coach, Adrian Lam, said. “We started really poorly in that second half and it was pretty much all over from there.”Isaiah Vagana scored a decisive try to make it 18-6 shortly after the restart before Faatili’s score put daylight between the teams. From there it felt as though Wakefield would run out convincing winners before Guler’s moment of madness, striking Owen Trout and being sent off, appeared to reopen the door for Leigh.They looked as though they would take it too when Lachlan Lam scored with 15 minutes remaining, but Wakefield tightened the proverbial screw and closed the game out with minimal fuss, with Max Jowitt’s penalty giving them a significant buffer. The final scoring act went to Leigh when Innes Senior touched down, but by then, their season was over.As for Wakefield? They break new ground again next week – and given the speed of their rise so far, do not rule out them creating more history once again.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueRugby leagueWakefield TrinityLeigh Leopardsmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Keely Hodgkinson shows off Catwoman style to steal Athlos London event | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Keely Hodgkinson destroyed a women’s 800m field dressed in a hooded black bodysuit, as Athlos London provided a radically different spin on track and field
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Keely Hodgkinson destroyed a women’s 800m field dressed in a hooded black bodysuit, as Athlos London provided a radically different spin on track and field
Content: Keely Hodgkinson, in unusual attire, wins the 800m in the Athlos all-female athletics meeting at the StoneX Stadium.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson, in unusual attire, wins the 800m in the Athlos all-female athletics meeting at the StoneX Stadium.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAthleticsKeely Hodgkinson shows off Catwoman style to steal Athlos London eventBriton destroys 800m field in hooded black bodysuitMill Hill event more like a rave than an athletics meetingSean Ingleat the StoneX StadiumFri 18 Sep 2026 17.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAthlos arrived in London promising that its all-female spin on athletics would provide a radical departure from the status quo. Long beforeKeely Hodgkinsonstepped on to the track dressed in a hooded black bodysuit – part ninja assassin, part Catwoman – it had emphatically made its point.Throughout the two-hour event, the bassline from the aptly named DJ Trauma carried enough force to make eardrums bleed. The stadium PA’s dial appeared to be permanently stuck on Spinal Tap’s 11. And those who successfully scanned a barcode were then shown dancing and waving on a giant screen.But the youngish crowd largely lapped it up. As Hodgkinson was introduced, the stadium MC told the cheering crowd: “Wait until she comes around the corner, she looks bad, bad, bad. In a custom Nike suit, Keely Hodgkinson!”Keely Hodgkinson reveals how freak canal accident ruined world record bidRead moreSoon the roars had become even louder.Athleticssometimes resembles a vicarage tea party. This was more like a rave. Mill Hill has surely never seen anything like it.Afterwards, the Paris Olympic 800m champion insisted that the suit and its aerodynamic design, which also contained openings for her sunglasses and ponytail, had given her an edge. But she could have been running in a thick duffle coat and she would still have won the $65,000 first prize and Tiffany crown with ease.“I think it’s a mixture of fashion, speed and science all coming together, for maybe the future of athletics potentially,” said Hodgkinson, after winning in 1min 56.40sec, more than 2sec clear of the Swiss athlete Valentina Rosamilia. “We weren’t sure when we were going to wear it, but in hindsight an all-women’s event, which is all about glitz and glamour and putting eyes on women, was perfect.”There was, Hodgkinson acknowledged, a nod to Cathy Freeman’s famous suit worn at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. But she insisted that this was a new version, legal under World Athletics’ rules, and with better technology.“The material, they’ve learned so much about making skin faster, humans faster, there’s so much science behind it that you wouldn’t believe. Technically, with the air drag you’re slower with your hair out, but I was like: ‘That’s a non-negotiable.’”Traditional track and field fans probably would have hated most of the night, which featured just 42 athletes and seven events. And the long gaps between events surely didn’t go down well on TV. But this was designed for a different audience. When Hodgkinson arrived on the red carpet in a baggy tracksuit, for instance, she was accompanied by the sound of dozens of screaming teenage girls.“I wasn’t expecting such a warm welcome, but it was fun,” she said. “My outfit was last minute, but for inspiration, I feel like it’s Liam Gallagher. I’m from Manchester, he’s from Manchester, I feel like I look like him.”View image in fullscreenKlaudia Kazimierska, in 4:19.43, just beats Georgia Hunter Bell to win the mile.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe stadium commentary was very different too. As the women’s mile entered the final lap, the stadium co-commentator Kath Merry asked: “Who wants the crown? Who wants the $65,000?” The race was decent, mind, with the Polish athlete Klaudia Kazimierska winning in 4:19.43, just 0.11 ahead of Britain’s Georgia Hunter Bell.Afterwards almost every athlete talked about the fun they had. Several even suggested such events were the future of the sport. But the sober-eyed would have left the StoneX Stadium with plenty of questions.Athlos offered a very generous prize fund of more than $1m for this event. But economically it must have stung. Only about 5,000 tickets, the size of the main stand, were sold. And with the event being shown on YouTube, there was no broadcasting rights windfall.At the moment Athlos appears to be operating on the Field of Dreams principle: if you build it they will come. Perhaps they will be proved correct – especially if the sport’s boom accelerates at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. But, as Michael Johnson’s Grand Slam Track has proved, it is fiendishly difficult to build a viable track and field start-up.Still, the fans saw some fine performances. Given how cold and late in the season it was, times were expected to be slow. Yet in the women’s 400m Marileidy Paulino ran a lightning quick 48.73, with Henriette Jaeger setting a Norwegian national record of 48.78 just behind her. Sha’Clarri Richardson won the women’s 100m in a very speedy 10.80.The night concluded with most of the athletes dancing to Beyoncé’s Run the World (Girls) on the large stage. Athlos isn’t there yet. But it has, at the very least, attracted a few converts.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsKeely HodgkinsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Kane smashes record for fastest to 100 Bundesliga goals in 98th game | Bayern Munich | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane beat the 49-year-old record for the fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals by 31 matches as Bayern Munich beat Union Berlin 7-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Harry Kane beat the 49-year-old record for the fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals by 31 matches as Bayern Munich beat Union Berlin 7-0
Content: Harry Kane celebrates scoring Bayern Munich’s fourth goal, his second of the match, against Union Berlin.Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPAView image in fullscreenHarry Kane celebrates scoring Bayern Munich’s fourth goal, his second of the match, against Union Berlin.Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPABayern MunichHarry Kane smashes record for fastest to 100 Bundesliga goals in 98th gameKane double helps Bayern Munich beat Union Berlin 7-0Dieter Müller’s record of 129 games had stood since 1977Press AssociationFri 18 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Kane smashed the 49-year-old record for the fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals in Bayern Munich’s 7-0 victory over Union Berlin, his 98th league game for the club.Cologne’s Dieter Müller set the previous mark in 1977, but it took him 129 matches and, with the England captain scoring at better than a goal a game, a new record had been inevitable for some time. Since his arrival in 2023 Kane had been averaging aBundesligagoal every 78.5 minutes and has now scored 152 in 154 appearances in all competitions, including 61 in 51 games last term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHarry Kane and Alessia Russo among nominees for this year’s Ballon d’OrRead moreHe blasted home a 39th-minute penalty to take the record before nodding in a Michael Olise cross early in the second half to send Bayern top of the table before the other weekend matches.The feat stole the spotlight from Olise, who scored his first Bayern hat-trick, and Jamal Musiala, who also scored a goal worthy of winning any game.“I’m very proud to have now scored 100 and 101 Bundesliga goals. I haven’t been around that long. I’ve loved every second of it,” Kane told Sky Germany. “With Michael, Lucho [Luis Díaz] and Jamal I naturally get chances and today was no exception.“So I just want to thank the team, the club, the coach, and the staff – everyone who has helped me achieve this. Let’s keep going like this. Scoring more goals in games is obviously a big step. Of course, there have been many important goals among them. I can only say that I’m enjoying every minute of it. Just like today.”Explore more on these topicsBayern MunichHarry KaneUnion BerlinBundesligaEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In almost every French game, there’s theatre’: Dean Richards on bringing joie de vivre back to English rugby | Dean Richards | The Guardian
description: Doncaster Knights’ new director of rugby tells Robert Kitson about his passion for the Champ, who Steve Borthwick should pick from overseas and why he wants players to have a bit of fun
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Doncaster Knights’ new director of rugby tells Robert Kitson about his passion for the Champ, who Steve Borthwick should pick from overseas and why he wants players to have a bit of fun
Content: Dean Richards wants to bring excitement and fun to Doncaster Knights in the Champ.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDean Richards wants to bring excitement and fun to Doncaster Knights in the Champ.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianDean RichardsInterview‘In almost every French game, there’s theatre’: Dean Richards on bringing joie de vivre back to English rugbyRobert KitsonDoncaster Knights’ new director of rugby is passionate about the Champ, who Steve Borthwick should pick from overseas and getting players to have a bit of funFri 18 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTurn up at Castle Park in Doncaster this week and, bang on cue, a pony and trap is being driven in stately fashion down the nearby main road. There is, some might argue, a similarly retro feel about the Knights’ latest choice of director of rugby. It is now 40 years sinceDean Richardsbarged his way into the public consciousness with two tries on his Test debut against Ireland at Twickenham but, at 63, he is still very much up for a challenge.As with vinyl records and fine wine, old-school rugby nous never goes entirely out of vogue. That, at least, is the rationale behind Richards’ return to the upper rungs of the English club ladder, commencing with a 740-mile round trip to Cornish Pirates on the opening weekend of the 2026-27 Champ season. “If it’s ingrained in you and you love the sport, then there’s no reason why you shouldn’t continue in some capacity,” he says softly, gazing out of the window at his latest field of dreams.View image in fullscreenDean Richards is congratulated by Nigel Melville (left) after the first of two push-over tries on his England debut, a 25-20 win over Ireland at Twickenham.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockAfter an illustrious 22-year association with Leicester,the Bloodgate eraat Harlequins, a decade at Newcastle Falcons and briefer spells at Grenoble and, most recently, Wymondham in Norfolk, his latest rugby reincarnation in South Yorkshire certainly lends extra intrigue to this year’s Champ as the league seeks to frame itself as an attractive standalone alternative to the Prem after years of slashed Rugby Football Union funding.Because Richards has seen it all in his time and has plenty of interesting views on the English game. For starters, he thinks the RFU has been guilty of underestimating the Champ’s potential value as a breeding ground for aspiring players, coaches and referees alike. In his opinion, the standard is improving and a glance at his Knights squad underlines the increasing depth in the second tier since the Prem was reduced to 10 teams. Semesa Rokoduguni, Telusa Veainu and Logovi’i Mulipola are all former standout Prem performers while Newcastle’s erstwhile head coach Alan Dickens is now on the coaching staff and the legendary Sir Ian McGeechan, now 79, is also on board as a consultant.double quotation markIf I was in Steve Borthwick’s shoes I’d be pushing to pick the Willis brothersDean RichardsThe caveat is that Doncaster’s playing budget is believed to have shrunk by around 45% compared with last season, when they finished eighth. Richards, however, has long argued that rugby success “is not all about money”, having secured second-tier titles with Quins and Newcastle. During both those campaigns his players were actively encouraged to buy their opposite numbers a post-match drink. This time he is thinking about organising a post-match eating contest, involving the club’s renowned “cow pie”, after the Knights’ opening home game against Hartpury on 27 September. “With Quins we set our stall out to have fun and I did the same at Newcastle. You ask a lot of the boys and it was probably one of the most enjoyable seasons they had. Preparation wasn’t key to everything. It was about having a bit of unity and fun. And it still is.”Richards, warming to his theme, also believes English rugby in general would benefit from lightening up a bit. He is not sure if the Red Bull era at Newcastle would have been his bag: “The way they’ve done it probably wouldn’t suit me … it’s become very corporate, as I understand it, rather than personal”, but remains a fervent admirer of France’s vibrant Top 14. “I went to the Nou Camp in Barcelona [in 2016] when they held the Top 14 final there and it was an unbelievable occasion. You go to Twickenhamto watch our Prem finaland … it’s all right. But it doesn’t get anywhere near that.View image in fullscreenDean Richards at Grenoble in 2015. He says: ‘The French have got some things right. Their style of play is absolutely fantastic. Here we’re inherently conservative.’Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The Guardian“The French have got some things right. Their clubs’ style of play is absolutely fantastic. In almost every French game, there’s theatre. And I love that. Here we’re inherently conservative. We don’t want to make a fuss.” Similarly he queries the value of excessively earnest preparation, at English club and international level. “I do think we are typically Anglo-Saxon. We put our noses to the grindstone every day. And I don’t think you need to do that.”In short, Richards would love to see English rugby display more imagination and vision on and off the field, not least in picking overseas-based players such as the Willis brothers. “If I was in Steve Borthwick’s shoes I’d be pushing to pick those boys.” At some stage he also reckons the Northampton duo of Phil Dowson and Sam Vesty would be a breath of managerial fresh air. “They’ve got a good handle on creating an environment where people want to come to work rather than have to come to work.“Dows is a real maverick and, for what it’s worth, I think Sam is as well. And I think with that goes the ability to manage people really well. If you’re looking at somebody in the future to be an England coach, I’d certainly look at those two boys. I also like Dave Walder. He is equally as capable but very different to Sam.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe also wonders aloud whether today’s young full-time pros need to get out more. “They’re far more like athletes than we probably ever were.“Having said that, I think there’s something missing in their lives. And it’s that balance between work and life. Years ago the life experiences you had prepared you to cope with setbacks. Because many of the guys don’t have life experiences these days, it’s harder for them to accept the adversity and the knocks.”Resilience was never a problem for Richards. During his days as a police constable, for example, he once attended a traffic accident on the M1 hours before playing for Leicester in a big East Midlands derby. A vehicle was stranded on the hard shoulder and its two occupants were Northampton fans travelling to the game. After racing back to fetch his kitbag and drop off his police car, Richards ended up giving them a lift to the game, which the Tigers duly lost. “Things like that, you wouldn’t think twice about,” he murmurs now.View image in fullscreenDean Richards, newly appointed director of rugby at Doncaster Knights, at the club’s Castle Park ground.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianRichards, however, is not one to wallow indefinitely in the past. After copping a three-year ban in the wake of the messy Bloodgate saga, he used his spare time to become a more skilful trout fisherman; now he is hoping to catch a few more opponents unawares and propel Yorkshire rugby back to the top table. “I’d love for Doncaster to get promoted. I think Cornish Pirates had us down the other day [on social media] as finishing 11th [out of 14]. [But] you look at what’s in place stadium-wise here and at Worcester. You’d want those clubs in the Premier league.” Whatever happens, Deano wants his hard-running Knights to enjoy the ride.Explore more on these topicsDean RichardsChamp RugbyRugby unioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Brydon Carse will not face charges after police drop investigation into alleged assault | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Brydon Carse will not face any charges after Derbyshire police dropped an investigation into an alleged assault by the England player last month
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Brydon Carse will not face any charges after Derbyshire police dropped an investigation into an alleged assault by the England player last month
Content: Brydon Carse was dropped from the England squad for the Pakistan series.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse was dropped from the England squad for the Pakistan series.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersEngland cricket teamBrydon Carse will not face charges after police drop investigation into alleged assaultEngland bowler arrested after Derby night outCricket Regulator to decide on disciplinary actionExclusive byMatt HughesFri 18 Sep 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse will not face any charges after Derbyshire police droppedan investigation into an alleged assaultin Derby city centre last month.The fast bowler was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly during a night out with his Durham teammates after a County Championship win over Derbyshire, which led to him being dropped from the England squad for the 3-0 Test series win over Pakistan.Somerset and Nottinghamshire title hopes hit by defeats: County Championship cricket, day four – liveRead moreCarse had been a non-playing member of the squad for the first Test at Headingley before being released to play for Durham, who beat Derbyshire by 338 runs to close in on promotion from Division Two, which has since been secured.Images circulating on social media the day after the game on Sunday 23 August showed Carse in handcuffs surrounded by police officers, which led to Derbyshire police confirming the following day that a man had been arrested outside Molly Malone’s bar. “A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night,” a police statement read.“However, the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area.”On the following Wednesday, the police gave a further statement, which added: “We are investigating allegations of an assault in Derby city centre. No arrests have yet been made and the investigation is ongoing.”The matter is now closed, however, with no action to be taken. In a statement released on Friday, the police said: “An investigation into reports of an assault in Derby city centre has been closed. Officers attended Molly Malone’s in The Wardwick, Derby, in the early hours of Sunday, 23 August.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarse will face a further investigation from theCricketRegulator to determine whether he will be subject to any disciplinary action from the England and Wales Cricket Board, which employs him on a two-year central contract that has 12 months to run. Carse was left out of the England squad for this month’s T20 and one-day international series against Sri Lanka, despite being available for selection, with the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, saying this week that he had to “work through the issues” around his arrest.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jon Rahm shoots 78-77 and slumps off in last place at PGA Championship | Golf | The Guardian
description: Jon Rahm was bottom of the field on 11 over par while Adam Scott, the 2013 Masters champion, said he was not putting pressure on himself to win
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Jon Rahm was bottom of the field on 11 over par while Adam Scott, the 2013 Masters champion, said he was not putting pressure on himself to win
Content: Jon Rahm takes a drop in a bunker. He went on to finish 11 over for his two days at Wentworth.Photograph: Warren Little/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Rahm takes a drop in a bunker. He went on to finish 11 over for his two days at Wentworth.Photograph: Warren Little/Getty ImagesGolfJon Rahm shoots 78-77 and slumps off in last place at PGA ChampionshipTommy Fleetwood also misses the cut at three overAdam Scott cards second 67 to be well placed at halfwayEwan Murrayat WentworthFri 18 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMissed cuts for Tommy Fleetwood and Jon Rahm at the PGA Championship would be notable enough even without contemplating the latter’s 36-hole score.The sight of Rahm dead last was remarkable – after rounds of 78 and 77, he was 11 over par. Fleetwood’s exit at plus three, while less dramatic, was another obvious blow to the tournament organisers at Wentworth. On a day of high-profile departures, injury forced Patrick Reed out of the event midway through his round. That scenario might have repercussions as Rory McIlroy seeks to prise the DP World Tour’s order of merit from the American’s grasp.Rahm did not stop for media duties but may have offered extenuating circumstance. It is just that seeing a player of such status and talent toil so badly turns heads. The Spaniard is awaiting the imminent arrival of his fourth child, a matter to which he referred before a ball was struck in Surrey.The LIV backdrop also cannot be ignored;Rahm is fully expected to depart the ailing circuitwhen the formalities of a voluntary bankruptcy filing are completed. This is, however, a situation now in the hands of the courts. It would be perfectly natural if Rahm finds himself unable to appropriately focus when inside the ropes. Two Wentworth rounds involved three birdies, 10 bogeys and two double bogeys.Fleetwood needed a change of fortune, albeit not a significant one, after Thursday’s 73. The 15th has proved his nemesis this week, with a bogey five during the first round followed up by a double bogey on day two. Despite delivering three birdies, the 35-year-old slipped to a 74.Reed – who looked a candidate to win after the first round – played his first nine holes in 44, nine over par. He grasped his left wrist after a pulled tee shot on the 10th, before his withdrawal was confirmed and he headed straight for medical treatment.Elements of normality were provided by Adam Scott, who is seeking to become the oldest winner of this event. The 46-year-old Australian backed up a 67 with an identical score. Scott would place huge stock in a Wentworth win.View image in fullscreenAdam Scott on the 7th fairway on day two at Wentworth.Photograph: Adam Davy/PA“Let’s put the majors aside for a minute,” he said. “I think there’s the Players Championship, Wentworth and the Australian Open for me at that level of importance. So it would mean a lot? Absolutely. I mean, it would be huge.“I’m not heaping pressure on myself to go and win this tournament. I feel like at this point I just need to put my head into a place where I can enjoy the next couple of days. I have done this many times in the past, not so much lately, but I think hopefully that kind of instinct and memory comes back in this position. If I can enjoy myself the next couple of days, I think I’ll get the best out of myself.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScott will form part of an International team trying to end a miserable run against the United States in the Presidents Cup. The event takes place next weekend at Medinah. Scott andRyan Fox, the Open champion, will fly straight to Illinois from this tournament.Not part of the Presidents Cup equation is JJ Spaun, which has left the American somewhat miffed. Spaun’s 66 here moved him to eight under and he made his shock at being omitted from Brandt Snedeker’s team plain.“It was disappointing to be left off,” the winner of last year’s US Open said. “I wasn’t expecting it, to be honest. I kind of hung my hat on my experience with the Ryder Cup last year. I made it to the Tour Championship this year. I won in San Antonio. I did everything I could. I was the odd man out.”Explore more on these topicsGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Earl Spencer SLATES the king. Charles DESTROYS Spencer. If only Diana were here to click on it | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: It’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeef, says the Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: It’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeef, says the Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Charles Spencer  on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, October 2024.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCharles Spencer  on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, October 2024.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockOpinionMonarchyEarl Spencer SLATES the king. Charles DESTROYS Spencer. If only Diana were here to click on itMarina HydeIt’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeefFri 18 Sep 2026 07.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareReading the extracts from Earl Spencer’s book about his sister Diana, and the king’s two-footedtakedown of it, it’s hard to escape the idea that Spencer and the Windsors are just elite content creators now. This entire thing is basically indistinguishable from a blockbuster influencer war, and I honestly won’t be happy till the king puts out a shade TikTok of him driving round the Sandringham estate in sunglasses captioned: “Threatening to release the receipts but never actually releasing the receipts … kinda chic.” Soundtrack: Mariah Carey’s Obsessed.Meanwhile, perhaps trying to disguise his full descent into the algorithm mines, Charles Spencer has started talking like one of those adverts for twee porcelain plates that you used to see in magazine supplements. You know the kind of thing – “these three little kittens are waiting to steal your heart”.Here is the earlon his Diana book, which he has called Swan Song: “At heart, this is a brother’s simple tribute to an extraordinary sister.” Mmm. And simply bound, very simply, into paginated form as a precious, simple keepsake that also functions as one of Penguin Random House’s lead titles for autumn and the run-in to Christmas. Favourite charming tribute from today’s serialisation in the Mail? Probably the bit when Diana drags Spencer for lunch in the London restaurant San Lorenzo to announce: “My husband is in love with his valet”. Nkay.View image in fullscreenKing Charles, then the Prince of Wales, with Charles Spencer, following a banquet in Cape Town not long after Princess Diana’s death in 1997.Photograph: John Stillwell/PABut the biggest tea-spill so far has been Spencer’s claim that Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after Diana’s death, then hissed: “Rest assured … we’ll forget about her soon enough.” Which definitely sounds like the kind of thing a father of two shockingly bereaved children would say if they were the future king character in a book written by someone quite bad at writing.By way of rejoinder,Buckingham Palace issued a statementthat began with the words “while we do not comment on books as a matter of principle”, and then – hilariously – went on to comment on the book. I mean, what principles? You always see these kinds of royal statements described as “highly unusual”, and yet in recent years their sheer frequency suggests they really aren’t. The royal family – and Spencer – do absolutely everything for the ’Gram. It’s all veryAlex Cooper v Alix Earle. I kept reading this week that Charles and William and Kate were “out in force” doing things likeplaying shinty on Buteand hosting AI summits. Yup, living for the timelines. Posting through it.And, indeed, posting about it, as that “we won’t comment on books” statement from the king continued in the more-in-sorrow-than-in-anger vein that is so particular to a contemporary social media drive-by. “His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”Wow. Apart from the pomposity, there is precisely nothing to distinguish this from the same kind of high-horse word salad you see farted out day after day by mid-tier creators involved in online beef about abortive podcast ventures or stolen brand deals. You know the kind of thing: “I’ve stayed quiet till now … But since you want to bring this to the internet, I have receipts. I’m done protecting people. The people who know, know.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Daily Star reports on Charles Spencer’s memoir Swan Song: Diana, My Sister.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty ImagesCharles Spencer has, of course, done a whole book of this stuff, probably making him the one the internet is less likely to side with. For just as it is possible to simply get up in the morning and decide not to post something on social media that makes you look like a complete shit, it is also possible to simply not do a whole book of this stuff. Why can’t Spencer just get a turret brand to sponsor his house upkeep like Molly-Mae would? “Loving our new #pediment and #pilasters! What’s one thing you love about your house? Tell me in the comments.”Instead, here is the earl on his Insta earlier this week: “A month ago I read ‘Swan Song’ out, over three days, for a recording so that it could be available on audiobook. When I finished the recording, I thought: ‘That is exactly what I wanted and needed to say – and she would, I reckon, have approved of every word.’” Oh for sure Diana would have approved. Nailed on.As we know, those who make money off Diana’s memory since she has died tend to do so with the absolute conviction that it’s what she would have wanted. Many of Diana’s indirect financial beneficiaries – her former psychics and energy healers,actors playing her in movies– give interviews announcing that her ghost has visited them to give the seal of approval to whichever commercial venture they’re involved in. Charles Spencer has yet to go down this route with Swan Song, though given the book isn’t actually published till next week – to permit the Mail the best run at the serial rights they paid him a fortune for – we definitely shouldn’t rule out the possibility that he’s keeping something spectral in the bag for the coming days.Ultimately, it’s increasingly impossible to escape the conviction that the royals and those familially connected with them behave as leading influencers – selling the absolute maddest form of lifestyle that you can still somehow pass off as a gift to your followers. The other day I rememberedan interview Prince Harry gavewhen his own book was out, where he said: “I genuinely believe, and I hope, that reconciliation between my family and us will have a ripple effect across the entire world. Maybe that’s lofty, maybe that’s naive.” Or maybe it’s just the lucrative way they all live now. Either way: #amazing.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyOpinionDiana, Princess of WalesKing Charles IIISocial mediaTikTokPrince HarryInstagramcommentShareReuse this content

title: An effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain? You read that right, and we will not settle for it | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: This scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability services, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: This scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability services, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: ‘Care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills.’Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreen‘Care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills.’Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFOpinionDisabilityAn effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain? You read that right, and we will not settle for itFrances RyanThis scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability servicesDisabled people in UK need right to travel abroad, say MPs, after ‘ridiculous’ restrictionsFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.34 EDTShareDisabled people are being barred from leaving the country. This isn’t the first line of a dystopian novel but a scandal quietly happening across swathes of England. For the past six months, myself and my colleague Patrick Butler havespoken to disabled peoplewho have effectively been blocked from going abroad on a holiday or to a work event by their local care provider.There’s 38-year-old Lucy from Oxfordshire who needs to travel internationally as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. And Chelsea from Lancashire, a 25-year-old with cerebral palsy who dreams of swimming in Spain again. Then there’s 40-year-old Joel*, who has a muscle weakness and works for a global marketing brand but hasn’t been able to leave the UK for nine years.Some have live-in personal assistants (PAs) via NHS continuing healthcare, the non-means-tested home support for people with high needs. Others have 24/7 social care through their local authority. But when they try to leave the country, all hit the same wall: they are told they are not allowed to use their care package abroad, sometimes even if they pay any extra costs themselves.Here’s the plot twist. Some areas of the country are permitting care users to go on holiday or travel for work – while disabled people just a few miles down the road can be stopped. Others are told they can travel but have to pay any extra expenses – effectively still barring them financially from going – while some care boards offer to cover the cost. As there is limited to no national guidance on the issue, disabled people’s right to travel depends on a postcode lottery, with local care officials inspecting their plans for a trip away and having the power to rule “go” or “stay”.This week,MPs and peers called for national guidelinesto end this injustice. Figures such as the work and pensions select committee chair, Debbie Abrahams, the crossbench peer Jane Campbell and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn told the Guardian that the government must guarantee the rights of disabled people to travel and ensure they have the support they need to do so.You can practically hear the right preparing to oppose the move with a cry of “Free holidays on the NHS!” But care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills. Disabled people who need 24/7 support for everyday activities already have care funding in place, and in many cases use their own money to pay PAs’ travel expenses, such as accommodation and plane tickets (on top of the already extortionate price of accessible travel). When Lucy was told by her care board she couldn’t take her PAs to a spinal cord conference in Germany this spring, her employer had already offered to pay any additional costs.View image in fullscreenBlocked from travel: Lucy, who needs to travel as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe question, then, is why would authorities want to stop disabled people going abroad? If it’s not just about tight budgets, why should it matter to them how an adult chooses to use their care package? You could say that it’s about practicalities: it’s easier not to worry about insurance or visas (disabled people largely sort this themselves for their PAs anyway). But it seems naive not to think there’s some prejudice lurking under the bureaucracy. Blocking disabled people from going on holiday or working abroad goes to the heart of cultural assumptions about disability: that we don’t have careers or families or friends like other, “normal” people.Sixty years afterdisabled people left institutionsand were able to live independently, alongside the vast gains, the stain of paternalistic control still lurks in disability services. It’s the social worker who suggests you get a commode next to your sofa because it’s cheaper than an accessible bathroom. It’s the care worker who speaks very slowly to you and picks your clothes out on your behalf. It’s the occupational therapist who suggests you get a hospital-style bed that your husband can’t fit in (and is visibly surprised you have a husband).We’re not supposed to talk about this stuff. There’s an unwritten rule that says disabled people should be just grateful for what they’re given by the state, lest we appear to be scroungers or burdens. I say “unwritten”. It’s written in some newspapers most weeks.It is uncomfortable, I suppose, in part because it is so ordinary. This isn’t the sort of prejudice that comes with an ableist slur or a violent push. It is the gentle, everyday belief that certain kinds of lives – certain kinds of people – come with low expectations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI had an amazing experience as a disabled person at school in the 70s. Since then, discrimination has got far worse | Mik ScarletRead moreJust look at the way much of the political and media class discuss social care. In the rare instances that younger disabled people are mentioned alongside elderly people, social care is still solely spoken about in terms of personal care – say, help to wash or prepare a meal. As Andy Burnham has put reform of the care sector on the agenda in recent months, it’s notable there has been little talk of its role in supporting a disabled person’s family role or career: whether that’s help to drop the kids off at school on the way to the office or to get to the pub to celebrate a friend’s birthday.That’s understandable. Underthe current system, as many as 1.5 million disabled people in England are left without access to even the most basic help. If you are suffering the indignity of sitting in soiled clothes because a care worker hasn’t arrived to assist you to the bathroom, it can feel pointless – delusional, even – to mention you’ve not seen the sea in years.But to settle for this state of affairs forces disabled people to accept a half-life, to be relieved to at least be clean and fed, and to try to forget the colour that defines being human. It diminishes not only our humanity but the principle that disability campaigners fought for decades for and underpins the modern care system: for disabled people to have choice and independence over our lives, just like everyone else.When I recently spoke to Campbell, who has 24/7 PAs herself, about the care abroad scandal, she said something telling: “It’s as if those controlling [these decisions] believe disabled people don’t deserve the same experiences they enjoy.”As pressure for national guidelines mounts, I can’t help but think that is a wise litmus test. Would you expect a non-disabled person to live like this? And if not, why do you think it’s OK for disabled people?*Name has been changedFrances Ryan is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDisabilityOpinionSocial careCare workersEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big response, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big response, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionDevolutionSlowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UKSimon JenkinsIt’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big responseFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.19 EDTShareMonday must have been a historical first. Never before have three of the four “nations” of the United Kingdom jointlydemanded freedomto vote for its dissolution. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have lost confidence in England. They declared in Cardiff that the unionist government at Westminster is “coming to an end”.There was no such Celtic alliance against the Normans, Edward I or Cromwell. Celtic MPs have never formed a voting coalition in parliament. The Victorian Liberal party advanced “home rule for all”, but that was not independence and it got nowhere.Irelandrebelled, but it did so alone. When this eventually succeeded, Britain said good riddance, kept hold of Belfast and continued to centralise power in London.So this is serious stuff. Yet London politics this week treated the declaration as on a par with the Oxfordshire village of Piddingtonvoting to go it aloneto ward off the possibility of asylum seekers being housed nearby.The UK’s only serious geographical devolution came in 1999. It was half-hearted, mostly decentralising the running of the welfare state. But it surged the vote for Scottish and Welsh separatism and fed rather than abated the cause of independence. We can only imagine if ruling parties in Bavaria or Provence or Sicily had opted for independence from Germany, France or Italy – or if California said it had enough of Donald Trump’s US. The result would be political eruption.What does theCardiff “memorandum of understanding”actually mean? The answer is not much in detail. There was advocacy of policy collaboration, as on childcare and economic growth. There were hints of moves towards further devolution, of the sort promised by Andy Burnham. But there was no suggestion of a new Celtic state, a British Celtica. The talks seemed to concentrate on self-determination, which Burnham had described as “off limits”, at least in the case of Scotland. Yet this was a man who declared self-determination for the Falklands would be defended even at the cost of tens of millions of pounds a year.The reality is that these three nations of the union have markedly different relations with England. Northern Ireland’s bipartisan government, a legacy of civil war and the Good Friday agreement, is clearly dysfunctional.As Donald Trump remarked last week, it really should advance toward Irish union.As interfaith relations slowly improve, a possible majority in favour of reunion also becomes more plausible. Support for union in Northern Irelandis now around one-third, with a majority among the young. Self-determination is not in Burnham’s gift but is written into Northern Ireland’s constitution. Observers accept that it must and will happen one day.Wales may also have a majority of its under-35sin favourof independence. But only a bare Welsh majorityvoted foreven mild devolution in 1997 and support for independencehovers at 32%. The poor performance of the Welsh health and education services makes self-government ever more alarming, and the generosity of the London Exchequer ever more essential. Perhaps the novelty of the new Plaid Cymru government can transform things, but Welsh independence is at best a distant fantasy.This leavesScotland. Here independence is an active issue. The population of 5.5 million puts the country in the 5-10 million band of Europe’s medium-sized states, such as Denmark, Norway, Finland, Austria and Switzerland. “Small is beautiful” appears to suit Europe’s distinctive welfare economies and keeps them ahead of their larger neighbours.Scottish unionists keep pointing toScotland’s £25bn fiscal deficit, financed by London’s Treasury and sustaining the country’s struggling health service. But independence is a dynamic not static state. In 1922 Ireland wasamong the poorest countries in Europe, far behind Scotland. Its economic self-sufficiency seemed hopeless, and for some 30 years it was indeed in desperate straits. Yet by the 1990s Irish membership of the EU and the adoption of a fierce fiscal autonomy had utterly transformed it into the celebrated “Celtic Tiger”. From limping behind Scotland and other poorer European regions, Dublin raced ahead. It has become one of Europe’s richest nations per capita, albeit partly thanks to its status as a base for corporate tax avoidance.Ireland’s burst of economic vitality in the late 20th century could never have taken place had it remained an adjunct of Britain. Income per head is now ahead of Scotland’s, having once lagged far behind. It grew between 2012 and 2022by 9%on average, against Scotland’s 1%. Whether Ireland is richer than Denmark is much debated, but the performance of an autonomous Ireland cannot be gainsaid. It is a lighthouse for the macro-economics of smallness.There is every reason why Scotland could feel held back by longstanding English dominance. Its economy, like the rest of Britain’s, has always been down the queue from London and the south-east. It has long felt cheated of its maritime oil and gas reserves. Trade has been crippled by Brexit. Unionists argue that theBarnett formula subsidy of £50bn a yearis fair compensation. But Ireland’s experience suggests that dependence on foreign subsidy is a curse, not a blessing. The most glaring comparative statistic is that health outcomes in both Ireland and Denmarkare now well ahead of Scotland’s. The scale of Glasgow’s drug deaths are a horror story.British loyalist though I may be, if I were a Scot I would have no hesitation. This is a real nation, and has been throughout history. Scotland has a personality and a culture recognised worldwide. Its capital, Edinburgh, is among Europe’s finest cities. Its “Silicon Glen” should be leading Europe’s AI revolution. Tourism is an obvious attraction. That the country should stumble behind its Nordic neighbours is absurd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland would have a tough transition to self-reliance, as did Ireland. But experience everywhere suggests that small autonomous democracies fare well, witness other relative newcomers such as Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the Baltics. Their governments can concentrate on their own priorities and promote their own virtues.An independent Scotland would be bespoke. It could retain its royal figurehead and Commonwealth membership. It could even honour a “united kingdom” and the king could stay in Balmoral. Relations with other states, EU and non-EU, would be complicated, as they are at borders across the continent. That is for diplomacy to resolve. The issue is self-determination, not convenience.Burnham is the first British prime minister to appear sincere in decentralising political power. How far he understands its significance is moot. His beloved “metro mayors” are accountable regionally, not representatives of truly local loyalties. They appear as his agents, enacting his policies and enforcing his planning quotas on subordinate councils. He has shown he will stamp the Piddingtons of England into the ground.That is why Burnham should welcome any Scottish desire for “independence”. It would be the most exciting constitutional reform of the UK in centuries and one that, on current figures, would save the Treasury around £25bn a year – the cost of the Scottish fiscal deficit. It would also release the Tartan Tiger.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDevolutionOpinionScotlandNorthern IrelandIrelandWalesScottish independenceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: BuzzBallz signed by Tory leader builds excitement for conference | Lucy Mangan | The Guardian
description: Kemi Badenoch-autographed cocktail offered as raffle prize. Plus, Bruce Springsteen’s surprisingly normal nightwear
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Kemi Badenoch-autographed cocktail offered as raffle prize. Plus, Bruce Springsteen’s surprisingly normal nightwear
Content: Kemi Badenoch makes a cocktail during a visit to the Johnnie Walker Experience in Edinburgh this year.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch makes a cocktail during a visit to the Johnnie Walker Experience in Edinburgh this year.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PADigested weekKemi BadenochDigested week: BuzzBallz signed by Tory leader builds excitement for conferenceLucy ManganKemi Badenoch-autographed cocktail offered as raffle prize. Plus, Bruce Springsteen’s surprisingly normal nightwearFri 18 Sep 2026 06.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.21 EDTShareMondayIt’s funny, isn’t it, how many things we take for granted in life? How many things go wholly unmentioned, even wholly unconsidered in any even minutely conscious way – and yet, when they are suddenly kicked away you realise just how much of your internal organisation, your mental integrity, your structural soundness altogether, rested on these unexamined pillars.One of mine, it turns out, is the belief – no, surely more than that? The sure and certain knowledge, in my bones if never alas vouchsafed by my mere mortal eyes – thatBruce Springsteendoes not wear pyjamas.This is fundamental, surely? The Boss sleeps naked. This is an eternal verity.But no. According to what I can only describe as reports, he is a loyal customer of the venerable sleepwear shop Schostal in Rome, which was opened in 1870 by two brothers from Vienna. There’s a photo of Bruce hugging the manager, Shirley Braine – to whom he apparently sends regular postcards – and everything.So. There you have it. The Boss sleeps in pyjamas. Acceptable province of 1950s boarding school boys, your worst boyfriend, and your dad. Please go carefully about your day and from the fragments of your shattered psyche may you rebuild better soon.TuesdayParty conference season is almost upon us – I know! Try to contain yourselves! – and the preparations for fun times are gathering pace. News breaks that Blue Beyond, a youngConservativesgroup (and I always like to know that they’ve found each other rather than roaming free and confused), is offering as a grand raffle prize a BuzzBallz signed by Kemi Badenoch! I said try to contain yourselves! And not only is it signed, but it is a large BuzzBallz! I SAID TRY TO CONTAIN YOURSELVES.In case you are not as young as a youngster or as cool as a Conservative, I should explain: a BuzzBallz is a spherical plastic container that contains a cocktail, usually of a lurid hue and unsubtle flavour profile (the inscribed orb itself is Berry Cherry Limeade and whyever not?). They come in two sizes – small, which is a bit larger than a tennis ball, and large, which is a bit smaller than a football.Tickets are available now. The winner will be drawn at the Tory conference and must be over 18 to collect. Rumours that Michael Heseltine will launch it at your head for a small further fee are popular but as yet unsubstantiated.View image in fullscreen‘No! I am considerably better at humaning than you!’ … ‘No! I have it now! Watch this!’Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersWednesdayI find myself unaccountably drawn to the story of theHyrox poo-er. Not because of any coprophiliac inclinations, you understand, but because the idea of exerting myself to the extent that I might lose control of my bowels is so out of my realm of personal possibility that I am increasingly intrigued by the question of whether Joanna Wietrzyk and I technically qualify as the same species at all.Again, for the uninitiated/hitherto and possibly blissfully ignorant, a recap: Hyrox Beijing is an intense indoor fitness event and Wietrzyk one of its world record- holding contestants. About halfway through the insanely difficult competition, which comprises a series of horrendous things – I don’t know precisely what, I passed out after reading the word “burpees” – Wietrzyk suffered what was later termed “a severe faecal event”, which went down her leg but didn’t stop her progress round the course.Cue a roar of outrage against her and the organisers, who didn’t disqualify her immediately before she touched any other equipment, and eventually an apology from Wietrzyk and a forfeit of her points.To hell with the critics, say I. Biohazardry be damned! You push yourself so hard you crap yourself and keep on going, you’re a winner in my book. Now, someone unwrap this Mars bar for me. Typing is exhausting, you know.ThursdayNot all heroes wear capes. Or a light coating of faeces down their legs. Some of them are headteachers who suspend 25 students in the first week back after the summer holidays, including one for the crime of zipping his bag too loudly. The head’s name is Dan Jeffries and, while he denies parents’ claims of suspension for minor infractions, it is clear that whatever measures he has indeed taken, he has no regrets about any of them.Parents of some of those suspended from Frome college have compared the school to “a military base” and say the strictness demotivates pupils. Whatever, whatever. The world is made up of two types of people: those who want to hear the children’s side of things and those of us who just want Jeffries put in immediate charge of a new government department called The Whole of Modern Life, Starting With Quiet Coaches on the Train and After That I Have a List.View image in fullscreen‘I mean, sure, you can sprinkle flowers everywhere and sell jam, or you can have mad shinty skillz like me. You decide.’Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockFridayMy mother summons me and my sister home. Apparently she needs to clear out the attic before she dies, but ideally before Sunday.“What’s happening on Sunday?” I ask.“Sunday,” she replies.Deadlines by fiat were a mainstay of my childhood and so I ask no more.My mother has lived in our house for 50 years. We brace ourselves for a hard 48 hours’ work and climb up into the loft.Three small cardboard boxes of stuff await us.“There are – there are just three small cardboard boxes of stuff up here.”“Yes,” she says. “I can’t believe I’ve let it get this bad.”We bring them down.My wedding shoes and some papers – including my first book, The Story of Esmerelda, written when I was nine and some letters home from university – are in the first one. The second one contains my son’s baby clothes. The third has my sister’s childhood attempts at making a working model of Sizewell B and some postcards she wrote to Dad when he went on his first trip to America. “Come hom. Shez insane.” On reflection, she shouldn’t have given them to Mum to post.“Excellent,” Mum says. “We can bin the lot.”Ah, fiats. Ah, memories.View image in fullscreenGod, AI really is coming for all of us.Photograph: Vernon Yuen/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockExplore more on these topicsKemi BadenochDigested weekBruce SpringsteenCocktailsAlcoholConservative conferenceConservativescommentShareReuse this content

title: Think it’s time for gen Z to ‘grow up’? You’re even more out of touch than the British state | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: We can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching on, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: We can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching on, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Young people at the London job show in Westfield White City shopping centre, May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYoung people at the London job show in Westfield White City shopping centre, May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianOpinionYoung peopleThink it’s time for gen Z to ‘grow up’? You’re even more out of touch than the British stateGaby HinsliffWe can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching onFri 18 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTShareWhen did you realise you had finally grown up? It’s a trick question, obviously: maturity is just realising that life is full of things you don’t feel old enough for but somehow manage anyway, while getting better at pretending to know what you’re doing. But the question is worth asking nonetheless, because for gen Z the goalposts of grownup life are clearly shifting.It’s a truism that adulting now comes later than it did to generations who still don’t consider adulting a verb, with43% of 25-year-olds still living at homeand plenty more jobless university graduatesboomeranging back there this summer, thanks to a grim labour market. Since they’ll probably be working longer into what were once retirement years, perhaps it’s only natural that they’re taking longer to get started. But there’s a fine line between choosing to grow up more slowly and becoming trapped into a kind of limbo between childhood and adulthood, with nobody to pull you out of the morass beyond parents who aren’t sure how to handle this new life stage either.If your unemployed 22-year-old is getting rejection after rejection, should you rewrite their job applications for them, or let them figure it out for themselves? What do you do with an 18-year-old too depressed to leave their bedroom, now they’re old enough to make their own GP appointments but not mature enough to know they need one? Kidulthood can be a minefield.The idea that the state should recognise the years roughly between 18 and 25 as a phase distinct from either childhood or full adulthood, which needs its own tailored policies, is catching on around Westminster.The Nuffield Foundationcharitable trust, which has spent two years researching changing journeys to adulthood, held a seminar this week drawing together threads from academia to Alan Milburn’s genuinely thoughtful review of what is causing so many young people to be Neet (not in education, employment or training). As Milburn put it to theNuffield Foundation’s Carey Oppenheim, councils have to ensure that teenagers are studying or training up to 18, but what happens after that is not their problem. Yet in the Netherlands, the state’s responsibilities extend up to 24 or, in some cases, 27. Guess which country has fewer Neets.More broadly, he suggested, the British state may be too quick to shrug off responsibility for young people struggling with the transition to adulthood. “We haven’t aligned now with the reality of the transitions that young people are going through in their lives,” he said.In Australia, Oppenheim points out, the equivalent of Britain’s children and adolescent mental health services runs from age 12 right up to age 25, recognising a growing argument within medicine that adolescence doesn’t end neatly at 19. But in Britain, teenagers still hit a cliff edge, tumbling abruptly out of children’s mental health services into adult ones where the threshold for intervention can be far higher. Even the new social media ban for under-16s assumes teenagers are mature enough at 17 to handle what they couldn’t the day before.Meanwhile theIPPR thinktank’s State of A Generationproject, another deep dive into the coming of age process, warns of a society where “transitions to adulthood are blocked” and young people are increasingly nihilistic about their future.There’s much we still don’t understand about this evolving life stage, including how far to accept it and how far to push back. If a quarter of 18- to 34-year-olds living with their parents say they’re genuinelyhappy at home or not ready to leave, rather than feeling stuck, does that imply a worrying failure to launch? Or, asthe demographer Prof Ann Berringtonargues, a new form of “privileged dependence”, where some young people enjoy a financial and emotional security that ultimately boosts them into adult life, and it’s the young people who can’t go home in a crisis we should worry about?There’s an obvious danger here of over-babying young people, potentially making them even more anxious in the process, or of the state intruding too far into the lives of twentysomethings who are coping fine. As the parent of a 19-year-old, I’m well aware that gen Z are often far more resilient and competent than they get credit for.But a significant minority do seem to be falling into a gap between childhood and adulthood, and in a chilly economic climate they look increasingly exposed. Maybe the real mark of having finally grown up is feeling ready to help someone else do the same.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis article was amended on 18 September 2026. An earlier version described the Nuffield Foundation as a “thinktank”. In fact it is constituted as a charitable trust.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsYoung peopleOpinionYouth unemploymentGenerational inequalityInequalityUnemploymentcommentShareReuse this content

title: Sydney Sweeney’s cartoonish provocation has sparked a culture war but let’s just admit sport can be sexy | Sport | The Guardian
description: Yes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appeal
Author: Emma John
Headline: Yes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appeal
Content: Sydney Sweeney’s advert for a sports betting site caused a storm of controversy this week.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney’s advert for a sports betting site caused a storm of controversy this week.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesSportSydney Sweeney’s cartoonish provocation has sparked a culture war but let’s just admit sport can be sexyEmma JohnYes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appealFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTShareHave you seen the 40-second video that will change the way you think about women’s sport, women’s bodies, just, you know, women? It’s been unavoidable on social media this week – brazen, unapologetic, dominating the algorithm like an AI kitten hacking a banana-bread recipe while lip-syncing to Cardi B. I for one have enjoyed it at least 50 times already.It starts with some carefully curated passive-aggression – “Dear Sydney”, “Hey Sydney”, “Respectfully Sydney” – and follows up with clips of what, in its own words, “a woman in sport actually looks like”. It shows its subject pounding the treadmill or powering down the back straight, flooring a rival with a tackle or a roundhouse kick, lifting weights or throwing herself through the air. It is, inevitably, soundtracked by Dua Lipa. Training Season is getting a serious bump this week.‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advertRead moreThealmighty backlashto the Novig advert that everyone would rather not have talked about at all has generated more montages than we’ve seen since Rocky IV. My own feed is swamped with inspo-insta reels from grassroots and elite athletes alike. Some might argue it’s the best thing to happen to women’s sport this week – unless, you know,they’re the European Solheim Cup team. Either way, a positively cartoonish piece of provocation lit the five-second fuse to the powder-keg stamped CULTURE WAR, and the resultant explosion has enveloped us all in its cloud of colourful outrage and content confetti.The noisy reaction to an actor posing almost naked with various items of sporting equipment demonstrates the power and importance of solidarity within women’s sport. For decades, being a woman in an incorrigibly sexist sector left you one of two responses. Either you ignored uncomfortable and demeaning situations so you could just get on with the thing you wanted to be doing, or you spoke out, braving either devastating indifference or a cacophony of scorn. These days, we’re privileged to have a far louder voice, and for it to be taken seriously.There is, however, a danger in taking every piece of deliberate provocation too seriously. And the danger is that it robs us of some of the delight of the thing we love in the first place. Instead of spending this week talking about Lottie Woad’s singles match in the Netherlands, or Chelsea’s 5-0 demolition of Manchester United in the WSL, we’ve surrendered billboards’ worth of brain space to an American celebrity who hasn’t even invested in a Premier League club yet.Personally I have also, as discussed, spent quite a lot of time scrolling other people’s highlights reels, and I won’t lie that they got me pretty pumped, but then that was very much their goal. From spiralling gymnastic tumbles to grunting deadlifts, all these women look fire. Even a unitedly earnest effort to remind us that sport is about effort and sweat and inclusivity can’t and shouldn’t hide the fact that it’s also, thrillingly, about human bodies and the gloriously impressive things they can be honed to do.View image in fullscreenAmy Hunt has led the backlash against Sydney Sweeney’s controversial betting advert by telling the US actress that ‘this is what women in sport look like’.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAHaving to argue that sportswomen aren’t sexual objects, on the other hand, feels as dated as the advert. Part of the problem of the ad is its almost comically regressive throwback to the era of Page 3 girls and 1980s erotica – the kind of aesthetic we now knowingly indulge within the safe confines of a Jilly Cooper TV adaptation. If we’re jumping this far back in the timeline, will we have to revisit, too, whether it’s appropriate to wear make-up on track, or skorts on court, or any other of the subsidiary arguments that determine how sexy or not a female athlete is required – or allowed – to be?Or can we unclench and leave them in the past where they belong? Might we even skip a bit further into a more confident future and say out loud the thing that we have always had to be extremely careful expressing? Which is that sport is a primarily physical pursuit that tends to turn the people at its apex into magnificent specimens of humanity. And that those aesthetics are a part of what makes it appealing in the first place.The bulging neck on the rugby pitch and the rock-hard calves on the marathon runner have a functional purpose, as opposed to the fantasy one that prompts today’s Hollywood actors to get superhero-buff. But that doesn’t mean we’re not allowed to admire them. Sport is an environment that invites us to witness and thrill to the power and grace of the human body. It’s not only our tribal allegiances and the dopamine hit of vicarious victory that we’re indulging when we marvel at our sporting heroes: it’s also our appreciation of their physical attributes, whether that’s Rafael Nadal’s arms or Jessica Ennis-Hill’s abs or Serena Williams’s everything.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd sometimes, when those attributes are in motion, sportcanbe sexy. Not in the ball-cradling way that Sydney Sweeney’s performance allows delusional men to believe. But in a way that nevertheless holds hostage to the eye and makes the pulse race. It’s rather absurd – and a little self-deluding – for sports fans to pretend either to ourselves or others that we don’t find some of our heroes pretty attractive.And no, as Amy Hunt so properly pointed out in her own clapback to the Sweeney ad, being an athlete is “not sexy all the time”. If anyone needed proof, the second most notorious viral video of this week was, in fact,a Hyrox competitor soiling herselfas she powered to victory. There has, in other words, been plenty of crap circulating on the internet this week. The sanest choice is to avert our eyes.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSportUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: The spectre of ‘remigration’ is haunting Europe. Slovenia in 1992 gives us a blueprint for this state terror | Miha Mazzini | The Guardian
description: In February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrants, says writer and film-maker Miha Mazzini
Author: Miha Mazzini
Headline: In February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrants, says writer and film-maker Miha Mazzini
Content: Pedestrians crossing a bridge in Ljubljana, Slovenia.Photograph: DavorLovincic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPedestrians crossing a bridge in Ljubljana, Slovenia.Photograph: DavorLovincic/Getty ImagesOpinionSloveniaThe spectre of ‘remigration’ is haunting Europe.
