Slovenia in 1992 gives us a blueprint for this state terrorMiha MazziniIn February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrantsFri 18 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.48 EDTShareSo much of your daily life – your job, your health, your home – hinges on the fact that your name is in a government database. Are you a legal citizen of your country, with everything that entails? You are, until an anonymous bureaucrat hits a key one night and strips it all away, turning you into an illegal immigrant. It happened inSloveniain 1992.“I took my son to register for secondary school. The clerk rifled through the papers, then stared at me as if refusing to see the boy standing right next to me. Finally, she said: ‘But you don’t have a son. He doesn’t exist.’” I can’t forget the look on the face of the woman who was telling me this story. It was a mixture of deep hurt and bewilderment, with a pause after every sentence, as if she were walking through a minefield. During the research for my book Erased, I compiled countless stories like this: stories I once would have thought impossible.On 26 February 1992, the Slovenian government quietly deleted 1.3% of its citizenry overnight. The criterion was frighteningly simple: anyone born in another part of the former Yugoslavia who was a permanent resident of Slovenia (regardless of whether they considered themselves naturalised) suddenly lost their citizenship, their right to reside, their healthcare, their pension: everything. They were transformed into illegal immigrants overnight, without prior notification, and with no right to appeal. The goal was to cleanse Slovenia of a Balkan “fifth column” and pivot closer toEurope.I have long felt this dark piece of Slovenian history to be an ugly stain on the conscience of my nation; but its spirit is spreading across Europe and beyond. The horrors of migrant deaths in the Mediterranean and the English Channel are regularly witnessed and documented, the victims dying at the very gates of “fortress Europe”. But even if you are already inside the fortress, even if you consider yourself fully naturalised, you are perhaps no longer safe. In an age of constant video surveillance, there is nothing fantastical about an official refusing to renew a permit, or unearthing a minor “offence” committed decades earlier, to strip away your citizenship.The spectre of “remigration” is haunting Europe, and its shadow looms ever larger. What Slovenia did in 1992 has become a blueprint for a quiet, bureaucratic form of state terror.The woman who told me about her son lived in a village equidistant between two towns. During her pregnancy, she had to choose between two maternity hospitals. After the collapse of Yugoslavia, the town she had picked was across the new border in Croatia, while her village remained in Slovenia. And so, on that fateful day in 1992, her son ceased to exist. His story had a happy ending: Slovenia is a very small country, and if you have a wide enough network, you’ll eventually find someone who knows someone. So the boy emerged from the ranks of the disappeared and was able to attend school. But for those without friends in high places, things rarely ended happily.View image in fullscreenA 2015 exhibition in Ljubljana showing passports belonging to the erased.Photograph: Jure Makovec/AFP/Getty ImagesOne man was rushing to work, speeding, when he was pulled over by the police. Unable to find him in the registry, they took him to an asylum centre. He had been born in Serbia, but Slovenia’s only border with the former Yugoslavia is with Croatia. So they deported him there instead. Croatia was at war with Serbia at the time, and the man was treated as a prisoner of war. He was lucky: had he been born in Croatia, he would have been conscripted and sent straight to the frontlines.For six years, 1.3% of the population hid and survived however they could. They worked illegally for subsistence wages, at the mercy of bosses and landlords. One man locked himself in his flat, eating old canned food, refusing to open the door to anyone. It was a wise strategy. There were cases of the erased returning home to find their locks changed: someone had simply claimed and occupied their flat, realising the victim would have no recourse to call the police.There were also stories of profound kindness: a citizen who officially contracted every disease imaginable because he kept lending his healthcare card to the erased; a waitress who walked out of her shift with a first aid kit to treat an injured, erased man who had just been thrown out of the hospital. Relying on the kindness of strangers, however, is a lottery I wouldn’t wish on anyone.In 1998, the Slovenian constitutional court ruled the erasure unconstitutional, and the immediate threat subsided. But thelong road to restoring rightsand securing measly compensation for the victims turned into agruelling odysseythat, for some, continues to this day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA monument has sincebeen erectedfor the erased in Ljubljana, and a park named after them. But it is always easier to build a monument than to issue an apology, let alone settle dues. The UK has its own unresolved equivalent in the Windrush generation – andtheir monument is standing, too.Many of the erased never doubted their status because they considered themselves Slovenians. Overnight, they were expected to deport themselves to countries they had no meaningful connection to. I was reminded of their fate when reading about the US administration’s “operation second look”, which entails ICE agents scavenging decades-old files for minor administrative discrepancies in the hope of stripping people of their citizenship.As it so often does, Europe follows America’s lead.Gregory Bovino,the former US Border Patrol “commander-at-large”, was recently in Europe and treated like a rock star. At arightwing gatheringin Portugal he noted that he and the Austrianethnonationalist Martin Sellnerare “on the same sheet of music”. Perhaps the original Slovenian experiment in “remigration” was indeed exactly what it was claimed to be back then: a step closer to Europe, but a meaner and more sinister version of Europe.Miha Mazzini is a writer, film-maker and anthropologistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on youth unemployment: too few jobs in too many places | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Young people in Britain’s poorer towns have far fewer opportunities. Changing this will require targeted support – and industrial strategy
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Young people in Britain’s poorer towns have far fewer opportunities. Changing this will require targeted support – and industrial strategy
Content: ‘If today’s young people are to find employment that will sustain them into adulthood, the government will need an industrial strategy capable of creating long-term opportunities.’Photograph: Marcin Rogozinski/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If today’s young people are to find employment that will sustain them into adulthood, the government will need an industrial strategy capable of creating long-term opportunities.’Photograph: Marcin Rogozinski/AlamyOpinionYoung peopleThe Guardian view on youth unemployment: too few jobs in too many placesEditorialYoung people in Britain’s poorer towns have far fewer opportunities. Changing this will require targeted support – and industrial strategyFri 18 Sep 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareThe ideas that Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) simply aren’t trying hard enough to find a job, or don’t want one, are “myths,” Alan Milburn wrote in his interim report on the subject earlier this year – “sometimes cruel ones”. Although84% of Neetssay they want to work, their prospects are unfairly limited by where they live. Rotherham has one suitable vacancy for every 22 young adults. The Cotswolds has one for every four. For too many young people, particularly those in deprived parts of Britain, there simply aren’t enough jobs.This is the finding from an index published last week by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which ranked British towns according to the availability of jobs for young people. Like so many features of Britain’s Neet crisis, from poor mental health to school drop-out rates, the index is a map of disadvantage. At the top areaffluent townsin southern England that account for nine in 10 of the areas with the highest numbers of vacancies. At the bottom are places such as Inverclyde and East Renfrewshire, where young people might once have followed their parents into manufacturing and industry. Deindustrialisation destroyed those jobs, and such places never recovered.Given thathalf of the risein Neets aged 18 to 24 since 2019 is due to changes in the labour market, jobs are a good place for the government to focus. In 2024, the Starmer government launched a “youth guarantee,” including a pilot jobs programme that provides six months’ paid work to 18 to 24-year-olds who have been receiving universal credit for18 months. This was a positive step, but 18 months is far too long for young people to wait for support, and almost half of Neets don’t claim benefits, so aren’t eligible for this scheme.View image in fullscreenAlan Milburn.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe IPPR has called for the creation of a new “youth contract”, comprising short-term placements for all people at risk of becoming Neet in areas where jobs are scarce, more apprenticeships at the smaller firms that dominate Britain’s labour market, and more dedicated work coaches. These would all be improvements to the status quo. But if today’s young people are to find employment that will sustain them into adulthood, the government will need an industrial strategy capable of creating long-term opportunities in places where few exist.The devolution ofvocational trainingto local authorities, which are better placed to understand the demands of regional labour markets than Whitehall civil servants, is welcome. But ministers will need a dose of realism about where “good” jobs will come from. Andy Burnham’s talk of“reindustrialising”regions resembles a Westminster pipe dream. As manufacturing has developed, it has lost the ability to reliably create widespread employment. Even in the US and China, where governments have generously subsidised industry, manufacturing jobs continue to fall as a share of total employment.As the economist Dani Rodrikrecently observedin an essay collection about reindustrialisation, much of Britain’s future employment won’t be in manufacturing or high-productivity service sectors, but in industries such as retail, hospitality and care. If Mr Burnham wants to create “good growth in every postcode”, his government must transform the conditions of work in these industries so they provide gainful employment – and opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: It’s not just ‘spermageddon’ that’s stopping us having children | Society | The Guardian
description: Letters: Aubrey Foard and Nina Plummer respond to Zoe Williams’s interview with Camilla Cavendish about the reasons behind plummeting birthrates worldwide
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Aubrey Foard and Nina Plummer respond to Zoe Williams’s interview with Camilla Cavendish about the reasons behind plummeting birthrates worldwide
Content: ‘As an older, childless millennial, climate change figures profoundly in my desire to not have children.’Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘As an older, childless millennial, climate change figures profoundly in my desire to not have children.’Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty ImagesSocietyLettersIt’s not just ‘spermageddon’ that’s stopping us having childrenAubrey FoardandNina Plummerrespond to Zoe Williams’s interview with Camilla Cavendish about the reasons behind plummeting birthrates worldwideFri 18 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTShareI appreciate Zoe Williams’s excellent interview with Camilla Cavendish (Spermageddon, ‘greedy jobs’ and abject fear: why birthrates are plummeting – and why it matters, 17 September), but I have to take issue with one of her statements: “Of course, the climate crisis is playing a big part in that, but it still doesn’t wholly stack up – in the 80s, there was the wraparound threat of nuclear annihilation and it didn’t seem to dent anyone’s joie de vivre.”Yes, the buildup of nuclear arms and the terror surrounding it reached its peak in the 20th century, but it was kept in check by policies of Mutually Assured Destruction: a singular launch of a nuclear arsenal would have instantly ended humanity.As an older, childless millennial, climate change figures profoundly in my desire to not have children: the cause of climate change has been known for 50 years, it’s happening before our eyes, and there is not enough being done about it.While it’s true that we may overcome rising emission rates with renewable energy, the current and near-future effects of the climate crisis mean we are in for a very difficult road ahead as a society – and that’s if we succeed. If I’m going to go through the financial, physical, emotional and psychological burden of raising a child, I don’t want to also have to explain to them that there’s a very good chance that they’re doomed, because billionaire, capitalist greed couldn’t figure out how to stop itself from ruining the world for human civilisation.Aubrey FoardBaltimore, Maryland, USCamilla Cavendish notes that the falling birthrate is fundamentally “a story about pessimism”. I would like to offer an additional perspective we can begin to hold alongside (not in lieu of) this bleak view.The link between women’s education and empowerment and the falling birthrate is well established. It is only two generations since contraception became widely available in western countries. It is therefore only a split second since human beings have collectively been given the opportunity to consider what other forms of joy, meaning and fulfilment are available to us as a species. While children are an enormous source of joy and meaning for many, we are now also discovering other ways to build beautiful, meaningful, fulfilling lives that include loving communities of non-biological kin, as well as deep affinity for our home and the other beings that inhabit it.Beyond pessimism, choosing not to have children or to have fewer children might be the exact investment of hope in the future that Cavendish is struggling to see. It is not just an act of “giving up”, but an investment in the belief that the decisions we make today can create a better future. By acting now to reduce the strain on the planet while simultaneously reducing competition for future generations; by becoming more mindful of our individual limitations as potential parents as well as the systemic limitations of our circumstances; by considering deeply and ethically whether here and now is the best time to bring more people into the world; by learning to savour deep connections alongside our biological relatives; and by finding a story of hope, meaning and fulfilment beyond the cycle of biological reproduction alone, people, and women in particular, might be making hope out of the freedom that has been offered through being able to control our own fertility.For some, choosing not to have children, or choosing to have fewer children, in order to dedicate ourselves more fully to helping, as well as savouring, the world already here, might be as much an act of hope as deciding to have (more) children is for others.Nina PlummerEdinburghHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: On assisted dying, MPs grappled with a difficult bill | Assisted dying | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the bill’s narrow defeat in the Commons earlier this month
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the bill’s narrow defeat in the Commons earlier this month
Content: Pro-assisted dying campaigners in Parliament Square react after MPs voted against the assisted dying bill on 11 September.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenPro-assisted dying campaigners in Parliament Square react after MPs voted against the assisted dying bill on 11 September.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAAssisted dyingLettersOn assisted dying, MPs grappled with a difficult billReaders respond to the bill’s narrow defeat in the Commons earlier this monthFri 18 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTShareFor many, the failure of the assisted dying bill (MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales, 11 September) has brought relief that a manifestly unsafe law will not be entering the statute book. But it should also prompt reflection about how it got this far.Two hundred and seventy MPs voted for the bill despite multiple warnings from themedical royal collegesandother professional groupsresponsible for implementing it that it was unsafe and unworkable. Supportive MPs appeared to be voting on an abstract principle rather than engaging with the concerns raised.But an MP’s role is not that of a campaigner. If MPs believe there is a case for assisting some people to end their lives, their role is to consider whether and how that could be achieved safely. Instead, parliament was presented with the latest iteration of a proposalfirst drafted in the 1930s by medical eugenicist Killick Millard, who held disturbing views about “a last service to society by relieving it of a useless burden”. His proposal has returned to parliament repeatedly over the past century, vigorously promoted by the organisation he founded,now calling itself Dignity in Dying.Only its justification, not its content, has been updated as social values have changed.If parliament returns to this issue, it should approach it afresh andhonestly grapple with the complex ethical and practical trade-offs. I, and many others with relevant expertise, would welcome the opportunity to help.Lucy ThomasPalliative care and public health doctorAndy Burnham talked at length about the importance of leadership in his recent campaigns. His decision to abstain in the assisted dying bill gave a clear compass bearing to those Labour MPs keen to follow their leader. It led to the defeat of the bill and will literally cause untold suffering to innocent citizens. This is not leadership, and to hide behind the barricade of “we must improve social care and palliative care first” is disingenuous in the extreme.Gary NethercottWoodbridge, SuffolkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Sweden’s soul and worrying political shift | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Letters: Alvin Engström and Jean Fridh respond to an article by Martin Gelin in which he argues that the country has entered a new era of cruelty
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Alvin Engström and Jean Fridh respond to an article by Martin Gelin in which he argues that the country has entered a new era of cruelty
Content: Öresund bridge. ‘I have seen how border controls with Denmark affect an Öresund region whose everyday life has long depended on easy movement.’Photograph: Bengt Hultqvist/AlamyView image in fullscreenÖresund bridge. ‘I have seen how border controls with Denmark affect an Öresund region whose everyday life has long depended on easy movement.’Photograph: Bengt Hultqvist/AlamySwedenLettersSweden’s soul and worrying political shiftAlvin EngströmandJean Fridhrespond to an article by Martin Gelin in which he argues that the country has entered a new era of crueltyFri 18 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTShareI am writing in response to Martin Gelin’s article (How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, 11 September). Gelin is right to lament how far Swedish politics has moved from the liberal internationalism of the Fredrik Reinfeldt era. Having grown up in Malmö, I have seen how border controls with Denmark affect an Öresund region whose everyday life has long depended on easy movement across the strait. Gelin is right to see this retreat from openness as consequential.But to say that Sweden has therefore “lost its soul” goes too far. Its political shift is neither uniquely Swedish nor evidence that the country has somehow ceased to be itself. Reinfeldt’s “open your hearts” Sweden faded in much the same European political moment as Angela Merkel’s “Wir schaffen das” Germany. Across the European mainland, mainstream parties have adopted more restrictive positions on migration.The cases involving British citizens that Gelin describes are troubling, but Britain’s departure from the EU is also part of the explanation for why Britons inSwedennow face immigration rules from which freedom of movement once spared them. Sweden has changed. So has Britain. Neither exists in a vacuum.There is nothing wrong with romanticising an open, internationalist Sweden. As a young Swede studying at Cambridge, I am susceptible to that image myself. But defining one particular political settlement as Sweden’s “soul” risks turning nostalgia into national essentialism.PerhapsJantelagen– the Scandinavian suspicion of thinking oneself exceptional – offers a more Swedish conclusion. We should not imagine that our political upheavals make us uniquely fallen. Sweden has changed, considerably and sometimes regrettably. It has not stopped being Sweden.Alvin EngströmCambridgeMartin Gelin’s analysis of how Sweden is losing its soul rings true – unfortunately. After living in Sweden for 33 years, I have never felt more like a foreigner than I do now. I am British (of Scottish origin) and moved to Sweden in 1993, at the age of 37, to live with my Swedish husband and our two children. I remember being so impressed by the social benefits, the access to good and affordable childcare and the job opportunities for women – precisely the ideals Martin describes. Over the past 10. years, opposition to immigration has grown in the wake of the so-called refugee “flood” of 2015, when the door was wide open. Sadly, that door is now permanently closed, and locked.In recent years, I have repeatedly been asked whether I consider myself Swedish (I have dual nationality). At first, I didn’t think much of it, but over time, I began to find the question very irritating. On one occasion, an older Swedish woman said it didn’t matter if I didn’t feel Swedish, because “we see you as one of us anyway”. I am ashamed to admit that I snapped at her over the word “us”; I know she meant well, but it made me realise just how divisive the question was. The mere fact that it was being asked by nice, ordinary, polite people was playing right into the hands of the far right.I love my life in Sweden and have no plans to move, but the divisiveness has got under my skin and is hard to ignore.Jean FridhKatrineholm, SwedenExplore more on these topicsSwedenEuropelettersShareReuse this content

title: Spot the conversation hogger – and do something about it | Friendship | The Guardian
description: Letter: Penelope Mavor suggests that listening is not a passive act, so you could interrupt the flow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Penelope Mavor suggests that listening is not a passive act, so you could interrupt the flow
Content: ‘A great listener can help to transform the conversation.’Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A great listener can help to transform the conversation.’Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesFriendshipLettersSpot the conversation hogger – and do something about itPenelope Mavorsuggests that listening is not a passive act, so you could interrupt the flowFri 18 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTShareThese conversational hoggers … don’t they know we were born with two ears and one mouth for a reason? Thank you, Anita Chaudhuri, for a fun, well observed and useful article (‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpers,13 September).It is an interesting reflection to see which of the five hoggers more frequently turn up in our own lives. As a people pleaser and introvert, I have a track record of meeting many monologuists. I pretend to listen, but secretly resent them and their audacity. I just want them to ask about me.I have learned that although interruption can feel violent, sometimes it is a courageous act. When the speaker has just lost connection with the audience and themselves, we have to bring them back. That is what I loved most about the article – it reminded us that we do have options. We can start noticing how we turn up. How am I listening and speaking? What is my responsibility here?A great listener can help to transform the conversation – listening is not a passive act. And in talking, am I actually being interesting? Am I talking as if being listened to?Life is always inviting us into a conversation … with ourselves and each other.Penelope MavorDirector, Earth ConverseHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Swedish teenager jailed for attempted murder, rape and assault committed online, with victims in Germany and Australia | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: Eighteen-year-old known as Chai was active in networks notorious for their sadistic exploitation of young people
Author: Ariel Bogle
Headline: Eighteen-year-old known as Chai was active in networks notorious for their sadistic exploitation of young people
Content: Chai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person in Germany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against an Australian girl.Photograph: xijian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person in Germany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against an Australian girl.Photograph: xijian/Getty ImagesCybercrimeSwedish teenager jailed for attempted murder, rape and assault committed online, with victims in Germany and AustraliaEighteen-year-old known as Chai was active in networks notorious for their sadistic exploitation of young peopleAriel BogleFri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Swedish teenager known as Chai has been sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for attempted murder, rape and aggravated assault – crimes committed via the internet,including against a teenage girl in Australia.The district court found that Chai, 18, was active in online networks notorious for their sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people, coercing them to create sexually explicit material or engage in acts of violence – and for the youth of those involved.The teenager was between 15 and 17 when the offences were committed.Chai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person inGermany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against the Australian teenager, among other offences.Jenny Östling, a senior public prosecutor at Sweden’s national unit against international and organised crime, said the court had clearly understood the phenomenon of “nihilistic violent extremism” and the Com – an umbrella term for a loosely connected online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.“I’m really glad that they realise how serious this is and what it is,” she said.Inside the horrifying online network where children coerce others to commit violence and self-harmRead moreShe noted that the sentence was among the longest possible in Sweden for someone of Chai’s age. The court also found that it was possible for someone to be convicted of violent offences even where they were committed remotely via the internet.“That is a very important tool for us when we proceed [with] these kinds of cases,” Östling said.The crimes committed by those involved with sadistic extortion networks, such as one globally known as “764”, often cross borders, with cases in the US, the UK, Germany and Australia, and alleged victims in multiple jurisdictions.Material is often created and traded among participants to build status and control, lawyers and researchers told the Guardian as part ofits investigationinto these groups, as well as a means of accessing closed servers and chatrooms.“These are young people recruiting other young people,” Bjørn Ihler, the founder of the security firm Revontulet, said at the time. “It is a youth phenomenon.”Chai’s conviction is one of several cases that have resulted in significant terms of imprisonment for young men found to be involved in this ecosystem, including anAmerican, Kyle Spitze, 27, who was sentenced in August to 77 years in prison – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on someone the US government has labelled a “nihilistic violent extremist”.During the trial, Chai underwent a forensic psychiatric examination that found he was not suffering a serious mental disorder when the offences occurred.His lawyer, Emily Tovedal, told the Guardian: “The defence’s view is that the court has made an error of judgment regarding a large proportion of the charges.”Authorities internationally have increasingly raised the alarm about sadistic online exploitation of young people, detailingpotential warning signsincluding self-harm and isolation.“Sadly, I’m confident that … they will probably grow,” Östling said of these networks. “And we will also be aware of more of them, because now we know what to look for.”In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeYoung peopleInternetInternet safetyCyberbullyingSwedenEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform donor Ben Delo loaned £350k to academic later found to have engaged in online bullying  | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Judge said Nina Power and her friend’s social media posts had ‘the whiff of threat and antisemitism’
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Judge said Nina Power and her friend’s social media posts had ‘the whiff of threat and antisemitism’
Content: It has not been previously reported that Delo gave funding to Power before the case went to court.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationView image in fullscreenIt has not been previously reported that Delo gave funding to Power before the case went to court.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationReform UKReform donor Ben Delo loaned £350k to academic later found to have engaged in online bullyingJudge said Nina Power and her friend’s social media posts had ‘the whiff of threat and antisemitism’Rowena MasonandJuliette GarsideFri 18 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK’s new mega-donor Ben Delo gave a £350,000 loan to a conservative writer fighting a legal case in which a judge later found she had engaged in online bullying and regrettable conduct with a “whiff of threat and antisemitism”.Nina Power and her friend, the writer Daniel DC Miller, brought the legal action for defamation against the performance artistLuke Turner, who they had accused of falsely calling them antisemitic. At the same time, Turner brought a counter-claim against the pair accusing them of harassment.Their libel action failed on the grounds that Turner’s online reach was not big enough to have caused harm to their reputations, while the harassment case also failed on the basis that their conduct was not unlawful.The loan from Delo to help fund Power’s case before the 2023 trial shines a light on the Reform supporter’s involvement in backing a landmark legal tussle over the boundaries of free speech.It is understood Delo did not and does not believe Power and Miller held antisemitic views as alleged by Turner, and would never knowingly provide financial or any other support to those who did.In the case, Miller, who is Jewish, and Power denied promoting fascist or antisemitic views, and said they did not know Turner was Jewish. The judge found there was “no overt antisemitism” displayed by the pair.But in the counter-claim of harassment, the judge described social media posts by Miller and Power as having “the whiff of threat and antisemitism which they themselves can fairly be held to have created”, although she ruled it was “too occasional, intangible, diffuse and unconsolidated” to have been unlawful.She said the “radio frequencies of macabre imagery and casualness around antisemitic tropes into which Mr Turner tuned do yield a discernible signal but not one strong enough to be recognised objectively as antisemitic hate speech or a resolved engagement with physical violence sufficient to render this conduct quasi-criminal”.The judge also said: “Mr Turner evidently had been harassed to a quasi-criminal (or indeed criminal) degree by other people. But what Mr Miller and Ms Power did was not of that order.”View image in fullscreenNina Power is a former leftwing academic who has written in publications including the Guardian about feminism.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAfter the failure of the cases, Turner was awarded costs of £1m amounting to 80% of the total, and Power was declared bankrupt. In the course of the bankruptcy proceedings it emerged that Delo had loaned her a sum in the region of £350,000 to help pay her lawyers.It is understood the loan was made by Delo weeks before the trial started when Power’s conditional fee arrangement with her lawyers collapsed. The loan was made on a commercial basis and secured against the value of a London property she owns, with a repayment schedule.Delo has been known to be a supporter of the Free Speech Union, run by the Conservative peer Toby Young, and has funded a base known for anti-woke causes.Power is a former leftwing academic who has written in publications including the Guardian about feminism. She has since described her journey towards being “conservative in the true sense of that word” and wrote a book, What Do Men Want? Masculinity and Its Discontents, in which she argues men have been demonised.The 2023 high court ruling describes how Miller and Turner were involved in an online incident which emerged from Turner’s involvement in the London arts scene. The artist had risen to prominence thanks to his creative collaborations with the Hollywood actor Shia LaBeouf.The pair took opposing sides in relation to the London art gallery LD50, which had staged a symposium featuring neo-reactionary speakers and a show advertised online with a quotation from Adolf Hitler, in German gothic font. While Turner described the venue as an alt-Nazi gallery, Miller joined the counter-protest, standing outside LD50 with a placard calling for “the right to openly discuss ideas”.Miller, who told the court he was of Jewish heritage, is closely associated withthe magazine IM-1776, which platforms hard-right views, having previously contributed to the title as an editor and an author. Among the articles published by IM-1776 are pieces celebratingthe “Unabomber” Ted Kaczynskiand the proto-fascist Italian nationalist Gabriele D’Annunzio.In the trial, Turner acknowledged he had been wrong to claim Miller was the author of a blog advocating a Hitler-style disability policy.WhatsApp chats between Miller and Power, disclosed as part of the 2023 trial, did show them dismissing anti-racism as a “psyop”. The term refers to psychological operations used by the military or governments to influence public behaviour.Power wrote: “The social disapproval for ‘racism’ is a psyop to stop people realising that there *are* alien and fairy races,” and that “black and white were alien races and very different”.In a later exchange Power brought up Hitler’s autobiographical political manifesto, Mein Kampf, writing “I think … at some point … we need to read Mein Kampf properly …”, adding that she wanted to “understand it”.In an episode referenced in the judgment, Miller performed at a public event in Athens, delivering a lecture in the persona of the Italian far-right philosopher and antisemite Julius Evola. During the rise of fascism, Evola called for measures to counter “the Jewish menace”. He opposed democracy in favour of a caste-based aristocratic order and was convicted on appeal during the 1950s of trying to revive fascism.The judge found the pair had between them labelled Turner “low IQ’, ‘sociopathic’, ‘paranoid’, ‘deranged’, ‘obsessive’, ‘paranoid schizophrenic’, ‘dangerously mentally ill’ and so on and on – sometimes accompanied by messages to ‘get help’.” She said in her ruling that Power told her from the witness box that the latter proceeded from genuine and empathetic concern. The judge was unconvinced.During the trial, Miller and Power denied promoting antisemitic philosophies, describing their interest in the subject as a quest to “critically understand” the issues.Power and Delo declined to comment. Miller said the story was “based on a systematic distortions of facts”, adding: “I am myself Jewish and proudly Jewish.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKOnline abuseDefamation lawFar rightAntisemitismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Error first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says report
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Error first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says report
Content: Passengers caught up in the delays at Heathrow airport last week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPassengers caught up in the delays at Heathrow airport last week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesAir transportFlight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software errorError first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says reportGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading toa six-hour outage and mass airline cancellationsand delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared.‘Baggage reclaim was pandemonium’: passengers hit by airport IT chaos in UK recount their ordealsRead moreThe transport secretary,Heidi Alexander, said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) industry regulator would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats more widely.Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which ended up delaying and cancelling flights across the UK and beyondlate into the next day.Airlines have called for compensation and a “credible plan”, with Ryanair demanding the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023.A government source said the CAA review would be “a chance to fundamentally investigate” if Nats was fit for purpose.Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures. He said he could “confirm that it was a software issue and not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators”.The preliminary report said the failure was a “legacy and previously unknown software defect and a combination of very specific events occurring simultaneously” in part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which allocates codes to individual aircraft to identify flights on radar.Nats said the software error occurred at 10am, with engineers first notified at 10.02am that the link between the NAS and London area control system had dropped. The engineers reported at 10.06am that the system had apparently recovered with no operational impact, but continued to investigate.The report said the fault presented when a manual request for an aircraft code was being processed but paused for another, unspecified “higher priority activity” request. It said: “When processing of the aircraft code request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted, and affected some subsequent flight data updates. This happened in the space of a millisecond.”At 12.32pm the link between the national and London airspace management dropped again and a major incident was declared, with controllers having to conduct some tasks manually. By 12.45pm, Nats was restricting flights as the system continued to glitch, before failing completely at 1.32pm.At 1.40pm airlines were advised of restrictions, and between 2.50pm and 4.09pm Nats rebooted the system, eventually resuming full operations at 7.30pm – but leaving mass congestion, displaced aircraft and hundreds of thousands of delayed passengers in its wake.It took more than two days for the backlog of passenger disruption to be cleared, with more than 2,000 flights cancelled in total and hundreds of thousands of people’s travel plans disrupted.Rolfe said: “The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week. It’s our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong. However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question.”The transport secretary said: “The disruption we saw last week was completely unacceptable and I know how frustrating it was for passengers, airlines and airports.”Alexander said she had received Nats’ report, adding: “It’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos.“I have therefore tasked the CAA with conducting an independent review to check Nats’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability.”The CAA’s review will be published within six months.Tim Alderslade, the chief executive of Airlines UK, a lobby group representing the industry, said: “The CAA’s review must mandate real investment in Nats’ resilience so a single fault can never again descend into nationwide disruption.”He said his members were writing to Nats to “demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience”.TheEasyJet chief executive, Kenton Jarvis, said: “Passengers deserve more than just another promise that lessons will be learned. Firm actions must be taken … and there must be a fair solution to ensure that airlines are not left to pick up the bill.”The Ryanair chief operations officer, Neil McMahon, said: “‘The software ate my homework’ is not an acceptable explanation … How many times must the UK ATC system collapse before Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility and resigns.”Explore more on these topicsAir transportAirline industryTravel & leisureTransportEuropeHeidi AlexandernewsShareReuse this content

title: Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy murder trial speaks out | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Michael P Desronvil was sole juror to vote guilty, resulting in deadlocked jury and judge declaring a mistrial
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Michael P Desronvil was sole juror to vote guilty, resulting in deadlocked jury and judge declaring a mistrial
Content: Lindsay Clancy looks on as Judge William F Sullivan declares a mistrial in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 4 September 2026.Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy looks on as Judge William F Sullivan declares a mistrial in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 4 September 2026.Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersMassachusettsLone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy murder trial speaks outMichael P Desronvil was sole juror to vote guilty, resulting in deadlocked jury and judge declaring a mistrialRon DeSantis offers ‘asylum’ to holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trialMaya YangFri 18 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lone holdout juror in theLindsay Clancy murder trialis speaking out, saying that he “didn’t have any doubts” during the jury’s deliberations of the case which ended in a mistrial.“I didn’t have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present,” the 48-year-old male juror, Michael P Desronvil, said in astatementto NewsNation on Thursday.“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” he added.Lindsay Clancy: five key moments from ‘America’s saddest murder trial’Read moreDesronvil’s public statement followswidespread debateonlineover the controversial caseabout whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse who fatally strangled her three children in Massachusetts in 2023, should be held criminally responsible.3:41A look inside the courtroom during the Lindsay Clancy murder trial – videoClancy has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder charges by reason of insanity, with her defense team arguing that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time.The trial, which brought nationwide attention to systemic gaps inmaternal mental health care, lasted nearly six weeks and culminated in a mistrial after nearly 40 hours of deliberation over seven days.Several members of the 11-1 deadlocked jury, which comprised nine women and three men, have since publicly commented on the case.Speaking toNBC10 earlier this month, Roni Carlson, the jury’s foreperson, said the single holdout juror “admitted he had reasonable doubt, and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited”.“There were three forms I had to fill out and I started filling them out, I wrote my signature on each one, and then he said, ‘But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity,’” she added.Another juror, Kellie Farina,said: “He had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children … Every one of us in the hours of our frustration would get up and walk the room because you just couldn’t sit anymore.”Meanwhile, juror Paula Devlinsaid: “He was very arrogant,” adding: “He really did not take anything that anybody said.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDesronvil’s lawyer, Edward Andrew Paltzik, has publicly defended his client, describing Desronvil as an “American hero and champion of justice” who will “not be giving any interviews at this time”.In a Friday statement on X, Paltziksaid: “Any attempts to contact our Heroic Lone Holdout Juror will not be well-taken. Please respect his dignity, humanity, and privacy. Stay away from his home, stop calling him, and don’t even think about deciphering his location.”Since the mistrial, Desronvil’s personal legal issues have come to light, raising questions over the jury selection process.Numerous outlets, includingNBC10and theBoston Globe, report that he has a past domestic violence charge from 2021 and an active civil restraining order for allegedly assaulting his nephew, and was facing eviction proceedings while deliberating the Clancy case.Plymouth district attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet publicly stated whether he will retry Clancy while Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, hassaidhe will ask for the jury to be sequestered in a new trial.Judge William F Sullivan has set a hearing for 29 September todetermine next steps.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS justice systemUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children
Content: Family members of those who died gather outside Minna general hospital in Niger state.Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/ReutersView image in fullscreenFamily members of those who died gather outside Minna general hospital in Niger state.Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/ReutersNigeriaSurvivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 diedPolice fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were childrenEromo Egbejulein Abidjan and agenciesFri 18 Sep 2026 13.27 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSurvivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.NSCDC – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.The state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. “There are issues of illegal mining and it is taking a toll on our children,” he said.Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.AFP reported that another survivor, who asked not to be named, said he had made it out alive because he was near the cell’s entrance, where he could breathe better. “We were screaming for help,” he said, with detainees telling the guards that “people are dying one after the other. They did not believe us.”President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials.But protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – ​some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called ‌for justice. Some protesters tried ‌to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make ‌a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.View image in fullscreenFamily members outside Minna general hospital. Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in the city.Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/ReutersAs ⁠curfew began at 6pm local time on Friday, security forces appeared to have at least temporarily restored order to the streets of the city.The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of an investigation.Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and is more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolice and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNigeriaAfricaMiningGoldCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: From old railways to an oasis of art, food and nature: how an eco-park was born in Greater Manchester | Access to green space | The Guardian
description: Northern Roots is launching Britain’s biggest urban farm and eco-park, in an effort to boost people’s health and wellbeing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Northern Roots is launching Britain’s biggest urban farm and eco-park, in an effort to boost people’s health and wellbeing
Content: Mary-Ellen McTague, a chef, food writer and restaurateur, has a leading role in shaping the food offer at Northern Roots.Photograph: Darren Robinson PhotographyView image in fullscreenMary-Ellen McTague, a chef, food writer and restaurateur, has a leading role in shaping the food offer at Northern Roots.Photograph: Darren Robinson PhotographyAccess to green spaceFrom old railways to an oasis of art, food and nature: how an eco-park was born in Greater ManchesterNorthern Roots is launching Britain’s biggest urban farm and eco-park, in an effort to boost people’s health and wellbeingNatalie WintFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStanding in the open green space of Northern Roots, it is hard to imagine the landscape as it once was.Two cotton mills, two coalmines and an industrial railway once occupied this 65-hectare (160-acre) site in Oldham,Greater Manchester. Later, about 24 hectares became a tip, with much of the space left to nature.Over the past five years, Northern Roots, a charity, has been developing this once industrial land, running community programmes including a NaturalHealthService.On 19 September a new facility will open to the public, featuring a cafe, shop, production kitchen, performance space, forestry skills centre, outdoor play areas and an urban farm. The charity’s ambition is to turn what was once a “burden” into the UK’s largest urban farm and eco-park.View image in fullscreenVisitors to the cafe and shop will be able to enjoy and buy fresh seasonal produce grown on site, helping strengthen connections between local communities, sustainable food production and healthy living.Photograph: Darren Robinson PhotographyThe idea began with Oldham council, which wanted to explore green space as an asset. Today the council works in a unique partnership with Northern Roots.“We wanted to look at what this land could do for Oldham, rather than simply seeing it as land that needed maintaining,” said Anna da Silva, the founder and chief executive of Northern Roots.The charity’s seven activity programmes, which include farming and food, arts and culture, sports, business and learning, have been designed to appeal widely.“The hardest part is getting people … physically and psychologically out of their house, down to the site, meeting people where they are on that journey,” said da Silva.Once they are through the doors, the aim is to encourage continued engagement so they can unlock the environmental, economic and social benefits – a challenge that led to the creation of “participation pathways”.This philosophy is perhaps best demonstrated by Faiza Awan and Louise Gibbs, who both grew up in the area and became involved with Northern Roots as community champions. Awan said: “It’s really important to have something for everyone.”Gibbs added: “There’s just so many doors to come in through Northern Roots, and then to continue development.”Both now have roles as Natural Health Service guardians. Unlikegreen social prescribingprogrammes that are centred on exercise or gardening, Northern Roots’Natural Health Servicefocuses on intentional connection with nature. In doing so, it embodies the wider aims of creating opportunities for people who might not otherwise come together.View image in fullscreenThe pioneering project spans 65 hectares of former industrial land in Oldham.Photograph: Darren Robinson PhotographyThe site sits between two different and historically divided communities, and its outdoor setting helps to make it a space where people feel able to participate. “It’s a very welcoming, inviting environment,” said Gibbs. “With it being outside, people automatically feel comfort.”Awan said: “There’s something really levelling and very democratic about doing things outside in nature,” adding that it could create a sense of belonging that might be harder to achieve in other settings.The importance of connection is reflected in the relationship between the community and the site. Gibbs said: “Because [people] are local they feel more connected to the space … it’s giving the ownership to the community.”The Natural Health Service was commissioned through Northern Roots by NHS England. It launched in 2023 as a six-month pilot with patients from the Hill Top GP surgery in Fitton Hill. It now works with healthcare providers to support people experiencing mental health challenges.A session may involve foraging, bushcraft, making something from natural materials or simply noticing what is around you. The principle is that being outside, in an environment without the clinical associations of a healthcare setting, can create room to slow down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA participant from Oldham takes part in the Natural Health Service project at Northern Roots.Photograph: Darren RobinsonGibbs said: “People might come in and they might be flustered from the morning, the school run or the next 10 things they need to do, but we really encourage people to slow down, to take that breath, to give themselves permission, to spend this time on themselves and to simply just be in this space.”Independent NHSresearch published in 2025 found that participants in Northern Roots’ Natural Health Service improved their wellbeing scores by an average of 8.15 points on the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale, a seven-item questionnaire used to measure a person’s recent wellbeing. The project generated an estimated £4,940 in social value per participant.However, the benefits extend beyond metrics. “You can’t put it in facts and figures, in black and white,” said Gibbs. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up when they’ve said they have not been out for years. They’re excited to come the next week.” The benefits were mutual, she added. “It makes me feel good within myself, seeing that person is happy in that moment.”Northern Roots is intended to be a model for others. “There are bits of land like this all over the place,” said da Silva. “They’re seen as a problem. We have got an approach to evaluating the place where you are, the site that you have, the needs of the community, the opportunities within the site.”View image in fullscreenThe forestry skills centre will provide specialist training in sustainable industries, including landscape management and crop growing.Photograph: Darren Robinson PhotographyNorthern Roots aims to attract 300,000 visitors a year by 2030, dispense hundreds of Natural Health Service social prescriptions – connecting people to non-medical community-based services – and create employment and training opportunities.The idea that land can be a resource is part of Northern Roots’ wider proposition: that urban green space should be treated as critical infrastructure in the same way as hospitals and schools. Da Silva said it should be seen as “part of an arsenal of tools that can be used to address issues and support communities”.The challenge is not simply to demonstrate what the land can provide, but to build the case for investment to make that possible.“We need commissioners to invest in these spaces in the same way they would built infrastructure,” said da Silva. The aim is to show that relatively modest investment in land can help to reduce pressure on other public services.For da Silva, however, the value of the project is not only in what it can deliver for public services. It is also in how it changes people’s relationship with the land. The ambition is to change “the way people feel about a place, themselves and their place in that place”.Explore more on these topicsAccess to green spaceCommunitiesMental healthSustainable developmentGreater ManchesterHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Private jets pollute up to 14 times as much as commercial planes and are undertaxed in US, report says | US news | The Guardian
description: Number of private jets has surged in recent years, but they do not pay commensurate portion of fees to FAA operations
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Number of private jets has surged in recent years, but they do not pay commensurate portion of fees to FAA operations
Content: The boom in private aviation is also driving demand for additional infrastructure.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe boom in private aviation is also driving demand for additional infrastructure.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesUS newsPrivate jets pollute up to 14 times as much as commercial planes and are undertaxed in US, report saysNumber of private jets has surged in recent years, but they do not pay commensurate portion of fees to FAA operationsMarina DunbarFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new report has put a spotlight on the rapid expansion of private jet travel in the US, revealing that owners are not paying their fair share of aviation tax despite the average owner’s wealth being $190m and private jets being up to 14 times more polluting than commercial flights.The Institute for Policy Studies’ new report,High Flyers 2026, examines the growing use of private aircraft, the public infrastructure supporting them and the tax policies benefiting private jet owners.The institute worked with a worldwide community of more than 20,000 open-source trackers to develop thePrivate Jet Emissions Tracker(PJET), which analyzes private jet flights arriving at and departing from specific locations during certain events, including the Super Bowl, the Kentucky Derby and every game of the World Cup.Super-rich’s assets cause outsized amount of climate harm, study saysRead moreThe number of private jet flights hassurged in recent years, with climate-heating emissions linked to that mode of travel rising by 50%, according to the most comprehensive global analysis to date.At the same time, private jets and charter services now account for roughly 16% of flight operations handled by the Federal Aviation Administration, according to the institute’s report.The US Department of Transportation estimates that noncommercial private jets represent 7% of airspace activity but contribute less than 0.6% of the taxes flowing into the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, which helps finance FAA operations.Private flights, used by an estimated 256,000 people (just 0.003% of the world’s population), are the most polluting form of transport, producing direct carbon emissions 10 to 14 times greater per passenger than commercial aviation travel, the report said.Private jet ownership has expanded alongside the growth of the ultra-wealthy, the report said. The median wealth of a private jet owner is $190m, while the median wealth of someone with fractional ownership in a private jet is $140m.“The rest of us should not have to pay for the luxury excess of the private jet billionaire class,” report co-author Chuck Collins said in a statement. “Our hard-earned tax dollars shouldn’t subsidize their reckless air travel habits that further harm our warming planet.”Between 2019 and 2025, fractional jet ownership, a program in which one buys an equity share of a private aircraft in exchange for a guaranteed number of annual flight hours, increased 6%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe boom in private aviation is also driving demand for additional infrastructure, including expanded private aircraft hangars and greater runway capacity at local and regional airports.The report also highlightslobbying and tax policybenefiting private aircraft owners. The National Business Aviation Association spent approximately $2m lobbying in 2025 in support of legislation providing major tax breaks to private jet owners, the report said.Collins added: “At a time when most ordinary people are struggling to afford groceries, rent and healthcare, our report exposes how the ultra-rich and greedy corporations are private jet-setting at the expense of the rest of us, while trying to dodge accountability for fueling the climate crisis.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsThe super-richAir transportAir pollutionClimate crisisShareReuse this content

title: Stephanie Cole, Coronation Street and Open All Hours actor, dies aged 84 | Television | The Guardian
description: Cole, described as an ‘extraordinary talent’, also appeared in Waiting for God, Tenko and had an extensive theatre career
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cole, described as an ‘extraordinary talent’, also appeared in Waiting for God, Tenko and had an extensive theatre career
Content: Stephanie Cole in 2014. Her agent said she would also ‘be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities’.Photograph: Mike Lawn/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStephanie Cole in 2014. Her agent said she would also ‘be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities’.Photograph: Mike Lawn/ShutterstockTelevisionStephanie Cole, Coronation Street and Open All Hours actor, dies aged 84Cole, described as an ‘extraordinary talent’, also appeared in Waiting for God, Tenko and had an extensive theatre careerPA MediaFri 18 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actor Stephanie Cole, best known for roles inCoronation Street, Waiting for God and Open All Hours, has died aged 84.She also appeared in the prisoner-of-war drama Tenko, A Bit of a Do and Doc Martin.A statement from her agent, John Grant, on behalf of her family, said: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Stephanie Cole, OBE.“She passed away this morning at the age of 84. Stephanie had been living with Alzheimer’s disease for some years.My TV hero: Stephanie Cole on Innes LloydRead more“Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television. She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama.“She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities. During this incredibly difficult time, the family kindly requests privacy.”View image in fullscreenCole (right) as Sylvia Goodwin in Coronation Street.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockCole appeared on Coronation Street between 2011 and 2013 as Sylvia Goodwin, the mother of Roy Cropper. She won the British Soap award for best comedy performance for the role.Her other notable performances included roles in Still Open All Hours, in which she reprised her Open All Hours character Mrs Featherstone, The Cleaner, Gentleman Jack and Talking Heads: Soldiering On.She won the British Comedy award for best actress for the 1990s sitcom Waiting for God, about residents of a retirement home.Cole also had an extensive career in the theatre, with roles in King Lear, A Passionate Woman and Noises Off.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionCoronation StreetSoap operaDramanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with culture | Arts Council England | The Guardian
description: In first interview since starting job – and after visiting school where arts are central – Dawn Airey says she wants to fix ‘shocking’ lack of access
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: In first interview since starting job – and after visiting school where arts are central – Dawn Airey says she wants to fix ‘shocking’ lack of access
Content: ‘When I was at school you went on cultural trips. It was just accepted,’ Airey said.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘When I was at school you went on cultural trips. It was just accepted,’ Airey said.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianArts Council England‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with cultureIn first interview since starting job – and after visiting school where arts are central – Dawn Airey says she wants to fix ‘shocking’ lack of accessMark BrownNorth of England correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly half of children in England have been to a museum or the theatre in the past year, while three-quarters have not been to an art gallery, research shows.Dawn Airey, the new chair ofArts Council England, said the figures were “shocking” but also “an amazing opportunity to ensure they do have that experience to enrich their lives”.In her first interview since taking up the job six weeks ago, Airey said experience of arts and culture “should almost be a human right”.“When I was at school you went on cultural trips. It was just accepted that you would go to your local gallery. You can have great art but if there is no access it might as well not be there. That is the challenge,” she said.Airey, a TV industry veteran and former Channel 5 boss, spoke to the Guardian while on a whistlestop tour of arts projects in Barrow-in-Furness, Cumbria.View image in fullscreenPrimary school pupils in a music session led by musicians and conductors from Liverpool Philharmonic at the Barrow Youth Hub.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianShe succeeds Nicholas Serota as chair of an organisation that has had a bumpy few years, beginning with huge cuts imposed by the Conservatives.Anindependent review of ACEby Margaret Hodge this year levelled a number of criticisms, including that it had overly complicated application processes, which “stifled creativity and innovation”.Arts organisations were also last year put through the wringer when ACE’s grant processing platform, Grantium, crashed,causing widespread funding limbo.Airey recalled that on her first visit as chair to ACE’s London office, “it felt quiet, a little bit subdued. I didn’t expect that.”She said she wanted ACE to get its “swagger” back. “I want the Arts Council to be open, I want it to be confident, I want it to be leading conversations, I want it to have a sense of fun, a sense of energy.“We’ve been quite process-driven and it doesn’t need to be. We’ve got to relax. I want us to be loud.”Airey was speaking as ACE published its first Creative Young Lives survey, one of the biggest of its type undertaken. It looks at how children and young people engage – or don’t – with arts and culture.View image in fullscreenAirey meeting pupils at Dowdales secondary school in Dalton-in-Furness.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThefigures showedthat in the past year 51.79% of young people had been to a museum, 48.56% to the theatre or a show, 26.31% to an art gallery or exhibition, and 22.25% to a music event.In the survey, 74% of children said being creative was important to them, and 60% said they would definitely like to do more creative and cultural activities.Cost is one of the biggest barriers, with 32% of respondents saying it prevented them from making more visits to cultural places. More than half (55%) said making creative activities more affordable would help them increase their participation.ACE said the detailed survey provided “robust data”, with previous studies “not conducted a scale to allow such granular analysis”.On her visit this week, Airey saw first-hand the value of giving young people easy access to culture, at the arts-madDowdales schoolin Dalton-in-Furness.Its headteacher, Emma Aubrey, has fostered close links with the Royal Shakespeare Company, Birmingham Royal Ballet and the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra,which performs in Barrowand has a youth hub.Aubrey said it had been a battle to ensure arts education was “front and centre” at her school while watching it being marginalised nationally.“It has been tough to say: no, we will continue to do that, and we teach drama and dance as well as music to every child in key stage 3 every week.”View image in fullscreenPupils taking part in a dance class at Dowdales school.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianOn the day the Guardian visited, 12- and 13-year-olds were rehearsing Romeo and Juliet – and also considering their town centre. It was “rough”, said one child. “There’s nothing good going on,” said another. It was “run down”. People “feel there’s not much they can do about it, it’s already happened”.The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school | EditorialRead moreThey were talking about Barrow, but it could be almost any English town centre: the nation’s problems summed up in seconds by children rehearsing Shakespeare.Aubrey is clearly proud of the school’s arts focus, and not necessarily because it is going to create lots of artists. “It’s about opening up a world that can be very insular and isolated and very industry-driven. It’s about making them believe they can be anybody,” she said.ACE distributesmore than £650m a year of public and lottery moneyto arts organisations and individuals, and will next week publish new, “simpler” guidance for the next national portfolio funding round.In Barrow, Airey met a number of organisations that had benefited from Arts Council money.View image in fullscreenAirey at a roundtable session with arts leaders in Barrow-in-Furness.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianAt one roundtable she told participants: “The Arts Council has been through a bit of a tough time … I want us to get our swagger back.”Airey said ACE would be actively involved in the government’s ambition to “rewire the nation”, adding: “We have been doing that a long, long time.”The idea of ACE getting its swagger back was enthusiastically received by panellists, who spoke of the challenges of getting everyone on board when arguing for embedding art and culture in places such as Barrow, a town dominated by its shipyard building nuclear submarines.Jo Reilly, the deputy directorof Art Gene, said: “We need you to be an advocate for us at all levels.”Explore more on these topicsArts Council EnglandDawn AireyArts in schoolsArts fundingArts policyMuseums (Education)Creativity in the classroomnewsShareReuse this content

title: Disabled people need right to travel abroad, say UK MPs amid ‘ridiculous’ restrictions row | Disability | The Guardian
description: Outcry over ‘brazenly discriminatory’ funding practices among NHS care boards and local councils, with wide variations in rules
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: Outcry over ‘brazenly discriminatory’ funding practices among NHS care boards and local councils, with wide variations in rules
Content: People who require full-time personal assistants have questioned whether local care boards are breaching human rights law with respect to travel funding.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople who require full-time personal assistants have questioned whether local care boards are breaching human rights law with respect to travel funding.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesDisabilityDisabled people need right to travel abroad, say UK MPs amid ‘ridiculous’ restrictions rowOutcry over ‘brazenly discriminatory’ funding practices among NHS care boards and local councils, with wide variations in rulesOpinion: An effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain?
