We will not settle for itFrances RyanandPatrick ButlerFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDisabled people must have a guaranteed right to travel abroad, MPs and peers have said, as further cases emerged of individuals barred from taking holidays as a result of “ridiculous” rules imposed by localNHScare boards and local councils.Leading figures have called on the government to bring in clear national guidelines to ensure people who requirefull-time personal assistants(PAs) are not prevented from using funding for their 24/7 support team for breaks and work trips.Wide variations in local rules governing foreign travel mean whether a disabled person can take their care team abroad can depend on where they live, the whim of local officials or whether they are prepared to mount a legal challenge.The call came as it emerged two men with the same health condition and care packages, living 40 miles from each other, are subject to different rules regarding overseas travel with their PA support team.While Joel, 40, a graduate who works in marketing for a global brand, is barred by his local health board from using his personal health budget to contribute to the travel costs of his PAs when going abroad, David, 25, who lives in a neighbouring health board area, receives a travel costs allocation.While Joel (not his real name) has been effectively prevented from travelling overseas for the past eight years – he can afford his own travel costs but not those of his two PAs – David was free to take a trip to Europe this summer with his PA support team.“This is really unfair and brazenly discriminatory,” Joel said. “It is a fundamental human right that individuals with disabilities should have the same freedoms, opportunities and choices to travel as any able-bodied person would.”Jane Campbell, a leading disability rights campaigner, said: “These ridiculous care restrictions are against common sense. Stipulating where and when the person can use the support they’ve been assessed as needing is like tagging somebody, as if a prisoner out on parole.”The Guardianpreviously revealedNHS care boards and local councils were refusing to allow disabled people to use their care funding outside the UK, even when they paid PA travel expenses themselves. Joel’s case suggests other care boards are indirectly barring disabled people from travelling: while overseas travel is in theory allowed, in practice it is unaffordable without NHS funding for PA expenses.Lady Campbell said: “It’s as if those controlling the purse strings believe disabled people do not deserve the same experiences they enjoy. The government constantly says how important it is for disabled people to work and take responsibility for their lives and yet when we do, these kind of rules are imposed.“We need national guidelines on using care abroad now to protect disabled people’s rights and end this nonsense once and for all.”Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the Commons work and pensions select committee, said the restrictions potentially breached the UN convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, which the UK has ratified.“Disabled people should have the same freedom as everyone else to travel for work, to visit family or simply to go on holiday,” said Abrahams.Joel, who has spinal muscular atrophy, was initially allowed to use his health budget to pay for his PAs to travel with him and had two short breaks in Europe, at his own cost. Eight years ago, his NHS funder, now Cheshire and Merseyside NHS integrated care board, reversed its decision, ruling travel costs were valid for the UK only.He challenged the ruling but was rebuffed, being told earlier this year by the care board that the period in 2017 when it permitted him to use his personal care budget for overseas PA travel costs was a “historical error in decision-making”.Just 40 miles (64km) away David (not his real name) said his local care board made very different rulings. Greater Manchester integrated care partnership blocked his requests for holiday PA expenses for five years. Officials finally relented last year after he submitted detailed evidence suggesting its decision would breach NHS guidance and human rights law.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt allocated £2,370 annually to enable David to contribute to his PA team’s travel and accommodation costs. David, a graduate with a first-class degree, last year took his first trip abroad without his parents, paid for by himself.He said: “It can feel like being in a prison for a person with my condition. I want to live how my peers live. I want independence. I want a change of scenery from time to time.”The MP Marsha de Cordova, who is a former minister for disabled people, said local variations highlighted the urgent need for national guidelines: “Disabled people’s right to travel should not be decided by the mood of local officials.”Cheshire and Merseyside’s mostrecent policy, approved last week [10 September] states that while disabled individuals can request holiday travel expenses for their PAs it would “not ordinarily” pay for them. It states it has an obligation to use NHS funds “in a way which is fair and equitable”.NHS Greater Manchester said it had no ratified policy on holiday travel.The Department ofHealthand Social Care’s (DHSC) position is that care boards should examine all requests for PA travel support and consider the health and wellbeing benefits for the applicant of overseas travel for the applicant.A DHSC spokesperson said: “Personal health budgets work best where people have real flexibility over how they use their budgets and we expect integrated care boards to examine each proposal on a case-by-case basis, in line with national policy and legislation.”NHS Cheshire and Merseyside and NHS Greater Manchester separately issued the following statement: “While we cannot comment on individual patient cases, all requests for personal health budget funding are assessed according to our personal health budget and integrated budget policy on a case-by-case basis according to patient need. This policy has been developed in line with national NHS guidance.”Explore more on these topicsDisabilityNHSHealthSocial careHealth policyPublic services policyWelfarenewsShareReuse this content

title: British Sikh man granted bail in India nine years after arrest | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Jagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offences
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Jagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offences
Content: Jagtar Singh Johal claims he was tortured in detention in an attempt to extract a confession.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenJagtar Singh Johal claims he was tortured in detention in an attempt to extract a confession.Photograph: Family handout/PAScotlandBritish Sikh man granted bail in India nine years after arrestJagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offencesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 18 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested inIndiain 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.Johal, fromScotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges weredismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-basedbrother Gurpreet Singh Johalsaid: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”View image in fullscreenGurpreet Singh Johal has fought tirelessly for his brother’s release.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianGurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStarmer urged to intervene in ‘rigged’ Indian prosecution of British human rights activistRead moreThe UK governmentrecently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular casesand he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.Explore more on these topicsScotlandIndiaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Critics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s elections
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Critics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s elections
Content: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a candidate for re-election for the workers' party (PT), speaks at a campaign rally in Brasilia, Brazil, on 16 September 2026.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a candidate for re-election for the workers' party (PT), speaks at a campaign rally in Brasilia, Brazil, on 16 September 2026.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersBrazilBrazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of electionCritics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s electionsTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroFri 18 Sep 2026 13.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election.On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has beengaining groundin recent weeks.The rise in the monthly payment, from about £98 to £113, that he announced on Thursday is due to take effect on 19 October, just before the likely runoff vote on 25 October.The increase is expected to benefit between 15% and 20% of voters in what promises to be one of theclosest ever presidential racesin Latin America’s largest country.Lulasaidit was not really an increase, but an adjustment in line with inflation to “protect the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families”, but his opponents have criticised its timing so close to the election.Flávio Bolsonaro called it an “act of desperation” after polls showed him gaining ground – although the most recent survey, released on Thursday night, still showed Lulanumerically aheaddespite the technical tie. The senator added that Lula was trying to “buy the votes of the poor”.Created in 2003 during his first term as president, the programme, calledBolsa Família, was a flagship cash-transfer policy that helped lift millions of families out of poverty during his first two terms.Currently, families with an income of up to £32 per person are eligible, covering about 50 million people, or roughly 27 million of voting age.The programme has long been fiercely criticised by rightwing politicians, including byJair Bolsonaro, although he kept it in place during his presidency.On the eve of the 2022 election, Bolsonaro announced a 50% increase in the monthly payment, prompting Lula’s campaign to file a case with the electoral court alleging abuse of political power and electoral use of the state machinery.The similarities have sparked a debate between those who say Lula isdoing the same thingBolsonaro did four years ago, and others who argue that the two cases are different.The journalist Miriam Leitão wrotefor O Globothat although both Bolsonaro and Lula made the adjustments “out of electoral interest”, the current incumbent’s increase is in fact limited to inflation over the past four years, during which there had been no adjustment.She also noted that Bolsonaro’s increase had an expiry date – precisely at the end of the electoral period – while Lula’s is permanent.Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, agreed. He said that although Lula, like his predecessor, is also being criticised for unveiling a package of benefits on the eve of the election – including apromise to distributeweight-loss jabs free of charge through the public health system – Bolsonaro’s measures were “even more irresponsible from a budgetary point of view”.In addition to increasing benefits for poor families, Bolsonaro introduced temporary monthly payments of up to £727 for two groups that broadly formed part of his support base, taxi drivers and truck drivers, along with a series of other social benefits whose projected impact on the budget was so large that critics dubbed them the“kamikaze” package.Escobar acknowledged that Lula’s intention was also electoral, but said that, as long as the measures comply with the law, “it’s something entirely expected when we’re talking about an incumbent running for re-election, who will try to use the legal mechanisms available to improve their voting numbers”.Some electoral law expertshave saidthat an inflation adjustment is not, in principle, prohibited, but another far-right candidate, theinfluencer Renan Santos, filed a case with the electoral court seeking to suspend the increase until the president-elect takes office. Although critical of the measure, Flávio Bolsonaro has not done the same,reportedlybecause of concern about the impact such a move could have among voters who benefit from the programme.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasJair BolsonaroWeight-loss drugsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position
Content: Houthi troopers on patrol in Sana'a, Yemen. The Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi troopers on patrol in Sana'a, Yemen. The Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAYemenYemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapseRout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon positionPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 18 Sep 2026 10.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.Some Yemeni politicians are claiming that billions of dollars were offered to persuade the forces defending the west coast to abandon their position. It is thought as many as 30,000 well-equipped fighters retreated, raising questions about coordination, readiness and morale.The claim made by the governor of Hadramaut, one of Yemen’s largest governorates, did not identify the source of the payment, but others have tried to draw conclusions from the past links between the United Arab Emirates and the pro-government National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh. The UAE left Yemen in January, but remains bitter at the role played by Saudi Arabia in forcing it out and in the outlawing of the separatist Southern Transitional Council.The Yemeni Nobel peace prize winner Tawakkol Karman has called for an investigation, while another political activist, the Mocha resident Abdu Mukabib, described the withdrawal of forces from the now Houthi-held port city in the early hours of 10 September as a great betrayal.Saleh’s National Resistance Forces have said they made a necessary tactical retreat.Hours before, theHouthishad captured the headquarters of the National Resistance Forces operating along Yemen’s western coast, situated on the high ground of Jabal al-Nar (Fire Mountain) and supposed to contain six military brigades and sophisticated weaponry provided by Saudi Arabia.Mukabib said on his Facebook page that by the time the Houthis entered the city at 6am their forces numbered less than 20: two military vehicles, each carrying five people, and four motorcycles, each carrying two people.He said that what happened, in his words, caused “humiliation” and betrayal to those who trusted the forces they fought alongside. “We are not accusing anyone, but they all participated in betraying us, conspiring against us, selling out our cause and abandoning us.“It was not a withdrawal from weakness or lack of equipment and supplies, but rather a cowardly and shameful withdrawal.”The National Resistance Forces said they had withdrawn after the death of 500 of their soldiers and to prevent encirclement. Saleh has said he is now forming the “Tihami Resistance”, a group that was entirely independent of Yemen national forces.Others point to explanations for the reverse including poor command and control communications that led to slow decision-making, high-level Houthi intelligence and divisions within the anti-Houthi military forces, including the influence of Saudi commanders.Alongside the inadequacies of the UN-backed forces, the Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army, bolstered by Iranian intelligence. They have benefited from the cut-price nature of modern warfare, using cheap drones to harass maritime traffic. But more than 10 years in control of many of Yemen’s key regions and the occasional payoff from Saudi Arabia have swelled their coffers enough to not only buy ballistic missiles, but develop their own indigenous weapon-making infrastructure, becoming less reliant on Iran in the process.Iranian officials insist the Houthis are not a simple proxy force, but have their own unified command structure and set of priorities.The inquest into what is widely regarded as a military catastrophe is not entirely retrospective. Both Yemen government and Saudi forces are urgently reviewing the lessons of defeat to better understand whether the Houthi gains can still be reversed.‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in YemenRead moreIt was claimed that a limited force from the Giants Brigades, a group once linked with the UAE-backed southern separatists, managed to repel the Houthi advance and recapture positions in the days before the fall of Mocha, which could have served as a springboard for regaining the initiative. However, the withdrawal of neighbouring National Resistance units weakened this advance and turned it into a series of retreats.Prof Dr Abdulwahab al-Awaj at Taiz University in Yemen said: “The collapse of the western coastal fronts is not merely a conventional military defeat, but a warning sign of a breakdown in coordination and trust among the anti-Houthi forces. The Houthis exploited this breakdown more than any decisive military superiority.“Regaining the initiative cannot be achieved simply by sending reinforcements. What is needed is a reorganisation of government forces and allied formations under a unified operational vision, addressing security gaps, and building genuine trust on the ground to prevent a recurrence of this scenario.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms | European Union | The Guardian
description: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders
Content: A display board shows prices at a fuel station in Leezen, Germany. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% up on a year ago, while diesel is up 38%.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersView image in fullscreenA display board shows prices at a fuel station in Leezen, Germany. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% up on a year ago, while diesel is up 38%.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersEuropean UnionRecord fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firmsGerman minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leadersJon HenleyEurope correspondent andJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right.With elections due next year in eight EU countries includingFrance, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades.Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on ‌the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies.“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a ⁠barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more ​supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not ‌expect a near-term drop in ‌prices.Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland.Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100.The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an ⁠EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free ​to impose their own taxes.Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France andItaly, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices.In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this weekit would scrap road taxfor 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn.“We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said.France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz.In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38.The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with ​cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest ⁠loans and support measures ​would ​to be ​tied ‌to ​fuel price changes.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all.“Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.”In August, Spaindoubled its diesel tax discountto €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has promised action “soon” to ease the impact of record fuel prices.Berlin cut fuel taxes for two months in May, but that lapsed just as renewed clashes in the Middle East began further pushed up oil prices. Merz’s centre-right CDU was this monthheavily defeated in state electionsin Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD.Two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOil and gas companiesEnergy industryFranceGermanyEuropeFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: BrewDog creditors owed £190m will not be paid in full, say administrators | BrewDog | The Guardian
description: There are ‘insufficient funds’ to pay unpaid wages, tax owed to HMRC and overdue bills, accountants say
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: There are ‘insufficient funds’ to pay unpaid wages, tax owed to HMRC and overdue bills, accountants say
Content: The investments of BrewDog’s 200,000 ‘equity punks’ are now worthless.Photograph: Islandstock/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe investments of BrewDog’s 200,000 ‘equity punks’ are now worthless.Photograph: Islandstock/AlamyBrewDogBrewDog creditors owed £190m will not be paid in full, say administratorsThere are ‘insufficient funds’ to pay unpaid wages, tax owed to HMRC and overdue bills, accountants sayRob DaviesFri 18 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAccountants picking over the remains of BrewDog, the“punk” beer company that collapsed earlier this year, have said that creditors who are owed about £190m will not be paid back.In an update on their progress, administrators at AlixPartners warned there were “insufficient funds” to pay debts in full related to unpaid wages, tax owed to HM Revenue and Customs, and overdue bills from other businesses.Earlier this year, the US cannabis and drinks company Tilray snapped up BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars in a rescue deal for about £33m, agreed after the brewer fell into administration.But the deal in March did not includemost of BrewDog’s chain of bars, with 38 closing and 440 staff losing their jobs.The collapserendered worthlessthe investments of 200,000 “equity punks”, the small investors who crowdfunded the business.AlixPartners admitted on Thursday that creditors owed more than £190m were also unlikely to get their money back.It cited increased costs owing to “unauthorised occupiers” having to be removed from BrewDog’s shuttered bars and the limited sums recovered from the sale of assets, such as vehicles of “old age and varying roadworthiness”.Supposedly “preferential” creditors of the bars business who will not get their money back in full include the UK government.View image in fullscreenThe US cannabis and drinks firm Tilray snapped up BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars in a rescue deal for about £33m earlier this year.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianStaff who were owed £489,000 in wages and holiday pay have already been compensated under the government’s redundancy payment scheme.But AlixPartners said there were not enough funds to repay the government, or to pay £2.4m in taxes owed to HM Revenue and Customs. However, a separate sum of £3.6m owed toHMRCwill be paid back.Unsecured creditors, including a host of British businesses such as Lord’s Cricket Ground, West Ham United FC and Manchester University, will receive less than a penny in the pound.Private equity investor TSG, which bought a 22% stake for £213m in 2017, had its investment wiped out and will not recoup debts of nearly £28m.Lender HSBC is expected to recover about £42m of about £61m it is owed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJames Watt, who co-founded BrewDog with friend Martin Dickie in 2007, has previouslysaid that he was left “heartbroken”by the brewer’s collapse.Watt’s tenure at BrewDog was marked by controversies, including criticism for the dubious taste of marketing stunts and anallegedly “toxic” working culture, for which he apologised.He has since set up several new businesses, including Social Tip, which pays people to make social media posts about brands.After being rebuffed in a bid to buy BrewDog back, he also launched a new beer business, Second Best, and has offered former BrewDog investors free shares in the business.However, multiple people who received offers of sharescomplained to the Information Commissioner’s Office, which regulates data privacy, saying they were concerned Watt had not obtained their contact details legally.Watt has denied any wrongdoing.Explore more on these topicsBrewDogBeerFoodPubsHMRCData protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC cash reserves hit lowest level in a decade after big single-year spend | BBC | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Reserves at public service arm drop 66% as broadcaster undertakes large cuts in effort to save £500m
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Exclusive: Reserves at public service arm drop 66% as broadcaster undertakes large cuts in effort to save £500m
Content: Staff questioned how the BBC’s finances had been allowed to deteriorate so badly.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenStaff questioned how the BBC’s finances had been allowed to deteriorate so badly.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersBBCBBC cash reserves hit lowest level in a decade after big single-year spendExclusive: Reserves at public service arm drop 66% as broadcaster undertakes large cuts in effort to save £500mMichael SavageMedia editorFri 18 Sep 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBBChas spent hundreds of millions of pounds of its cash reserves in a single year, increasing concerns at the corporation over the perilous state of its finances.Cash reserves at the BBC’s public service arm slumped by 66% in the last financial year, from £369m in 2025 to just £125m, according to analysis by the Guardian. This is the lowest figure in the last decade of accounts.Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, usedan internal call with staff last weekto warn that slumping cash reserves and maxed-out dividends from the corporation’s commercial operation meant there was “not a lot of elbow room for anything”.He made the call after staff questioned how the BBC’s finances had been allowed to deteriorate so badly. The broadcaster is currentlyengaging in huge cuts, including up to 2,000 jobs, designed to save £500m.BBC insiders said cash reserves were being spent to ensure the BBC could keep investing in content and make the changes needed to adapt to digital audiences.TheBBC licence feehas lost about £1.3bn in value in real terms since 2017. This has been a result of fee freezes and a faster than predicted rise in the number of people choosing not to pay it.The broadcaster is having to make painful changes to deal with the rising costs of TV production, growing competition from the likes of Netflix and YouTube, and rapidly changing patterns of how people consume media.The financial decline has coincided with a huge amount of staff turnover at the top of the corporation. Its chief financial officer, chief technology officer and chief operating officer have all left in the last 18 months. They will soon be joined by the chief people officer.Tim Davie, the BBC’s previous director general, resigned last year after criticism over a Panorama episode that spliced together parts of a Donald Trump speech. The US president hassince taken legal action. The BBC has apologised for the cut, but maintained it did not defame him.The cash crunch comes at a difficult time for Brittin, who took over from Davie in May. He wants to transform the BBC to cope with the demands of digital audiences, but major changes require upfront investment.He is also engaged in delicate negotiations with the government over the BBC’s future funding model, under which those who watch streaming services could be asked to pay the BBC licence fee. Currently, only those who watch live TV and the BBC’s iPlayer have to pay the fee.Abi Watson,﻿ at Enders Analysis, said the fall in reserves was part of an underlying depletion of the BBC’s financial cushion that had been “building for years”.“The BBC hasn’t run out of money, but the fall in public-service cash leaves it with considerably less room to absorb further pressures or fund change,” she said. “And this isn’t a new problem.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The latest savings requirement predated [Brittin’s] arrival. The BBC has already reduced headcount, rationalised its estate and changed its commissioning mix. Commissioned hours, excluding news and sport, are down 20% since 2016-17. Further savings increasingly mean decisions about output.”Alex DeGroote, an independent media analyst, said the upcoming redundancies would add extra costs in the short term: “[It] will drain further the cash as staff are paid off upfront, before the benefit emerges from a lower cost base.”He also said a bumper £197m in dividends the BBC received from its commercial arm in the last financial year could not be relied upon. “The internal dividend amount is well above trend and it’s hard to believe it’s sustainable at that level, particularly in this trading environment.”The BBC reported a £121m deficit for the last financial year, more than the £33m deficit it had predicted.A BBC spokesperson said: “Like many in the media industry, the BBC is facing considerable financial challenges, which is why we’re making significant cost savings across the organisation.“The drawdown of cash reserves has enabled us to manage pressures on licence fee income while continuing to prioritise spending for audiences and invest in our digital transformation.”Explore more on these topicsBBCBBC licence feePublic service broadcastingMedia businessJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Retail sales bounce back in Great Britain amid brighter signs for economy | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Latest data to defy economic gloom shows 0.5% rise boosted by purchases of sports items, aircon units and fans during heatwaves
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Latest data to defy economic gloom shows 0.5% rise boosted by purchases of sports items, aircon units and fans during heatwaves
Content: The 0.5% rise in sales marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a 0.5% fall registered in July.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe 0.5% rise in sales marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a 0.5% fall registered in July.Photograph: Yui Mok/PARetail industryRetail sales bounce back in Great Britain amid brighter signs for economyLatest data to defy economic gloom shows 0.5% rise boosted by purchases of sports items, aircon units and fans during heatwavesBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyFri 18 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRetail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget.TheOffice for National Statistics(ONS) said the volume of goods sold rose 0.5% month on month in August, defying analyst expectations of a 0.2% fall.It marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a0.5% month-on-month fall in July.The summer heatwaves fuelled increased sales of items including fans, air-conditioning units, sports merchandise and clothing in the three months to August.Next forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts salesRead moreThe unexpected sales boost is the latest positive update on the state of the economy for the government, after asurprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic productin July that was reported by the ONS last week.“August’s warm weather delayed the usual shift towards autumn purchases, but retailers successfully kept consumers spending,” said Sandra Prince, the head of corporate consumer at Lloyds. “The late bank holiday weekend and back-to-school shopping are also likely to have supported demand, with online sales among the areas seeing the biggest boost.”Across the three-month summer period sales rose 2.4% year on year, again significantly above forecasts of a 1.9% rise.Among the strongest performers were department stores, which recorded a sales rise of 1.8% month on month in August – a bounce back after a fall in July, which the ONS attributed to stock availability problems.Non-store retailing, primarily online shopping, rose by 1.7% month on month, a major bounce back after sales fell 3.7% the previous month due to heavy promotional activity driving June sales.Overall, non-store retailers enjoyed a strong summer with a 5.4% sales rise across the three-month period.Retailers selling alcohol and beverages performed well across all three months to August 2026, the ONS reported, which they attributed to promotions, the hot weather and the men’s football World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFuel sales dropped again, down by 1.3% in August and 2.5% across the three-month period as motorists cut back on non-essential journeys after big increases in the price of petrol and diesel since the start of the Iran war in February.UK petrol prices have hit thehighest level in four yearsas the conflict in the Middle East intensifies.On Thursday the Bank of England monetary policy committee voted tohold the base rate at 3.75%. However, it indicated that the latest rise in energy prices because of the conflict was likely to result in a rates increase to keep inflation in check. Inflationrose to 3.1% in August, from 2.9% in July.“There are some challenging headwinds for consumers to navigate as we head into autumn,” said Andy Carlisle, the consumer goods and retail lead at Accenture.“Higher energy bills, food, fuel and transport prices continue to weigh on purse strings. We’re beginning to see consumers preparing for these pressures, prioritising everyday needs while showing greater caution around discretionary and bigger-ticket purchases.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryConsumer spendingEconomic growth (GDP)EconomicsEnglandScotlandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Warren Buffett steps down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway after over 50 years | Warren Buffett | The Guardian
description: ‘Father Time always wins,’ Buffett, 96, says as his son, Howard, steps in as the $1tn conglomerate’s new chair
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: ‘Father Time always wins,’ Buffett, 96, says as his son, Howard, steps in as the $1tn conglomerate’s new chair
Content: Warren Buffett attends the Berkshire Hathaway Inc annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on 3 May 2024.Photograph: Scott Morgan/ReutersView image in fullscreenWarren Buffett attends the Berkshire Hathaway Inc annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on 3 May 2024.Photograph: Scott Morgan/ReutersWarren BuffettWarren Buffett steps down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway after over 50 years‘Father Time always wins,’ Buffett, 96, says as his son, Howard, steps in as the $1tn conglomerate’s new chairLauren ArataniFri 18 Sep 2026 10.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWarren Buffett is stepping down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway, the company that he took from a faltering textile manufacturer into a $1tn conglomerate over the course of 60 years.Buffett’s son, Howard, 71, will take over as chair. Buffett, 96, cited his age as the main reason behind the transition, noting that he has a one-year-old great-grandchild who is “moving a bit faster than I am these days”.“Serving as your chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted,” Buffett, 96, said in aletterto shareholders. “Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me. He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead.”Buffett said he will remain as chair emeritus and a director on the board. He left his post as CEO ofBerkshireHathaway in May 2025, shocking the audience of thousands at the company’s annual shareholder meeting in Omaha, Nebraska. Greg Abel, vice–chair of the company, replaced him as CEO.‘Be fearful when others are greedy’: Warren Buffett’s sharpest lessons in investingRead moreKnown as the “Oracle of Omaha”, Buffett built a reputation as a sharp-eyed investor, building up Berkshire Hathaway into a $1tn conglomerate. The company owns dozens of companies in construction, manufacturing, consumer goods and insurance, along with being a major investor in some of the biggest companies on the stock market, including Nvidia, Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta.Bloomberg places Buffett’snet worthat $145bn, making him the 10th richest person in the world.Howard Buffett, known as “Howie”, is Buffett’s second child out of three and was long planned to be his father’s successor as chair of the company, having served on the board since 1993.“He is getting it because he’s my son,” Buffett told the Wall Street Journal in January 2025. “I’m very, very, very lucky in the fact that I trust all three of my children.”In a statement, Abel said that Buffett’s impact on the company “is without parallel in the history of American business”.“The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian,” he said.Explore more on these topicsWarren BuffettBerkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The man’s a psychopath when it comes to hedgerows’: Derek vs Derek, the unexpectedly heartwarming doc about farmers at war | Movies | The Guardian
description: One Devon farmer, called Derek, is committed to rewilding his land. His neighbour, also a Derek, tends cattle and crops. What happened when a film-maker decided to follow the bickering pair?
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: One Devon farmer, called Derek, is committed to rewilding his land. His neighbour, also a Derek, tends cattle and crops. What happened when a film-maker decided to follow the bickering pair?
Content: At loggerheads … Derek Gow and Derek Banbury.Photograph: Joss BarrattView image in fullscreenAt loggerheads … Derek Gow and Derek Banbury.Photograph: Joss BarrattMoviesInterview‘The man’s a psychopath when it comes to hedgerows’: Derek vs Derek, the unexpectedly heartwarming doc about farmers at warPatrick BarkhamOne Devon farmer, called Derek, is committed to rewilding his land. His neighbour, also a Derek, tends cattle and crops. What happened when a film-maker decided to follow the bickering pair?Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerek Gow and Derek Banbury should hate each other. Gow is an outspoken rewilder widely credited with bringing back the beaver in England. As he returns his Devon sheep farm to wild nature, he is also breeding storks, wildcats, red-backed shrikes, glowworms and even adders to return to the countryside. Over the hedge, Banbury, his neighbour, is proud to be an intensive farmer, producing milk and beef cattle behind tightly clipped hedges.“It’s like he’s just gone mad,” says Banbury of Gow at the start ofDerek vs Derek, an illuminating and unexpectedly funny new documentary that follows the pair over three years. “And the madness is now crossing the road on to my land.”What begins as a portrait of neighbours at war, with no hope of bridging the chasm between modern chemical farmers and idealistic rewilders, or between the needs of food production and the worsening extinction crisis, is slowly and subtly upended, as the two Dereks learn to live alongside each other and hopeful seeds of common ground are sown.Documentary-maker James Dawson started following Gow as he sold the last of his sheep, planning a film about the dramatic changes brought about by rewilding his farm. Then, when Dawson first visited Gow, he was put up at the Banburys, where wife Linda has turned former pigsties and old sheds into holiday cottages. As soon as Dawson met Derek Banbury over breakfast in the farmhouse kitchen, he knew he had to make a rather different film.As well as a boundary, both Dereks share a certain charisma, bloody-mindedness, business acumen and, actually, a love of animals. Gow is an imposing, fast-talking, sweary Scot who criticises “showers of morons” in conservation for convening endless committees while species plummet towards extinction. He’s equally disdainful of farmers “spaffing” public money on Land Rovers and sticking sheep on overgrazed pastures and feeding them fish-meal from the Gambia, “raping what’s left of a disastrous environment to produce something that nobody wants”.Meanwhile, Banbury, who has an impish grin and quick wit, is unrepentant about agribusiness. “I love farming,” he declares in the film. “Intensive farming, that’s supplying the world with food. The population’s getting bigger. It’s not getting smaller, and everyone is going to be happy if they’ve got full bellies. I’ve done it for 50 years and I won’t change. I won’t change.” Or will he?double quotation markThe auctioneer called out: ‘Derek, hair and makeup’s waiting,’ right in front of everyone, and they all started laughingDerek BanburyI find both Dereks in the Banburys’ kitchen, where Linda is doling out tea and cake and Banbury’s four grownup children (three daughters and one son) and dogs are bustling around. They are preparing to welcome an audience of farmers, neighbours and friends to a special preview of Derek vs Derek, which is being shown on a temporary screen erected in the Banburys’ biggest, newest barn.Banbury is laughing, but he is also raging: the production company was duty-bound to bring in a health and safety officer, and he’s been instructed to reduce the number of chairs in the barn. “It’s my farm! Nobody tells me what to do!” he says. “I’ve done what I wanted for 50 years.”“It’s in case there’s a fire,” reasons his eldest daughter, Katie.“Oh, for God’s sake! It’s a steel building and concrete walls. If there’s a fire, people will run out quickly.”“My Derek doesn’t get cross often,” says Linda. “But he’s cross now.”It takes all four Banbury children to calm Derek down. A few chairs are shuffled around to enable a swift evacuation. Meanwhile, Banbury admits he was “a little bit” reluctant to appear in a film where he assumed Gow would be the hero. “Then James [Dawson] started going outside and filming some of my animals. Then they came up with a little payment, and it started from there.”View image in fullscreenField of dreams … Farmer and rewilding advocate Derek Gow.Photograph: Joss BarrattWhen Dawson’s cameras followed Banbury to the local cattle market, the farmer got some stick. The auctioneer called out “‘Oh Derek you’re needed, hair and makeup’s waiting for you,’ right in front of everyone, and everyone started laughing.” When Banbury told a spraying contractor that he and Gow would soon be on The One Show, the contractor replied: “What, as the Teletubbies?”Banbury doesn’t mind because, in a way, he is the hero of the film. As well as documenting the transformation of Gow’s land from grim mudbath to natural paradise, the film follows Banbury’s journey from feeling a visceral dislike of wild boar, storks and beavers to acknowledging the losses brought about by intensive farming. Linda, his perceptive wife, who preaches tolerance and an acceptance of beavers, is a second breakout star.The Banburys and Gow received a standing ovation at film festivals in Thessaloniki, Greece, and in Sheffield. Banbury, who has never before visited Mayfair in central London, thinks he might have to buy a new suit for the film’s UK premiere there. How does he feel he comes across? “I’ve got more confident as I’ve got older and I know what I’m talking about. I’m proud to be a farmer and I’ve tried to do the best I can. We’re tied a bit by the price of milk, but we just keep going, we keep struggling on and we love what we do.”His father started out with just 14 cows, and in those days he could support his family with a small farm of less than 150 acres. Like most farmers, Banbury has had to expand – and intensify production – to survive. His farm has become a small village of barns housing 200 milking cows, with 600 in total. While sparrows still chirrup on the farm and swallows dip over the pond, Banbury has noticed the loss of nature as he fertilises, sprays and takes three or four cuts of silage each year. “I wish there was more insects and birds and bees but I don’t study that. I study my crops,” he says in the film.Dawson documents the tensions when rewilding and intensive farming share the same corner of north-west Devon. Gow’s wild boar escape and rootle up Banbury’s pasture. Banbury has the boar shot. Banbury “hates” storks, and don’t talk to him about beavers, which are acclaimed by conservationists for creating new wetlands that become havens for wildlife: “I can’t see that they do any good at all. They just do vicious damage,” he thunders. When Gow writes a book about the history of wolves in Britain and hosts a conference considering their reintroduction, Banbury and other local farmers are apoplectic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd yet, Banbury is taken to see Gow’s meadows, which after unpromising beginnings, are today burgeoning with rare birds, wildflowers and butterflies, and admits “we’ve got to have areas like this for the wildlife”. Gow does not want to rewild the world, but suggests if every farmer set aside 10% of their least productive land for wildlife, it could reverse the extinction crisis. “I hate to say it but sometimes he’s right,” nods Banbury on film.View image in fullscreenBattle fields … Dereks Banbury and Gow.Photograph: Joss Barratt“The man’s a psychopath when it comes to hedgerows,” Gow initially says of Banbury, but as the film progresses, there is talk of Banbury allowing hedges to grow wild and create corridors for nature to move through his neat green fields. So will he? “It depends on the land. It depends if we’re paid for it,” he tells me. Banbury is due to re-fence his fields this autumn; Gow hopes he will make a bit more space for nature.For all Gow’s bristle, Linda recognises him as a “big Scottish softie at heart”. Has Gow’s view of farmers softened as well? “I do have great sympathy for them, especially the older men,” he says. “Some of them are just bastards. They are hard, hard farmers but they know what has happened. They know of the loss of nature. These inflexible and difficult old men are the last generation who understand that.”Today, Gow gives rewilding talks with illustrations from the Ladybird books of the 1950s and 60s that recall a lost British countryside – “pictures of the redshanks with chicks and hedgehogs and bats in these beautiful woodlands under a full moon at night. And you look and think: that’s attainable. It’s not alarming. It’s not scary. It’s actually something that’s quite alluring.”’double quotation markMost conservationists have to understand farming and farmers better and, despite all the rhetoric, I’m not sure they doDerek GowGow’s latest big idea is that farmers could be paid to do what he does: breed rare wild animals in captivity and release them. They would then be invested in seeing local populations of “their” wild animals thrive. “They’re the guys that are sitting in the pubs at night, they’re talking to their neighbours. If there are issues, it’s much easier to resolve them amongst themselves,” he says. “As a farmer, you become part of the solution. You’d feel good. But most conservationists have to understand farming and farmers better and, despite all the rhetoric, I’m not sure they do.”Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to GazaRead moreMore than 300 farmers and neighbours turn up for the Banburys’ special screening, where they are served local cider, pasties and ice-cream. They laugh loudest at Banbury’s put-downs of rewilding. But, as Gow says afterwards, “when the film finished, no one was arguing” against the facts of nature loss. As well as a cinematic release, Derek vs Derek will be shown at special on-farm screenings across the country. Its makers hope it might forge new conversations and even new working relationships between farmers, conservationists and rewilders.Has the two Dereks’ relationship been strengthened by the film? Gow took the Banburys to see flamingoes when they visited the film festival in Thessaloniki together. He also ensured Derek and Linda found a cab after the show in Sheffield. The first thing Gow asks when he pops into the Banburys’ kitchen the morning after the screening – after ribbing them about their St George’s flags flying from their farm buildings – is whether he can borrow their trailer. While he’s there, Linda serves him another of her generous cooked breakfasts.Are Derek and Derek friends? I ask Banbury. “Yeah!” he beams. A big sincere smile. “You can’t be no other can you, when you’re neighbours? He’d do anything for me. And I’d do anything for him.”Derek vs Derekisin UK cinemasfrom 2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFarmingWildlifeConservationinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I toured with a hole in my brain. I don’t regret a thing’: punk duo Lambrini Girls on fighting extreme times with extreme measures | Music | The Guardian
description: Their debut stormed the charts and wowed Iggy Pop, but health crises threatened to derail the Brighton duo. Now they’re back, taking aim at the manosphere, fascism and the ruling class
Author: Kate Hutchinson
Headline: Their debut stormed the charts and wowed Iggy Pop, but health crises threatened to derail the Brighton duo. Now they’re back, taking aim at the manosphere, fascism and the ruling class
Content: ‘Do we get branded misandrists? Of course we fucking do’ … Phoebe Lunny (left) and Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Jessie MorganView image in fullscreen‘Do we get branded misandrists? Of course we fucking do’ … Phoebe Lunny (left) and Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Jessie MorganMusic‘I toured with a hole in my brain. I don’t regret a thing’: punk duo Lambrini Girls on fighting extreme times with extreme measuresTheir debut stormed the charts and wowed Iggy Pop, but health crises threatened to derail the Brighton duo. Now they’re back, taking aim at the manosphere, fascism and the ruling classKate HutchinsonFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt a last-minute surprise show in London, the British punk duo Lambrini Girls are sharing their stage with a continuous tide of crowd surfers. They move almost as one, a jumble of limbs rippling over a sea of bodies – emboldened, perhaps, by the band’s vow to double up as security guards. “If you don’t feel safe, tell us and we’ll punch them in the dick!” shouts Phoebe Lunny, the lead vocalist and guitarist.She also requests that people pick up anyone who falls over in the moshpit and goes around with the mic asking fans to introduce themselves if they are “queer legends” (there are many). “This show is as much yours as it is ours,” Lunny announces, before she and the bassist Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez pummel everyone with shouty rants, furious beats and sludgy grunge.Backstage, before the gig, the two Lambrini Girls are sitting on a battered sofa. Lunny, 29, is the chattier of the two, with bleached-blond waves and broken Mary Janes. Macieira-Boşgelmez is a year older, with red hair and a quiet poise, that seems at odds with her headbanging stage presence. They’re not long back from a European tour where their visuals made their politics plain. In France, the screen read “Fuck Marine Le Pen”. For London, it’s “Fuck Nigel Farage”.“The issues we address are not specific to the UK,” says Macieira-Boşgelmez. “Oppression is growing. People’s anger is growing.”View image in fullscreen‘The system is so unfair’ … Phoebe Lunny and Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez on stage in London last year.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsTheir second album, No Refunds, was announced this week, capping a successful few years for the band who formed in Brighton in 2019. There have been magazine covers, support slots with Iggy Pop, Idles andAmyl and the Sniffersand a remix by the queer idol Peaches. In January 2025, their debut albumWho Let the Dogs Outcharted at No 16 – not bad, given that it contains a song called Cuntology 101. Recently, they’ve been able to pack in their 9-to-5s, although they feel a little ashamed about it. “The guilt is extremely prevalent,” says Macieira-Boşgelmez. “It is on my mind every single day. You watch your friends work so fucking hard …” Lunny agrees: “The system is so unfair.”The band has a sense of humour – their debut EP featured a cover illustration of a giant flaming turd and one early song is effectively just a call-and-response of “Craig David” – but they’re serious about confronting that unfair system. At the London show, their touring drummer, Misha Phillips, delivers an impassioned speech about transgender liberation before they unleash one of their most popular songs, Terf Wars. These biting calls for social justice mean they’re often compared to riot grrrl bands such as Bikini Kill (for whom Lambrini Girls will be opening next week in Brooklyn). As the duo have evolved, so has their mission to represent “the disenfranchised, disaffected and disillusioned”, Lunny says.Lunny was raised in Sussex by a single mother, a primary school teacher and socialist, who politicised her. Lunny did a music BTec: “I didn’t pass and went to the University of Burger King.” Macieira-Boşgelmez, who is of Turkish and Portuguese heritage, moved to the UK to become a musician and says she has always had “a really strong sense of justice” from growing up “financially privileged. My parents made sure that I knew that.”In September 2025, just as Lambrini Girls were really popping off, Macieira-Boşgelmez took time out from touring (a friend stepped in to cover her). She had been diagnosed with autism and bipolar disorder four years prior andwrote a candid, moving social media postabout the distressing effect of touring on her health. “It was slowly accumulating and gradually getting worse and that was influencing my behaviour and me not being aware of my limits,” she says now.When Macieira-Boşgelmez returned in February 2026, the duo went to play Australia for the first time. During one gig, Lunny leapt from a balcony and injured herself. She was told it was “just whiplash”. It was six weeks before she discovered what was up. “It was only when I was in a hotel at 2am, fitting and passing out on the floor, that it was obvious that something was really wrong,” she says.Lunny had a small bone fracture in her neck, which had punctured a hole in her brain membrane. Fluid had been draining out. “So now I have a lopsided brain,” she says, matter-of-factly.She was forced to rest for nearly four months, but being laid up in bed wasn’t her style. “So then I started touring with a hole in my brain. It was the hardest thing I’ve ever had to do.” She took flights in a wheelchair. “I had to lay side of stage, force myself up with willpower and rely on adrenaline to carry me. As soon as I was off stage, the pain would disorient me to the point where I didn’t know where I was. The thing is, I insisted on touring as it offered me 40 minutes of feeling like myself again. I don’t regret a thing.”View image in fullscreen‘The world is a far darker place than it was two years ago’ … Lunny (left) and Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Jessie MorganShe had two rounds of surgery in July this year and feels as if she is finally recovering, but says: “I’d kill to have a body that was capable of what it was able to do before.” The new album includes an acoustic track, Spilt, an unwavering look at her booze-fuelled party era. “I feel very fortunate that I can’t really relate to that song any more and that’s testament to growing up a bit,” she says. “I’ve had so many health scares. I’m very restricted with my drinking.”But, for the most part, No Refunds is bigger and beefier, railing against fascism and “the ruling class”, Lunny says. “We’re trying to shake people and say fucking get off your asses. The world is a far darker place now than it was two years ago. Even though we thought it couldn’t get any worse, it has.”Musically, it strikes a balance between corrosive grunge low-end, bristling punk intensity and the arch delivery of Britpop, with some of their peppiest songs yet – although a suggestion of Elastica, a female-fronted band, elicits the subtlest of shared sideways glances. “The majority of my influences from that era, because it was so male-dominated, are men,” says Lunny. “I’m a huge fan of Blur.”There is some classic Lambrini Girls sarcasm, such as Is This AI?, Don’t Talk to Me Till I’ve Had My Abortion and the lead single Cult of Celebrity, which references the Epstein files (“Oh, how the other half live / … on Lolita island”). But the fun-poking has largely been replaced by fury; the lyrics are less direct, more conceptual. “I don’t want to go through a list of societal ills and be like: right, we’ve done that,” Lunny says, mimicking ticking off a list. “Because I feel like that trivialises it.” A lot of the last album was “I don’t like this and here is why”, but No Refunds is more about “trying to build a world”.View image in fullscreenStrength and secuirty … Lunny (left) and Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/RedfernsRegarding another new song, Gaza Beach, Lunny says she “wanted to write a song about Palestine for years, but I couldn’t do it. Obviously, to encapsulate a genocide is incredibly difficult to do in a way which doesn’t sensationalise the suffering of hundreds of thousands of people”. But seeing an AI-generated video of how a glitzy new resort in the territory might look gave her the idea. “I started thinking: well, what would that actually look like? I felt like I was able to convey the moroseness and the insidiousness of this genocide [but also] encapsulate the imperialist settlement, which was really important to do.” She is encouraged to see more artists speaking out about it, too. “You don’t have to write a song about it, but you have to use your voice.”Macieira-Boşgelmez cites Macklemore being criticised by Pink forhis pro-Palestine commentson Ed Sheeran’s tour (we spoke before Macklemore was kicked off the tour and Sheeran faceda retaliation of his own). “Even though there are some artists that are speaking out about this, the backlash you face is still incredibly disproportionate,” she says.In April, Lunny revealed that she was oncearrested for harassmentand faced a possible six-month jail sentence after she emailed promoters to warn them about booking an allegedly “dodgy” male musician. The case was dropped, although Lunny was made to write a letter of apology to the man. “It was a long time ago; I can’t say specifics,” she says now.Abusive men and abuses of power are recurrent themes on No Refunds, including one track that is specifically about the manosphere (The Basement).Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutralityRead more“We talk about male violence a lot, we talk about the oppression of women a lot,” she says. “Do we get branded misandrists? Of course we fucking do. The people that brand us that are ‘incels’. We are not misandrists. We both have a lot of male friends that we adore.” It’s more, they say, about taking aim at the “capitalist patriarchy”.It’s a grim world, but Lambrini Girls aren’t without optimism. “There is still a lot of value to be found in community,” Lunny says. “When I feel hopeless about the rise of the far right and us edging towards a new iteration of techno feudalism and that AI might kill us all, I have strength and security in my friends around me. I look at Selin and she gives a real fuck.Thatgives me hope.”The community at Lambrini Girls’ shows is just as strong. Towards the end of the London gig, a fan scales a large circular rig in the centre of the space. For a moment, their legs dangle down precariously, hovering above the pit. There is a collective sharp intake of breath. But soon hands are thrust aloft, fingers clasp around their ankles and the lone ranger drops into a throng of arms.“Solidarity will prevail in times like these through listening to each other, uplifting each other, supporting each other,” says Macieira-Boşgelmez. “As much as you might feel it, you are not alone.”No Refunds is released via City Slang on 15 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockBrightonPunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The damage was much worse than I had imagined’: the shocking inside story of Salman Rushdie’s survival | Movies | The Guardian
description: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life
Author: Claire Armitstead
Headline: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life
Content: Eliza Griffiths, Salman Rushdie and Alex Gibney.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEliza Griffiths, Salman Rushdie and Alex Gibney.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘The damage was much worse than I had imagined’: the shocking inside story of Salman Rushdie’s survivalClaire ArmitsteadAfter ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous lifeFri 18 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic friend, who told her the man she had married just a year earlier, and who had set off the previous night for a speaking engagement nearly 400 miles away, had been hurt. “What kind of hurt?” she panicked. Turning on the television, she was assaulted by blurry images of chaos on stage as audience members surged to the rescue. Her husband, SirSalman Rushdie, had been stabbed multiple times and was fighting for his life.Within days of desperately chartering a plane to fly her to Rushdie’s hospital bedside, not knowing if he was alive or dead, Griffiths – a poet and photographer who works under her full name Rachel Eliza Griffiths – had begun to make a video diary recording his treatment and recovery. “When it had become likely that I was going to survive,” says Rushdie drily, “I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this. By which I meant something very modest: maybe she would take a picture of me on her iPhone every couple of days just to document the recovery, but Eliza had bigger ideas.”One of her first ideas was that it needed to be shot not on a phone but with a proper camera. “I explicitly remember when the box arrived with my camera,” Griffiths says. “I cried because it was reconnecting me to my identity as an artist. The person I used to be, even just 24 hours ago, was being returned to me. It was giving both of us this permission to continue to be artists and tell our stories together.”The couple are sitting in separate rooms of their New York home to tell their shared story over video link. Griffiths is warm and animated, as the memories rush out. Rushdie is more reserved and sardonic, smartly turned out, with only a black lens over his right eye to attest to the horrific injuries he suffered.Both have already published memoirs about the experience: Rushdie’sKnife, in 2024 and Griffiths’The Flower Bearersearlier this year. Now they are the subjects of an unflinching film, Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, which combines Griffiths’ video diary with archive footage from the period following the fateful day in 1989 when a fatwa was issued against Rushdie for the offence allegedly caused to Islam by the supposed blasphemy of his fourth novel, The Satanic Verses. Iran’s then supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini called for the execution of the 41-year-old author and his publishers, forcing him into hiding, where he remained, under armed guard, for nine years.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a very intimate point of view from love between two people in a new marriage’ … Griffiths and Rushdie.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIt is hard to say which time zone of the film is more viscerally shocking: the grisly footage of Rushdie being stitched and stapled back together in 2022, or the murderous hatred that roars out from news headlines in the months and years following the fatwa. In the US, the office of the Riverdale Press newspaper is firebombed after it runs an editorial about the book defending free expression; in Pakistan, six people are killed in riots; in Japan, a translator is stabbed to death; in Italy, another translator is stabbed in his home, while, in London, an effigy of a mutilated Rushdie is paraded through the streets by a furious crowd, some of whom declare on camera that nothing less than hanging will satisfy them.Incorporating the archive footage was the idea ofAlex Gibney, an Oscar-winning documentary maker (his newest film is a four-hour study of Elon Musk) who was invited by Rushdie and Griffiths to direct – or, as he describes it, “curate” – the film. Rushdie was initially opposed to dredging up the past, reasoning that his attacker – known simply as “A” in both his memoir and the film – was “just one crazy kid”. “I don’t see it as being representative of a larger matter,” he insists. “I think I was unfortunate in that this person was motivated by who knows what influences, and at this venue where he came to attack me, there was absolutely no security protection at all.”The venue he was speaking at was at the heart of an idealistic community at Chautauqua in upstate New York, whose naivety in not having a single security guard in the hall Rushdie now sharply questions. Yet just three years before the attack, at a talk hosted by the Guardian at the Sheldonian in Oxford for his Booker-shortlisted novel Quichotte, he was tetchy to find plainclothes police at the entrances, complaining that only in the UK was such security still deemed necessary. “Well the thing is,” he says now, “in the preceding 20 years, I’d done hundreds of public events all over the world with no trouble, and it didn’t seem necessary to surround the Sheldonian with armed men.”double quotation markThere was absolutely no security protection at allAs the film reveals, not everyone shared his confidence. The Palestinian-American historian Edward Said predicted that the main threat Rushdie faced would not be soon from a religious fanatic, but at some time in the future from a random individual. The film’s power lies in the connection it forges between the two time frames: it demonstrates that the body in the bed in 2022, with a destroyed eye bulging from its socket, is what happens if the right to free speech is violently and publicly opposed.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to understand this story as a kind of healing film’ … Alex Gibney.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianGriffiths, who is Rushdie’s fifth wife, was an 11-year-old growing up in Delaware when the fatwa was issued. Gibney was “a wayward film-maker in search of a career” who had made a few TV documentaries and was trying to write some scripts. “I was doing a lot of reading because I didn’t get much work, so I was well aware of Salman as a novelist and an essayist,” he says. “But I think we [he and his editor] had forgotten, too, how vast it was. You know, you go through a process, starting by saying, OK, let’s see what kind of clips there are about the fatwa, and we were stunned.”He concedes that Rushdie would have preferred less of the footage. “Salman doesn’t want to be defined by this. He bristles, and I understand it. You want to be defined by your artistic work, not by the political opportunism of a down-on-his-luck tyrant. But at the same time, I think it was hugely important for the audience to understand just how global it was.”Gibney’s original idea was to model the film on Dennis Potter’s hit 1980s TV series The Singing Detective, based on Potter’s experience of struggling with the chronic skin disease psoriasis. “The simple story is that he comes in, in terrible shape, and over the course of the series, he recovers physically. But in the meantime, his life passes before his eyes. He thinks about his childhood. He hallucinates … and he imagines bits and pieces of his life through his own detective fiction. Salman was on his own path with Knife, and in some ways, they kind of coalesced. But ultimately, I did the smart thing with a writer of Salman’s stature, which is just to use enormous portions of Knife as the narration for the film.”Though Rushdie wryly complains that he is the only one of the trio to receive no production credits, apart from “based on the book by …” (Griffiths has two, as cinematographer and executive producer), it gives full range to his “free-associating” mind, flitting from literary citation to animation and movie excerpts.View image in fullscreen‘The film becomes a third perspective’ … Rushdie.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn one scene, he recalls a famous image from Georges Méliès’ classic short of 1902, Le Voyage dans La Lune, of a spacecraft crashing into the eye of the moon. “This is the literary device known as foreshadowing,” he wrote in the memoir.
