The night before the attack, happy because he was in love and had just signed off the proofs for his next novel (2023’s Victory City), he sent Griffiths a photograph of the moon seen from his hotel balcony. “Here’s a man in the dark, ignorant of the danger that’s already very close … the future rushes at him while he sleeps … Except strangely it’s really the past returning, my own past rushing at me … a masked man with a knife seeking to carry out a death order from three decades ago.”Seeing the image reproduced for reference in a printed text is nothing like experiencing it on the big screen, juxtaposed with Griffiths’ unstinting footage of what Rushdie described as “my bulging boiled-egg eye [hanging] out of my face, the iris improbably perched on the swollen white …”Why did Griffiths – and by extension the film – put so much emphasis on the horror of Rushdie’s damaged eye? “I think for me, the camera is part of how unbearable it was, and the shock for anyone to see their loved one being so wounded, so damaged, so violently attacked by another human being,” she replies. “And so I feel that, though the camera could be a sort of screen, also it was so open and you can’t look away.”She continues: “It’s a very intimate point of view from love between two people in a new marriage, and this is where we’re at. It was just I’m moved to pick up the camera, or I can’t believe we’re in this situation. The camera is real, and I’m not. This can’t be happening to us. But then I’m like: ‘Well, it’s real because I can see it in the camera.’”In the early days, when Griffiths was filming by day and camping out in Rushdie’s hospital room by night, she knew she could not show him what he looked like, any more than she could reveal her own fear and distress, which spill out in a tearful selfie monologue. It was only after he was finally allowed home that she asked if he’d like to see it. “I hadn’t really sat by myself and looked at much of it either,” she says. “When we finally did look at it, we did it together, and then it kind of became: ‘Oh, this is bigger than us, and maybe other people need to see it.’”For Rushdie, the viewing was a rollercoaster. “First of all, I thought I looked really much worse than I thought I looked – the damage was much worse than I had imagined it to be. And then I felt quite pleased because I thought I don’t look like that any more. I look like this. So it actually dramatised the recovery.”View image in fullscreen‘I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this’ … Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie.Photograph: Altitude FilmThe final minutes of the film show the couple revisiting the scene of the attack, and laying to rest some of the misrememberings. Early on, Rushdie berates himself for submitting to his attacker. “I ask myself: why didn’t I do anything? Why did I just stand there? Well, in the film, you see that I didn’t just stand there. I tried to get away from him. So memory and reality are sometimes at odds with each other, and the film becomes a third perspective.”Gibney tried, and failed, to get an interview in jail with “A”, the destroyer, who was wrestled to the floor and whose motives remain a mystery. “I wanted to understand this story as a kind of healing film, which I think we all of us need, and also about their investment in their love for each other,” he says. “So while it’s gruesome in parts and difficult and deals with the dark places of the human psyche, nevertheless, it finds a way out to a really good place.”Rushdie and Griffiths had been together for five years when the attack happened, having met at the opening night of a festival that he had co-founded and chaired for the writers’ charity PEN. Though they didn’t hide their relationship, they did not flaunt it either, so that at the time of the attack, few people beyond their immediate friends and family knew they were married. “Being private is part of my personality,” says Griffiths. While the attack shoved Rushdie back into the spotlight, it forced her into it for the first time. She recalls looking out on this new reality as the plane carrying her to her husband’s bedside landed on an airstrip packed with law enforcement troops and realising she was just going to have to deal with it, “which is another part of my personality”. In an epigraph to his memoir, Rushdie quoted Samuel Beckett: “We are other, no longer what we were before the calamity of yesterday.” How much do they feel they have been changed by what’s happened? “Well,” he says, “I’m better than maybe I have any business to be. And Eliza, too.”He still travels back and forth to see his sons and grandchildren in the UK, and the couple will be with them for the film’s London premiere. Has the attack ever tempted them to leave Trump’s US, where the forces against free speech and human rights seem ever more entrenched and dangerous? “What, for Farage’s Britain?” scoffs Rushdie. I take it that’s a no, then.Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie is released in the UK on 30 September. It was released in the US on 17 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSalman RushdieAlex GibneyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Zack Snyder is angling to make another Batman movie. Stranger things have happened | Movies | The Guardian
description: Two Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Two Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns
Content: Anyone? … Ben Affleck in Batman v Superman, 2016.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures/Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenAnyone? … Ben Affleck in Batman v Superman, 2016.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures/Warner Bros./AllstarWeek in geekMoviesZack Snyder is angling to make another Batman movie. Stranger things have happenedBen ChildTwo Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight ReturnsFri 18 Sep 2026 07.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTShareThere cannot be too many film-makers who have spent quite so long being told that their version of a superhero universe is over, asZack Snyderhas. His Batman is gone, his Superman has been dismantled and the studio that once handed him the keys to DC is now run by James Gunn and Peter Safran, two men whose first order of business was to build something completely different. And yet here he is, determined not to give up, telling anyone who will listen about his proposal to bring the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns to multiplexes.In an interview with Varietyto promote his forthcoming film The Last Photograph, Snyder returned to an idea he has been talking about for years: adapting Miller’s famously grim 1986 vision of an ageing Batman coming out of retirement in a dystopian Gotham. “The reason why it’s The Dark Knight Returns, if anyone would ever let me do it outside of the DC Universe since it’s a novel that just happens to have superheroes in it, is if I could do Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, those two books next to each other, to me, represent the complete cycle of the superhero comic book medium,” the film-maker said.“You can do no more than those two books. Watchmen came at the beginning of the superhero movie phase, so it would be super fitting to have The Dark Knight Returns come now, at what I would say is possibly – I don’t want to call it the twilight, but – we’re down the road of the superhero movie genre, and I think audiences would understand the why of it.”View image in fullscreenA return with interest? Ben Affleck as Batman in 2016.Photograph: Clay Enos/Warner Bros./AllstarWhat’s this, you may ask? Isn’t this the guy who was in charge of the caped crusader and man of steel back when they were played by Ben Affleck and Henry Cavill, and didn’t he already spend a significant chunk ofBatmanv Superman recreating Miller’s seminal comic with the serial numbers only lightly filed off? It all seems pretty unlikely. For starters, comic book studios rarely make straight-up adaptations of iconic graphic novels – at least outside the animated sphere. Then there’s the small matter of the two existing Batman projects already running concurrently under DC Studios: Robert Pattinson’s grungy doom-laden version, about to embark on a second outing under the auspices of Matt Reeves (The Batman Part II), and a second dark knight who’s due to turn up in the forthcoming The Brave and the Bold, this time with It director Andy Muschietti attached.Wouldn’t a third caped crusader be taking things too far, even in a genre where multiversal alternates have increasingly become commonplace? Then again, stranger things have happened. Nobody expected Snyder’s four-hour version of Justice League to ever get made, either. The “release the Snyder cut” campaign remains one of the most bizarre examples of fan power to have emerged. Yes, Snyder’s early DC films, Man of Steel and Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice did well at the box office, especially given the studio’s later struggles, but the idea that Warner Bros would one day hand Snyder $70m to exhume Justice League, perform emergency franchise surgery on it and release two four-hour versions on TV (one entirely in monochrome) still feels closer to an AI fever dream than reality. Did Snyder really have the huge and dedicated following to justify it?There may be one glimmer of hope on the horizon for those who long to see a greying Batfleck battle Cavill’s Superman once again. Paramount Skydance’s planned takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, which could yet struggle to get over the line, might signal another shake-up of the Gunn-led DC Studios. There are even murkiercorners of the blogospherethat suggest Paramount boss David Ellison could bring Snyder back once Gunn’s contract (allegedly) expires next year.In the meantime, Snyder will keep on keeping on with his backdoor campaign to get The Dark Knight Returns into cinemas. This may not be “release the Snyder cut” just yet, but somewhere in the darker reaches of the internet, a hashtag is warming up.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekSuperhero moviesDC ComicsZack SnyderBatmanComics and graphic novelscommentShareReuse this content

title: MobLand season two review – why is Pierce Brosnan’s tedious crime drama so obsessed with testicle jokes? | Television | The Guardian
description: This Guy-Ritchie-directed gangland drama is deathly dull. It’s a charm-free watch with awful characters and humour so genital-based that at one point Helen Mirren yells a penis joke at a sausage
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: This Guy-Ritchie-directed gangland drama is deathly dull. It’s a charm-free watch with awful characters and humour so genital-based that at one point Helen Mirren yells a penis joke at a sausage
Content: In the market for fresh adversaries … L to r, Helen Mirren as Maeve Harrigan and Pierce Brosnan as Conrad Harrigan In MobLand, season 2.Photograph: Luke Varley/Paramount+View image in fullscreenIn the market for fresh adversaries … L to r, Helen Mirren as Maeve Harrigan and Pierce Brosnan as Conrad Harrigan In MobLand, season 2.Photograph: Luke Varley/Paramount+TV reviewTelevisionReviewMobLand season two review – why is Pierce Brosnan’s tedious crime drama so obsessed with testicle jokes?This Guy-Ritchie-directed gangland drama is deathly dull. It’s a charm-free watch with awful characters and humour so genital-based that at one point Helen Mirren yells a penis joke at a sausageSarah DempsterFri 18 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMobLand. It sounds like a regional nightclub. Or a boyband. But it’s not. It’s a Paramount+ crime drama starringPierce Brosnanas an Irishman unable to speak in a convincing Irish accent. This is his tragedy. His cross to bear. And now it’s ours, too, because MobLand is back for a second series, with Brosnan – as the veteran gang boss Conrad Harrigan – once again battling other gang bosses while attempting to say things like “Oi love ye loike a tramp loves paraffin” without his vowels shrivelling into tiny raisins of pseudo-Hibernian shame. Does he succeed? Oi tink not! But there are bigger problems afoot, to be sure.Created by Ronan “Top Boy” Bennett and directed byGuy Ritchie, the first series of the London-set MobLand (feel the width of that capitalised L!) was a sustained roar of nothing much; a rumble through every possible modern gangster drama cliche in the Every Modern Gangster Drama Cliche book. You know the sort of thing: car chases through suspiciously empty city streets; convoluted drug deals with mumbling eastern Europeans; tiny-eyed endomorphs in flat caps bellowing “Oi” in slow motion as they hurtle through the air to the strains of something unconscionable by Kasabian.In the middle of it all was Tom Hardy as the stoic fixer Harry Da Souza, lugging boxes of exposition from scene to scene while visibly longing to get back to his trailer. And who could blame him? For all its screeching wheels and strike-a-lighting cockneys, this was a terribly lacklustre affair: a propah front door (bore) that failed to generate much interest in either the characters or their Victoria Derbyshire’s Newsnight (plight).Anyway, here we are again, blasting into the new series with a visit to a greyhound track for some combatively accented hijinks with Conrad and his similarly “Irish” wife Maeve (a horrifyingly miscast Helen Mirren). Having disposed of several (if, crucially, not all) members of the rival crime family the Stevensons, the Harrigans are now in the market for fresh adversaries.Enter a Turkish mob composed largely of beards and excessive upper body strength. They are led by a man who looks like Mick Fleetwood, and Conrad doesn’t like them one bit, not least when they attempt to tell him “sweet little lies” about the fancy drug deal they’ve just reneged on. It seems they have bypassed Conrad in favour of a clandestine contract with wayward son Kevin (Paddy Considine). The nerve! What could it all mean?Here’s Harry with some mixed metaphors: “This family is in a death spiral. We’ve lost fentanyl. Now heroin is swinging in the breeze. Instead of keeping our powder dry, we’ve started a war.” A pause, for effect. “Wiv our own allies.”Could there be a shadowy “big bastard” behind it all? A shark, perhaps, circling the Harrigans, intent on “splitting this family into small pieces” and turning Conrad against his son?Let us ponder this unpleasant question over 10 48-minute episodes, plus ad breaks.Blimey, it’s dull. For all the guns and flying CGI viscera, it’s absent either the charm or wit that makes these sorts of fist-based capers bearable. The characters are all gits and their banter is as effortful as it is relentless. (There is the suspicion that production meetings involved liberal use of the word “craic”.)The characters are all awful. Gag-wise, it’s strictly back-of-the-bus stuff. There is a preoccupation with balls and the misuse thereof. Conrad threatens to place one flunkey’s potatoes “on me fuckin’ mantlepiece”, before promising another he’ll reduce him to “a bag o’ Turkish testicles”.If you tweezered out all the swear words, the whole thing would collapse like a game of Jenga. All that would remain would be a steaming pile of fists and Hardy’s huge face squinting dolefully into the distance, like a satellite dish struggling to pick up some distant television signal.At one point, apropos of nothing, Mirren shouts: “Dis tastes loike a tramp’s cock!” at a sausage. At another point, we’re given an unexplained closeup of a greyhound doing a wee on a racetrack. This feels like a metaphor, somehow. But for what? For the Harrigan family’s insistence on treating the world as their personal urinal, perhaps? Or for Ritchie continuing to take the proverbial? Jury’s out, squire.MobLand is on Paramount+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewPierce BrosnanHelen MirrenGuy RitchiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? review – Jarvis Cocker’s wit and warmth upstage the hits | Movies | The Guardian
description: Wonderful archive footage charts the Sheffield outsiders’ unlikely rise, but the distant camerawork struggles to capture the thrill of their triumphant O2 gigs
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Wonderful archive footage charts the Sheffield outsiders’ unlikely rise, but the distant camerawork struggles to capture the thrill of their triumphant O2 gigs
Content: National treasure … Jarvis Cocker at the 02, London, in Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Photograph: MUBIView image in fullscreenNational treasure … Jarvis Cocker at the 02, London, in Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Photograph: MUBIMoviesReviewPulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? review – Jarvis Cocker’s wit and warmth upstage the hitsWonderful archive footage charts the Sheffield outsiders’ unlikely rise, but the distant camerawork struggles to capture the thrill of their triumphant O2 gigsLaurence PhelanFri 18 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1978, in the classroom of a comprehensive school in Sheffield, a skinny, shortsighted 15-year-old wrote a mission statement in the back of an exercise book – a masterplan for reaching the top with the band he had recently formed with some classmates who, like him, weren’t picked first for sports.In 2023, after a hiatus of a decade, his band Pulp started touring again, and last year played to 20,000 people at each of two nights at the O2 in London. This film features concert footage from those gigs in which a still lithe, still-got-it-at-60-oddJarvis Cockersings his hit art-pop anthems backed by most of the classic lineup and a 10-piece string section. And interspersed with the concert footage are autobiographical musings, nostalgic archive footage, interviews with Jarvis’s mum and gran, and Cocker narrating the story of how he got from there, almost half a century ago, to here.The total package, in typicalPulpstyle, is a mixture of the exuberant and celebratory with the bittersweet and reflective. In voiceover, Cocker says that songs “contain pockets of energy from your past life that’s released again when you perform them”. And hearing them performed in the present, you notice how many of the lyrics were about young people wondering what life would be like when they were older. (“Let’s all meet up in the year 2000/Won’t it be strange when we’re all fully grown?”) Which was another way of them wondering whether they were making the right decisions in the present.Obviously it’s ironic that Cocker achieved national treasure status by being the patron saint of outsiders – all those “misshapes, mistakes, misfits / Raised on a diet of broken biscuits”. He sounds a little bemused by it himself, although, of course, he understood the transformative power of pop from a young age, and how even the gawkiest kid might strike a pose and become a sex symbol.But the band were outliers even at their Britpop-era peak. There’s a clip of Cocker playing in a charity football tournament in 1996 along with the more classically laddish Liam Gallagher, Damon Albarn and Robbie Williams, and while he briefly enjoyed being in the starting XI, as one of life’s shrewd observers, he did look more suited to the sidelines. In fact the implication of much of the 90s footage is that getting everything he had ever dreamed of in his youth was an anticlimactic trauma from which he has only lately recovered.‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on PulpRead moreBack in the film’s present day, Pulp’s first album in 24 years has just gone to No 1 and the concert opens with a song from it, Spike Island, and its defiant refrain “I was born to perform … I exist to do this”. The gigs are apparently Pulp’s 566th and 567th live shows, and there is no reason why there shouldn’t be many more.It is a shame, though, that the O2 gigs were the only ones filmed. Even by the standards of soulless, corporate enormo-arenas it is an absolute enjoyment-vortex of a venue, and while the attenders are singing along and do look as if they’re having fun, very little of the energy that was presumably there is transmitted through the screen. Pulp thrived and thrilled because they seemed to speak to (and for) us so directly. But in this film the cameras seem too far away, the stage too big and the musicians too far apart. The bio-documentary and archival parts of What Do You Do for an Encore? are wonderful: droll, heartfelt and inimitably Cocker. To enjoy the concert section, you probably had to be there.Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? is in UK and Irish cinemas on 18 September and onMubifrom 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmMusic documentaryDocumentary filmsPulpJarvis CockerPop and rockMubireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Phaedra Ensemble: The Music of Meredith Monk review – fleeting rough edges amid polished beauty | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Works by the not-quite-minimalist composer’s included her Realm Variations and quartet Stringsongs in a compelling concert
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Works by the not-quite-minimalist composer’s included her Realm Variations and quartet Stringsongs in a compelling concert
Content: Injecting colour: Phaedra Ensemble at Kings Place, London.Photograph: Monika S. JakubowskaView image in fullscreenInjecting colour: Phaedra Ensemble at Kings Place, London.Photograph: Monika S. JakubowskaClassical musicReviewPhaedra Ensemble: The Music of Meredith Monk review – fleeting rough edges amid polished beautyKings Place, LondonWorks by the not-quite-minimalist composer’s included her Realm Variations and quartet Stringsongs in a compelling concertFlora WillsonFri 18 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no one quite likeMeredith Monk. So often grouped with her lionised contemporariesPhilip Glass,Steve Reich,Terry RileyandLa Monte Young, she is 83 to their 90-odd years and sports long plaited hair as reliably as Reich wears a baseball cap. Yet she refuses the label “minimalism” for her music, and composition is just one element of a creative life that also takes in singing, choreography, film-making and drawing.Monk was not present at this performance marking the launch of Phaedra Ensemble’snew album of her music, though she did loom briefly over the audience on video, professing “it’s a dream of mine for this music to be recorded and played”. (Compare that to the fortunes of Glass’s works.) But she had been closely involved, having invited the group to record some of her music after hearing them play.It was therefore a shame that the ensemble on stage atKings Placewasn’t quite the lineup of musicians that had joined Monk on her exploration of how voices might become instruments and vice versa. There were fleeting rough edges – pinched soprano sound, rather abrasive violin – in her Realm Variations, and some uncomfortable tuning in her quartet Stringsongs, which I can’t imagine feature on the album.But there were also some moments of pure, polished beauty. None more than in the opening extracts from Monk’s film score Book of Days, where the softly keening loop of a single tenor blossomed into the otherworldly polyphony of six unaccompanied voices. The texture was always limpid, communication between the singers intense. The rapid exchange of bell tones in Stringsongs was similarly transparent, the string instruments audibly reaching towards a kind of abstract sound. Voluptuous clarinet lines and the weird slow clang of oboe multiphonics injected colour into the otherwise rather austere repetitions of Backlight. In Realm Variations, the sculpted phrasing of the singers and woodwind was not matched by the strings. But conductor Lucy Goddard wove this larger ensemble into a compelling warp and weft: a thread of metallic piccolo, a grainy growl of contrabass clarinet and, in between, the mellow, breathing warmth of amplified voices.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicKings PlaceChoral musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the euphoric ‘Bollywood electronic’ of the Twins and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Omar and Jamal Ikram, 21-year-old brothers, are making lo-fi glitchy dance-pop with the melodic sensibilities of Bollywood music
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Omar and Jamal Ikram, 21-year-old brothers, are making lo-fi glitchy dance-pop with the melodic sensibilities of Bollywood music
Content: ‘We don’t want brown kids to feel like they have to fit into anything’ … the Twins.Photograph: Arran Ashan/PR imageView image in fullscreen‘We don’t want brown kids to feel like they have to fit into anything’ … the Twins.Photograph: Arran Ashan/PR imageAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the euphoric ‘Bollywood electronic’ of the Twins and the week’s best new tracksOmar and Jamal Ikram, 21-year-old brothers, are making lo-fi glitchy dance-pop with the melodic sensibilities of Bollywood musicShaad D'Souza,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromAldershot, HampshireRecommended if you like2hollis, the Hellp, Jai PaulUp nextNew single Wish U out nowYou, like me, may be growing tired of the 2020s’ so-called “indie sleaze” revival, which has so far yielded a few good parties and not that much good music. But the music of the Twins – Aldershot-born brothers Omar and Jamal Ikram – is made of sturdier stuff. The 21-year-olds are progenitors of a sound they call “Bollywood electronic” – a strain of loud, lo-fi, ultra-glitchy dance-pop that sounds like 2hollis if his songs were heavy with screwy samples of south Asian pop. Their debut album, last year’s Turmeric, captures the still-potent appeal of Jai Paul’s classic Str8 Outta Mumbai – which fused the lackadaisical sheen of 2010s electronic pop with the shining rhythmic and melodic sensibilities of Bollywood music – and, as is de rigueur for the contemporary era, makes it bolshie and frenetic, taking in the euphoric aggression of early Skrillex and unnerving noise of Aphex Twin.Turmeric was a minor hit, thanks in part to Fuckersby, a collaboration with on-the-rise British rapper Fakemink, as well as the Twins’ monthly NTS show,also called Turmeric, which turns one this month. (Its combination of classic British pop stars such as Lily Allen, Punjabi artists such as Sukshinder Shinda, and contemporary electronic acts the Hellp and Sophia Stel gives it the feeling of a late-night pirate radio station totally out of time and place.) The duo’s follow-up EP There&Back, released in May, polishes up the Twins’ sound a little, but not that much – if anything, their collaborations with Rada and Varg2TM on There&Back are even louder and wilder than anything on Turmeric. The duo’s future plans aren’t clear, but their mission is: “We don’t want brown kids to feel like they have to fit into anything,” Jamal said in an interview. “People are always gonna try to label what you’re doing, but you don’t have to move like that.”Shaad D’SouzaThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenPleasingly candid … Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul.Photograph: Courtesy of Paul KooikerCharlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul – Googoo GagaOnly this puckish Belgian duo could make a gorgeous choral refrain from “poo and pee and poo and pee”, which is the prelude to their pleasingly candid, dark electropop account of new parenthood.LS​Voice Actor – High-RiseWith a stunning beat by Lukid, like a house track heard throbbing across a wind-buffeted body of water, Noa Kurzweil ruminates about the psychological damage of apartment block living.BBTSex Week – Life Is a CircleWhat starts as prettily precious folk-pop à la Big Thief or@wilds out into thrilling hyperpop that keeps one foot on the ground (including whinnying horse samples) while spiralling ecstatically skywards. Rare to hear music so surprising.LSJGrrey – BelieveConversational verses slam into a spirited chorus with gospel overtones – appropriate for the London neo-soul singer’s search for something to have faith in as the world goes asunder.BBTOR – Nokik MessiahJohn Talabot pivots to his actual initials (Oriol Riverola) for an album of “the most euphoric possible variant of ambient”. The first taste sounds ready to blow, with piercing synth shards colliding into an unbroken crescendo.LSOscar Later – The Moon Belongs to YouFrom the Londoner’s awesomely accomplished new EP of big-room rollers, this track has an inspired conceit: old-time comical folk song Yon Yonson is turned into Ibiza-grade techno with hard-rock guitar detailing.BBTDana Margolin​ – Big Beautiful SoundThe frontperson of UK indie band Porridge Radio strikes out solo, and the squall of that band has abated to leave bright, clear air on this timeless folk song. Lovely Mike Mills-directed video, too.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Baka Beyond: Sing the World Awake review – powerful Cameroonian vocals burst through fussy arrangements | Music | The Guardian
description: This fusion of western folk and the traditional music of the Baka people is an uneven patchwork of sound – but there is remarkable power in its yearning ululations
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: This fusion of western folk and the traditional music of the Baka people is an uneven patchwork of sound – but there is remarkable power in its yearning ululations
Content: A distinct fusion … Baka Beyond.Photograph: Carla WordenView image in fullscreenA distinct fusion … Baka Beyond.Photograph: Carla WordenGlobal album of the monthMusicReviewBaka Beyond: Sing the World Awake review – powerful Cameroonian vocals burst through fussy arrangements(March Hare Music)This fusion of western folk and the traditional music of the Baka people creates an uneven patchwork of sound – but it astonishes when their vocals are placed front and centreAmmar KaliaFri 18 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the past 30 years, British folk musicians Su Hart and Martin Cradick have been developing a distinct fusion of traditional Cameroonian vocal music with western instrumentation. Their 1993 debut record Spirits of the Forest, released on Joe Boyd’s Hannibal Records, focused on the female singers of the Baka people, who use a polyphonic style of yodelling to evoke dawn spirits. Hart and Cradick have maintained the relationship over the decades, splitting royalties equally and supporting the community through their Global Music Exchange charity. Sing the World Awake, their first album in 12 years, centres field recordings made with a new Baka generation and deepens their exploration into an ancient oral tradition.View image in fullscreenBaka Beyond: Sing the World Awake album coverCradick’s instrumental arrangements are expansive and wide-ranging. Topé Malangui Kpode features sprightly, Ghanaian highlife-inspired guitar melodies and percussive polyrhythms. Fair Molly (Mál Bhán Ní Chuilleanáin) features Gaelic vocals from guest singer Irene O’Meara, and The Swift harnesses the intricate folk sound of Ben Moneypenny’s violin playing. Each song alights on snatches of Baka vocals, although the overall effect of splicing these unique melodies into different genres creates an uneven patchwork of sound.The album reveals its remarkable power when the Baka ensemble are front and centre. Dance the Dawn beautifully interweaves Mbakolo Elaine’s yearning ululations with finger-picked acoustic guitar and a soft bed of synth melody, gently embellishing her piercing song, while the powerful group vocals of Nahwia Hélène, Loni Julienne, Barma Thérése and Mayo Jacqui ricochet like dub echo on the reggae-inspired We Miss You! The title track is a highlight, featuring a large ensemble of Baka singers who each respond to the soaring yodelling of lead vocalist Loni Julienne to produce an enveloping soundscape of undulating voices. Deeply skilful and strangely moving, when the Baka voices are presented unadorned in full force they are unlike anything else you are likely to find on record.Also out this monthTurkish psychedelic innovatorsBaba Zulamark 30 years as a band withXXX (Glitterbeat). Delving into murky, dub-influenced territory, the record blends droning bass with twanging saz melody and sparse darbuka rhythm to produce a charmingly ambient odyssey. A gem of a find, the rerelease of a rare album of 1980s Ethiopian synth experiments byTeodros Makonnen,Teodros Makonnen With His Organ (Muzikawi), is a wistful exploration of Ethio-jazz melodies and early electronic dancefloor sounds. Syrian composerKhaled Kurbeh’s latest albumIthā Sajā (Research)is a profoundly tender collection of solo piano pieces that weave dextrous Iraqi folk rhythms with soothing neoclassical melodies, each inspired by recording at dawn and dusk.Explore more on these topicsMusicGlobal album of the monthCameroonFolk musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Empress Of: Dream House review – a tender and openhearted rebirth after wildfires razed her house | Music | The Guardian
description: Lorely Rodriguez contemplates the meaning of home – both physical and emotional – on a gorgeously humid, hopeful album that makes a virtue of her searching nature
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Lorely Rodriguez contemplates the meaning of home – both physical and emotional – on a gorgeously humid, hopeful album that makes a virtue of her searching nature
Content: Feeling right at home … Lorely Rodriguez AKA Empress Of.Photograph: Courtesy of Luca MastroView image in fullscreenFeeling right at home … Lorely Rodriguez AKA Empress Of.Photograph: Courtesy of Luca MastroMusicReviewEmpress Of: Dream House review – a tender and openhearted rebirth after wildfires razed her house(Major Arcana/Giant Music)Lorely Rodriguez contemplates the meaning of home – both physical and emotional – on a gorgeously humid, hopeful album that makes a virtue of her searching natureLaura SnapesFri 18 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince the early 2010s Lorely Rodriguez has cut a restless, inventive figure. She’s slipped from raucous pop to silkier sounds, explored her Honduran-American heritage and, on her last album, flipped the staple awards season phrase “for your consideration” into a full-frontal club-pop meditation on uneven relationships. Her gorgeous fifth album makes a feature of this searching nature. Written after her family home burned down in the 2025 California wildfires, Dream House is about the rebuilding of that home – birdsong-dappled field recordings of its construction keep popping up – but also contemplates what it means to feel at home in yourself and with others.View image in fullscreenThe album artwork for Dream House by Empress Of.Photograph: PRFor all the violent loss behind the record, it sounds amazingly airy, free and open-hearted. The directness of For Your Consideration softens to a humid atmosphere that’s bright with hope, Rodriguez’s undulating synth lines bubbling with impatience and ecstasy as they cushion her soaring arrow of a voice. The bangers leap above the fray: SYW, featuring Cecile Believe, elegantly twists EDM to evoke an uncontainable desire; the equally yearning HandsOn sparks with glassy chimes and battering percussion. I Pray 4 U evokes the frisky joy of Jayda G, and Machete, dwelling on defiant post-breakup rebirth, slices like a laser through the night sky.Impressively, the calmer moments are no less arresting. Blue Light taps Dev Hynes for a slinky trawl through alienation and the title track wipes away trip-hop’s murk to expose its sweetness, more than fulfilling Rodriguez’s promise that “good things are coming”.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockDance musicElectronic musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best books to read in September: new paperbacks from Margaret Atwood, Kiran Desai and Richard Holmes | Books | The Guardian
description: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some great new paperbacks, from an epic multigenerational saga by a Booker winner to a biography of an iconic Victorian poet
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some great new paperbacks, from an epic multigenerational saga by a Booker winner to a biography of an iconic Victorian poet
Content: View image in fullscreenThis month's best paperbacksBooksThe best books to read in September: new paperbacks from Margaret Atwood, Kiran Desai and Richard HolmesLooking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some great new paperbacks, from an epic multigenerational saga by a Booker winner to a biography of an iconic Victorian poetFri 18 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTShareFictionFictionThe Loneliness of Sonia and SunnyKiran DesaiView image in fullscreenThis Booker-shortlisted novel is about work as much as it is about the relationship between Sunny Bhatia and Sonia Shah, whose families are neighbours and whose attempts to make a match begin their on-off liaison. Where Sunny dreams of journalistic success, Sonia’s heart and mind lie in writing fiction. The dilemma facing an Indian writer, she ponders, is one of obeisance to the west’s appetites and projections.Desai’s solution to the problem in this immensely entertaining and generative novel is to dart continually between modes of representation and register. The gothic novel appears with the early introduction of the monstrous Ilan de Toorjen Foss, a narcissistic artist who seduces Sonia, suppresses her literary endeavours and then abandons her. The predicaments and predilections of Sunny and Sonia’s Allahabad relatives create a low-key bourgeois comedy: stranded single aunts, genteel impoverishment, the wrangle over a cook famed for his kebabs.Capacious and shape-shifting though the novel is, filled with subtexts and shadow narratives, it is still a challenge to hold the contradictions and demands of multiple identities. Desai pictures Sonia and her father listening to the Pakistani singer Iqbal Bano, and reflecting on what the music conjures in them: “To be a citizen of a troubled postcolonial nation gave a person gravitas. To be holding out against the crass new world gave a man gravitas. To be wounded yet fighting on against the barbarians gave one gravitas. To be exiled, abandoned by love and luck, gave them gravitas. What happened within a family, what happened between a couple, was no different from that which happened in a nation under dictatorship, running on fear.”Whether or not a novel can accurately and productively capture this yearning for gravitas, or the continuum between the personal and the political, is one of the questions posed by The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny. Another is the sheer exhaustion – mental, physical and artistic – caused by the constant need for self-invention and reinvention, whether individual, societal, national or global; and how the form of the novel, created in the European consciousness, can complexify itself to take account of an accelerated, fractured modernity. Desai’s answer to these questions is to make her story both dizzyingly vast and insistently miniature; to make us feel that there is as much at stake in the lives of Vini-Puri, a pair of servant girls not even accorded single-name recognition, as in the grand ambitions of the novel’s title characters. She pulls it off, not only in her manoeuvring of cast and incident, but in her ability to elicit apprehension, laughter, compassion and curiosity in the reader.Alex Clark£11.04 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionWe Love You, BunnyMona AwadView image in fullscreenWe Love You, Bunny, is the much-anticipated sequel to Mona Awad’s beloved campus horror/satire of 2019, Bunny. Both books are set at an Ivy League university in a crime-ridden New England town; from various well-seeded clues, we can identify this as Brown University. Here it is called Warren, because the Bunnyverse is unabashedly silly and self-referential. Rabbit jokes abound.The first book followed Samantha, an alienated, cash-strapped creative writing student cold-shouldered by her workshop cohort, a cabal of four ultra-feminine rich girls who all call each other Bunny. The Bunnies wear fluffy dresses, eat mini food and – as Samantha learns when she’s finally inducted into their cult – express their creativity through demonic rites that involve exploding rabbits. Samantha has to transcend them to find her voice as an artist. The story of Bunny is the result.We Love You, Bunny begins with Samantha bound and gagged in an attic. The Bunnies surround her, congratulating her venomously on the success of her book. Now they want to tell their story. Passing an axe like a talking stick, they introduce us to four versions of their Bunny-centric world. Then they pass the mic to a special guest.This follow-up has the key strengths of the original, particularly its scabrous satire on upper-middle-class American femininity. However, it suffers from a certain sequelitis. It’s baggier than the original. Its metaphors for creativity feel less earned. The game of visiting each Bunny’s point of view also disappoints. This is redeemed, however, when we come to the last voice of the novel.Toward the end, a writing professor passes judgment on the story we’re in: “A touch too camp.Zany.A sort of zanyromantasy,isn’t it?” Yes, it is, but Awad is here to show us that romantasy can be serious literature, andnothingcan really be too camp. And if We Love You, Bunny has weaknesses endemic to sequels, it also has their strengths. There’s the fun of meeting the old characters and seeing areas we wondered about before, but it also builds on the original, opening up new territory and making new jokes. And though it’s better to start with the first novel, We Love You, Bunny can be read alone. It’s a goofy, overblown flower of a book with lots of thorns that pleasurably scratch.Sandra Newman£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionBuckeyePatrick RyanView image in fullscreenOpening in the first decades of the 20th century, this luminous and tender novel follows the interwoven lives of two married couples in the fictional town of Bonhomie, Ohio. One half of the first of these couples is Cal Jenkins, the sweet-tempered son of a traumatised first world war veteran, born in the spring of 1920 with (to use the parlance of the era) a mild deformity: “The day you were born and one of your legs came up short,” his father, Everett, tells him, “right then I thought, well, that’s it. If we get into another big one, he’ll never be in it.” The delights of prolepsis!The US gets into another big one in quite short order, of course. Cal, just as his father predicted, is turned away from the recruitment office and ends up spending his days in drudgery at the local concrete factory instead. A chance meeting with Becky Hanover, a young woman with a dark bob and a loveably whimsical way about her, sees Cal married by the end of the first chapter.On 8 May 1945, Cal is working a shift at the hardware store owned by Becky’s father when a gorgeous, confused redhead stumbles in. Together, they listen to President Truman announce allied victory in Europe over the wireless – and then she kisses him. The gorgeous, confused redhead is Margaret Salt. Her own equally gorgeous and strangely aloof husband is away on a cargo ship in the Pacific. From here, the novel takes off at full thrust, and, as one of Ryan’s characters summarises it: “people get laid, babies get made, everybody lies to their kids”.It is no surprise that Ryan cut his teeth writing short fiction: Buckeye iselevated throughout by the precision with which he captures the tiny, haunting glories of everyday suburban life. And for all its quotidian charm, a deep melancholy prevents Buckeye from ever tipping into saccharine nostalgia. Ryan strips away the Bakelite glaze of the American dream to expose the raw flesh beneath.AK Blakemore£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionThe Wax ChildOlga RavnView image in fullscreenOn 26 June 1621, in Copenhagen, a woman was beheaded – which was unusual, but only in the manner of her death. According to one historian, during the years 1617 to 1625, in Denmarka “witch” was burned every five days. The first time this happens in Danish author Olga Ravn’s fourth novel, the condemned woman is “tied to the ladder, and the ladder pushed into the bonfire”. Her daughter watches as she falls, her eye “so strangely orange from within. And then in the heat it explodes.”The child is watched, in turn, by a wax doll who sees everything: everything in this scene, and everything everywhere, through all space and all the time since it was fashioned. On a basic level, the wax child is a useful narrative device. But it also complicates everything. The temptation, from the distance of the 21st century, is to assume charges against so-called witches to be baseless. But in this case, a well-known one in Denmark, the charges included the making of wax children – and Ravn begins with Christenze Krukow, a real Danish noblewoman who wasaccused of witchcraft three timesduring her lifetime, making this wax baby.Ravn began as a poet, and even in English this lineage is clear. Her work asserts that knowledge inheres in objects, comprehension through smell and taste and blood and guts; through metaphor. “How do I know this?” demands the wax child, at one point. “It is like a gash in me to know it.”At its best The Wax Child is richly evocative, beautiful, creepy and visceral. “It is the darkest of times, December. From the curvature of the earth, minutes run like droplets from the day.” At other times, there’s a bit too much research just out of sight; the novel can feel elliptical, even baffling. One misses the space, the clarity and freedom of Ravn’s International Booker-shortlisted novel The Employees. But maybe that’s the thing about weaving spells. About poetry, too: demand it makes neat sense, and you begin to have too much in common with the witch-hunters.Aida Edemariam£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionKing SorrowJoe HillView image in fullscreenSix oddball but doughty kids fall into the path of a vast and terrible supernatural evil which has come into our world from the outer limits of darkness. They must spend their lifetimes battling it, facing horror after horror in the process.This is the plot, roughly, of Stephen King’s novel It (his best; no arguments). It is also the plot, roughly, of King’s son Joe Hill’s new horror doorstopper, in which six friends summon the ancient, infinitely malicious dragon King Sorrow from the Long Dark to help them defeat some baddies. Needless to say, their supernatural ritual backfires.Joseph Hillström King started his career making great efforts to avoid any connection with his famous father, publishing under the pen name he still uses today and avoiding meeting his agent in person (he bears a striking resemblance to his dad). But in this latest novel, he leans into it. There are lines that deliberately echo some of King’s most famous (“The man in black fled across the desert …”); a moment that brings to mind a King plot point (a riddling contest). In this whopper of a novel, Hill is delighting in his family connection, and we delight along with him. King Sorrow is huge, sprawling – and absolutely fantastic.Alison Flood£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirMemoirBook of LivesMargaret AtwoodView image in fullscreenBook of Lives is less a memoir than an autobiography, not a slice of life but the whole works, 85 years. Where most such backward looks are cosily triumphalist or anxiously self-justifying, hers is sharp, funny and engaging, a book you can warm to even if you’re not fully au fait (and few people are) with her astonishing output, which in the “also by” contents list here fills two pages.At the co-ed high school Atwood opted for, she soon graduated to the “brain class”. A small, “flat-chested weirdo”, with horn-rimmed glasses, a snaggle tooth, frizzy hair, astigmatism and anaemia, she put her energies into sewing and fancy dress. By 14 she was dating: older, artsy boyfriends “somehow just appeared, like mushrooms after rain”. Poetry pursued her, too: her adolescent efforts were “heavily sensational, sometimes macabre”. According to her school yearbook, her “not-so-secret ambition is to write THE Canadian novel”. But her first publications were poems that appeared under the name ME Atwood, “so I wouldn’t be tagged as a girl”.From university in Toronto, she moved on to Harvard, a tweedily unglamorous scholarship girl. There she researched the Salem witch trials, which along with the patriarchal norms of Harvard graduate school fed into The Handmaid’s Tale many years later. She wasn’t an active feminist in her 20s, when the idea that “domestic tasks might be shared equally” hadn’t arrived. But the oppression of women increasingly troubled her. And by the time the TV version was made, in the era of Trumpism, it was more salient than ever.At a party in 1969 she met Graeme Gibson, novelist, trickster, spendthrift, high-energy oddball. He was wearing blue denims, she a “white crocheted lace mini dress with wooden buttons down” (Atwood is scrupulous in recording her changing outfits and hairstyles), and at first she had no awareness of his “non-platonic interest” in her. There were complications: she’d married an American poet, less from love than to spare him being drafted to Vietnam, and Graeme had a child by a woman with whom he had an open marriage, Shirley. A cautious courtship followed; Graeme wooed Atwood with yearning letters. If she’d not met him she’d still have been a great novelist, he said, but she’d have had a lot less fun.His decline, dementia and death bring a sombre tone to the book’s last pages. Ever the workaholic Ms Fixit, Atwood keeps going rather than miss out on the publicity whirl for The Testaments (her sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale): “Ask yourself, Dear Reader: The busy schedule or the empty chair? I chose the busy schedule. The empty chair would be there when I got home.” She has a pacemaker these days and eventually her body “will decide to go off on an adventure of its own”. But for now mind and body are still together and so, in friendly opposition, are the many selves she unveils here in a “blizzard” of memories and photos: nerdy brainiac, waifish poet, Medusa-eyed feminist, uncanny prophet and one of the great novelists of our time.Blake Morrison£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopHistoryHistoryIndignityLea YpiView image in fullscreenIt starts with a photo. A black-and-white image of a couple relaxing on a pair of sun loungers in front of a luxury ski hotel: him, squinting against the sun; her, smiling at the camera, wrapped in a white fur coat. It is their honeymoon in Cortina, up in the Italian Alps.The year is 1941, and the woman is Lea Ypi’s grandmother. Ypi saw the picture after it had been posted online by a stranger, gone viral acrossAlbania, and attracted a stream of abuse. “Morally degenerate” was one comment. “Fascist collaborator” another.And so, in Indignity, Ypi sets off to find out exactly who her grandmother was. It is, she writes, partly out of a sense of duty, to defend her family member from the trolls – a kind of 21st-century version of EP Thompson’s famous call for history to rescue the dead from “the enormous condescension of posterity”. But partly, Ypi admits, it is because she finds the photo unsettling. How to reconcile her beloved, compassionate grandmother with this glamorous young woman living it up in Mussolini’s Italy?From here, two parallel stories unfold. The core of Indignity is a richly reimagined retelling of Ypi’s grandmother’s life. Born in Salonica (now Thessaloniki) in 1918, Leman Leskoviku came into a world that was already falling apart. Cosmopolitan empires were collapsing into nation states, unsure how to treat families like hers: Albanian-speaking, living in Greece, with a proud record of service to the Ottoman state. Leman’s childhood is shaped by the uncertainty of those years: the trauma of wars just ended, economic decline, and blunt, brutal social engineering. As Ypi describes, millions were forcibly moved across newly drawn borders. Leman’s nanny, one of Salonica’s many Muslim Turks, is barely able to hold back tears as she is packed off to central Anatolia.Amid the ambiguity, and to escape an unwanted suitor, Leman sets her own life on a different path. At just 18, she decides to move to Albania alone. Ypi’s Ondaatje prize-winning memoir,Free, was haunted by stories of Albanians fleeing to neighbouring countries to escape the violence of the 1990s. This story hinges on a young woman’s extraordinary choice to move the other way.Sami Kent£11.04 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopPoliticsPoliticsOne Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against ThisOmar El AkkadView image in fullscreenPalestine has many eloquent defenders, and El Akkad is one of them. Born in Egypt, raised in Qatar and Canada, and now a US citizen, he has reported from the Middle East, Afghanistan and Guantánamo. His new bookis a response to events inGazaafter 7 October 2023. It is his voice, his bafflement, spilling out after decades of having to keep quiet for the sake of journalistic neutrality or artistic show-don’t-tell, of having to bite his tongue after readers responded to his journalism with racist doubt: “I don’t trust any story about terrorism written by a guy named Omar”.He turns his back on these old strictures and tells the world what’s wrong as himself, not just reporting but processing all that he has seen and heard. “This is an account of a fracture,” he writes, “a breaking away from the notion that the polite, western liberal ever stood for anything at all.” It is a deft, broken-hearted, rhetorical savaging of comfortable people who say nothing (or pay lip service) but care only about preserving normality, convincing themselves that these things only happen “to certain places, to certain people”.One Day is passionate, poetic and sickening. It is full of well-earned rage, frustration with those who need this morality to be spelled out. For me it was cathartic, almost spiritual, to have these ugly truths articulated. It stoked and tempered the fires of my own rage. It is an important book, a must-read, if only for the reminder that history always comes down to one simple question: “When it mattered, who sided with justice and who sided with power?”Dina Nayeri£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopBiographyBiographyThe Boundless DeepRichard HolmesView image in fullscreenAlfred Tennyson was a divided soul. He even wrote a poem called The Two Voices in which dual versions of himself argued out the pros and cons of suicide. In this illuminating book, Richard Holmes has chosen to focus on the lesser known of the poet’s personae.The Boundless Deep is not about the bestselling author of the nation’s favourite poem – The Charge of the Light Brigade – or the laureate lord, pacing along the clifftops of the Isle of Wight or posing for Julia Margaret Cameron’s famous photograph (known derisorily in his family as “the dirty monk”). Instead, Holmes gives us “young Tennyson”, the wildly talented youth whose story is far more rich and strange than that of the bearded celebrity.The Tennysons, wrote Alfred, were a “black-blooded race”, meaning prone to moods and melancholy. His father, a reluctant clergyman, was angry and very often drunk. There was an incident, the details of which are obscure, that resulted in the family cook being burned to death in the rectory kitchen. One of Alfred’s brothers was confined to a lunatic asylum as a boy and stayed there for life. Another suffered from profound depression and followed his father into alcoholism. A third became addicted to opium. Alfred himself suffered from episodes of paralysing gloom and what he called “weird seizures”. His Maudis narrated by a madman: he must often have wondered whether he was or would become one himself.Holmes is not an uncritical fan – he is tart about the pseudo-medieval flim-flam of Idylls of the King – but when he loves a poem, he writes about it with a wonderful capacity for noticing every pulse of metre, every flicker of nuance. This biography is a compelling story of an odd, brilliant, charismatic character, and a reappraisal of a man who had become so very established we could no longer see him. In giving us young Tennyson – gauche, beautiful, veiled in stinking tobacco smoke – Holmes has given the great poet back to us.Lucy Hughes-Hallett£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopBiographyCrickMatthew CobbView image in fullscreenMost people could tell you that Francis Crick, together with James Watson, discovered the double helix structure of DNA, and shaped our understanding of how genes work. Fewer know that Crick also played a key role in modern neuroscience and inspired our continuing efforts to understand the biological basis of consciousness.Crick once said the two questions that interested him most were “the borderline between the living and the non-living, and the workings of the brain”, questions that were usually discussed in religious or mystical terms but that he believed could be answered by science. In his new biography of the Nobel prize-winning scientist, Matthew Cobb, emeritus professor of zoology at the University of Manchester, does an admirable job of capturing the rare thinker who not only set himself such ambitious goals but made remarkable progress in achieving them, radically remaking two scientific disciplines in the process.Far from being the stereotypical reclusive genius, labouring in isolation, Crick was loud-talking and charismatic, a philanderer, poetry lover and thrower of risque parties. Crick’s inspiration and breakthroughs came through intense encounters with others, and he was skilled at bringing researchers from different disciplines together to solve scientific puzzles.In Cobb’s telling, Crick was bold and arrogant, with an uncanny ability to uncover connections and to identify new theoretical and experimental approaches, often challenging far more established experts. Lawrence Bragg, the head of the Cavendish lab, is said to have described him as “the sort of chap who was always doing someone else’s crossword”. This approach meant he often stepped on people’s toes and was occasionally wildly off mark.Cobb sets himself an ambitious task in trying to do justice to both Crick’s prolific scientific career and his colourful personal life, and this biography is an impressive work of research and scholarship. It is intended to be accessible to the general reader, with the advice that those who are struggling with the science should “follow Crick’s advice to readers of his own books and skip the hard bits”. This general reader struggled often with the technical detail and vocabulary. Some difficulty may be inescapable simply because the science is complex. Nonetheless, it is a relief whenever Crick is quoted, describing his research in his own words, because he had a knack for translating hard science into lay terms.Sophie McBain£12.74 (RRP £14.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopTechnologyTechnologyIf Anyone Builds it, Everyone DiesEliezer Yudkowsky and Nate SoaresView image in fullscreenWhat if I told you I could stop you worrying about climate change, and all you had to do was read one book? Great, you’d say, until I mentioned that the reason you’d stop worrying was because the book says our species only has a few years before it’s wiped out by superintelligent AI anyway.We don’t know what form this extinction will take exactly – perhaps an energy-hungry AI will let the millions of fusion power stations it has built run hot, boiling the oceans. Maybe it will want to reconfigure the atoms in our bodies into something more useful. There are many possibilities, almost all of them bad, say Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares in If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, and who knows which will come true. But just as you can predict that an ice cube dropped into hot water will melt without knowing where any of its individual molecules will end up, you can be sure an AI that’s smarter than a human being will kill us all, somehow.Yudkowsky and Soares present their case with such conviction that it’s easy to emerge from this book ready to cancel your pension contributions. The glimmer of hope they offer – and it’s low wattage – is that doom can be averted if the entire world agrees to shut down advanced AI development as soon as possible. Given the commercial and strategic incentives, and the current state of political leadership, this seems a little unlikely.There are certainly moments in the book when the confidence with which an argument is presented outstrips its strength. And Yudkowsky and Soares exhibit more than a touch of confirmation bias. “History,” they write, “is full of … examples of catastrophic risk being minimised and ignored,” from leaded petrol to Chornobyl. But what about predictions of catastrophic risk being proved wrong? History is full of those, too, from Malthus’s population apocalypse to Y2K. Yudkowsky himself once claimed thatnanotechnology would destroy humanity“no later than 2010”.The problem is that you can be overconfident, inconsistent, a serial doom-monger, and still be right. It’s important to be aware of our own motivated reasoning when considering the arguments presented here; we have every incentive to disbelieve them. It still feels like everyone with an interest in the future has a duty to read what Yudkowsky and Soares have to say.David Shariatmadari£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMusicMusicNight PeopleMark RonsonView image in fullscreenNight People is intended as Ronson’s memoir but is as much an attempt to immortalise the people and scenes he came up in as it is a reflection on a childhood shaped by the late-night parties hosted by his parents – first in London, where a distant memory of Robin Williams tucking him in to bed with “Nanu nanu” floats through, then later in Manhattan, when his mother marries Mick Jones from Foreigner.By his own, self-aware account, Ronson has led a gilded life. Elite schools (Collegiate, Vassar, NYU); sleepovers with Sean Lennon and a cast of New York’s nepo who’s who; hanging out with Michael Jackson; the abundant creative freedom gifted by the safety net of generational wealth. It would be enough to make many readers roll their eyes before turning a single page. Their loss.Ronson’s talent as a writer enables him to render this privilege, the background glamour, his awkward stumbles as well as successes, with a kind of wry, soft self-deprecation that is genuinely endearing. It helps, of course, that he is a massive nerd. Ronson would rather spend paragraphs enthusing about the thickness of slipmats required for a specific DJ setup than he would recalling the wild-eyed buzz generated at an afterparty close to dawn. On balance, this is a good thing. There is more than enough bad writing on hedonism in the world. I’ll take the earnest, qualitative review of turntable cartridges.The one-man hit factory, the force who famously drove Amy Winehouse to create her best work, the mega producer – none of that is here, of course. At the centre of this book is a Ronson much closer to the teenage crate-digger whose mum bought him his first Technics turntables and who blagged his way to the booth. It shouldn’t be as compelling as it is, but for the accompanying soundtrack of deep cuts alone, Night People is well worth a spin.Nosheen Iqbal£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

title: Paul, John … and Yvonne? The French novelist asking: what if a woman had written the Beatles’ greatest hits? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Celebrated thriller writer Michel Bussi explains why the plot of his new novel Code Yesterday isn’t so far fetched, saying ‘I wanted to give women revenge’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celebrated thriller writer Michel Bussi explains why the plot of his new novel Code Yesterday isn’t so far fetched, saying ‘I wanted to give women revenge’
Content: With a little help from their friend? The Beatles in 1964.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWith a little help from their friend? The Beatles in 1964.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesFictionPaul, John … and Yvonne? The French novelist asking: what if a woman had written the Beatles’ greatest hits?Celebrated thriller writer Michel Bussi explains why the plot of his new novel Code Yesterday isn’t so far fetched, saying ‘I wanted to give women revenge’Bertrand BouardFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRelations betweenFranceand England have rarely looked brighter. The recent loan of the Bayeux tapestry has become a symbol of a renewed friendship between the two countries, evidenced further by the numerous smiles exchanged on the occasion between prime minister Andy Burnham and French president Emmanuel Macron. A new book released in France at the start of this month, however, could soon darken the sunny skies of a revitalisedentente cordiale.In Code Yesterday, author Michel Bussi proposes that every single song credited to the Beatles was in fact written by a woman … of French descent.Before you clench your fists in anger, rest assured: Code Yesterday is a work of fiction. “I hope British people have a good sense of humour,” says Bussi, sitting in the garden of his house near Rouen on a sunny morning.Bussi is one of France’s most successful thriller writers, whose books have sold in the millions and been turned into several films. Seven years ago, he wroteJ’ai dû rêver trop fort(“I must have been dreaming too hard”), which drew its inspiration from the story of American folk singer Sixto Rodriguez. His latest, he says, is the outcome of a lifelong fascination with the Fab Four, or thegarçons dans le ventas they are called on his side of the Channel.View image in fullscreenPaperback writer … Michel Bussi.Photograph: Philippe Matsas“I discovered them through my older sister and the red and blue compilations when I was eight. A little later my sister came home with The White Album, and I assumed it was a third compilation, and could not figure out why it had all these songs that were already on the other two,” he remembers, laughing. While his desire to write a story around the most iconic of rock bands was something he’s envisioned for years, his starting point came from an observation: “There are absolutely no women among all of the classic rock bands. Things have changed, thankfully, but for a long time, rock was exclusively a male thing. So I wanted to give them a revenge.” That’s how his plot began. And Bussi went all in.According to his story, a certain Yvonne McKenzie (a relation to “Father McKenzie” in Eleanor Rigby is implied) meets John and Paul near St Peter’s church on 6 July 1957, the same fateful day the pair first run into each other. Yvonne, a customs inspector born in Normandy to a French mother and an English paratrooper and raised on Liverpool’s Penny Lane, develops a crush on them both. Hurt by their indifference, she one day starts humming a song while sat in front of the young McCartney on the bus: Love Me Do.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Presses de la CitéMacca can’t get the tune out of his head and has no qualms about passing it off as his own. When Yvonne hears it on the radio for the first time, she is overwhelmed, and when John and Paul come back to her to ask for more, she happily obliges. The collaboration that ensues is unconventional but professional: Yvonne sings melodies to them over the phone, they add middle-eights and vocal layers and churn out hits.The feedback on I Feel Fine? According to Bussi’s novel, that’s inspired by one of Yvonne’s household appliances interfering with the phone line. The rattle-and-shake of Can’t Buy Me Love? A rhythm she came up with while whisking an egg. “Ob-La-Di Ob-La-Da”? The first syllables uttered by her newborn son, of course.As a female songwriter of humble origins in the 1960s, Yvonne is resigned to remaining faceless. “However awkward my story may seem,” says Bussi, “it’s entirely credible that a female songwriter at that time would only have been able get her songs heard if they were sung by good-looking boys”.The only thing she demands in exchange for her silence is that the Fab Four include in their oeuvre a few nods to her French origins – hence La Marseillaise in the first bars of All You Need is Love, and Michelle, a tribute to her mother, Micheline.Bussi’s says his wild fantasy is supported by years of deep-diving into books, movies and documentaries. His favourite records are Rubber Soul and Revolver,“where you hear an energy that was still pure and simple, they go experimental yet remain accessible”. He retains a deep fascination with the many myths surrounding the scouse quartet, and his story touches on many of the more mysterious aspects of the Beatles story, such as the deaths of Stuart Sutcliffe and Brian Epstein.In the novel, a grumpy old rock critic (and ardent Stones fan) backs Yvonne when she decides to tell her side of the story. And just as the whole country starts to believe her – in spite of a MI5 disinformation campaign – there’s a twist in the tale and Bussi’s outrageous story makes some kind of sense after all.‘It’s a more expansive, inclusive version’: how women reshaped the history of the BeatlesRead moreTo the author, Code Yesterday is above all a homage to the enduring charm of the Beatles’ music. The novel’s central premise may stretch credulity, but it demonstrates that the Beatles’ appeal – especially the wild romanticism of the early years – is so universal precisely because their songscouldjust as well have been written by or about a woman.“What I find fascinating is that they have this image of nice-looking boys, yet they did things that were much bolder than artists who are considered avant garde,” Bussi says. He pauses for a second, then adds: “I was pretty happy to come up with the part of Yvonne’s French ancestry, it was good fun. But let’s be honest, we French people are nowhere near as good as the English when it comes to rock music.” No hard feelings, then. France might even get the Bayeux tapestry back.Explore more on these topicsFictionMusic booksFiction in translationFranceThe BeatlesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No Land to Stand On by Mahmoud Khalil review – a searing account of political imprisonment | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury
Author: Houman Barekat
Headline: The Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury
Content: Mahmoud Khalil at a news conference in New York.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APView image in fullscreenMahmoud Khalil at a news conference in New York.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewNo Land to Stand On by Mahmoud Khalil review – a searing account of political imprisonmentThe Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet furyHouman BarekatFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMahmoud Khalil was completing a master’s degree at Columbia University when, in March 2025, plain-clothed officers from the Department of Homeland Security snatched him from his home in New York and took him to an immigration detention centre; he was then transferred to another facility in Louisiana, more than 1,000 miles away. As a green card holder, Khalil has permanent US residency, but secretary of state Marco Rubio had determined that his continued presence in the country would have “adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States”, and sought his deportation under a legal provision dating back to the McCarthy era. Khalil was released on bail in June 2024 after a federal judge ruled his detention unconstitutional, but the Trump administration is still trying to have him removed.Khalil – who was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria – had been targeted because of his advocacy on behalf of pro-Palestinian protesters during campus protests over Columbia University’s links to Israel. They were calling for Columbia to cut its ties with Israeli academic institutions and companies profiting from Israel’s onslaught on Gaza; in response, the universitycalled in the NYPD.There was no suggestion that Khalil had done anything unlawful, and no criminal charges were brought against him; the government had simply identified him as an influential pro-Palestinian voice on campus, and for that reason alone they wanted him gone. He spent a total of 104 days in detention, missing the birth of his son.Khalil recounts this Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury in his memoir, No Land to Stand On. The episode is a damning snapshot of the Trump administration’s creeping authoritarianism and the cruelty of its immigration enforcement policy. Khalil was a high-profile detainee whose case drew considerable public scrutiny; he had access to lawyers, and was eventually able to extricate himself. Many of his fellow prisoners at the facility, hailing from places as diverse as Georgia, Romania, Senegal, Nepal, El Salvador and Chechnya, were less fortunate. They languish in detention for months on end, at the mercy of an opaque and glacially slow legal bureaucracy, “forgotten in a system designed to forget them”.Khalil notes that the private ownership of the detention centre produced a perverse incentive structure. It “was not operated by the government, it was operated by shareholders. By people who made money when beds were filled and lost money when they were empty … Every man in this facility was a line item on a balance sheet. Every day we spent here was revenue.” This might explain why, whenever an asylum claim is successful, the state appeals the decision as a matter of course, needlessly extending the applicant’s detention by many more months. So much for the land of liberty.At Columbia, too, the prerogatives of the private sector impinge on the public interest. The university, Khalil quips, “turned out to be a real estate empire with a campus attached”; its board of trustees is “not so much a neutral administrative body as a deeply ideological one … drawn overwhelmingly from finance, real estate, corporate law, and weapons manufacturers”. So when students called out the university’s entanglement with a state credibly accused of committing war crimes, the college administration treated it “as a crisis to be managed rather than a grievance to be heard”.In the meantime, a broad coalition characterised by reading groups, fundraising bake-sales and solidarity with anti-Zionist Jewish groups was smeared as an antisemitic hate movement. There was much hand-wringing about student safety, at least some of which was in bad faith: “When pro-Israel students showed up at our events to film and harass us, the administration called it a legitimate expression of campus discourse. When we held a silent vigil, they described it as a security risk.” People may quibble over who is harassing whom in any given flashpoint, but one thing is undeniable: only those on one side of this argument are at risk of being spirited away by unidentified agents of the state on spurious pretexts.Khalil dislikes being referred to as an activist because the term implies some degree of volition, when in reality he had no choice: “From the moment I was born Palestinian, my existence was political.” His personal backstory, told here in parallel with the account of his arrest and detention, is indeed shaped by political turmoil. As a teenager he was shot in the leg by Bashar al-Assad’s security forces; in 2013, aged 18, he fled Syria for Lebanon, where eventually he ended up working for the British embassy in Beirut. It was there that he met his future wife, a US citizen, before moving to New York in 2022.What happened next is a warped travesty of the American dream: having grown up under a brutal dictatorship, Khalil settles in the US and exercises its much-vaunted political liberties, only to be locked up without charge alnd threatened with deportation. Palestinians, he concludes, “are the exception to every rule the supposed free world claims to hold sacred”. Given the horrors of the past three years, it’s hard to disagree.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMahmoud Khalil, No Land to Stand On: Protest, Palestine and Being Unfree in America is published by Picador (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsAutobiography and memoirBook of the dayMahmoud KhalilPolitics booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels | Teen books | The Guardian
description: A tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and more
Author: Imogen Russell Williams
Headline: A tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and more
Content: Making a splash … a detail from Once Upon a Tiger by Sarah Massini.Illustration: Simon and SchusterView image in fullscreenMaking a splash … a detail from Once Upon a Tiger by Sarah Massini.Illustration: Simon and SchusterChildren's book roundupTeen booksReviewChildren’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novelsA tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and moreImogen Russell WilliamsFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnce Upon a Tigerby Sarah Massini, S&S, £14.99Tiger is irate to find three cheeky human cubs climbing on his back – but when they refuse to be scared off, he becomes increasingly attached to them. A sweet, classic-feeling picture book fable, heightened by tender, expressive illustrations.View image in fullscreenMama’s Weddingby Circle Yuen, Lantana, £12.99Mama is getting married, but Ruby has mixed emotions – how will Daddy Albert feel on the day? A gorgeous, nuanced picture book about blended families and new milestones.I Am a Squirrelby Scott Rothman, illustrated by Tom Tinn-Dinsbury,Happy Yak, £7.99Big brother won’t believe that little brother’s a squirrel, even though he loves gathering nuts and leaping from tree to tree. But wait – is it time for a hawk to join the game?
