A funny, acutely observed picture book about sibling dynamics and imaginary play.View image in fullscreenThe Mole Construction Companyby Shingo Nagasaki, translated by Lisa Wilcut, Do Re Mi, £12.99Oh no, the Squirrels’ treehouse is tipping over! Enter the Moles with cranes and diggers to rebuild in this hugely engaging 4+ read-aloud story, translated from Japanese and perfect for vehicle-loving preschoolers.Three Brides for the Devilby Sally Nicholls, illustrated by John Broadley, Andersen, £12.99Charismatic and wealthy, the Devil rides into town in search of an obedient wife. Will one of the widow’s three daughters fit the bill? This elegant, subversive revisiting of Bluebeard, fascinatingly illustrated in intricate pen and ink, will grip 7+ readers as well as older children.View image in fullscreenGhost and Toastby Phil Corbett,Piccadilly, £8.99Trying to remember how he arrived in a haunted mansion, Ghost is surprised to find a cheery companion in Toast, a perfectly ordinary sentient slice of browned bread. Surreal jokes abound as the unlikely duo attempt to thwart the nefarious Croissant in this daft, delicious 7+ graphic novel.Henry Tudor: The Incredible Diaries of Me!by Danny Wallace, illustrated by Tor Freeman,Simon & Schuster, £7.99Eight-year-old Henry Tudor is the best at everything - especially making rude and obnoxious demands. When he’s challenged by a mysterious opponent, however, he’s forced to acknowledge that he might not be completely infallible in this highly illustrated, laugh-a-minute, subversively “historical” 7+ diary.View image in fullscreenHow the Rivermaid Grew Her Tail and Other West African and Caribbean Mythsby Jessica Wilson, illustrated by Sophie Bass,words & pictures, £12.99Weaving together the storytelling traditions of West Africa and the Caribbean, this lush, joyful 8+ collection offers tales ranging from the trickster Anansi to the Jamaican rivermaid of the title, describing the origins of each story with enticing details of food, culture and landscape. Wilson’s ornate text is enhanced by Bass’s boldly coloured, swirling illustrations.The Haunting of Old Splinterby Jack Mackay,Rock the Boat, £8.99When he makes a grisly discovery in his uncle’s sinister mansion, Peter wonders if the old stories are true. Can Old Splinter’s mysterious Wishing Claw actually grant wishes - and if so, at what cost? A superlatively creepy revisiting of The Monkey’s Paw for 8+, from a brilliant new horror writer.View image in fullscreenTackling Racism Togetherby AM Dassu, illustrated by Mia Saine,words & pictures, £10.99Informative and timely, this straightforward little book, produced in partnership with Show Racism the Red Card, provides a broad understanding of racism and its impacts, looking at systemic inequality, how our views are formed and how we can challenge racism in all its forms. A classroom must for 8+ readers.Impossible Creatures: The Neverfearby Katherine Rundell, Bloomsbury, £16.99When a dear friend is kidnapped from the Glimt Midsummer Feast, Christopher and Anya must undertake a desperate series of tasks to win her release. Funny, bloody, and richly underpinned with classical mythology, Rundell’s return to the world of Glimourie is layered with powerful themes of conservation, love, sacrifice and hope for readers of 9+.View image in fullscreenAnd Then We Screamedby Holly Bourne, Usborne, £9.99In the small town of Maple Lakes, everything is perfect – until cheerleader Abigail starts screaming in the middle of an exam. As more girls follow suit, student journalists Clover and Brody investigate the cause, only to discover the sad, terrible secrets beneath the town’s tranquil exterior. A fiercely feminist, gripping and emotionally resonant thriller from a much-loved YA author.Dead Girlsby Beck Kubrick,Simon & Schuster, £12.99When five teenage girls are found murdered in Clossdale, suspicion falls on 17-year-old Ash, daughter of notorious serial killer “Evil Evelyn”. Determined to clear herself, Ash devises a plan to stop the killings, teaming up with her foster sister and best friend. But the girls aren’t expecting to discover a dark conspiracy dating back through generations of power. This blackly comic, splendidly camp graphic novel is a must for YA slasher-film fans.View image in fullscreenThen We’ll Be HappybyAlan Carrigan, Chicken House, £8.99Seventeen-year-old Sam, who has cerebral palsy, just wants some control over his life. When an inaccessible bus bars him from a school trip, he decides to campaign for change – but soon finds himself well out of his comfort zone, confronting his own internalised ableism as he investigates what happiness might look like for him now, rather than in a remote future. Carrigan’s YA debut is a humorous, sometimes painful, deeply engaging account of coming of age as a disabled teenager.Between Ghosts and Godsby Ann Sei Lin, Walker, £16.99As a mortal, Kasu sold her soul to a demon; now she works in a lower-world gambling den, exchanging ghosts’ treasures for gambling tiles, and living virtuously in the hope of reincarnation. When Arun, a mortal prince, arrives in the underworld looking for his mother, Kasu wants nothing to do with him - but as she and Arun are drawn closer, she may risk all her hopes to help his quest. A lush, delectable dark YA fantasy, rooted in Chinese mythology.Explore more on these topicsTeen booksChildren's book roundupChildren and teenagersChildren's books: 7 and underChildren's books: 8-12 yearsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Susan Calman: Tall Tales review – comic’s first tour in 10 years is raw and riotous | Comedy | The Guardian
description: Faux truculent and palpably adorable, the standup is in her element exposing her supposed flaws and the unseen idiocies of her TV career
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Faux truculent and palpably adorable, the standup is in her element exposing her supposed flaws and the unseen idiocies of her TV career
Content: Peachy and bulletproof set pieces … Susan Calman.Photograph: Steve UllathorneView image in fullscreenPeachy and bulletproof set pieces … Susan Calman.Photograph: Steve UllathorneComedyReviewSusan Calman: Tall Tales review – comic’s first tour in 10 years is raw and riotousPerth Concert HallFaux truculent and palpably adorable, the standup is in her element exposing her supposed flaws and the unseen idiocies of her TV careerBrian LoganFri 18 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTall Tales isSusan Calman’s first new standup set for 10 years, designed to show us the real Susan behind the cuddly personality we see on TV. Given that was the premise ofher 2016 touring showtoo, it’s clear that a decade away has done little to develop – but also nothing to diminish – the Glaswegian’s onstage shtick. This is a compelling return, stuffed with experiences and insights gleaned from that standup downtime, and which undergirds familiar tales of cat fancying, being small and entering menopause with a heartfelt reckoning with recent bereavement and rocky mental health.That last material feels raw, as she tells us she only returned to standup (the thing she feared the most, she says) to shock herself out of a bad depression. That would be hard to credit based on her show alone, which finds Calman in her element: faux truculent but palpably adorable, fulminating at the indignities of short, lesbian, middle-aged womanhood, revealing to us the unseen idiocies of her gilded TV career. Her supposed flaws are arrayed for our pleasure: her catastrophising (cue a fun anecdote about being trapped on a hotel balcony), her addictive personality, and – in the peachy set-piece that closes act one – her hormonal lust for righteous revenge.Tilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumnRead moreThat number, about her newfound love for golf, finds Calman at her best, when the occasionally generic midlife patter becomes uniquely, idiosyncratically her. See her story about her granny’s recipe for “Italian mince”, her penchant for the80s TV show Hart to Hart, or the tale of terrorising her neighbour with the Weeping Angel (from Doctor Who) she keeps in her back garden. The behind-the-scenes stories culled from her work on daytime telly are homelier, although she does derive fromher Strictly Come Dancing stinta bulletproof standup set-piece about, ahem, personal grooming.All of this is given emotional heft by the recent parental loss and experience of depression, which – while the point isn’t laboured – clearly knocked Calman for six. This may, she says, be her last standup show. If so, this pint-sized tall tales teller goes out with her head held high.Touring until 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsComedySusan CalmanTelevisionStrictly Come DancingDoctor WhoreviewsShareReuse this content

Content: Growing mystery  … La Voix du sang by René Magritte.Photograph: Fredrik Nilsen Studio/© 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, LondonView image in fullscreenGrowing mystery  … La Voix du sang by René Magritte.Photograph: Fredrik Nilsen Studio/© 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, LondonArt Weekly newsletterArt and designMindboggling Magritte, artists respond to a world in peril and a squished Citroën – the week in artThe surrealist still confounds, artists look at the past, present and future of the planet and Rachel Kneebone’s crazed delights blend into the Wallace Collection –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekThisIs Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of MagritteThe confounding, mind-boggling genius of Magritte is explored through remarkable loans of his paintings plus contemporary responses by Sarah Lucas, Matthew Barney and more.Gagosian Grosvenor Hill, London, from 24 September until 12 DecemberAlso showingRachel Kneebone– Metamorphoses: Porcelain SculptureKneebone’s porcelain sculptures are crazed reworkings of the kind of Rococo delights that fill the Wallace Collection, so this is a match made in Versailles.Wallace Collection, London, 23 September until 25 AprilExtinction: Renewal, Art of a Living PlanetDavid Nash, Cristina Mittermeier and other Bangladesh.Serpentine North Gallery, London, 23 September until 31 JanuaryGabriel Orozco: ChronotopicA retrospective of the artist famous for cutting open and remaking a Citroën DS, from early works to his latest conundrums.White Cube Bermondsey, London, until 8 NovemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPollenarium by Luke Jerram.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianA new installation that gives visitors a bee’s eye view of the world is landing by the Thames in east London. Created by Bristol artist Luke Jerram the outside represents a grain of pollen, and the inside represents an insect’s compound eye. Jerram hopes it will make people think about how we need to protect pollinators, whose numbers have declined by 60% in 20 years.Read more here.What we learnedManchester’s Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art has a new name and a new missionDonald Trump wants a 30ft “Colossus statue” of George Washington erectedA show about Emmett Till, whose lynching fired the US civil rights movement, invites audiences to reckon with racismYasmin David is the greatest British landscape painter you’ve never heard ofMagazine designers have picked their favourite ever coversPreviously unseen drawings by Moomins author Tove Jansson are to go on show in Londonskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Women’s Art Collection in Cambridge features some of the industry’s biggest names including Maggi Hambling, Paula Rego and Bridget RileyMasterpiece of the weekTwo MenWith a Sleeping Woman by Gabriel Metsu, about 1655-60View image in fullscreenPhotograph: AlamyPipes play a slightly surreal part in this 17th-century Dutch painting in which objects and people interact suggestively. A woman has passed out with her white clay pipe in her hand, its stem leading the eye towards what amounts to a still life arrangement beside her: there is a richly decorated cup for spirits, presumably gin, beside a fanned out deck of cards, a mirror, another pipe and a jug of booze. The implication is pretty clear that she’s fallen asleep after a long session of drinking, smoking and card playing – but what about the mirror? It suggests vanity, and in this picture that may mean loose morals or even prostitution. title: Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison drama | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Rona Munro’s understated untangling of a fractured relationship is revived with Christine and Lois Mackie
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Rona Munro’s understated untangling of a fractured relationship is revived with Christine and Lois Mackie
Content: Estranged and unalike … Christine and Lois Mackie in Iron.Photograph: Shay RowanView image in fullscreenEstranged and unalike … Christine and Lois Mackie in Iron.Photograph: Shay RowanTheatreReviewIron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaHome, ManchesterRona Munro’s understated untangling of a fractured relationship is revived with Christine and Lois MackieMark FisherFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can see why they cast real-life mother and daughter Christine and Lois Mackie in the central roles ofRona Munro’s 2002 prison drama. With Christine playing Fay, a lifer who is inside for murder, and Lois as Josie, her daughter and only visitor, it is no stretch to believe they are related.The irony, though, in this probing, slippery play, is not just that they are estranged but they have become quite unlike each other. It has been 15 years since Josie saw her mother and, having been raised by a grandmother, has grown into a sensible career woman, all suits, business parties and international travel.Mackie junior plays her with an air of detachment: you can imagine her drifting frictionlessly through the world of personnel just as you can see her struggling for definition in her private life. Whatever happened in her childhood has stripped her of an identity. She comes to the visiting room to be coloured in.Compared with such middle-class smoothness, Fay is all sharp edges. Mackie senior plays her like a captive bird, her eyes forever searching for danger, her body contained but ready for flight. It is a superb performance, inconsolable one moment, manipulative the next, hungry for trust but untrustable. Is her “erratic impulse control” a consequence of being locked up or a character flaw? She leaves us guessing.Fences review – August Wilson’s classic family drama is as smart as paintRead moreAs they meet, month by month, they only seem less alike. That is part of Munro’s point: in other circumstances, someone like Josie could forget that people like Fay exist, still less consider the purpose of prison, its effects on mental health and the degree to which women, in particular, can be incarcerated less because of malice than because of a bad roll of the dice. Whether Fay is guilty or innocent, the women’s trauma starts with a man.Sam Holland-Bunyan’s bare-bones production forBest Girlis quiet and subdued, the better to untangle the psychological knots in the women’s relationship as they are watched over by the seen-it-all prison guards (Ellaney Hayden and Jamie Smelt). The low-key approach mutes Munro’s humour and makes a long play seem longer, even as it renders a fractured relationship compelling and sad.AtHome, Manchester, until 19 September. Then atThe Dukes, Lancaster, 30 September–3 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreRona MunroHome in ManchesterPrisons and probationUK criminal justicereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a mess. I had to do something’: the personal struggle that inspired rap star Giggs to start a special needs school | Giggs | The Guardian
description: After a battle to get his autistic children properly assessed, the London MC has co-founded a specialist centre in Kent to help neurodivergent kids realise their potential
Author: Ian Gittins
Headline: After a battle to get his autistic children properly assessed, the London MC has co-founded a specialist centre in Kent to help neurodivergent kids realise their potential
Content: A remarkable venture … Giggs pictured at St James House, the new Send school he has co-founded in Kent.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianView image in fullscreenA remarkable venture … Giggs pictured at St James House, the new Send school he has co-founded in Kent.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianGiggs‘It was a mess. I had to do something’: the personal struggle that inspired rap star Giggs to start a special needs schoolAfter a battle to get his autistic children properly assessed, the London MC has co-founded a specialist centre in Kent to help neurodivergent kids realise their potentialIan GittinsFri 18 Sep 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been a busy few weeks for the London rapperGiggs. Two weeks ago, he was in New Jersey with his fiancee Valerie as she gave birth to the couple’s daughter, Noa. The next day, he flew home and went straight to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium to guest on stage with Jay-Z. “Yeah, it’s been crazy,” he smiles.Remarkably, as soon as Noa was delivered, he also found time to livestream from the US hospital to the launch event for his latest project: not an album, but a specialist school and assessment centre for neurodivergent children.Giggs, 45, has teamed up with education charity the OMG Foundation, to launch St James House, a secondary school for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) and those in alternative provision, in Gravesend, Kent. It’s a project with extremely personal origins.“I’ve been fighting for my seven-year-old son, Israel,” Giggs says when we meet at the school on his return to the UK. “He’s autistic but the system was failing him. We couldn’t get him diagnosed and he wasn’t getting the support and assessments he needed. It was a mess. I thought, well, I’ve got to do something.”If Giggs is tired, you can’t tell from the way he bounds around the former business offices now being converted into a 75-pupil school.View image in fullscreenGiggs (right) and OMG Education CEO Jamal Miah.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianThe Peckham-born musician has four children including his newborn; all three older kids are autistic. His eldest son, the rapper ML, was diagnosed more than a decade ago, in his early teens. Last year, the father-and-son duo made a joint track about living with autism, Own Motion. “When I was young, I was ashamed, now I just own it,” ML raps.“At the time, I read ML’s diagnosis and thought, this is me as well,” recalls Giggs. “So, I went to get assessed. It was just a man and woman in a room with a notepad and I thought, this is bullshit. How the fuck are they going to know if I’m autistic or not? After five minutes, I walked out. I didn’t hear anything, but then 10 years later I was in the doctor’s and he looked at my notes and said, ‘It says here that you’re autistic. I was, like, ‘Is it?’ Because I didn’t even know.”View image in fullscreenThe under-construction St James House school in Gravesend.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianGiggs belatedly learning his own diagnosis coincided with his battle to obtain diagnoses and education, health and care plans (EHCPs) for Israel and his daughter, Isla. Last year, he went on Newsnight to rail against the flaws and inadequacies in the Send educational system. Israel was given his EHCP the next day.Yet this clearly isn’t an avenue for most parents struggling with the difficult, opaque Send system. Prime minister Andy Burnham recently acknowledged that the overladen system is “broken” and pledged greater assistance for the parents of special needs children attempting to navigate it.The difficulties Giggs had getting these crucial assessments for his children was a primary motivation when he decided to launch St James House. He and his co-founder, OMG Foundation CEO Jamal Miah, have long been acquainted.“I’ve known Giggs since he used to record in a south London music studio that I ran 20 years ago,” says Miah, when we meet on an earlier visit to the school. “We kept in touch then coincidentally we found that we had both moved out to Kent. We saw a lot of disadvantaged kids around Gravesend and decided to do something for them.”OMG Foundation already runs one school in east London. When Miah and Giggs decided to start one in Kent, Giggs insisted it needed an assessment centre built in. “Because a lot of parents don’t know how to get EHCPs,” says Miah. “Until their kids have got those, it’s hard to do anything for them.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘What Giggs is doing with this project is tremendous’ … Frances Akinde, executive head teacher at St James House.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianThe school and assessment centre will be overseen by executive head Frances Akinde, a specialist in neurodivergent education who praises the value of art and music therapy. “I also used to do parental advocacy work, and one of the parents I advised was Giggs,” she explains. “What he is doing with the St James House project is tremendous.”The assessment centre, employing educational psychologists, occupational therapists and speech-and-language specialists, opened this month. The school is due to follow suit in January. Miah reports that OMG Foundation are well on the way to raising the £930,000 they need to begin operations, spurred by Giggs pulling in big names for a recent charity auction.“I reached out to people that I know,” he says. “Damien Hirst gave us seven artworks. Dynamo agreed to do two private shows. Stephen Fry gave us stuff, and Ed Sheeran and Robbie Williams. They all wanted to be get involved. They’re all proper, man.”It’s a remarkable venture, and when St James House opens in the new year, Giggs knows exactly what he wants it to do for the autistic and ADHD children thronging through its doors.“I want us to be Professor Xavier for the neurodivergent universe,” he concludes, referring to the founder-educator figure in the X-Men comic books. “The X-Men started as a school before they all became superheroes. We can help autistic children to realise that they are geniuses and show them how to use their superpowers.”Explore more on these topicsGiggsSpecial educational needsAutismNeurodiversitySchoolsParents and parentingnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to answer for its ‘dismal record’ in Eurovision before committee of MPs | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Digital, culture, media and sport committee expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses and music industry experts
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Digital, culture, media and sport committee expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses and music industry experts
Content: The UK finished last this year with Eins, Zwei, Drei by Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UK finished last this year with Eins, Zwei, Drei by Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesEurovisionUK to answer for its ‘dismal record’ in Eurovision before committee of MPsDigital, culture, media and sport committee expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses and music industry expertsJamie GriersonFri 18 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe and Jake. Daz Sampson. Electro Velvet. Who could forget them?Most people, probably. They are some of the many acts who represented the UK at theEurovisionsong contest in the last 20 years that have failed to find a place in the country’s cultural pantheon.Now, the chair of an influential parliamentary committee has decided to interrogate exactly why the UK has been performing so poorly.Dame Caroline Dinenage, who heads the digital, culture, media and sport committee,told the BBC: “We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years is the result of bad song choice, weak performance … or something else.”Prior to 2000, the UK could be proud of its efforts: it finished in the top 10 every year except 1978, 1987 and 1999, and won with Love Shine a Light by Katrina and the Waves in 1997.View image in fullscreenKatrina and the Waves after winning Eurovision in Dublin in May 1997.Photograph: John Giles/APBut since then it has reached the top 10 only three times and finished in last place six times – in2003,2008,2010,2019,2021and2026– with Jemini and James Newman scoring nul points in 2003 and 2021 respectively. The exception was Sam Ryder’s Space Man in 2022,which came second.The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC with support from a record label or music management company.The Commons committee is reportedly expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses as well as music industry experts over the coming months.In 2026, Bulgaria won the contest when Dara swept to victory with the songBangaranga. The 27-year-old singer’s triumph was the first victory for Bulgaria, which joined Eurovision in 2005 and had sat out the past three editions.View image in fullscreenDara in Vienna in May.Photograph: Lisa Leutner/ReutersThe UK finished last with Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle. The YouTuber, who makes his own synthesisers, failed to win over neutral voters with the song Eins, Zwei, Drei. The song received zero points in the public vote, meaning it did not make it into the top 10 in any of the voting countries.The contest has become increasingly political, primarily over the inclusion of Israel, which has been participating since 1973. Ireland is to boycott the contest for the second year running over the Gaza war. It wasone of five countries, along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.Explore more on these topicsEurovisionArts policySam RydernewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthony Page obituary | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Stage and screen director behind landmark productions of Samuel Beckett, John Osborne and Edward Albee
Author: Michael Coveney
Headline: Stage and screen director behind landmark productions of Samuel Beckett, John Osborne and Edward Albee
Content: Page at the Longacre Theatre, New York, on the opening Night of Edward Albee's revival of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, March 2005.Photograph: Bruce Glikas/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenPage at the Longacre Theatre, New York, on the opening Night of Edward Albee's revival of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, March 2005.Photograph: Bruce Glikas/FilmMagicTheatreObituaryAnthony Page obituaryStage and screen director behind landmark productions of Samuel Beckett, John Osborne and Edward AlbeeMichael CoveneyFri 18 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Page, who has died aged 90, was one of a group of talented and individual – sometimes wilful – directors who helped establish the English Stage Company at the Royal Court in London at the end of the 1950s and the early 60s.The company, led by George Devine and Tony Richardson, became the seedbed of modern playwriting, notablyJohn Osborne’s Look Back in Anger (1956) in a repertoire that embraced Beckett, Brecht, Ionesco,Arthur Millerand Tennessee Williams, as well as the native voices ofArnold Wesker,Ann Jellicoe,John ArdenandNF Simpson.Page, quietly spoken but tough as old boots, shared a general predilection for waspishness in this fearsome company that included John Dexter,William Gaskilland Lindsay Anderson, with Devine a benign and pipe-smoking presence; his “old school” professional connections to the likes of Peggy Ashcroft and Laurence Olivier stamped the enterprise with their status and eminence.Page started at the Court as an assistant director in 1958 and emerged as Osborne’s ideal director after Richardson had supervised the rough and tumble of Look Back in Anger and then Olivier in The Entertainer (1957). He directed six Osborne premieres, notably Inadmissible Evidence (1964), withNicol Williamsonas the washed-up, craven solicitor Bill Maitland; A Patriot for Me (1965), with its Viennese 1890s drag ball and infiltration of Russian intelligence agents; and the still underrated Hotel in Amsterdam (1968), withPaul Scofieldas an acidic version of Osborne himself on the other side of a decade of success.The one thing shared among all the Court directors was a regard for the primacy of the author’s text. Page, highly civilised and literate, tall and not a little forbidding, had an almost faultless ear for music, tone and rhythm, which led him to be as adept with Beckett and Shaw as he was, in the later part of his career, with the more inflamed and baroque poetry of Tennessee Williams andEdward Albee.View image in fullscreenAlbert Finney, left, and Brian Cox in Page’s 1973 production of David Storey’s Cromwell at the Royal Court.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyHe was born in Bangalore (now Bengaluru), India, the son of a British brigadier, Frederick Page, and his wife, Pearl (nee Hall). Educated at Oakley Hall, Cirencester, and Winchester college, Hampshire, he studied English at Magdalen College, Oxford. He then went on a free passage with the Royal Canadian Air Force to visit his parents, who were now based in Canada, and hitchhiked to New York, where he studied at the Neighbourhood Playhouse School, an offshoot of the Stanislavski-influenced GroupTheatreof the 1930s.He became obsessed with a form of method acting, developed by the directorSanford Meisner, that replaced the Stanislavskian use of affective memory with an emphasis on “the reality of doing”, a technique devised to find a fresher way for an actor to speak the truth. He returned to London and, with Anderson, instigated a series of workshops along those lines. The future Court alumniAlbert FinneyandAlfred Lynchcame along. So didMaggie Smith, whom Page would direct in three of her finest performances in plays by Albee.His first production at the Court wasHarold Pinter’s The Room in 1960, with Michael Caine and Vivien Merchant in the cast. He then went off to work in various reps around the country and was artistic director of the old Dundee Rep for a couple of seasons before it burned down in 1963.Williamson was in the Dundee company and followed Page to the Royal Shakespeare Company’s 1962 experimental season at the Arts theatre in both Henry Livings’s Nil Carborundum, a comedy about national service, and Thomas Middleton’s Jacobean shocker Women Beware Women, withElizabeth SpriggsandJohn Thaw.As Devine fell ill, Page took over the reins in Sloane Square with Anderson and embarked on an incredible quartet of productions at the Royal Court in 1964-65: Inadmissible Evidence, Ben Travers’s 1925 Aldwych farce A Cuckoo in the Nest (the cast including Alan Bennett,Arthur Loweand Osborne, as well as Williamson), the first British revival of Waiting for Godot (with Williamson and Lynch as the tramps) and A Patriot For Me.Following the death of Devine, Gaskill returned to take on the artistic leadership in 1969, with Page, Anderson andPeter Gillhis associates. Page directedAlan Batesas Hamlet at the Nottingham Playhouse and the Cambridge theatre in London, and Pirandello’s The Rules of the Game (in a version co-written by David Hare, his first NT credit) at the National in 1971.His last productions at the Court, in the early 70s, wereTed Whitehead’s coruscating Alpha Beta, with Finney and Rachel Roberts tearing up the stage; Jill Bennett as Hedda Gabler; a double bill of Beckett’s Not I (Billie Whitelawas the mouth in a black hole) and Krapp’s Last Tape with Finney; and Finney again, with Brian Cox, inDavid Storey’s Cromwell (1973).Page’s American career continued in the 80s with television films featuringJason Robardsas Franklin D Roosevelt,Mickey Rooneyas a lost soul in Bill, and Dirk Bogarde andGlenda Jacksonas Roald Dahl andPatricia Nealin The Patricia Neal Story. He had also worked in British television since 1963, notably on The Parachute (1968) by David Mercer – with Bennett, Osborne and Anderson in the cast – and a superb six-part version of George Eliot’s Middlemarch in 1994.A 1991 TV revival of Rodney Ackland’s Absolute Hell (1952, when, as The Pink Room, it was dismissed by one critic as a libel on the British people), with Judi Dench as the hostess in a West End drinking den between VE Day and the Labour landslide in 1945, was a reimagined revelation on the National Theatre stage in 1995, again with Dench.View image in fullscreenMaggie Smith, left, and Eileen Atkins in Page’s ‘blistering revival’ of A Delicate Balance at the Theatre Royal Haymarket, October 1997.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAll of Page’s work was about finding the right style and the right cast for each play or film, never trying to make a name for himself at the expense of the text or script. This scrupulousness went right back to the early Royal Court days.And it went hand in hand with a sensitivity for the most difficult of Albee’s plays, for instance The Goat (at the Almeida and the West End in 2004), which dealt in the limits of tolerance rather than bestiality in the fable of a securely married architect (Jonathan Pryce) falling in love with, well, a goat; Eddie Redmayne made a touching West End debut as the architect’s gay son.His reinvention, almost, as a go-to director of American and European classics occurred in the West End and on Broadway, where he directed a Tony awardwinning A Doll’s House with Janet McTeer (1996-97).The three “Maggie Smith in Albee” collaborations marked an Indian summer for Page with commercial managements: Three Tall Women (1994) at Wyndham’s he described, and treated, as a Restoration comedy about death; his blistering revival of A Delicate Balance in 1997 at the Haymarket teamed Smith, unforgettably, with Eileen Atkins as viciously intemperate siblings; and, also at the Haymarket, in 2007, Smith wasThe Lady from Dubuque, an angel of death who brings bad tidings to a drunken party where the hostess is dying of cancer. This was Greek tragedy with cocktails and laughter, and ornately macabre dialogue.For one of his last productions, Page returned to New York, and to Beckett, in 2009 to stage an acclaimedWaiting for Godotat Studio 54 with Nathan Lane and Bill Irwin as the tramps and John Goodman as Pozzo.Page was predeceased by a younger sister, Jane. He is survived by his husband, Ken Butler, an artist. Their 40-year relationship was formalised by a civil partnership in 2006 and a marriage in 2014.Anthony Frederick Montague Page, theatre director, born 21 September 1935, died 11 September 2026Explore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Court theatreobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules | House of Lords | The Guardian
description: Switch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressed
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Switch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressed
Content: Men will no longer be required to wear a tie in the House of Lords, as they are in this May photo.Photograph: Roger Harris/Roger Harris/House of Lords 2026View image in fullscreenMen will no longer be required to wear a tie in the House of Lords, as they are in this May photo.Photograph: Roger Harris/Roger Harris/House of Lords 2026House of LordsIs the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rulesSwitch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressedSammy GecsoylerFri 18 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHouse of Lordshas long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”.One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”.Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-pagebook, they can add a touch of undeniable class.Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”.“Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties.View image in fullscreenGuy Hills.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianHe called them “little works of art”, and decried those who shunned them while dressing formally. “It looks as if you’re not completely dressed, or you’ve forgotten something,” he said.On Savile Row, views on ties were mixed. “I don’t think ties are completely dead, they’re just having a down moment,” said Guy Hills, 58, a fashion photographer and owner of Dashing Tweed, who was sauntering down the street in a green tweed suit. Something else was also green: his moustache.He said his dyed facial hair might be allowed in the House of Lords, and is in support of the relaxed dress code, believing that members have a responsibility to keep up with fashion trends.“They used to be the driving force of fashion, especially around Savile Row. They would go to their tailors and try to outdo each other. When you stop all that, and it becomes like a living museum, then the whole menswear fashion world stops,” he said.Hills usually has something around his neck. “I can’t go out without a scarf because it looks too slovenly,” he said. But Thursday afternoon was, unluckily, one of the rare occasions he was without a silk scarf or cravat.While ties aren’t totally “in”, Hills thinks they could make a comeback. “The younger generation is now getting more interested in sustainability and proper clothing. A tie really finishes a whole outfit off,” he said.View image in fullscreenChaand Singh.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianAmong the few wearing a tie on Savile Row was Chaand Singh. The 25-year-old, who works in marketing, had decided to wear a navy tie from Next because of an important work meeting. “Dressing up and adding a tie elevates the look,” he said – so much so that he had received compliments from people. “Someone said that I look a bit more sharp today.”Ties were no longer an office must, said Singh – but he thinks they still have their place. “I’ve got some from the 80s with cool patterns. They’re usually wider and designed when fashion was a bit more experimental,” he said. “I would wear them at work for the right scenario, but casually as well. Some girls even wear ties as belts.”View image in fullscreenJames Sleater.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianWhat do tailors on the Row think? “The House of Lords should be a mirror of society. What better way of doing it than reflecting current trends?” said James Sleater, 45, the owner of Norton & Sons. “Women don’t have to wear ties, and if men have the option, it’s OK by me.”Sleater said that in the “post-Covid era, there has been a huge decline in neckwear and the number of people wearing ties to the office”, adding that the “relaxation of dress codes is symptomatic of people working several days a week at home”.Norton & Sons sees people from all walks of life. “Yesterday we had an ex-prime minister and today we’ve got a Hollywood star having a fitting. We also see people wanting a suit for their first job and people celebrating a wedding,” he says. Have these customers shunned ties and other neckwear in droves? Actually, no. “We’re seeing the reversal of this trend,” says Sleater. “We’re selling more neckwear this year than we did in previous years.“If you’re no longer forced to do something, it almost becomes a pleasure to it,” he adds. “To wear a suit to work when you don’t have to is a joy. When you’re told to do it, you’re almost feeling rebellious and you don’t want to do it.”People have opted for “more characterful textures rather than just plain silks or bright brash colours”, though Slater sees a limit to a potential neckwear revival. “I don’t see cravats or bow ties coming back,” he said.As for Lords who can keep their ties at home, some are in favour of the new rules. “In truth, the only people now wearing ties for business purposes are estate agents and funeral directors,” Lord Davies of Brixton, a Labour peer, told the Telegraph. “The tie is disappearing.”It remains to be seen if Davies’ fellow Lords will heed the message.Explore more on these topicsHouse of LordsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I survived being buried in an avalanche | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I was at the mercy of the mountain, heading towards a 20-metre drop, about to discover what it felt like to die
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was at the mercy of the mountain, heading towards a 20-metre drop, about to discover what it felt like to die
Content: ‘I felt as if I was falling for ever’ … Jacob Wester in Stockholm.Photograph: Josefine StenersenView image in fullscreen‘I felt as if I was falling for ever’ … Jacob Wester in Stockholm.Photograph: Josefine StenersenExperienceLife and styleExperience: I survived being buried in an avalancheI was at the mercy of the mountain, heading towards a 20-metre drop, about to discover what it felt like to dieJacob WesterFri 18 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrowing up in Sweden, I was as comfortable on skis as I was walking on my feet. As a teenager, I became a professional free skier, a style that features jumps and tricks. In my 20s, I moved into content creation. Now, at 38, I spend the winter months filming extreme ski videos with my photographer wife, Sofia.In March this year, we’d been staying at the base of the Lyngen Alps, northern Norway. Nonstop rain had prevented us from filming but, finally, we had fresh powder and clear skies. The plan was for me to go up the mountain with a friend, Lovisa, and make our way down as the sun was setting. Sofia would film us from the bottom using a drone.We climbed to the summit, arriving just before sunset, but it was cloaked in cloud. I was disappointed. I was hooked up to audio and ready to go.I suggested we ski down anyway, just for fun. I dug into the snow to make sure it was stable. If it’s not, the top layer of snow slides off the icier layer underneath. It didn’t move, so we took turns to zigzag slowly down, with me in the lead. Once we broke through the clouds, we had breathtaking views of the orange skies and blue fjords.Experience: I didn’t know I was pregnant until I gave birthRead moreThen a dark line shot out from under my skis, a deep crack in the surface. I knew what it meant. My movement had caused a slab of snow to break away beneath me. I’d triggered an avalanche.Lovisa was above me, so she was safe. An avalanche picks up speed and more snow as it travels down the mountain. I’d been in small slides before and had outskied them. This time, however, the snow was moving too fast to do that.If I didn’t get out of its way, I wouldn’t survive. I spotted some rocks to the side. I dug my poles down hard and turned towards them. Moments from safety, I hit something under the snow and my skis pinged off. I was at the mercy of the mountain, heading towards a 20-metre drop. I started tumbling downwards. It would go dark as I was pushed deep into the snow, then light as I circled to the surface again. I frantically dug my poles and boots into the slope, trying to slow myself down. Suddenly, I was weightless, and everything went silent. I’d been flushed off the cliff edge. I felt as if I was falling for ever, but I later discovered the drop lasted less than two seconds.double quotation markFuelled by adrenaline, I ignored my injuries and started kicking towards the surfaceI realised I couldn’t survive this and curled myself into a foetal position. I was about to discover what it felt like to die. Would it go all black, like the end of a film? Instead, there was an incredible impact. I’d crashed on to a thin layer of snow, littered with ice and rocks. The air was knocked out of my lungs, and I felt my right leg buckle painfully. I thought: “I’m not dead.”As the snow continued to push me down the slope, I checked myself over. I could move my toes, so knew my back wasn’t broken. My leg was numb, but my pelvis felt like it was in one piece.The intensity of the snow surging over me had eased and the incline was beginning to level out, but I knew if I didn’t stay near the surface I’d be buried. Fuelled by adrenaline, I ignored my injuries and started kicking towards the surface. Finally, I slowed to a stop. I ended up in a sitting position, buried to my waist with my legs in front of me. “I’m alive!” I shouted into my mic, “but I need help.”Lovisa made it down in 10 minutes, navigating the rocky cliff face and sections of pure ice. Minutes later, Sofia and two friends began trekking to where they’d seen me land, bringing blankets and hot-water bottles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSofia and Lovisa had both watched as the avalanche overwhelmed me, and endured an agonising wait to find out if I’d survived. When we listened to the audio recording, the entire ordeal had lasted just 75 seconds.A rescue helicopter flew me to the nearest hospital. X-rays confirmed I had broken some ribs and snapped my femur. I was rushed into surgery, where they pinned my leg. I was in hospital for three days and felt like a celebrity. Everyone wanted to meet the man who’d survived the avalanche.I’m currently recovering in Stockholm, but I plan to get back on the slopes next year. We’ve lost friends in avalanches and accidents before. Unfortunately, it’s part of the deal you strike with the mountain. I’m just grateful to be here to tell my story.As told to Jacqui PatersonDo you have an experience to share? title: Cocktail of the week: Buster’s stout punch, from The Prince Bar – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A velvety, Guinness-based, punch-style pick-me-up
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A velvety, Guinness-based, punch-style pick-me-up
Content: ‘Warm the cockles’: Buster’s stout punch.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Jack Hall.View image in fullscreen‘Warm the cockles’: Buster’s stout punch.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Jack Hall.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Buster’s stout punch, from The Prince Bar – recipeA velvety, Guinness-based, punch-style pick-me-upWill HawesFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePunch isn’t just for summer parties, and this Caribbean-inflected one, featuring rum, brandy, stout, lemon and nutmeg, will warm the cockles of a crowd on any autumn evening. It’s named afterPrince Buster, the Jamaican ska legend and inspiration for our bar’s name.Buster’s stout punchServes20250g demerara sugar, or cane sugar4 large unwaxed lemons900ml Jamaican dark rum, ideally a well-aged one –Myers’sorPlanteray Original Darkfor preference400ml VSOP cognac– we useMartell300ml Guinness– we useGuinness Foreign Extra StoutorGuinness West Indies PorterFreshly grated nutmeg, to garnish and to taste (optional)Put the sugar in a large bowl, then finely grate in the zest of all four lemons(use a Microplane, if you have one); save the rest of the fruit for later. Gently massage the lemon zest into the sugar, to release the oils, then pour in a litre of hot water from the kettle and stir to dissolve the sugar. Strain the sugar water through a fine sieve and into a punch bowl, to sift out the spent zest.Measure in the rum, cognac and stout, squeeze in the juice of all four lemons, stir and put in the fridge to chill until your guests arrive.To serve, stir a good couple of handfuls of ice into the punch, grate over the nutmeg to taste, then ladle into glasses of your choosing. Top each serving with a light dusting of grated nutmeg, if you like.Will Hawes, co-founder,The Prince Bar, London EC1Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodCaribbean food and drinkBeerFruitHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns | Baking | The Guardian
description: Everyone loves an iced finger bun, but these light and moist bakes with a blackcurrant fondant topping might be your new favourite afternoon treat
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: Everyone loves an iced finger bun, but these light and moist bakes with a blackcurrant fondant topping might be your new favourite afternoon treat
Content: Helen Goh’s blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotBakingHelen Goh’s recipe for blackcurrant and vanilla finger bunsEveryone loves an iced finger bun, but these light and moist bakes with a blackcurrant fondant topping might be your new favourite afternoon treatHelen GohFri 18 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoft, feather-light and topped with a thick strip of icing: few things are as irresistible to me as an iced finger bun. Here, I’ve flavoured the fondant with blackcurrant jam, which lends a gentle tartness to balance the sweetness, though almost any good-quality jam will work. A simpletanzhong(a cooked flour-and-milk paste) gives the buns their wonderfully fluffy crumb and keeps them soft for longer. For a more indulgent version, split the buns along the top and fill with whipped cream and a spoonful of jam instead. They’re best assembled just before serving, and make a particularly lovely afternoon treat.Blackcurrant and vanilla finger bunsPrep10 minProve2 hr+Cook1 hr 15 minMakes12For the dough270ml whole milk7g dried instant yeast400g strong white bread flour,plus extra for dusting50g caster sugar1 large egg, lightly whisked¾tsp fine sea salt1 tsp vanilla paste60g unsalted butter, cut into small cubes and softened, plus a little extra for greasingFor the blackcurrant fondant70g blackcurrant (or other) jam180g icing sugar, sifted2 tsp lemon juice1 tiny pinch fine sea salt1-2 tsp hot water, as neededPour the milk into a small saucepan and heat gently until just lukewarm. Measure 140ml into the bowl of a stand mixer, stir in the yeast and leave until bubbly.Meanwhile, whisk the remaining milk in the pan with 25g of the flour, then cook, whisking constantly, on a medium heat for about five minutes, until it thickens into a smooth paste. Set aside to cool until just warm.Whisk the milk and yeast mix, then add the remaining 375g flour, the sugar, egg, salt, vanilla and the cooled milk/flour mix. Attach the dough hook and mix on low speed for about three minutes, until it turns into a rough dough. Turn up the speed to medium, add the butter a few cubes at a time and mix for eight to 10 minutes in total, scraping the base and sides of the bowl occasionally, until the dough is smooth and elastic. The dough should start to pull away from the sides of the bowl while still feeling soft and slightly tacky. Transfer the dough to a large, lightly greased bowl, cover and leave in a warm place for one to two hours, until doubled in size.Line a large baking tray with baking paper. Turn out the dough on to a lightly floured work surface and weigh it. Divide the total by 12, then cut the dough into 12 equal 60g pieces. Shape each one into a tight ball by pulling the edges into the centre and pinching to seal underneath. Put the balls seam-side down on your worktop and, using lightly cupped hands, roll until smooth. Gently roll each ball back and forth to form neat, 12cm-long logs; if you like, taper the ends slightly.Arrange the buns on the lined tray, leaving about 3cm between them (they’ll expand and just meet as they bake, which helps keep the sides soft). Cover loosely and leave to prove for an hour, until risen and puffy.Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, then bake the buns for 15 minutes, rotating the tray once halfway, until lightly golden. Transfer to a rack to cool completely.Meanwhile, make the fondant. Warm the jam gently until loosened, then pass it through a fine sieve – you should have about 50g. Whisk in the sifted icing sugar, lemon juice and salt, until smooth, then add just enough water to make a thick, spreadable fondant. Transfer to a shallow bowl wide enough to dip the buns into.Dip the top of each cooled bun into the fondant, allowing any excess to drip back into the bowl, then put on a rack for the icing to set before serving.Explore more on these topicsBakingThe sweet spotFoodSnacksCakeFruitrecipesShareReuse this content
