title: Felicity Green obituary | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Innovative journalist who as fashion editor of the Daily Mirror brought the latest 1960s looks to millions of readers
Author: Veronica Horwell
Headline: Innovative journalist who as fashion editor of the Daily Mirror brought the latest 1960s looks to millions of readers
Content: Green in 1962, when she was an associate editor of the Daily Mirror. ‘Readers and advertisers responded to the confident sexuality of 60s clothes as shown in Green’s pages.’Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGreen in 1962, when she was an associate editor of the Daily Mirror. ‘Readers and advertisers responded to the confident sexuality of 60s clothes as shown in Green’s pages.’Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesFashionObituaryFelicity Green obituaryInnovative journalist who as fashion editor of the Daily Mirror brought the latest 1960s looks to millions of readersVeronica HorwellFri 18 Sep 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFelicity Green made a career on tabloid newspapers in their most masculine era when, after secretaries and tea-trolley ladies went home, whole buildings could be as all-male as a foundry or a battleship. By 1961 she was an associate editor across Mirror Group newspapers; in 1973, as the group’s publicity director, she was the first woman on the main board of a publisher. When she found out in 1978 that a new – less experienced, male – director was paid £30,000 a year, more than twice her salary, she resigned, insulted.Green, who has died aged 100, knew how extraordinary her value had been to the group. TheDaily Mirror, at its peak of five million-plus readers, besides being a household’s source of news and sport, offered families access to what we would now call pop culture – showbiz, celebrity and especially style. Newspapers were a main advertising medium through the 1950s, 60s and 70s, and agencies yearned for content to attract women, who controlled household purchases, and young people, a new market for discretionary spending.Green was working at the ad agency WS Crawford in 1955 when Hugh Cudlipp, editorial director of the Mirror Group, asked for her opinion on the Women’s Sunday Mirror, a new paper he had launched to appeal to demographics the advertisers desired. She detailed its faults fiercely; he recruited her to its staff. The paper did not last, but Green moved to his Sunday Pictorial (later the Sunday Mirror) and then the Daily Mirror, with overall responsibility for women, and as “Felicity Green on the fashion scene”.That was the perfect position at a moment when the long-operating trickle-down-from-the-grand-couture-top process was beginning to be challenged by new designers for customers who had limited money but youth to flaunt. A graphic idea sewn from a couple of yards of cheap cloth and modelled with attitude for, say, David Bailey shooting in black and white, could hold a tabloid spread: Green laid out her own pages, integrating text and pictures, inviting participation.View image in fullscreenA 1969 Daily Mirror meeting with the editor, Lee Howard, far right. Felicity Green is in the centre, with Marjorie Proops, left, the only other woman present.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty Images“This is Barbara,” she wrote in May 1964, between a tiny closeup of designer Barbara Hulanicki and a single column shot of Paulene Stone modelling a shortish, sleeveless, gingham shift dress with matching scarf. “And this is one of her designs. Interested? … twenty-five bob isn’t a fashion fortune …” Hulanicki expected 3,000 mail orders for the dress, tops. She got 17,000, and so enough money to start her first bricks-and-mortar Biba shop.Readers and advertisers responded to the confident sexuality of 60s clothes as shown in Green’s pages – a classless look, up from the streets, more at home in the Mirror than Vogue. Green’s superiors, though, were apoplectic. The chair of the Mirror, Cecil King, threatened to fire her after a feature on Mary Quant miniskirts, saying, “How long are you going to continue to put those ridiculous clothes in my newspaper? Can you imagine the wife of a Sheffield bus-driver wearing that?”Cudlipp was shrewder, telling Green in 1964: “I don’t understand what you’re doing but I trust you. So I’ve decided to give you the front and back pages of the Mirror to tell our readers what the swinging 60s are all about.” He did that in 1964: “The Year That Changed Our Lives … Khrushchev sacked, China explodes atomic bomb …” the big print began, eventually reaching, “And of course, skirts got shorter, boys’ hair got longer, smart girls wore the trousers …” When she once wore a trouser suit to the office, it was suggested she go home (she didn’t.)Tiny, with a powerful presence and voice, Green personally preferred her clothes undramatic, long favouring Jean Muir, but was amused in later years to buy a clever piece from Zara.She had developed her interest in style during her childhood in Dagenham, east London, when she would skip school at Clark’s college, Ilford, every Thursday to go with her father to the cinema to see two movies, especially their wardrobes. He was Emanuel Green, who ran a small shoe shop, and Felicity’s mother, Anne (nee Mazin), did not go with them because she was deaf.Theirs was an unhappy marriage, and Green learned early in life to cope with difficult behaviours. Equipped only with nerve and deplorable shorthand, she begged for a job as secretary, dog walker, coffee maker and lighter of the office coal fire on Woman & Beauty magazine, and found a mentor in its eccentric editor, Phyllis Digby Morton.It was a superior publication, expanding fast with postwar advertising. Green learned about ads, layout and sharp headlines, and – the odd one out among its half-dozen genteel dogsbodies – was promoted to fashion editor. She recalled that Digby Morton once invitedHarold Wilson, then president of the Board of Trade, for drinks: Green had just given herself an early home perm, and Digby Morton “wanted me to give one to [Wilson’s wife]Mary… I did the perm in the bathroom and got a thank you poem from Mary.”View image in fullscreenThe Biba Story exhibition at Dovecot Studios, Edinburgh, featuring an article by Green, February 2026.Photograph: Craig Brown/AlamyMagazines were rife with office politics, but when Green agreed to work for Cudlipp she was surprised at rough life in the Fleet Street bearpit, where there were two daily shifts of drinking, and senior executives kept booze fridges in their offices. She survived initial patronisation and resentment by not registering them, and then got her way publishing pieces on sex, abortion, contraception, equal pay and all the tough topics of the 60s through patience and non-confrontation.Men gave in in the end, she found, if she did not give up. The shortest version of her oft-repeated advice on how to deal with an all-male work meeting is “always allow men to leave the room with their bollocks intact”. But she would not accept any insult to her mastery of the crafts of journalism, or the status they had won her – hence the Mirror resignation.In the late 70s Green briefly ran the hair stylistVidal Sassoon’s expanding empire, then returned to journalism as an associate editor at the Daily Express in 1980, and the Daily Telegraph from 1986 to 1996. Well into old age she was invited to consult on retail magazines for organisations ranging from Marks & Spencer to Harrods. Her education had been patchy – only that Pitman shorthand certificate – so she was intrigued to teach fashion journalism at Saint Martin’s School of Art in London in the 80s and Central Saint Martins in the 2010s.In 2014 she published Sex, Sense and Nonsense – not the memoir expected from an 88-year-old media dowager, more an anthology of her 60s pages, still blasting the excitement of freedom and a tabloid rawness. She was made an OBE in 2012.Green encouraged young women who began to join newspaper staffs in the mid-60s as more than just secretaries, saddened that their careers stopped short if they left to have a family. Her own firm belief in equality in all things led her to the Fawcett Society and the 300 Group, which worked in the 80s to increase the number of female MPs.Green married Geoffrey Hill, a cigar importer, in 1952, and he was the rock in her landscape until his death in 1992. She did not regret choosing not to have children, only the consequential absence of grandchildren.Felicity Green, journalist, born 26 June 1926; died 10 September 2026Explore more on these topicsFashionDaily MirrorNewspapers & magazinesNewspapersMagazinesobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Why did a high-profile fashion CEO physically restrain Peta protesters at New York fashion week? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Steven Kolb tried to stop activists demonstrating against the use of wool – but he can’t curb consumers’ growing concern about where their clothes come from
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Steven Kolb tried to stop activists demonstrating against the use of wool – but he can’t curb consumers’ growing concern about where their clothes come from
Content: Steven Kolb, the chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, at a gala in New York in 2022.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APView image in fullscreenSteven Kolb, the chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, at a gala in New York in 2022.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APFashion Statement newsletterFashionWhy did a high-profile fashion CEO physically restrain Peta protesters at New York fashion week?Steven Kolb tried to stop activists demonstrating against the use of wool – but he can’t curb consumers’ growing concern about where their clothes come fromChloe Mac DonnellFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Sunday afternoon, Mason Melito took a front row seat at the Cos show atNew York fashion week. A campaigner at Peta (People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals), Melito wasn’t on the guest list – instead, he and four other activists had planned to briefly disrupt the catwalk show with the aim of drawing attention to the use of wool by the Swedish brand.Protests on the catwalk have a long, rich history. Since the 90s, Peta have regularly stormed shows in an attempt to draw attention to the industry’s use of fur and leather. It’s a typically peaceful practice that happens regularly – during some shows, the catwalk is so long and security so swift that show-goers don’t even notice. (Sometimes, Peta take a different approach: in 1996, during a lunch, a protester famously dropped a dead raccoon on to Anna Wintour’s plate.)However, rather than causing a temporary interruption during the Cos show, Melito and a fellow protester found themselves being physically restrained by Steven Kolb, the chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA). A video of the incident went viral, and has since led to the Cos show unexpectedly becoming one of the most talked about events at fashion week.Melito, speaking to the Guardian by phone from New York City, described his shock at how the incident unfolded.View image in fullscreenA Peta activist staging a protest outside an H&M store this week in the Harajuku district of Tokyo in Japan.Photograph: Franck Robichon/EPAAs the show started and the models emerged, one of the activists on the other side of the room took to the catwalk holding a poster and shouting their concerns about the wool trade. They were quickly escorted away by security.Shortly afterwards, Melito signalled to Andrija Barak, a fellow disruptor who was sitting close to Kolb, that it was their time to take to the catwalk. “As soon as she got up, Kolb assaulted her,” Melito claims.In a video captured by the news site Fashionista, Kolbcan be seenseemingly wrestling Barak to the ground. He snatches a poster out of her hands and then covers her mouth with his hand while restraining her using his arms and a leg.After Barak freed herself, Melito stood up. “I attempted to follow her to console her and make sure that she was OK,” he says. Instead, he too found himself being restrained by Kolb in another incident that was also captured on camera.On Monday, Kolbissued a statementon Instagram saying he had “inappropriately restrained” two activists, and that “there is no justification” for his actions. “As I review the videos, I understand the reaction they have generated,” he added. “Frankly, I don’t recognise that person. As a result, I am taking a voluntary leave from work and meeting with a professional to ensure it never happens again.”On Tuesday, Kolb was placed on leave by the CFDA, pending a full review. In a statement, the organisation said it is “committed to working with dissenting voices to find commonality and is engaged in efforts to move the American fashion industry forward while upholding the values of our membership, including respectful engagement with differing viewpoints”. A spokesperson for the H&M Group, which owns Cos, added that the company was “deeply sorry” about the confrontation.Melito describes the situation as “a scary one”. Asked if he felt unsafe, he said: “Absolutely – Kolb just went completely rogue and decided to take matters into his own hands.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe confrontation has opened a can of worms. But, most of all, the incident must be a reminder of the issues fashion has with some of its supply chains. Fromthe illusion of Made In Italytowasteand alleged “wage theft”, whether it’s a giant global corporation that sells pieces for less than £30 or a luxury house that sells items for four figures, when it comes to failures to protect people and animals, the industry is quick to pass the buck. For many, what will have been most alarming about the incident isn’t the pinning of protesters to the floor, but the fact that its consumers will now be questioning just exactly how their clothes are made.Melito, for what it’s worth, considers this a victory for sheep, who he describes as the “real victims”. “Wool belongs to sheep and it should stay on sheep.”The incident hasn’t dissuaded PETA from storming the catwalk. On Thursday night at a H&M show at London fashion week, the show was interrupted three separate times by protesters who were met with boos by several audience members. Each one held a sign stating “H&M: Wool is bloody cruel. Drop it.” After walking up and down the catwalk twice they left voluntarily and were escorted out of the venue by security.To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure and your wardrobe dilemmas solved –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterNew York fashion weekFashion weeksnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Gateways to heaven’: readers’ favourite trips in Europe’s mountains | Travel | The Guardian
description: From the foothills of the Pyrenees to the peaks of the Dolomites, you share your top views, meals and adventures at altitude
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From the foothills of the Pyrenees to the peaks of the Dolomites, you share your top views, meals and adventures at altitude
Content: That’s a bit steep … the Stanserhorn funicular in Switzerland near Lucerne.Photograph: Denis Linine/AlamyView image in fullscreenThat’s a bit steep … the Stanserhorn funicular in Switzerland near Lucerne.Photograph: Denis Linine/AlamyReaders' travel tipsTravel‘Gateways to heaven’: readers’ favourite trips in Europe’s mountainsFrom the foothills of the Pyrenees to the peaks of the Dolomites, you share your top views, meals and adventures at altitudeTell us about a trip to Germany– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll the fun of the funicular in SwitzerlandNo doubt your first thought on hearing the words “double-decker” is of a bus. But in the Swiss village of Stans, an old wooden funicular carriage ascends to the station, where a double-decker cable car awaits. Inside, a spiral staircase leads you to an open upper viewing deck. At the summit, the views back to Lucerne are superb, and there are alpine marmots to spot too. There was a wedding ceremony going on at the summit on our trip!MartinLiechtenstein’s Route 66View image in fullscreenLooking across the Three Sisters.Photograph: GanzTwins/Getty ImagesSteinbock, marmot and elderflower jam are in abundance on Liechtenstein’s Route 66 track – a  multi-day hike that is popular with locals, but little known to others. The route traverses the Drei Schwestern (the Three Sisters), where you’ll experience white knuckles and lush valley views. After an easy 5km hike, you land at the first mountain hut, where a succulent homemade three-course dinner awaits you. Befriend the other walkers over a game of cards, as golden hour lights up the mountains.InezProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Picturesque French PyreneesView image in fullscreenLuz Saint Sauveur is surrounded by tall peaks.Photograph: Chris Craggs/AlamyLuz Saint Sauveur in the French Pyrenees is the gateway to heaven. Whether it be by bike, car, motorbike or on foot, stunning surroundings, wildlife-a-plenty and quaint French shops await you at this picturesque market town. Eat the local saucisson, drink the jurançon white wine, marvel at the blue skies in the shadows of the legendary Tour de France Cols, jump in canyons and be merry with the surroundings. Simply beautiful and fun for all ages.WillHigh on the hog in DonegalView image in fullscreenMuckish is a flat-topped mountain to the north of Glenveagh national park.Photograph: Steven Granville/Getty ImagesFor mountain scenery without Alpine crowds, head to north-west Donegal. Errigal gets the attention, but don’t overlook flat-topped Muckish, whose name comes from the Irish for “pig’s back”. Drive the small roads around the Poisoned Glen and through Glenveagh national park, where each bend reveals another reason to stop. Allow far longer than the satnav suggests: our best moments came from pulling over for an unexpected view rather than racing between sights. Pack walking shoes and a picnic, then reward yourself afterwards in a cosy pub. Here, a mountain day can include Atlantic beaches and a well-earned pint.Niamh KerrThe quiet side of Italy’s DolomitesView image in fullscreenAlpine hut Rifugio Agostini was the highlight of Ben Bryant’s trip.Photograph: Johannes 86/Getty ImagesThe Brenta Dolomites seem to go strangely unnoticed, while the main Dolomites heave with Instagrammers. We based ourselves in Pinzolo, an alpine town an hour north of Lake Garda, then took the lift from Madonna di Campiglio for a three-day hut-to-hut trek, tackling two via ferrata routes across knife-edge ridges and limestone spires. Rifugio Agostini was the highlight: a warm welcome and hearty mountain food after a hard day’s climbing, with jagged peaks filling every window. We descended into the town of Molveno for a well-earned aperitivo by the lake.Ben BryantA spectacular climb in KosovoView image in fullscreenThe Lumbardhi River in Prizren.Photograph: Engin Korkmaz/AlamyAfter exploring Kosovo’s historic monasteries and wartime memorials, we escaped to the Sharr mountains national park, a 40-minute drive south of Prizren. The road winds through the spectacular Zhupa valley and follows the bubbling Lumbardhi river through its steep-sided gorge. At Prevallë, we left the car and began what turned out to be a strenuous climb over rocky paths and grassy slopes. We kept expecting the summit to appear, but every turn revealed another, until we finally reached our destination and were met with spectacular mountain views. Afterwards, we rewarded ourselves at Hotel Krojet with coffee and a reviving glass of raki.Roy Messengerskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeaceful paths above Lake ComoView image in fullscreenThe Via dei Monti Lariani passes close to Mount Bregagno.Photograph: Mauritius/AlamyThis spring, my partner and I hiked the Via dei Monti Lariani, a 78-mile (125km) trail through the mountains on the western shore of Lake Como between Cernobbio and Sorico. Skirting the border between Italy and the Swiss canton of Ticino, the route passes through mountain pastures with views towards the Alps, and remote villages shaped by a history of cross-border smuggling. The accommodation is a highlight, ranging from Alpine rifugios to agriturismi, where we sampled regional specialities, includingpolenta uncia, polenta with local cheese and butter, andpizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta with cabbage and potatoes. Quiet trails, excellent food and complex history made it an especially rewarding route.Ross CameronGrand canyons of the Spanish PyreneesView image in fullscreenSanta Engràcia, high in the Pyrenees.Photograph: Chris Craggs/AlamyThis summer my family and I stayed atFox Housein the tiny village of Santa Engràcia in the Tremp valley, in the foothills of the Spanish Pyrenees. Perched on a cliff edge, the beautifully renovated guest house has panoramic views, eclectic art and a warm homely feel. Laura and Carl were excellent hosts, creating a relaxed atmosphere and serving delicious evening meals. Days were a mix of poolside downtime and outdoor adventure, including rafting, mountain biking, canyon kayaking and swimming in crystal blue lakes.MariaCampsite with a view in AustriaView image in fullscreenCamping Grubhof is on the Saalach River.Photograph: APA/AlamyCamping Grubhof,in the small town of Lofer between Salzburg and Zell am See, is simply beautiful. It’s an immaculate campsite, surrounded by mountains. Lofer (and the campsite) have direct access to a huge network of cycle trails as well as to the beautiful village swimming pool (free with the local access pass). Walking high in the mountains, surrounded by cows with bells is simply beautiful. Come the afternoon, there’s time for an apple strudel at a mountain hut and a glass of radler low alcohol beer. There is a camping meadow where you can pitch a tent and cabins to rent, as well as the best shower blocks I’ve come across.MarkWinning tip:Stars, sunsets and glaciers in ItalyView image in fullscreenRifugio Bertone has commanding views of surrounding peaks.Photograph: Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesThe views over Mont Blanc fromRifugio Bertonein Italy are incredible, but it’s the whole experience that makes it special – great food, proper mountain atmosphere, and the Balconata Val Ferret has some of the best walking in the area. It’s also near Courmayeur, which is a lovely town. Arrive for sunset, watch the light move across the glaciers, then look up at the stars as Mont Blanc disappears into the darkness. A brilliant place to eat, walk, breathe and simply take in the mountains. And it’s very affordable.Eddie CampbellView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsTravelReaders' travel tipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like a Bond villain’s lair’: I climbed the Dolomites to the world’s most spectacular mountain hut | Dolomites holidays | The Guardian
description: Perched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisine
Author: Andrew Gilchrist
Headline: Perched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisine
Content: ‘Santnerpass Hut is perched on a sheer cliff and resembles a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eye-popping hit of modernity and innovation’.Photograph: Andrew GilchristView image in fullscreen‘Santnerpass Hut is perched on a sheer cliff and resembles a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eye-popping hit of modernity and innovation’.Photograph: Andrew GilchristDolomites holidays‘Like a Bond villain’s lair’: I climbed the Dolomites to the world’s most spectacular mountain hutPerched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisineAndrew GilchristFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ithink my boots are falling apart!” shouts Nigel just as we hit the pinnacles, a whole range of them jutting up and out from the mountainside, all thrillingly tall, spiky and knobbled. Through them we painstakingly step, fingers aching in gloves, heads sweating in helmets – squashing up narrow chimneys, squeezing through mighty boulders and inching along slender ledges on a twisting path that’s only just discernible through swathes of sharp white scree.I know how Nigel’s boots are feeling: the going is far harder than I was expecting. This is only the first day of our annual trip to the Dolomites, a vast range of breathtaking sawtooth peaks in northern Italy, but my head’s already full of the thought I have every year as we start out: “If only you’d got fitter.”View image in fullscreenBut it should be worth all the scrapes, bumps, scares and sweat. Somewhere up ahead, hopefully not too far, is Rifugio Passo Santner, or Santnerpass Hut, a spectacular mountain refuge that, as everyone who sits near my desk at work knows, has been obsessing me ever since I first saw a picture of it eight months ago.Allowing you to stay deep in the mountains for days on end, the high-altitude Dolomites huts we overnight at all have their charms, from hearty food to giddying views to a generous way with the grappa. But in terms of appearance, they tend to fall into two not particularly pulse-quickening camps: stone block or cuckoo clock. Although you’re almost always overjoyed to see them, none could ever pass for a Bond villain’s lair, however much grappa you’ve had.double quotation markHuts tend to fall into two not particularly pulse-quickening camps: stone block or cuckoo clockYet that is exactly what Santnerpass Hut resembles. Perched on top of a sheer cliff, this elongated triangle encased in a gleaming wrapper of galvanised steel looks like a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eyepopping hit of modernity, originality and innovation in a place where tradition usually dictates more of the same.After one final push, the five of us scramble up on to the summit and there it is just ahead, side on and glowing silver in the late afternoon sun, like a star that has touched down on Earth to enjoy the stunning views of the surrounding peaks with the rest of us, up at the bracing height of 2,734m.“Welcome!” says the bartender as we enter. “You made it. Well done!” With the customary relief – if not actual jubilation – that follows a tough climb finally ending, we ease off our backpacks, gloves and boots then look around, slowly realising that Santnerpass Hut isn’t just a treat for the eyes from the outside.Inside, what you first notice is the unbroken parade of huge windows wrapping around the refuge’s front and flanks. This doesn’t just turn every spot of the roomy ground floor into a light-filled observation point. It also means the hut achieves passive heating since it’s effectively one big solar collector. So there’s no need for log-devouring stoves. That’s quite an achievement at ground level; at more than 2km up, with no road access, it’s verging on miraculous.View image in fullscreen‘Santnerpass Hut was built in 1956 but was taken over, closed and rebuilt, finally opening to the eager climbing public in the summer of 2023.’Photograph: Andrew GilchristThen there’s the wood. It’s blond and everywhere. Guests are basically cocooned within a spellbinding timber tapestry that casts everything in a warm yellow glow, quite a novelty to anyone used to the dingy two-watt corridors and bedrooms of most refuges.The flooring is larch, the restaurant furnishings maple and the load-bearing A-frame spruce, its hefty angular joists exposed on the sundeck, where we soon find ourselves sinking well-earned ice-cold drinks and marvelling at this beacon of sustainable architecture.There are other things to marvel at. Off in the distance, piercing up through an immense blanket of cloud, the lofty peaks of the Latemar group are catching the last rays of the sun, turning pink, orange and purple in a ravishing Dolomites phenomenon known as theenrosadira, triggered by calcium and magnesium in the rock. “This place is incredible,” says Donnie, sipping an Aperol spritz. “I’ve never been anywhere like it in my life.”double quotation markGuests are basically cocooned within a spellbinding timber tapestry that casts everything in a warm yellow glowSantnerpass Hut was built in 1956 but in the last decade or so was taken over, closed and rebuilt, finally opening its generous glass doors in 2023. Designed by alpine specialistsSenoner Tammerle Architects, the new refuge is not just meant to please the eye: the shape lets it shed thick snow and deflect howling winds.There are more surprises when we take our pre-dinner showers. Not only does the wood here give way to zesty yellow laminated panels that wouldn’t look out of place in a chic nightclub, the showerheads also actually stay pointing at your body for the full three minutes of hot water a token gets you.Dinner, however, may have been the biggest surprise of all. It was completely vegetarian – a shock for all of us and a treat for veggies Sam and Nigel. No goulash, no ragu, no pork chops. Instead, out of the kitchen came herb-sprinkled lentils with asparagus, radish and onion, pea and mint soup, then beetroot dumplings on a rich bean, tomato and yellow pepper broth, washed down with superb local wine in actual wine glasses and finished off with creme brulee.“A delicious and nutritious meal,” said Sam, running his spoon round his plate. “What an eye-opener. A win-win for hiker and planet.”Curfew was at 10pm but the restaurant was clearing out anyway. This may have been due to the fact that, in high spirits after our action-packed day, we had taken the hut’s guitar off the wall and treated everyone to that Proclaimers Alpine classic Sunshine on Leith, managing to get a singalong going with the very up-for-it, very international audience.View image in fullscreen‘Made it’ … the writer on the summit, nearing the refuge.Photograph: Donald LivingstoneThe refuge sleeps 4o in 16 rooms. Ours was a spacious affair with bunkbeds, a dainty dormer window and two large cubbyholes each, one for your bag, the other for your stuff – so much more useful than the usual pointless wardrobes and drawers that no one ever unpacks into, since you’ll be gone in a hurry at the crack of dawn.We reached Santnerpass Hut via the König Laurin cable car, 22 miles (35km) from Bolzano, gateway to the Dolomites. After that, it’s a rising, fairly straight line to the refuge, a two-to-three-hour hike through loose scree, then boulders and pinnacles. But be warned: the last section is a via ferrata, meaning there’s a metal cable for you to clip your harness to, and grab hold of as you reach trickier, more treacherous passages. It’s not for beginners.I’d heard, though, that there was another route and, keen to take it back down to the cable car, asked at reception. “Yes, there’s another way,” said Romina Huber, who co-owns and runs the hut with her husband (and chef) Michel Perathoner. “It’s not a via ferrata and it’s super beautiful.”Truly, madly, steeply: a via ferrata tour of the DolomitesRead moreShe wasn’t kidding. First it took us past the Vajolet towers, dramatic spires that lure climbers from all over the world. Then we swung right on to a winding path of fine white scree that rises sharply through meadows full of edelweiss, saxifrage, dwarf pine and boulders, leading to bulging cliffs and eventually the Coronelle Pass, an astonishing vantage point at 2,360m.“Well, that was a walk and a half,” said Mac as we descended in the cable car 30 minutes later, exhausted after the final knee-popping trudge down from the pass on timber-pinned switchbacks. “My boots,” said Nigel, lifting his feet to let us see a rip in one and a sole flapping off the other, “have completely had it.”Santnerpass Hutstarts at€105pp per night, including breakfast and four-course vegetarian dinnerHutiquette: the mountain hut codeMountain huts may occasionally be rather luxurious these days, but their original function, still relevant, is survival. There are, as you might expect, several very sensible codes that make great use of words like “respect”, “other users”, and “environment”. My own code is no less worthy and comes from hard-won experience.No complainingHuts are not hotels. If there’s a problem, go sort it out. Certainly, never complain about snoring, even when you are convinced it is about to trigger an avalanche. I once did, only to be informed, rather too forcefully, that is was me doing the snoring, an outrageous lie that triggered grunts of approval from other grumpy insomniacs. Gel ear plugs work well.ShareIt’s sometimes hard to drop the urban habit of self-assertion to ensure survival. One night in a Corsican hut with a shared sleeping platform, an obnoxious Brit in a down bag shoved all the other sleepers into a pile at one end of the bench, claiming later that he was “dreaming of being pushed”. I pray never to run into him again.Clean up after yourself… and take your rubbish home. TheBritish Mountain Bothy Codehas a good reminder on this point. I’d go even further and say, try to leave absolutely no trace at all. Visiting one treasured wild swimming spot recently, I found the scorch mark of a campfire. Whoever it was had not left any rubbish, and there was nothing to mark their visit, except that dreaded black spot, as if Blind Pew had delivered a death sentence.The hut is for everyoneI once cycled to a remote Icelandic hut and found it blissfully empty of people. Lighting the fire, I prepared my simple meal, and apart from wishing I had packed a beer, looked forward to a night of splendid isolation. Then a large group of locals arrived. I felt my heart sink. My solitary bliss was gone. They sat down, gave me a beer, and two hours later, after helping to eat their huge delicious feast, I felt like I’d joined a tribe. When a hut generates that kind of gang conviviality, it’s uplifting.Look after othersIn Scandinavia, this is a social habit that is deeply embedded. You turn up in a hut in winter and there are logs because the last visitors left them for you. You cut your finger and they all have the plaster that you forgot to bring. TheNorwegian Mountain Codehas a list of essential reminders.Kevin RushbyExplore more on these topicsDolomites holidaysItaly holidaysClimbing holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysArchitectureAdventure travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: There’s a long history of athletes pooing themselves mid-race – why, and how can you avoid it? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Since the ancient Olympics, athletes like Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk have experienced runner’s diarrhoea. What does the science say about extreme exercise’s ‘mechanical jostling of the intestines’?
Author: Natalie Parletta
Headline: Since the ancient Olympics, athletes like Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk have experienced runner’s diarrhoea. What does the science say about extreme exercise’s ‘mechanical jostling of the intestines’?
Content: Joanna Wietrzyk’s unfortunate case of runner’s diarrhoea at the Hyrox games in Beijing is far more common than many people realise.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoanna Wietrzyk’s unfortunate case of runner’s diarrhoea at the Hyrox games in Beijing is far more common than many people realise.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesHealth & wellbeingThere’s a long history of athletes pooing themselves mid-race – why, and how can you avoid it?Since the ancient Olympics, athletes like Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk have experienced runner’s diarrhoea. What does the science say about extreme exercise’s ‘mechanical jostling of the intestines’?Natalie ParlettaThu 17 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoiling yourself in public sounds like a bad dream. But the Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has nowapologised for doing just thatat the Hyrox games in Beijing on Saturday.Wietrzyk won the fitness race but not before using communal equipment with faecal matter visibly running down her legs – and muddying Hyrox’s reputation.‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivalsRead moreApologies aside, Wietrzyk’s unfortunate case of runner’s trots, or runner’s diarrhoea, is far more common than many people realise, throwing a new light on the ominous rows of portable toilets stationed along the course of a fun run and the knowing nods between runners as they pass them (or not).About 60% of endurance athletes report some type of gastrointestinal symptoms during training or competition, according to Kayla Henningsen, a PhD candidate researching exercise gastroenterology and extremes physiology at Monash University. The American Medical Society for Sports Medicineestimates that the prevalence could be as high as 90%.Severity varies considerably. “Symptoms can range from mild bloating and cramping through to nausea, diarrhoea and, in rare cases, loss of bowel control,” Henningsen says. “High-intensity events such as marathons, ultramarathons and Hyrox can create the perfect conditions for gastrointestinal distress, urgency or diarrhoea.”Safety in numbersWietrzyk isn’t alone: other public mishaps published over the past three decades include the 1998 London Marathon winner, Catherina McKeirnan, whododged camerasalong the way while suffering several bouts of diarrhoea. Paula Radcliffe, the winner of the 2005 London Marathon, wasn’t so lucky; she waspublicly caughtrelieving herself of debilitating stomach pains by the road near the finish line, blaming it on too much gluten-free pasta and grilled salmon the night before. In 2024 the US athlete Taylor Knibb won the Dubai T100 despite having to relieve herself during the race, utteringthe immortal line to a camera operator: “I just shit myself … so can you not get my ass? Thank you.”double quotation markThe gut is an ‘athletic organ’ and can be trained to tolerate nutrient loadingProf John HawleyAlthough runner’s trots are more common in women, men aren’t immune. The TikTok celebrity Davis Clarke decided a toilet stop would impact his time so hecrapped his pantsduring the 2024 Boston Marathon. In a 50km race walk at the 2016 Olympics, the French world record-holder Yohann Diniz suffered stomach pain and had blood and possibly diarrhoea dribbling down his legbefore collapsing– then still managed to finish in eighth place.Perhaps most cringeworthy episode afflicted a Swedish runner, Mikael Ekvall, who ran a half-marathon in 2008 with diarrhoearunning down his leg, earning him the viral nickname “bajsmannen” (poop man). He finished in 21st place despite 10km of severe stomach cramps.An ancient ailmentThe scientific literature has recorded gut problems related to exercise stress, known less colloquially as “exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome”, for the past century,according to Prof Ricardo Da Costafrom Monash University and colleagues.They writethat it’s likely to have plagued competitive athletes since the ancient Olympics.Despite this, and the large volume of cases seen by sports professionals, they note that an understanding of why and how endurance exercise stresses the digestive tract only started to develop in the 1980s and 90s, and is still relatively unclear – possibly because it can’t be pinned to one straightforward cause.Exercise diverts blood to skeletal muscles, affecting the motility and absorptive ability of the digestive tract. Reduced absorptive capacity can especially affect the lower intestines when athletes load up with drinks, gels and bars during exercise, according to Prof John Hawley from Australian Catholic University.“Events in the heat make the problem worse,” he adds, “as blood that would normally go to the gut is diverted to the skin for cooling and to preserve core temperature.”He says that prolonged weight-bearing exercise for 90 minutes or more, such as running, can produce more severe symptoms than other endurance-based exercise. “This is because of the vertical up-and-down impact, and why cyclists can tolerate a lot more food and drink.”Henningsen refers to this as “mechanical jostling of the intestines” and adds dehydration and intolerance of certain foods or nutrition protocols to these potential causes.Da Costa’s teamrefers tothe gut-brain axis possibly directing performance stress to the gut – potentially through the hormonal stress response and/or the microbiome – among other factors including altered pH.Can it be prevented?From a sports physiology perspective, Henningsen says runner’s trots and other gut problems highlight the stress that extreme exercises places on the body: “These events are not necessarily a sign of poor preparation or poor fitness.”‘A drug that’s very safe and healthy‘: what ultrarunners can teach us about life | Sean IngleRead moreWhile risk can be reduced, it may not be completely eliminated, she notes, suggesting prevention strategies such as avoiding unfamiliar foods before a competitive event, staying well hydrated, managing heat exposure and gradually adapting the gut to tolerate carbohydrates and fluids while exercising. But because triggers can differ between individuals, she says, a personalised approach is usually most effective.Hawley explains that “the gut is an ‘athletic organ’ and can be trained to tolerate nutrient loading – that is, eating and drinking during exercise – so practise in training what you will be doing in a competition”.Henningsen agrees, saying the most important advice is “to treat your gut like any other part of your performance system and train it accordingly”. She recommends keeping a record of foods, fluids, symptoms and environmental conditions to look for any patterns.In addition to these recommendations, Da Costa and colleaguescite evidencethat ingesting carbohydrates during prolonged exercise may help. They also review positive findings that proteins, especially glutamine, may support gut integrity and note possible benefits from low-fibre and gluten-free diets. But the evidence for these remains unclear.Fortunately, according to Hawley, “most GI symptoms are mild, transient, and of no risk to long-term health”.But Henningsen offers a caution: “If symptoms are frequent, severe or worsening, see a healthcare professional. Persistent gastrointestinal issues should not simply be accepted as ‘part of the sport’.”Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingAustralia sportFitnessMarathon runningHealth (Australia news)Health (Society)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Legends of the fall: why autumn is the perfect time to plant grasses in your garden | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Whether tall or short, wafty or heavy, these versatile, texture-giving plants can be magical
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: Whether tall or short, wafty or heavy, these versatile, texture-giving plants can be magical
Content: Calamagrostis x acutifloradoes well in shadier spots.Photograph: Flowerphotos/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCalamagrostis x acutifloradoes well in shadier spots.Photograph: Flowerphotos/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesGardening adviceLegends of the fall: why autumn is the perfect time to plant grasses in your gardenWhether tall or short, wafty or heavy, these versatile, texture-giving plants can be magicalAlice VincentFri 18 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter four long months of warmth, the garden decided it was autumn prematurely. Yellow leaves piled up against the kerbstones. Everything might be dry and crispy, but for those who believe that planting should be done between September and April, it’s the start of a whole new school term in the garden.I won’t be planting anything just yet: my garden is currently home to steel girders and a cement mixer. Instead, I’ve been taking inspiration from other green spaces: other people’s gardens, parks, allotments and community growing spaces are far more interesting than mine. And when you can’t garden in your own plot, gardens become even more addictive. Which is why grasses are on my mind: my son was running through our well-landscaped local play park yesterday morning, the sun was low and yolky, and the seedheads were shimmering. Yes, I thought, I need more of these.double quotation markGrasses offer a shimmer to the spectacle of their more floriferous late-summer companionsI have an internal Rolodex of good grass inspiration. There’s a front garden near our old place that consisted purely of erigeron tumbling over steps and gravel, and goldenStipa gigantearising above. It was so magical and clean and confident. The Oudolf Field at Hauser & Wirth Somerset and the High Line in New York, where I first saw Piet Oudolf’s New Perennial design catch the light 16 years ago, show how magical these often overlooked wafty wonders can be. Visiting floral artist Hazel Gardiner’s garden for the first time, in early September six years ago, I was struck by the post-shower sunlight splintering through miscanthus plumes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWill we have to choose different plants for hotter, drier summers?Read moreGrasses offer a shimmer to the spectacle of their more floriferous late-summer companions (dahlias, I’m looking at you).Stipa giganteais massive, as the name might suggest, but it’s also airy, so if you have the space for it, it can create a beautiful sense of hide-and-seek in a garden. On the dinkier side isMelica uniflora, which is surprisingly tolerant of dry shade and, after taking its time to settle in, will cover ground with green leaves and tiny pale flowers.Much as grasses cover the spectrum of size and scale, don’t think they’re just for hot sunny spots. Beth Chatto’s water garden in Essex demonstrates how well grasses grow in moist conditions, withDeschampsia cespitosa‘Goldschleier’ turning a golden yellow about now after summer flowering. And as for shadier spots,Calamagrostis x acutiflora‘Karl Foerster’(pictured above) did well in the shade bed in my last garden.However many grasses you want to plant, I’d round up to the next odd number. It just looks better. Movement and texture come from repetition. Now is a good time to try some smaller pots of hardy varieties, which can establish over the cooler months before putting on a show next year.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: Dinner time for the buzzard family is not a dignified affair | Birds | The Guardian
description: Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: We have three breeding pairs on the farm, and one in particular has been a source of fascination and amusement
Author: Kate Blincoe
Headline: Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: We have three breeding pairs on the farm, and one in particular has been a source of fascination and amusement
Content: Trail cam footage of the juvenile buzzards scrapping on a hay bale.Photograph: Chris SkinnerView image in fullscreenTrail cam footage of the juvenile buzzards scrapping on a hay bale.Photograph: Chris SkinnerCountry diaryBirdsCountry diary: Dinner time for the buzzard family is not a dignified affairCaistor St Edmund, Norfolk:We have three breeding pairs on the farm, and one in particular has been a source of fascination and amusementKate BlincoeFri 18 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m out on the farm most days, but I miss so much. It took a few days to notice a mother mallard with her late brood of 12 ducklings until they were all dabbling in a yard puddle. Dad sees more than me. He told me of the lazy adult buzzard that waited in a tree, then dive-bombed a peregrine that had caught a pigeon. The peregrine dropped its prey, which the buzzard then delivered to a hay bale already strewn with feathers. A pair of juvenile buzzards swiftly followed, ready for a meal.Later, Dad placed the trail camera at the bale. The young buzzards were soon back in position with yet another dead pigeon. The footage tells a story that many parents will recognise after the long summer holidays.One young buzzard claims the pigeon, turns its back on the other and opens its wings around the food. Known as “mantling”, it creates a share-proof barrier. The other bird looks disgruntled, shifting around, head down, trying to work out a plan. It sticks a leg out under its sibling’s defensive wings and is told off with a shrill screech.Opting instead for being persistently annoying, it eventually provokes the pigeon-possessor to rise in attack. There’s a funny moment when both birds overbalance and plummet off the side of the bale. Another high-pitch squeak arises, off-camera. I shouldn’t anthropomorphise, but the expressions of the birds throughout this little drama do seem very familiar.View image in fullscreenOne buzzard ‘mantling’, the other waiting for a chance.Photograph: Chris SkinnerThere are three pairs of buzzards that nest on the farm, each wood has its couple. Usually seen soaring on thermals above the farm, or loafing around in the woodland canopy, they are in turn majestic and clumsy. Despite centuries of persecution, followed by the myxomatosis outbreak in the 1950s that reduced their favourite rabbit prey, buzzards somehow persisted, and more recently increased in numbers.The bales have now been cleared from the fields and this next generation of buzzards must fend for themselves.Meanwhile, back in the yard, each night there is a diminishing of ducklings. We’re down to eight now. Still an impressive amount in the numbers game of reproduction, but they have a long way to go until they too are independent.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsBirdsCountry diaryWildlifeRural affairsSummerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence
Content: The Hotel Bamy in Malabo, where migrants are being held.Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/APView image in fullscreenThe Hotel Bamy in Malabo, where migrants are being held.Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/APUS immigrationMen deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers sayGroup trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violenceMaanvi SinghFri 18 Sep 2026 19.08 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men that theTrump administrationexpelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions atthe Hotel Bamy– a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received$7.5mas part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.UN pleads for Equatorial Guinea not to send US asylum seekers to their home countries: ‘Their life would be in danger’Read moreAdvocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture,according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.Equatorial Guinea police point gun at migrants deported by Trump administration - loopIn the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone ​so he could contact relatives and a ​lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned byEquatorial Guineato their home country, where they face persecution.In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal askingEquatorial Guineato halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.A spokesperson for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said that “when an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them”, adding: “All of these illegal aliens were deported to a safe third country.” The agency did not engage with questions about the violence deportees have faced.A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationEquatorial GuineaAfricaICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children
Content: Family members of those who died gather outside Minna general hospital in Niger state.Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/ReutersView image in fullscreenFamily members of those who died gather outside Minna general hospital in Niger state.Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/ReutersNigeriaSurvivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 diedPolice fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were childrenEromo Egbejulein Abidjan and agenciesFri 18 Sep 2026 13.27 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSurvivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.NSCDC – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.The state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. “There are issues of illegal mining and it is taking a toll on our children,” he said.Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.AFP reported that another survivor, who asked not to be named, said he had made it out alive because he was near the cell’s entrance, where he could breathe better. “We were screaming for help,” he said, with detainees telling the guards that “people are dying one after the other. They did not believe us.”President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials.But protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – ​some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called ‌for justice. Some protesters tried ‌to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make ‌a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.View image in fullscreenFamily members outside Minna general hospital. Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in the city.Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/ReutersAs ⁠curfew began at 6pm local time on Friday, security forces appeared to have at least temporarily restored order to the streets of the city.The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of an investigation.Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and is more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolice and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNigeriaAfricaMiningGoldCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout | Malawi | The Guardian
description: Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week
Content: Nusrat Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and ‘not too shaken’ after her ordeal, her brother said.Photograph: Family HandoutView image in fullscreenNusrat Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and ‘not too shaken’ after her ordeal, her brother said.Photograph: Family HandoutMalawiBritish woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootoutFour of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last weekRachel Savagein JohannesburgFri 18 Sep 2026 07.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British woman kidnapped inMalawilast week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police hadoffered a rewardof 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.Malawian policeannounced Osman’s rescuelate on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwatold the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to theWorld Bank.In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outletNyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.Explore more on these topicsMalawiAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire | Louisiana | The Guardian
description: The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility
Content: An African serval in a transport carrier after being found in the back yard of a home by firefighters in New Orleans.Photograph: John McCusker, JPawsView image in fullscreenAn African serval in a transport carrier after being found in the back yard of a home by firefighters in New Orleans.Photograph: John McCusker, JPawsLouisianaLouisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fireThe African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facilityRamon Antonio VargasFri 18 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouisianafirefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, prompting an animal welfare agency to seek placing the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburbanNew Orleanscommunity of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws in effect in Marrero require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.View image in fullscreenAn African serval cat being transported after being found in an enclosure in the back yard a of a home.Photograph: John McCusker, JPawsThe statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.Servals share some similarities with domesticatedcatsthat make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.A social media post on Friday by Brignac said JPaws had managed to place the serval with a zoo “where he could have something very different: space, enrichment, appropriate care and an environment designed with his needs in mind”. Brignac’s post did not specify to which zoo she was referring.The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boomdriven in part by social mediacontent creators showing them in videos online.View image in fullscreenServals mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature and cannot be fully house-trained.Photograph: John Mccusker/John McCusker, JPawsCases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati areacapturedan African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated inheartbreakafter a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.View image in fullscreenThe Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity.Photograph: John Mccusker/John McCusker, JPawsAnd the news outlet Peoplereportedon authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.Explore more on these topicsLouisianaCatsPetsNew OrleansAnimalsWildlifeAfricanewsShareReuse this content

Habteab.Photograph: PEN InternationalBooks‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writersMore than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias AfwerkiElla CreamerFri 18 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.Nobel laureatesOlga Tokarczukand JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiledin the Guardianin 2015.The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.Earlier this year, PEN Internationallaunched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president ofPENInternational. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”Explore more on these topicsBooksEritreaPENAfricaJM CoetzeeOlga TokarczuknewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Critics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s elections
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Critics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s elections
Content: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a candidate for re-election for the workers' party (PT), speaks at a campaign rally in Brasilia, Brazil, on 16 September 2026.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a candidate for re-election for the workers' party (PT), speaks at a campaign rally in Brasilia, Brazil,
