Merz’s centre-right CDU was this monthheavily defeated in state electionsin Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD.Two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOil and gas companiesEnergy industryFranceGermanyEuropeFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position
Content: Houthi troopers on patrol in Sana'a, Yemen. The Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi troopers on patrol in Sana'a, Yemen. The Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAYemenYemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapseRout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon positionPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 18 Sep 2026 10.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.Some Yemeni politicians are claiming that billions of dollars were offered to persuade the forces defending the west coast to abandon their position. It is thought as many as 30,000 well-equipped fighters retreated, raising questions about coordination, readiness and morale.The claim made by the governor of Hadramaut, one of Yemen’s largest governorates, did not identify the source of the payment, but others have tried to draw conclusions from the past links between the United Arab Emirates and the pro-government National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh. The UAE left Yemen in January, but remains bitter at the role played by Saudi Arabia in forcing it out and in the outlawing of the separatist Southern Transitional Council.The Yemeni Nobel peace prize winner Tawakkol Karman has called for an investigation, while another political activist, the Mocha resident Abdu Mukabib, described the withdrawal of forces from the now Houthi-held port city in the early hours of 10 September as a great betrayal.Saleh’s National Resistance Forces have said they made a necessary tactical retreat.Hours before, theHouthishad captured the headquarters of the National Resistance Forces operating along Yemen’s western coast, situated on the high ground of Jabal al-Nar (Fire Mountain) and supposed to contain six military brigades and sophisticated weaponry provided by Saudi Arabia.Mukabib said on his Facebook page that by the time the Houthis entered the city at 6am their forces numbered less than 20: two military vehicles, each carrying five people, and four motorcycles, each carrying two people.He said that what happened, in his words, caused “humiliation” and betrayal to those who trusted the forces they fought alongside. “We are not accusing anyone, but they all participated in betraying us, conspiring against us, selling out our cause and abandoning us.“It was not a withdrawal from weakness or lack of equipment and supplies, but rather a cowardly and shameful withdrawal.”The National Resistance Forces said they had withdrawn after the death of 500 of their soldiers and to prevent encirclement. Saleh has said he is now forming the “Tihami Resistance”, a group that was entirely independent of Yemen national forces.Others point to explanations for the reverse including poor command and control communications that led to slow decision-making, high-level Houthi intelligence and divisions within the anti-Houthi military forces, including the influence of Saudi commanders.Alongside the inadequacies of the UN-backed forces, the Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army, bolstered by Iranian intelligence. They have benefited from the cut-price nature of modern warfare, using cheap drones to harass maritime traffic. But more than 10 years in control of many of Yemen’s key regions and the occasional payoff from Saudi Arabia have swelled their coffers enough to not only buy ballistic missiles, but develop their own indigenous weapon-making infrastructure, becoming less reliant on Iran in the process.Iranian officials insist the Houthis are not a simple proxy force, but have their own unified command structure and set of priorities.The inquest into what is widely regarded as a military catastrophe is not entirely retrospective. Both Yemen government and Saudi forces are urgently reviewing the lessons of defeat to better understand whether the Houthi gains can still be reversed.‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in YemenRead moreIt was claimed that a limited force from the Giants Brigades, a group once linked with the UAE-backed southern separatists, managed to repel the Houthi advance and recapture positions in the days before the fall of Mocha, which could have served as a springboard for regaining the initiative. However, the withdrawal of neighbouring National Resistance units weakened this advance and turned it into a series of retreats.Prof Dr Abdulwahab al-Awaj at Taiz University in Yemen said: “The collapse of the western coastal fronts is not merely a conventional military defeat, but a warning sign of a breakdown in coordination and trust among the anti-Houthi forces. The Houthis exploited this breakdown more than any decisive military superiority.“Regaining the initiative cannot be achieved simply by sending reinforcements. What is needed is a reorganisation of government forces and allied formations under a unified operational vision, addressing security gaps, and building genuine trust on the ground to prevent a recurrence of this scenario.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Iranian actor Laleh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speech | Movies | The Guardian
description: Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women of Iran’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women of Iran’
Content: Laleh Marzban with the Orizzonti best actress award for Falling House at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenLaleh Marzban with the Orizzonti best actress award for Falling House at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersMoviesIranian actor Laleh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speechMarzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women of Iran’Philip OltermannEuropean culture editorFri 18 Sep 2026 05.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Iranian actress who won the best newcomer award at theVenice film festivalhas come under severe attack from the country’s authorities and state media after highlighting the plight of women in Iran in her acceptance speech.Laleh Marzban last Saturday won the best actress award in the Orizzonti sidebar competition for emerging talent, for her role inMohsen Gharaei’s Falling House, a film revolving around three generations of women who are incarcerated in their own home by the family’s father.At the awards gala, Marzban dedicated her prize to “the women of my country who have paid the highest price for even the smallest measure of freedom”. Speaking in Farsi, she added that Iranians were experiencing some of the most difficult days of their lives but should not lose hope.On Thursday, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution, a conservative-dominated government body appointed by Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement condemning Marzban’s speech as “presenting a one-sided narrative of Iran’s proud society”.Referring only to “recent statements and behaviour made at the Venice film festival”, it said reducing Iranian women to “the stereotypes desired by western circles […] is not in line with the awareness-raising mission and social commitment of art”.The statement has come on the back of a raft of similarly worded attacks in state-affiliated Iranian media, some of which called for the actress to be disciplined by the regime.Zahra Chekhmaghi, a journalist and presenter associated with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), called Marzban “a two-faced person, […] self-interested, hypocritical, despicable and miserable”, while another IRIB-affiliated media personality, actress Zhila Sadeghi, criticised Marzban for not dedicating her speech instead to the children killed in a US missile strike on an elementary school in Minab on 28 February.On state TV IRIB, a Qu’ran expert said the actress had been “deceived by the enemy” and called on the government to not let her work in Iran. Another news agency, Student News Network (SNN), urged the ministry of culture to not let Marzban back into the country.The Iranian reaction to Gharaei’s film and Marzban’s speech appears to mirror the pushback against another film that premiered on the Lido this year, Guardian-produced documentary NAZA,about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said this weekhe would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating a campaign against NAZA’s directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Netanyahu seeks to strip citizenship from Israelis as threats to NAZA film directors intensifyRead moreGharaei’s Falling House thematises the collapse of traditional patriarchal family structures in Iran, and men’s efforts to keep them in place by force. Marzban plays twentysomething Ensi, who announces to her family her plans to leave the country and pursue a modelling career in Turkey. In a desperate effort to assert his authority, her father Rashid (Farhad Aslani) locks Ensi and the other female members of the household in their rooms.Asked after Falling House’s Venice premiere how the film would be received in Iran, Marzban said: “This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective,” she said.“I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalIranCensorshipFestivalsMiddle East and north AfricaWorld cinemanewsShareReuse this content

title: YouTube star Ms Rachel to match Macklemore’s $1m Palestine aid donation | Culture | The Guardian
description: Educator talks of ‘moral obligation’ and urges ‘every wealthy white celebrity’ to make similar donation
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Educator talks of ‘moral obligation’ and urges ‘every wealthy white celebrity’ to make similar donation
Content: Ms Rachel, right, said she would match Macklemore’s $1m donation to Palestinian groups.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMs Rachel, right, said she would match Macklemore’s $1m donation to Palestinian groups.Composite: Getty ImagesCultureYouTube star Ms Rachel to match Macklemore’s $1m Palestine aid donationEducator talks of ‘moral obligation’ and urges ‘every wealthy white celebrity’ to make similar donationUwa Ede-OsifoThu 17 Sep 2026 21.00 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYouTube starMs Rachelhas said sheis matching rapper Macklemore’s $1mdonation to organizations supporting Palestinians, calling on other public figures to follow suit.Macklemore, who wasfiredas the opening act on Ed Sheeran’s tour after saying “Free Palestine” on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, pledged to donate the entirety of his earnings from Sheeran’s tour to several organizations focused on the Palestinian people.Ms Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote on Instagram: “Over 20,000 precious Palestinian children have been killed, and children continue to be killed every day.”Accurso said her donation would go to thePalestineChildren’s Relief Fund.“We have a moral obligation to use our privilege and platforms to protect children and human rights,” she wrote.Accurso, a children’s entertainer with over 21 million YouTube subscribers, has been vocal about the hardships Gaza’s young people face amid the war with Israel. She encouraged “every wealthy white celebrity” to match her donation.Accurso is the latest public figure to backMacklemore, after he was dropped from Sheeran’s Loop tour for remarks he made at a 4 September concert about the plight of the Palestinian people.“Free Palestine! I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he said during a two-minute speech.Macklemore’s words prompted a flurry of criticism from Israel-aligned groups. The singer Pinkalso called onMacklemore to be removed from the tour, and referenced a 2014 incident where he wore a costume decried for bearing resemblance to Jewish caricature. Macklemoreapologizedfor the costume at the time.Pink expanded on her position in an Instagram post, saying she was not speaking on behalf of the Israeli government, but rather wanted to advocate for Jewish concertgoers who may have been alarmed by the rapper’s remarks.Macklemore directly addressed Jewish audience members at a second tour date on 5 September, saying: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”Sheeran has maintained the decision to fire Macklemore was led by stadium owners, including Gillette Stadium and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.Sheeran wrote on Tuesday on Instagram: “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”Kraft and Sheeran are bothdonating$2m each to “aid in the region”, Kraft said Wednesday, although it is unclear which organizations their funds will support.Four supporting acts, among them American singer Finneas and Danish pop band Lukas Graham, have quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.Explore more on these topicsCulturePalestineMiddle East and north AfricaCelebrityMacklemorenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration again denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly | United Nations | The Guardian
description: For the second year in a row, the administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel for the forum
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: For the second year in a row, the administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel for the forum
Content: The Palestinian Authority president, Mahmoud Abbas, at the general conference of Fatah in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on 14 May 2026.Photograph: Mohammad Torokman/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Palestinian Authority president, Mahmoud Abbas, at the general conference of Fatah in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on 14 May 2026.Photograph: Mohammad Torokman/ReutersUnited NationsTrump administration again denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assemblyFor the second year in a row, the administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel for the forumAnna BettsThu 17 Sep 2026 20.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’sUnited Nationsgeneral assembly gathering inNew York.The state department said in astatementthe Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations.“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said.Burnham and Trump expected to meet for first time next week as PM steps up presence on world stageRead moreThe move marks thesecond yearin a row the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person.The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against it in astatementon Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region”.Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US isMahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority,according to reports.The UN general assembly voted on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering via ⁠video, for thesecond year in a row.This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on22 September.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsPalestineTrump administrationWest BankUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north title: US court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 years | US news | The Guardian
description: Samir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were tortured
Author: Alice Speri
Headline: Samir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were tortured
Content: Photograph depicting Alsheikh and Bashar al-Assad on or about July 25, 2011, when Assad appointed AlsheikhPhotograph: US Department of JusticeView image in fullscreenPhotograph depicting Alsheikh and Bashar al-Assad on or about July 25, 2011, when Assad appointed AlsheikhPhotograph: US Department of JusticeUS newsUS court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 yearsSamir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were torturedAlice SperiThu 17 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTFirst published on Thu 17 Sep 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis article contains descriptions of torture.A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal juryconvictedal-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.Al-Sheikh’s legal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Assistant attorney general A Tysen Duva of the justice department’s criminal division said in astatementthe sentence sends a clear message: “Human rights violators who come to the United States will receive no safe harbor here. We will find them, and they will be prosecuted and punished for their heinous crimes.”Al-Sheikh, 74, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 atLos Angelesinternational airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 whichtoppled the regime in just 11 days.Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a courtsentencedal-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet” or “flying carpet” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” or “flying carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.Al-Sheikh is one of only five people to be prosecuted under the extraterritorial Torture Act, which allows the US government to prosecute individuals physically present in the US over acts of torture committed abroad.“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at theCenter for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsSyriaBashar al-AssadLaw (US)Middle East and north AfricaLos AngelesnewsShareReuse this content

title: British Sikh man granted bail in India nine years after arrest | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Jagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offences
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Jagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offences
Content: Jagtar Singh Johal claims he was tortured in detention in an attempt to extract a confession.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenJagtar Singh Johal claims he was tortured in detention in an attempt to extract a confession.Photograph: Family handout/PAScotlandBritish Sikh man granted bail in India nine years after arrestJagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offencesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 18 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested inIndiain 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.Johal, fromScotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges weredismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-basedbrother Gurpreet Singh Johalsaid: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”View image in fullscreenGurpreet Singh Johal has fought tirelessly for his brother’s release.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianGurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStarmer urged to intervene in ‘rigged’ Indian prosecution of British human rights activistRead moreThe UK governmentrecently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular casesand he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.Explore more on these topicsScotlandIndiaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Earl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s death | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Buckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Buckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’
Content: Spencer stood firm in his recollection after the palace suggested his memory had been clouded by ‘fraternal grief’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenSpencer stood firm in his recollection after the palace suggested his memory had been clouded by ‘fraternal grief’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAMonarchyEarl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s deathBuckingham Palace has rebutted claim by Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, that then prince told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’Sammy GecsoylerFri 18 Sep 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said ofDiana, Princess of Wales, “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her death, saying he is telling the truth.The alleged comments, revealed in Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, prompted Buckingham Palace to issue an extraordinary statement suggesting Diana’s brother had misremembered events, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise”.In an interview with the BBC, Spencer stood firm in his recollection, telling Laura Kuenssberg:“I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”Responding to the palace’s statement, Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious, or is he embarrassed?” When asked about the inference that his memory was coloured, Spencer said: “They’ve sort of smudged that one, haven’t they?They’ve said that recollections may vary.”View image in fullscreenDiana died in a car crash in 1997, at the age of 36.Photograph: Simon Kreitem/ReutersSpencer said the call was one of two he had with Charles in his lifetime and said he told his friends and family members at the time about the comment “because it was so monstrous”.The alleged comment was revealed on Wednesday in an extract from the memoir published in the Daily Mail. The comment by the then prince was allegedly made during a heated argument over funeral arrangements. Spencer says it reflected Charles’s“pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, the Daily Mail reported.Charles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after Diana’s death, claims Earl SpencerRead moreAmong other claims in the book are that Diana told a friend on the eve of her wedding to Charles that he said he was happy to marry her, but was not actually in love with her.On Friday, the second extract from the memoir was published. Spencer writes Charles was “polite and formal” on the day of Diana’s funeral and says Prince Philip told him to look ahead while walking in unison alongside his nephews and former brother-in-law.“It was hellish, entering that tunnel of grief, particularly because we were unable to put a face to it by looking at the individuals in the crowd,” said Spencer of the procession.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Prince Philip, Prince William, Charles Spencer, Prince Harry and King Charles, then a prince, walking in Diana’s funeral procession.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/APIn the extract released on Wednesday, Spencer says he insisted to Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, to walk in her funeral procession. In the end, her sons walked behind her coffin, which William later called “one of the hardest things I’ve ever done”.Spencer wrote that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer writing: “‘Rest assured,’” he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”Spencer wrote that he was stunned and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”Spencer also claimed that Diana “never would have wanted” her sons to walk behind her coffin, to which Charles allegedly replied: “That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty.”Swan Song is due to be published globally next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.Four copies of the Dutch-language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.Buckingham Palace did not issue a statement responding to the BBC interview, but on Wednesday a spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”Explore more on these topicsMonarchyDiana, Princess of WalesKing Charles IIInewsShareReuse this content

title: Sensitive UK police data vulnerable to ‘compromise’ by US government and foreign actors | Police | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackers
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Exclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackers
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyPoliceSensitive UK police data vulnerable to ‘compromise’ by US government and foreign actorsExclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackersAisha DownFri 18 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVast troves of highly sensitive police data are lying onMicrosoftcloud platforms which an oﬃcial UK security assessment deemed to be vulnerable to “compromise” by foreign actors and the US government, a Guardian investigation can reveal.The files include criminal records, victim statements, internal emails and sensitive information held by more than 40 police forces across the UK.Some files exceed “oﬃcial” classification, according to a policedocument seen by the Guardian, raising the possibility the information could be classed as “secret” or “top secret”.The cloud platform is Microsoft Azure, one of the main commercial offerings of the US tech company. It is used by businesses and governments globally and rests on a web of IT infrastructure – datacentres, networking gear, fibre optic cables – that spans more than 100 countries.In recent years, doubts have surfaced about how cloud platforms store data and whether they are truly secure.British police decided to put some of their most sensitive data on the Microsoft platform in a 2017 meeting, a record of which was examined by the Guardian.In doing so, officers accepted that “US government insiders” would be able to see the data, and that it could be “transmitted worldwide”, with “the extent of this … unknown”.According to five specialists who reviewed the Guardian’s findings, the risks identified in that document persist today. Almost every UK police forcenow depends onMicrosoft Azure, and the UK government spends at least £1.9bn on Microsoft software each year.“There’s no evidence that this has been properly understood,” said one source who has held senior roles in UK policing. The data is “some of the most sensitive that exists”, he added. “You’re talking about information that, if it gets into the wrong hands, or if the information is incorrect, [means] people can get hurt or may die.”When the Guardian approached the police about the possibility that sensitive information was not secure, they appeared to wave aside these risks, saying Britain’s contracts with Microsoft meant US authorities could not view data without express permission and that the data it stored on Microsoft remained in the UK.These statements appeared to contradict public admissions by Microsoft, which said in a disclosure toPoliceScotland in 2023 that data “can go outside the UK” and that it “cannot guarantee data sovereignty”.Microsoft said it “does not provide any government with direct or unfettered access to customer data”, and that it had not provided UK data in response to a US government request. It added that, like all US-based tech companies, it responded to US government requests made through valid legal processes.The threat of ‘US government insider attackers’In 2017, a senior police oﬃcer, Ian Dyson, chaired a meeting in which stakeholders considered15 risks the UK would face if police forces decided to transfer their data to Microsoft’s global cloud.View image in fullscreenIan Dyson, pictured in 2016.Photograph: Jamie SmithThat meeting considered both the police’s use of Microsoft’s software, such as Office 365, and the reliance on the cloud that underpins these services, Azure. Those risks, and the resulting police decisions, were set out in a summary document seen by the Guardian and signed off by Dyson.This was four years after the advent of a policy called “cloud first”. Introduced by the Cabinet Office in 2013, it became a government-wide effort to push almost all departments to migrate their data on to the “public cloud” – commercial offerings by tech companies, often based in the US. Departments that did not want to do this had to jump through burdensome administrative hoops.Dyson was the police commissioner of the City of London at the time, but he held another title: senior information risk owner for all of Britain, or the SIRO. It was his job to set the norms for how British police could safely handle their data.In their assessment, officers came to startling conclusions about what would happen if they put police data on Azure. Firstly, they considered it would be vulnerable to hackers: Microsoft’s software “carries vulnerabilities which will be exploited by cybercriminals and other threat actors in due course”.Separately, it added: “Police forces cannot be certain where their data will be processed or stored.“The hyper-scale and global nature of the Microsoft cloud means that police data, and metadata relating to police data could be transmitted and stored worldwide by Microsoft, and the extent of this will be unknown.”The document specifically identified the potential risk from what it described as “US government insiders”. It said: “There is a risk of compromise of sensitive data shared by, or taken from, Microsoft by the US government being released by US government insider attackers.”The document explained that the data intended for migration was sensitive. In fact, “a significant volume” of it exceeded the classification “oﬃcial”. In the UK, this suggests it was either “oﬃcial sensitive”, “secret”, or “top secret”.The assessment also suggested Microsoft’s platform was unable to guarantee this data would be secure. “This places sensitive data, inadequately protected in an environment which then becomes a significantly more attractive target for attackers,” it said.double quotation markWe really don’t know if the data has been breached or notFormer senior policing sourceAs well as risks, the report also listed mitigations. On the problem of cyber-attacks, it mandated that police servers should be repaired promptly, kept up to date and have antivirus software.To address the risk of “US government insiders” and the concern that Microsoft might store UK policing data “worldwide” it suggested “applying Microsoft’s ‘out-of-the-box’ native encryption” and leaving the final decision about using Microsoft up to individual police chiefs.Several experts interviewed by the Guardian, including cloud computing specialists and engineers working for Microsoft, suggested these mitigations were inadequate. Microsoft’s internal encryption does not prevent its employees accessing UK police data; nor would it stop the US government obtaining British policing files.The National Police Chief’s Council (NPCC) said access to data stored on the cloud is limited to those with a genuine need to access it and that this is subject to strict controls. Despite that claim, a Microsoft engineer who reviewed the Guardian’s findings said the information “could be viewed by hundreds of people around the world, some of them not vetted, many of them not directly employed by Microsoft”.Despite the risks identified by the assessment, every police force in the UK put its data, wholly or in part, on Microsoft’s cloud. Some began migrating their information in 2017. A few forces, such as Police Scotland, are still finalising their adoption of the technology.The files cover the “full gamut of data: intelligence, body-worn video, digital evidence and case files, as well as the non-law enforcement data any organisation has”, said the source who held senior roles in UK policing.‘We do not expect any sharing … without permission’The UK government spends billions each year on services oﬀered by three US tech companies: Amazon, Google and Microsoft.Up to 60% of its IT infrastructure ishosted on cloud platforms. Britain’s intelligence data is hosted on Amazon’s cloud services, as is its customs data. The Ministry of Defence uses Azure. There is “a deep dependency on US hyperscalers”, said Dave Michels, a researcher with the Cloud Legal Project, at Queen Mary University of London.This is the result of 13 years of decisions like Dyson’s. It is unclear if the potential consequences are broadly understood.When the Guardian approached the NPCC over the document signed by Dyson, it said: “UK policing as standard requires the use of UK-only datacentres,” but added that “on occasion” Microsoft employees could access the data “to provide support”.Asked whether the US government could access the data, a police spokesperson said they could not comment on the phrase “US government insiders”, because “terminology … changes continuously” and the document was “outdated”.“In line with the contract signed with Microsoft, we do not expect any sharing with the US government without the express permission of the UK government,” they added.Microsoft said: “The suggestion that use of Microsoft cloud services means customer data is inherently insecure or automatically exposed to foreign governments is inaccurate.” It said it had “never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”.Two legal experts, as well as several Microsoft engineers who spoke anonymously to the Guardian, suggested these assertions did not give an accurate picture of the potential risks.double quotation markThe risk is obvious, even though the providers of the cloud and the government both have an interest in talking it downDouwe Korff, professor of international lawBy default, Microsoft’s cloud was “a global network of datacentres”, said Michels. It had facilities on every continent and this meant, generally, that data stored on it was stored everywhere: pieces of a single file could be held across multiple countries, from Sweden to Ethiopia.In recent years, Michels said, Microsoft had begun to offer clients in Europe greater assurances about where their data was stored, including assuring some customers that their data would remain within EU borders. But “the focus on data location is a bit of a red herring”, he said.This was because thousands of engineers from more than 100 countries maintained Microsoft’s systems. Some were directly employed by Microsoft, others worked for subcontractors in countries potentially hostile to the UK, from Israel to Egypt, China and Kazakhstan. “You’ve seen the list of their sub-processors of people who have access to customer data,” said Michels. “It’s a long list.”Some of the engineers could access data, such as UK police data, directly as part of customer support. Many more could see key features of what the data included.View image in fullscreenA Microsoft datacentre in the Netherlands.Photograph: Ramon van Flymen/EPAMicrosoft said it had “strong guardrails” around data access by engineers.Douwe Korff, a professor of international law at London Metropolitan University, said the police statement that “we do not expect any sharing [of our data] with the US government” was “typical lawyers’ wriggling”.“The risk is obvious, even though the providers of the cloud and the government both have an interest in talking it down,” he said.Michels said: “As a cloud customer, if you’re relying on a contractual commitment from a cloud provider not to hand over data when forced to under foreign law, that is not worth much more than the piece of paper it’s written on.”US law, including the Cloud Act, allows US authorities to access any data held by US cloud companies, including data held abroad. US authorities do not need a warrant to do this, and they can require US companies to not disclose such access to cloud customers.Microsoft, Amazon and Google have insisted they would fight such requests, said Korff. But there is “nothing that is legally binding” that would prevent them from sharing other governments’ data if US authorities demanded it.In response to a query from the Guardian, Microsoft said it “has never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”. It added in a follow-up that it was bound by its “contractual commitments”.“If UK law prohibits us from turning over data to another government, that is a binding law that would govern our response to any hypothetical demand,” it said.‘The security guys expected a big breach by now’The Guardian spoke to six people who have closely followed the country’s data storage arrangements over the past decade. Several of them said that senior leaders did not view dependence on US tech companies as a concern, and trusted them not to give data to US authorities.“Government security departments are painfully aware of all the risks,” said Mark Butcher, a cloud expert who acts as a strategic adviser across government. “But the way that most senior leaders talk about it is: ‘Well, we’ve been reassured by Microsoft that it would never happen.’”But the source who has held senior policing roles said: “All the security guys I worked with when this policy came in expected a big breach by now, and we know it will take that to change the police’s position.“The truth is, however, the level of logging and information in the cloud systems would not necessarily tell us if there was a problem. We really don’t know if the data has been breached or not.”Explore more on these topicsPoliceCloud computingMicrosoftComputingInternetData protectionData and computer securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Polanski request to postpone Greens’ conference to focus on byelection refused by party | Green party | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against plan
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Exclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against plan
Content: Zack Polanski is standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyView image in fullscreenZack Polanski is standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyGreen partyPolanski request to postpone Greens’ conference to focus on byelection refused by partyExclusive: Leader understood to have wanted to concentrate on Holborn and St Pancras campaign in London but executive committee voted against planPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski requested that the Greens’ ruling executive committee postpone the party’s imminent annual conference so they could focus on theHolborn and St Pancras byelectionbut was refused.While party officials say the formal request came from staffers worried about diluting resources by staging a conference a week before Polanski tries to win Keir Starmer’s former Commons seat, the Guardian understands the party leader wanted this to happen.In the end, the executive committee of the Greens in England and Wales, which has about 25 voting members including Polanski, voted against the plan on Thursday.The party expects about 3,000 people to attend what would be its biggest gathering, beginning in Brighton on 2 October.Calling off the event at such short notice would have cost the party a significant sum given it has rented a conference venue, and risked annoying members who have taken time off work and booked travel and hotels.The byelection, in which Polanski hopes to challenge for a traditionally safe Labour seat, takes place on 8 October, just four days after the conference finishes.The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly ToynbeeRead moreThe end of a byelection campaign is traditionally marked by parties trying to canvass as many voters as possible. Having thousands of the Greens’ most active members gathered somewhere else for the final weekend greatly complicates their operation.Some Greens have also speculated that Polanski would have preferred to fight the byelection before the party votes on a contentious policy motion at its conference, which sets out a motion on Zionism.Polanskiis under pressureto take a stance on the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference, and is thus almost certain to feature.The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state in Palestine – with racism and would call for a single Palestinian state. Members who support Zionism would risk being disciplined for racism.A number of Greens fear passing the motion could alienate Jewish supporters. Polanski, who is Jewish, has not given a public opinion on the issue, but is understood to support a pair of amendments that would tone down the motion.A Green party spokesperson said: “The party was exploring different ways of allocating our resources effectively while fighting theHolborn and St Pancras byelection. One possible option was to postpone our conference.“After discussion we remain committed to running an incredibly ambitious Holborn and St Pancras byelection campaign and holding what will be our biggest ever party conference.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephanie Cole, Coronation Street and Open All Hours actor, dies aged 84 | Television | The Guardian
description: Cole, described as an ‘extraordinary talent’, also appeared in Waiting for God, Tenko and had an extensive theatre career
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cole, described as an ‘extraordinary talent’, also appeared in Waiting for God, Tenko and had an extensive theatre career
Content: Stephanie Cole in 2014. Her agent said she would also ‘be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities’.Photograph: Mike Lawn/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStephanie Cole in 2014. Her agent said she would also ‘be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities’.Photograph: Mike Lawn/ShutterstockTelevisionStephanie Cole, Coronation Street and Open All Hours actor, dies aged 84Cole, described as an ‘extraordinary talent’, also appeared in Waiting for God, Tenko and had an extensive theatre careerPA MediaFri 18 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actor Stephanie Cole, best known for roles inCoronation Street, Waiting for God and Open All Hours, has died aged 84.She also appeared in the prisoner-of-war drama Tenko, A Bit of a Do and Doc Martin.A statement from her agent, John Grant, on behalf of her family, said: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Stephanie Cole, OBE.“She passed away this morning at the age of 84. Stephanie had been living with Alzheimer’s disease for some years.My TV hero: Stephanie Cole on Innes LloydRead more“Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television. She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama.“She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities. During this incredibly difficult time, the family kindly requests privacy.”View image in fullscreenCole (right) as Sylvia Goodwin in Coronation Street.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockCole appeared on Coronation Street between 2011 and 2013 as Sylvia Goodwin, the mother of Roy Cropper. She won the British Soap award for best comedy performance for the role.Her other notable performances included roles in Still Open All Hours, in which she reprised her Open All Hours character Mrs Featherstone, The Cleaner, Gentleman Jack and Talking Heads: Soldiering On.She won the British Comedy award for best actress for the 1990s sitcom Waiting for God, about residents of a retirement home.Cole also had an extensive career in the theatre, with roles in King Lear, A Passionate Woman and Noises Off.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionCoronation StreetSoap operaDramanewsShareReuse this content

title: Marks and Spencer’s first LFW catwalk gamble pays off with compelling looks at affordable prices | Marks & Spencer | The Guardian
description: Retailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway show
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Retailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway show
Content: All of the clothes went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces priced under £50.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersView image in fullscreenAll of the clothes went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces priced under £50.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersMarks & SpencerMarks and Spencer’s first LFW catwalk gamble pays off with compelling looks at affordable pricesRetailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway showJess Cartner-MorleyFri 18 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoan Collins declared the coats “very chic”, and has her eye on a graceful ivory evening dress with caped shoulders. Kemi Badenoch plans to snap up the classic black tuxedo jacket. If the British public are as enthusiastic as the celebrity front row, Marks & Spencer’s first everLondon fashion weekcatwalk looks like a hit.The show, held at the Design Museum for 310 guests including Ian Wright and Jamie Carragher, was a gamble on both sides. Would snobby fashionistas be traumatised by elasticated waistbands and practical rainwear? Would M&S customers be alienated by a world of £2,000 handbags and shoes you can’t walk in?The style message was “fashion with a small f, not a capital F”, said the M&S womenswear director, Maddy Evans. The look was new enough to be compelling (sharp kilts instead of flouncy tiered skirts, low-rise slouchy denim replacing mom jeans), but pitched at a before-the-watershed comfort level. A judicious amount of catwalk theatre was added with some sauce (a very short skirt, the odd semi-visible nipple) and a little zeitgeisty styling (faux fur stoles, Charli xcx-adjacent sunglasses).The real stunner is the price. All the clothes in this collection went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces under £50. The most expensive, a leather coat, will retail for £450. The message – that catwalk style is for everyone – is a win for London fashion week, which has struggled to feel relevant to real lives as designer prices have soared during a cost of living crisis.View image in fullscreenThe show featured Lennon Gallagher modelling a classic grey office suit.Photograph: Ian West/PAAs a vision of where our wardrobes are going next, the collection will not give Phoebe Philo or Jonathan Anderson any sleepless nights. M&S is not seeking to define the next vibe shift. Instead, they picked up on the currents that make a wardrobe look contemporary: a colour palette of neutrals with pops of red (for men, as well as women) and a shift toward outfits built from separates over dresses. Menswear featured a classic grey office suit – worn, in a witty casting touch, by scowling nepo-rocker Lennon Gallagher – and centrist-dad chore jackets.M&S are now ranked in second place in style perception, behind Zara. “That’s exactly where we want to be”, said Evans. “Zara are the cutting edge of fashion, and we are fashion for everybody.”Many pieces felt intentionally familiar, with nods to the archives to celebrate the centenary of fashion being sold at M&S. There was a twinset, reworked as a cardigan over a knitted camisole, and a sage-green lace two-piece set which nodded to the proud history of M&S lingerie. Models of a broad range of ages and body sizes “were chosen to reflect our 23 million customers”, said Evans.After the show, Wright caught up with Carragher as a fashion week version of an M&S “picky tea” was served: smoked salmon finger sandwiches and champagne on silver trays.The show was a bold statement about how M&S sees itself, reflecting resurgent style confidence after fashion hits that have included suede loafers that could pass for Saint Laurent and a sellout collaboration with Bella Freud.M&S is not the only big name giving the London schedule fresh momentum and a renewed sense of occasion this season. McQueen is returning to London after showing in Paris, while Christopher Kane – one of the city’s most beloved and influential designers – is making a keenly anticipated return to the catwalk with a new job at Mulberry.Fashion editor’s top picksDouble-breasted tuxedo jacket, £85Modern party-dressing made simple. Double-breasted shape and satin peak labels bring just enough drama. Machine washable!View image in fullscreenTuxedo jacket, £85.Photograph: M&SIvory satin party dress, £89Crepe-back satin (one side matt, one side glossy) is the kind of high-end fabric you do not often find on the high street. Kimono sleeves and a train for real wow factor. Also comes in black.View image in fullscreenSatin mini dress, £89Photograph: M&SSequin fringe skirt, £50Swishy! The personality skirt is big in fashion and with gold sequins and silk fringing, this has main character energy.View image in fullscreenSequin fringe skirt, £50.Photograph: M&SRed half zip sweater, £40From tech bros to pop stars, everyone is in a half zip. The ketchup red is fun.View image in fullscreenHalf zip jumper, £40.Photograph: M&SLeather jacket with borg collar, £250Vintage style pilot’s jacket in tobacco leather with a cream shawl collar and waist tabs.View image in fullscreenPer Una vintage borg leather jacket, £250.Photograph: M&SExplore more on these topicsMarks & SpencerLondon fashion weekFashion weeksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Uber ordered to pay $40m over death of woman ejected by driver on freeway | Uber | The Guardian
description: California judge finds company ‘vicariously liable’ for driver’s negligence in death of Emily Normandin-Parker
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: California judge finds company ‘vicariously liable’ for driver’s negligence in death of Emily Normandin-Parker
Content: The Uber headquarters in San Francisco.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Uber headquarters in San Francisco.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUberUber ordered to pay $40m over death of woman ejected by driver on freewayCalifornia judge finds company ‘vicariously liable’ for driver’s negligence in death of Emily Normandin-ParkerJohana BhuiyanFri 18 Sep 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUber was ordered to pay $40m to the parents of a 23-year-old woman who was killed after a driver kicked her and a friend out of his car by the side of aCaliforniafreeway, according to newly public arbitration documents.An arbitrator, retired Calfornia judgeRichard A Stone, found that the ride-share company was “vicariously liable” for the driver’s negligence.In August 2023, two women, Emily Normandin-Parker and Luna Moore, hailed anUberafter a night out in Orange county. The driver pulled over on the 73 freeway after Normandin-Parker vomited in the car, attorneys said. While Moore and the driver argued over a cleaning fee, Normandin-Parker got out of the car, wandered into oncoming traffic and was struck by a car.Normandin-Parker’s parents accused the driver and Uber of negligence. The company argued it was just “a technology company that provides a software platform connecting riders with independent third-party drivers who perform the transportation”. In California, under Prop 22, Uber and Lyft drivers were categorized as independent contractors – not employees of the companies – a designation the company has used to argue it is not liable for the actions of its drivers. However, the arbitrator rejected Uber’s argument that it should be treated as a platform that merely connects drivers and riders.In arbitration documents released by the family’s attorney on Thursday, Stone wrote that Uber should be treated as a common carrier – which is any entity or individual that transports people or goods – and thus should be held “vicariously liable” for the incident. Vicarious liability is when one party is held liable for the negligence or actions of another party that it has a relationship with.“The fact that Uber uses a digital interface rather than street hails does not change the fundamental nature of the service being offered,” the arbitration documents read. Stone further asserted Prop 22 does “not immunize Uber from vicarious liability for the torts of its drivers stands”.Uber said that while the company respects the arbitration process, the arbitrator “was wrong in holding Uber legally responsible for the tragic events of that night”.“No family should have to suffer the loss of a child, and our thoughts continue to be with the Normandin-Parker family,” said Uber spokesperson Gabriela Condarco-Quesada.“We have continued to strengthen our approach to safety over the years, through new technology, policies and safeguards informed by safety experts, including additional guidance to drivers about avoiding drop-offs in unsafe locations.”The family further asserted that Uber at one point proposed a settlement that included a confidentiality agreement. As part of that agreement, the family said they would have been charged a $10m penalty any time they spoke about the accident and Uber’s connection to it. The family said they rejected thesettlementand Uber said it “ultimately did not pursue confidentiality in this case”.The ruling to hold Uber liable for the negligence or actions of its drivers is not binding and applies only to this case. However, the case is part of the company’s battle to be treated as merely an online marketplace for rides and in doing so distance themselves from the actions of their drivers by treating them as contractors rather than employees.Explore more on these topicsUberCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition | Tennessee | The Guardian
description: Angela Lipps, 50, alleges in suit that Fargo police wrongly relied on AI facial recognition to arrest and charge her
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Angela Lipps, 50, alleges in suit that Fargo police wrongly relied on AI facial recognition to arrest and charge her
Content: Fargo police department building.Photograph: Google MapsView image in fullscreenFargo police department building.Photograph: Google MapsTennesseeUS woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognitionAngela Lipps, 50, alleges in suit that Fargo police wrongly relied on AI facial recognition to arrest and charge herLucy CampbellFri 18 Sep 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 20.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Tennessee woman who wasfalsely chargedwith bank theft in North Dakota and jailed for six months has sued for $10m in damages, alleging in a federal lawsuit that Fargo police improperly relied on an artificial intelligence (AI) facial recognition system to wrongly accuse her.Angela Lipps, 50, was arrested at gunpoint by US marshals at her home in Tennessee while babysitting her neighbor’s four children in July 2025. The mother of three and grandmother of five was booked into a county jail and remained there for almost four months without bail while awaiting extradition toNorth Dakota, where she was held for about two more months.Lipps, who has lived most of her life in north-central Tennessee, had never been on a plane until authorities flew her toNorth Dakotaat the end of October, where she was charged with four counts of unauthorized use of personal identifying information and four counts of theft.The charges were ultimately dropped, and she was “released into the freezing cold … on Christmas Eve with no way to get home” after her lawyer, Jay Greenwood, provided bank records proving that she was inTennesseeat the time the fraud occurred in Fargo, the complaint says.Another attorney for Lipps, Eric Rice,toldTennessee television station WKRN that the $10m his client is seeking is “obviously … a significant number, but it reflects the specific harm that happened to Angela”.“Can you imagine being taken away at gunpoint, held in detention, taken from your family?” Rice said.A Fargo government spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.Lipps’s lawsuit names the city of Fargo and Lucas Heck, a city police detective identified in the complaint as having requested the arrest warrant for her, as the defendants.The plaintiff alleges that she “experienced traumatic conditions in the jails”.“She struggled with the fear of not knowing when she would be released or whether she would end up wrongly convicted and imprisoned for years,” the lawsuit continues. “She missed family birthdays. She spent her own birthday incarcerated, separated from her family. She missed holidays with her loved ones, including Thanksgiving and Christmas. While in custody, she was denied basic care, such as her medications and her dentures.”Lipps learned she had lost her residence, her car and her personal property once she was released from custody, her lawsuit states. The experience, it says, has left Lipps with “lasting hardships and trauma that might be managed but never erased”.The “Fargo police department (FPD) and its agents have refused to accept responsibility or apologize to Lipps despite multiple requests for them to do so”, the complaint says. The lawsuit says that it seeks to “repair what has been broken” over her false arrest and “seeks accountability” from the FPD.Lipps’s complaint recounts how a west Fargo police investigator used AI facial recognition software to identify bank fraud suspects. The software returned Lipps’s social media photo as a potential lead, which was provided to Heck.It alleges that the source of the facial recognition was a fake ID used by a female suspect who was captured in surveillance video footage. Lipps did not look like the female suspect and had also never been to North Dakota, according to the complaint.The complaint alleges that Heck falsely suggested that facial recognition systems had identified Lipps and did not conduct further investigation or find sufficient probable cause – but requested an arrest warrant anyway.Lipps maintains she was unlawfully arrested and imprisoned – as well as maliciously prosecuted – and that the FPD lacked policy, training and supervision of officers on the use of facial recognition technology.“They knew that AI facial recognition technology should not be used as the sole basis to extradite and charge a person,” Lipps’s complaint alleges. “Yet they ignored those issues and gave no care to the harm it would do to innocent people like Lipps.“As AI facial recognition technology becomes more accessible and widespread, Lipps hopes that her case will cause officers to use appropriate care and consider the harm their actions can have on those who are wrongly accused.”Lipps’s lawsuit further alleges: “FPD was aware that the lack of supervision of an officer using facial recognition in an investigation could result in the wrongful detention and prosecution of a subject. Despite knowledge of this risk, FPD refused to supervise its officers’ use of facial recognition technology in a criminal investigation.”Explore more on these topicsTennesseeUS policingNorth DakotaUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Warren Buffett steps down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway after over 50 years | Warren Buffett | The Guardian
description: ‘Father Time always wins,’ Buffett, 96, says as his son, Howard, steps in as the $1tn conglomerate’s new chair
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: ‘Father Time always wins,’ Buffett, 96, says as his son, Howard, steps in as the $1tn conglomerate’s new chair
Content: Warren Buffett attends the Berkshire Hathaway Inc annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on 3 May 2024.Photograph: Scott Morgan/ReutersView image in fullscreenWarren Buffett attends the Berkshire Hathaway Inc annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on 3 May 2024.Photograph: Scott Morgan/ReutersWarren BuffettWarren Buffett steps down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway after over 50 years‘Father Time always wins,’ Buffett, 96, says as his son, Howard, steps in as the $1tn conglomerate’s new chairLauren ArataniFri 18 Sep 2026 10.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWarren Buffett is stepping down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway, the company that he took from a faltering textile manufacturer into a $1tn conglomerate over the course of 60 years.Buffett’s son, Howard, 71, will take over as chair. Buffett, 96, cited his age as the main reason behind the transition, noting that he has a one-year-old great-grandchild who is “moving a bit faster than I am these days”.“Serving as your chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted,” Buffett, 96, said in aletterto shareholders. “Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me. He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead.”Buffett said he will remain as chair emeritus and a director on the board. He left his post as CEO ofBerkshireHathaway in May 2025, shocking the audience of thousands at the company’s annual shareholder meeting in Omaha, Nebraska. Greg Abel, vice–chair of the company, replaced him as CEO.‘Be fearful when others are greedy’: Warren Buffett’s sharpest lessons in investingRead moreKnown as the “Oracle of Omaha”, Buffett built a reputation as a sharp-eyed investor, building up Berkshire Hathaway into a $1tn conglomerate. The company owns dozens of companies in construction, manufacturing, consumer goods and insurance, along with being a major investor in some of the biggest companies on the stock market, including Nvidia, Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta.Bloomberg places Buffett’snet worthat $145bn, making him the 10th richest person in the world.Howard Buffett, known as “Howie”, is Buffett’s second child out of three and was long planned to be his father’s successor as chair of the company, having served on the board since 1993.“He is getting it because he’s my son,” Buffett told the Wall Street Journal in January 2025. “I’m very, very, very lucky in the fact that I trust all three of my children.”In a statement, Abel said that Buffett’s impact on the company “is without parallel in the history of American business”.“The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian,” he said.Explore more on these topicsWarren BuffettBerkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second term
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: President has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second term
Content: Trump speaks to the press onboard Air Force One in August.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump speaks to the press onboard Air Force One in August.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White HousePresident has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second termUS politics live – latest updatesLucy CampbellandRobert MackeyFri 18 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his latest attack on the US constitution’s first amendment and the press,Donald Trumpabruptly announced that he is banning outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage.In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the US president said he was expelling the news outlets “effective immediately” over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and threatened that bans for others outlets could follow.He went on: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”Trump defended the ban at an Oval Office event to promote his administration’s healthcare policies.“I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump told reporters, referring to friendly media outlets. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.”Reminded by one reporter that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, Trump said: “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.”He added: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.”Towards the end of a chaotic news conference, when a reporter asked Trump to explain how his ban on the three outlets would work, the president expressed confusion. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban?
