Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” Trump asked, seeming confused.After another correspondent rephrased the question, asking, “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?”Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?”On Friday, the Washington Postreportedthat more American service members have died in the war on Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed; CNNrevealedthat an “entirely false” intelligence report about a Chinese ship in the Middle East generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) had “almost started a war”; while a Politico reportuncovereda Hill investigation after sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology unexpectedly made its way to Hong Kong, possibly giving China access to them.Trump said his decision to ban the three outlets was unrelated to the stories. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said, beforethreatening more media prohibitions could follow.“There may be others to join them,” Trump said.In a statement, a spokesperson forCNNsaid the network “stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting”.“We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right,” the spokesperson said.Politico said its reporters would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones”.“We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” it added.Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), said the organization “stands in defense” of the banned reporters “who are being singled out for doing their jobs”.“This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Henrich wrote in a statement. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”A spokesperson forMS Nowdeclined to comment.Trump’s move drew swift condemnation from Democrats and free speech groups. Chris Coons, a Democratic senator, wrote on social media: “Trump is once again trying to use the power of the presidency to punish a free press, now banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. That is the behavior of an authoritarian, and we must defend the press’ right to hold those in power accountable.”The White House press pool is a “public forum” under the first amendment, so the president cannot expel journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director at Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. To do so, would be “doubly unconstitutional”.“The first amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent,” said Jaffer. “With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now.”Similarly, Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the first amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the ‘People’s House’ for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move.“The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”Since returning to office, Trump has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media at the White House, including the Associated Press, which wasbanned from press pool eventsin the Oval Office and on Air Force One after it continued to use Gulf of Mexico instead of Gulf of America in its coverage. The APsued, and that case remains in litigation.Trump’s White House also seized control over the organization of the presidentialpress pool, a rotation that determines which news organizations and reporters are allowed to follow – and question – the president in places such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One. The WHCA, an independent association made up of members of the media, traditionally coordinated rotating pool coverage of more than a dozen journalists allowed access to the president in smaller settings.The Pentagon also attempted to introduce a new press policy to restrict the ability of journalists to gather and report on sensitive information, which culminated in a mass walkout of news media outlets who refused to sign the pledge. A federal judge later ruled the policy was unconstitutional.The president has also launched high-profile legal battles with major outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and the BBC.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsUS press and publishingMS NowCNNNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Workers in New York seek to create first AutoZone union as company resists | US unions | The Guardian
description: Company may have spent about $200,000 to fight union effort in White Plains, where 11 people can vote to join UAW
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Company may have spent about $200,000 to fight union effort in White Plains, where 11 people can vote to join UAW
Content: An AutoZone store in Richmond, California, on 26 February.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn AutoZone store in Richmond, California, on 26 February.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesUS unionsWorkers in New York seek to create first AutoZone union as company resistsCompany may have spent about $200,000 to fight union effort in White Plains, where 11 people can vote to join UAWMichael SainatoFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorkers at an AutoZone in White Plains, New York, are seeking to become the first store at the US’slargestauto parts retailer to win a union election, set to begin 25 September, despite a heavy-handed union opposition campaign from the company.LaborLab, a non-profit workers’-rights watchdog,estimatesAutoZone has spent around $200,000 to oppose the unionization effort at the White Plains store, where 11 workers are eligible to vote to join the United Auto Workers Local 259. The estimate isbasedon external attorney costs and internal costs of executive salaries based on reports from workers at the store.AutoZone did not respond to multiple requests for comment.The company hasmore than 6,800 retail storesin the US and reported anet income of $2.5bnin fiscal year 2025.Nathan DuCongé has worked at an AutoZone store in White Plains, New York, for about two years, where he started as a sales associate making minimum wage.“I just remember that being very low, but I needed it very badly, and so I accepted the job,” said DuCongé. “For a job that just essentially pays minimum wage, it just makes no sense, that you’re doing all of this work, which essentially is service sales, and you’re also expected toupsellcertain products too.”He explained that the idea to unionize came from the low pay and working conditions, but took off after he attended an Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee training session and met an organizer with United Auto Workers.David Valencia, who also works at the AutoZone store in White Plains, said he began working there in May 2026, and became interested in the union after being scheduled to work the Fourth of July holiday and did not receive any sort of holiday pay or bonus for doing so.“When I got my paycheck and saw that they didn’t pay anything extra when part-time employees leave their families for holidays and sacrifice the time that they have with their families to come to work, you don’t get anything extra, any recognition, and that just blew my mind,” Valencia said. According toIndeed, AutoZone only provides paid holidays for eligible full-time employees.“Our goal is to get compensation, job security, just more things that closely reflect the value that we know that we bring to the company. We’re not getting close to what we’re worth,” Valencia added. “There is no bargaining when you’re alone. They’re only going to bargain when you’re together. So we don’t have a choice. Either we’re going to live in poverty and not be able to pay our bills, or we’re going to do this.”DuCongé and Valencia both explained that AutoZone management caught wind of the union organizing drive after they had collected enough union authorization cards to file for a union election with the National Labor Relations Board.They said the following day, the store became filled with regional and corporate managers and human resources executives.“They had sent in a whole fleet of managers, they were flying in people from around the country, and it was very bizarre, because even customers were kind of noticing how many managers were in the store,” said DuCongé.He noted the response from AutoZone was initially asking how they could help, but switched to deterring unionizing after the group issued a letter to management announcing their intent to unionize.“They were pulling people into the back. They had these long meetings where they would read: ‘Hey, we don’t think that the union is good. Here’s all the reasons why,’” said DuCongé.He explained that AutoZone threatened to delay the union election by challenging DuCongé’s eligibility to participate. He says the issue caused the union election petition to bewithdrawn initiallyin late July, thenrefiledin August.“We essentially had no choice. If we wanted to get to an election, I had to sacrifice my eligibility as a worker,” he said.DuCongé provided recordings where, he said, he is told by a manager “we will accept your invitation to fire you”, although DuCongé said he had never suggested that, and was told his social media posts were being monitored.He also shared a screenshot of AutoZone CEO Phil Daniele’s Facebook account appearing as an account that had watched one of his social media stories about the union campaign.Several letters from AutoZone management to workers plead for them to vote against the union, citing union dues and claiming “you could actually end up with less” because “nobody knows what tradeoffs will be made in bargaining” and “your wages could go up or down”.The letters did not cite the existence of any proposed union contract where workers would end up with less pay, nor explain why AutoZone or the union would propose regressive pay in a contract.“I believe local 259 will destroy the mutual respect, teamwork and culture you and I have built at store 2976,” one management letter states.LaborLab, with the help of workers in the store, identified at least 11 corporate executives at AutoZone who have appeared at the White Plains, New York, store whom they say were there to deter workers from organizing, and several regional and district managers.The Teamsters previously attempted to unionize an AutoZone distribution center in the early 1990s. They lost the election, though the National Labor Relations Board subsequentlyordereda rerun election due to AutoZone’s conduct during the election, which included prohibiting union discussions at work, threatening workers with loss of their jobs and withholding scheduled pay increases.“Seeing the amount of money, the managers, everybody that they’re sending in, it really kind of shows that you can make change at the store,” concluded Valencia. “You can make change within the company because the fact that you’re unionizing it and you’ve got this kind of a response is actually a good thing. It means that you really are out there changing things, and I believe that if we can do it, and hopefully we do win, then everybody else can too.”Explore more on these topicsUS unionsAutomotive industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: US wheat farmers navigate uncertainty amid drought and geopolitical chaos | US economy | The Guardian
description: Some experts worry factors affecting wheat exports could push global food prices even higher than they are now
Author: Debbie Carlson
Headline: Some experts worry factors affecting wheat exports could push global food prices even higher than they are now
Content: Unharvested wheat in a field on 29 July 2026 in Beloit, Kansas.Photograph: Joshua A Bickel/APView image in fullscreenUnharvested wheat in a field on 29 July 2026 in Beloit, Kansas.Photograph: Joshua A Bickel/APUS economyUS wheat farmers navigate uncertainty amid drought and geopolitical chaosSome experts worry factors affecting wheat exports could push global food prices even higher than they are nowDebbie CarlsonFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWheat prices are at their highest level in three years, which means farmer Merrill Nielsen should be getting more for his crops out of his 2,500-acre (1,010-hectare)Kansasfarm.Yet even as future prices for bread-type wheat are up 39%, Nielsen is unsure whether increased prices will raise his bottom line. The price of diesel fuel, which he needs to run his tractor, has hit record highs. Then there’s the erratic weather that made him lose his entire wheat crop in the spring, and drought has overtaken the southern Great Plains.“We’re not looking to plant any more wheat than we probably normally would, or maybe we won’t even plant that much. I don’t know. Really, we’ll have to see what the weather does for us,” Nielsen said.Panama canal traffic facing further cuts as drought from El Niño worsensRead moreThe combination of high costs, poor weather and geopolitics leave US farmers such as Nielsen with an uncertain growing season despite higher prices for their yields. It also leaves consumers, from millers and bakers to restaurants and grocery shoppers, at risk of feeling the pinch.Droughts across the US and Europe have been shriveling harvests, and weather forecasts for a “super” El Niño this year means “there are some alarming signals” about the impact of weather on wheat crops, said Joao Lampreia, a market strategist at the Lisbon-based Freedom24.The weather phenomenon, exacerbated by the climate crisis, causes warm waters to rise to the surface across the equatorial Pacific Ocean, along the coast of South America, and is known to imperil agriculture in the southern hemisphere significantly. Experts say wheat supplies in key exporting countries are at their second-lowest levels on record. Already, Australia’s wheat plantings are down 12% due to expectations of dryness and increased fertilizer costs.The good news for farmers and consumers is that El Niño can also bring wetter conditions for the southern Great Plains in the fall and spring. During the last big El Niño in 2015 and 2016, the US set an all-time record-high winter wheat yield, said Mark Welch, an economist who researches grain marketing at Texas A&M University.Even if the weather impacts turn out better than expected, recent Russian attacks on port facilities in the Black Sea, where one-third of the global wheat trade passes through, have also disrupted grain shipments. Black Sea farmers, who were some of the few global wheat exporters to experience a bumper crop, had just wrapped up their harvest before the attacks.Because of the fighting, supply is largely inaccessible, which has pushed prices up, Welch said. But if Black Sea farmers and shippers can find alternative routes, prices will backtrack somewhat.At best, about 35% to 50% of that wheat could find a way out, but it will take longer and cost more to get, Lampreia said.Dan Basse, president of the agricultural market research company AgResource, worries the that combination of weather-damaged harvests and the impact of geopolitics on wheat exports could leave global food prices even higher than they are today. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization’sfood price index, which tracks a basket of widely traded food commodities, was up 2.5% in August over a year ago, he said.The spike in wheat prices “has tentacles that go far beyond the war between the Ukrainians and Russians”, Basse says. “The world needs more harvested acreage of every grain. All of this resonates in higher grain and food prices for the world looking forward.”In the immediate future, US farmers will need to help make up the shortfall. Basse said he expected planted acreage for wheat this winter to expand about 10% more than last year as producers seek to capture higher prices.But harvested acreage for wheat in the US has been at its lowest levels since 1877, as US farmers have found it more profitable to plant corn and soybeans rather than wheat. One year of high prices isn’t likely to change a structural decline.Farmers will need higher production and strong values to benefit. “If it’s not an average yield or better, the breakeven cost really gets high very quickly,” Welch said.And it’s unclear how much weather will continue to affect harvests. Vance Ehmke, a wheat-seed seller in south-westKansas, said he’s been busy fielding more calls for seeds this year. But the weather in the southern Great Plains is now too dry for seeds to germinate and grow.“If you get your wheat up, you’ve got 90% to 95% odds that you’ll harvest something. But if you can’t even get it up, I mean, you’re just screwed,” he said.Prices will need to stay high to accommodate a surge in input prices, which have been exacerbated by ongoing trade wars. “We are the ones that get hurt by those policies,” Ehmke said.Explore more on these topicsUS economyFarmingEl Niño southern oscillationCereals and grainsDroughtClimate crisisEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Error first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says report
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Error first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says report
Content: Passengers caught up in the delays at Heathrow airport last week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPassengers caught up in the delays at Heathrow airport last week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesAir transportFlight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software errorError first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says reportGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading toa six-hour outage and mass airline cancellationsand delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared.‘Baggage reclaim was pandemonium’: passengers hit by airport IT chaos in UK recount their ordealsRead moreThe transport secretary,Heidi Alexander, said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) industry regulator would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats more widely.Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which ended up delaying and cancelling flights across the UK and beyondlate into the next day.Airlines have called for compensation and a “credible plan”, with Ryanair demanding the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023.A government source said the CAA review would be “a chance to fundamentally investigate” if Nats was fit for purpose.Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures. He said he could “confirm that it was a software issue and not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators”.The preliminary report said the failure was a “legacy and previously unknown software defect and a combination of very specific events occurring simultaneously” in part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which allocates codes to individual aircraft to identify flights on radar.Nats said the software error occurred at 10am, with engineers first notified at 10.02am that the link between the NAS and London area control system had dropped. The engineers reported at 10.06am that the system had apparently recovered with no operational impact, but continued to investigate.The report said the fault presented when a manual request for an aircraft code was being processed but paused for another, unspecified “higher priority activity” request. It said: “When processing of the aircraft code request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted, and affected some subsequent flight data updates. This happened in the space of a millisecond.”At 12.32pm the link between the national and London airspace management dropped again and a major incident was declared, with controllers having to conduct some tasks manually. By 12.45pm, Nats was restricting flights as the system continued to glitch, before failing completely at 1.32pm.At 1.40pm airlines were advised of restrictions, and between 2.50pm and 4.09pm Nats rebooted the system, eventually resuming full operations at 7.30pm – but leaving mass congestion, displaced aircraft and hundreds of thousands of delayed passengers in its wake.It took more than two days for the backlog of passenger disruption to be cleared, with more than 2,000 flights cancelled in total and hundreds of thousands of people’s travel plans disrupted.Rolfe said: “The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week. It’s our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong. However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question.”The transport secretary said: “The disruption we saw last week was completely unacceptable and I know how frustrating it was for passengers, airlines and airports.”Alexander said she had received Nats’ report, adding: “It’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos.“I have therefore tasked the CAA with conducting an independent review to check Nats’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability.”The CAA’s review will be published within six months.Tim Alderslade, the chief executive of Airlines UK, a lobby group representing the industry, said: “The CAA’s review must mandate real investment in Nats’ resilience so a single fault can never again descend into nationwide disruption.”He said his members were writing to Nats to “demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience”.TheEasyJet chief executive, Kenton Jarvis, said: “Passengers deserve more than just another promise that lessons will be learned. Firm actions must be taken … and there must be a fair solution to ensure that airlines are not left to pick up the bill.”The Ryanair chief operations officer, Neil McMahon, said: “‘The software ate my homework’ is not an acceptable explanation … How many times must the UK ATC system collapse before Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility and resigns.”Explore more on these topicsAir transportAirline industryTravel & leisureTransportEuropeHeidi AlexandernewsShareReuse this content

title: Alex Ovechkin claims he’s ‘not in politics’. His pro-Putin video says the opposite | NHL | The Guardian
description: After the NHL star appeared in an ad campaign for United Russia, it’s fair to start pressing about the impact of his stances – even if he doesn’t want to talk about it
Author: Colin Horgan
Headline: After the NHL star appeared in an ad campaign for United Russia, it’s fair to start pressing about the impact of his stances – even if he doesn’t want to talk about it
Content: Alex Ovechkin speaks after the Capitals’ first practice.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlex Ovechkin speaks after the Capitals’ first practice.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersNHLAlex Ovechkin claims he’s ‘not in politics’. His pro-Putin video says the oppositeAfter the NHL star appeared in an ad campaign for United Russia, it’s fair to start pressing about the impact of his stances – even if he doesn’t want to talk about itColin HorganFri 18 Sep 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Russian launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, reporters asked Washington Capitals captain Alexander Ovechkin for his thoughts. It was no secret, even then, that Ovechkin was close to Vladimir Putin. Years before, Ovechkin boosted the Russian president in a social media campaign and featured Putin in his own Instagram profile photo. “He is my president,” Ovechkinsaid of Putinshortly after the invasion. “But [like] I said, I’m not in politics, I’m an athlete.” That’s over. He’s in politics now.“The thing about the video: I’m Russian,” Ovechkintold reportersThursday. The video in question is one he taped for United Russia, a group supporting Putin, ahead of parliamentary elections. Ovechkin appears in the video alongside Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, Margarita Simonyan, the editor-in-chief of the state-controlled media outlet RT, and others. “I’m for peace and love, and I hope, in the world, it doesn’t matter who you are,” Ovechkin told reporters. “I hope everybody understands everybody wants peace, and everybody hope everything’s going to be OK in the world.”NHL star Alex Ovechkin appears in campaign ad for pro-Putin United Russia partyRead moreA day before, the Capitalsreleased a statementthat lauded Ovechkin and treated his video participation in the same mundane, neutral tone. “Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will live there following his retirement. This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign,” the team said. “As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, DC and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the continued impact he makes on the ice and in our city.”It’s undeniable that Ovechkin has had an impact on DC during his long NHL career, never playing anywhere else, bringing the Capitals their first and only Stanley Cup andbecomingthe sport’s greatest goalscorer. But now that Ovechkin is also into politics – by choice – it’s fair to start asking what the impact of those politics is, too, even if he doesn’t want to talk about it.In an awkward bit of timing, inan indictment unsealed Tuesday, US federal prosecutors accused five men of being part of a network planning to assassinate Russian dissidents and others on US soil, including one who reportedly lived in Washington. Just one concrete example of the Putin government in action – its continued impact, if you like – right in Ovechkin’s adopted home town. Elsewhere, on X, former NHL goaltender Dominik Hasek – a Czech icon who has been anoutspokenPutin critic for years –tore intothe Capitals’ statement on Ovechkin for turning a blind eye to the impact of that politics in Europe. “This statement ignores the hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of Ukrainians and Russians killed or maimed – casualties for which Ovechkin bears a significant share of responsibility through his public stance,” Hasek wrote.View image in fullscreenAlexander Ovechkin skates for Russia against the United States during their quarter-final at the 2019 IIHF Ice Hockey World Championship in Bratislava, Slovakia.Photograph: Martin Rose/Getty ImagesA “significant” share may be stretching it, but Hasek’s broader point is that there ought to be a reckoning here, that the people involved should take ownership. For Ovechkin, that would probably mean repeating the message that he supported as publicly in the US as he does in Russia, instead of distancing himself from it the moment it becomes uncomfortable and offering “peace and love”. For the Capitals, taking a moral stand could mean anything from making a donation to a Ukrainian charity to stripping Ovechkin of his captaincy, to barring him from playing.Alex Ovechkin is now the NHL’s greatest goalscorer. It’s debatable what else he isRead moreBut that would mean the organization would have to have the guts to address it as more than an uncomfortable topic to be endured just long enough to look like anyone cared, which is also what happened Thursday in the media scrum. After answering a couple of questions about the United Russia video, Ovechkin pivoted. “All right,” he said, “let’s do hockey questions.” “Happy birthday,” one reporter said almost immediately, ushering back the illusion of normalcy. “Did you get a cake?” Ovechkin replied he is on a diet. Everyone laughed. No one in the scrum made him answer for anything. When an ESPN reporterpressedhim later with questions on the video and the invasion, Ovechkinsaidhe is “not in politics” and “can’t say who’s right and who’s wrong” before abruptly ending the interview.Fans are now left to figure out an unwindable ethical quandary that was never theirs to solve. If you keep watching or keep wearing your Ovechkin jersey, you’re liable to be accused of tacitly supporting a repressive regime; if you choose to boycott, you’re accused of “politicizing” sports. The fans are left holding the bag, searching for accountability, while those responsible for it walk away behind a mealy mouthed word cloud.It doesn’t have to be that way. If Ovechkin, the Capitals and, by extension, theNHL, want the fans to hold them all accountable, so be it. Fans can keep asking the questions most ofthe media room wouldn’t – they make this all mean something. Just because Ovechkin can’t muster an opinion (outside Russia, anyway), it doesn’t mean fans can’t. We don’t have to pretend to be neutral.Explore more on these topicsNHLWashington CapitalsUS sportsIce hockeyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jon Rahm shoots 78-77 and slumps off in last place at PGA Championship | Golf | The Guardian
description: Jon Rahm was bottom of the field on 11 over par while Adam Scott, the 2013 Masters champion, said he was not putting pressure on himself to win
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Jon Rahm was bottom of the field on 11 over par while Adam Scott, the 2013 Masters champion, said he was not putting pressure on himself to win
Content: Jon Rahm takes a drop in a bunker. He went on to finish 11 over for his two days at Wentworth.Photograph: Warren Little/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Rahm takes a drop in a bunker. He went on to finish 11 over for his two days at Wentworth.Photograph: Warren Little/Getty ImagesGolfJon Rahm shoots 78-77 and slumps off in last place at PGA ChampionshipTommy Fleetwood also misses the cut at three overAdam Scott cards second 67 to be well placed at halfwayEwan Murrayat WentworthFri 18 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMissed cuts for Tommy Fleetwood and Jon Rahm at the PGA Championship would be notable enough even without contemplating the latter’s 36-hole score.The sight of Rahm dead last was remarkable – after rounds of 78 and 77, he was 11 over par. Fleetwood’s exit at plus three, while less dramatic, was another obvious blow to the tournament organisers at Wentworth. On a day of high-profile departures, injury forced Patrick Reed out of the event midway through his round. That scenario might have repercussions as Rory McIlroy seeks to prise the DP World Tour’s order of merit from the American’s grasp.Rahm did not stop for media duties but may have offered extenuating circumstance. It is just that seeing a player of such status and talent toil so badly turns heads. The Spaniard is awaiting the imminent arrival of his fourth child, a matter to which he referred before a ball was struck in Surrey.The LIV backdrop also cannot be ignored;Rahm is fully expected to depart the ailing circuitwhen the formalities of a voluntary bankruptcy filing are completed. This is, however, a situation now in the hands of the courts. It would be perfectly natural if Rahm finds himself unable to appropriately focus when inside the ropes. Two Wentworth rounds involved three birdies, 10 bogeys and two double bogeys.Fleetwood needed a change of fortune, albeit not a significant one, after Thursday’s 73. The 15th has proved his nemesis this week, with a bogey five during the first round followed up by a double bogey on day two. Despite delivering three birdies, the 35-year-old slipped to a 74.Reed – who looked a candidate to win after the first round – played his first nine holes in 44, nine over par. He grasped his left wrist after a pulled tee shot on the 10th, before his withdrawal was confirmed and he headed straight for medical treatment.Elements of normality were provided by Adam Scott, who is seeking to become the oldest winner of this event. The 46-year-old Australian backed up a 67 with an identical score. Scott would place huge stock in a Wentworth win.View image in fullscreenAdam Scott on the 7th fairway on day two at Wentworth.Photograph: Adam Davy/PA“Let’s put the majors aside for a minute,” he said. “I think there’s the Players Championship, Wentworth and the Australian Open for me at that level of importance. So it would mean a lot? Absolutely. I mean, it would be huge.“I’m not heaping pressure on myself to go and win this tournament. I feel like at this point I just need to put my head into a place where I can enjoy the next couple of days. I have done this many times in the past, not so much lately, but I think hopefully that kind of instinct and memory comes back in this position. If I can enjoy myself the next couple of days, I think I’ll get the best out of myself.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScott will form part of an International team trying to end a miserable run against the United States in the Presidents Cup. The event takes place next weekend at Medinah. Scott andRyan Fox, the Open champion, will fly straight to Illinois from this tournament.Not part of the Presidents Cup equation is JJ Spaun, which has left the American somewhat miffed. Spaun’s 66 here moved him to eight under and he made his shock at being omitted from Brandt Snedeker’s team plain.“It was disappointing to be left off,” the winner of last year’s US Open said. “I wasn’t expecting it, to be honest. I kind of hung my hat on my experience with the Ryder Cup last year. I made it to the Tour Championship this year. I won in San Antonio. I did everything I could. I was the odd man out.”Explore more on these topicsGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Josh Allen shines again as Bills celebrate new home with slugfest victory over Lions | NFL | The Guardian
description: Josh Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for two scores, and the Bills beat the Detroit Lions 41-31 in the first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Josh Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for two scores, and the Bills beat the Detroit Lions 41-31 in the first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium
Content: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen celebrates a rushing touchdown against the Detroit Lions.Photograph: Jeffrey T Barnes/APView image in fullscreenBuffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen celebrates a rushing touchdown against the Detroit Lions.Photograph: Jeffrey T Barnes/APNFLJosh Allen shines again as Bills celebrate new home with slugfest victory over LionsDetroit Lions 31-41 Buffalo BillsBills QB throws three TDs and rushes for twoJared Goff excellent in defeat for LionsAgenciesThu 17 Sep 2026 23.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosh Allen quickly put his stamp on the Buffalo Bills’ new stadium, which has been dubbed “The House that Allen built.”Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for two scores, and the Bills beat theDetroit Lions41-31 on Thursday night in the first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium.The Josh Allen rollercoaster is up and running again for the new NFL seasonRead moreIt was Allen’s fourth five-TD outing, and followed a four-touchdown outing (two passing, two rushing) in Buffalo’sseason-opening win at Houston.“[We won in a] short week against a really good team who kept us fighting until the last second there,” Allen said after the game.Allen followed the pregame fireworks celebration with more of his own by overseeing touchdown drives on each of Buffalo’s first four possessions.He scored the first regular-season TD in the stadium on a one-yard run 5:51 into the opening quarter. He followed that with a 43-yard scoring pass to a wide-open Josh Palmer. Tight ends Dalton Kincaid, with a 16-yard catch, and Dawson Knox, with a one-yarder, also scored for Buffalo in the first half.Allen finished the night 20 of 31 for 248 yards, and added 72 yards rushing. James Cook had 134 yards rushing and put the game away with a one-yard TD run late in the fourth quarter.“I got a little emotional during the national anthem, feeling super blessed and lucky to do what I do. This is a great spot, we’re going to be here for a long time, hopefully the fans enjoyed it,” said Allen.Allen’s two rushing TDs upped his career total to 83, moving him into a tie for 18th on theNFLlist with Jim Taylor. He also picked up his 90th regular-season victory, becoming one of just four quarterbacks to reach that milestone through their first nine seasons.The Lions were undone by their injury-depleted defense, and a banged-up offensive line that had difficulty opening holes for Jahmyr Gibbs and protecting Jared Goff.After rallying from a 21-0 deficit to cut Buffalo’s lead to 34-24, the Lions offense stalled midway through the fourth quarter. Backed up at their own 10, the Lions went three-and-out and were forced to punt after Goff had two passes tipped by Deone Walker, and Gibbs was stopped for no gain.Goff finished 26 of 38 for 327 yards and four touchdowns. Amon-Ra St Brown had nine catches for 142 yards and two scores. Gibbs also scored on an 11-yard catch but was limited to 52 yards rushing. Sam LaPorta scored on a one-yard catch.The Lions’ defense got off to a dreadful start, allowing the Bills to score 27 points and gain 299 yards in the first half alone. The struggles carried over from a season-opening 31-30 overtime win over New Orleans, in which the Saints rallied from a 21-0 first-half deficit and lost only after their two-point conversion failed in overtime.The Lions’ troubles began on Buffalo’s second drive when two defenders converged on DJ Moore, allowing Allen to find Palmer wide open deep for a 43-yard touchdown. On Buffalo’s next drive, a holding penalty against Rock Ya-Sin, negated Skyler Gill-Howard’s interception of a tipped pass.The Lions’ offense had its own sputters, with Goff sacked twice and also having a snap go over his head on Detroit’s first two series.The $2.1bn Highmark Stadium that officially opened last month was built across the street from the Bills’ former home. The new stadium has a capacity of just over 60,000, about 12,000 less than the old facility. What’s different is the layout, with the new facility’s seating structure built steeper, placing viewers more on top of the action. The new building also features a canopy, which helps project crowd noise directly on to field.Bills fans began arriving two and three days earlier, with a private lot nearly filled with RVs by Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsNFLBuffalo BillsDetroit LionsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: My son’s death during a college football workout was preventable. Lessons must be learned | College sports | The Guardian
description: Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich is fighting for his life after collapsing during practice. Tragedies like this can be avoided
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich is fighting for his life after collapsing during practice. Tragedies like this can be avoided
Content: Jordan McNair, pictured in 2016 while at McDonogh School in Maryland, died in June 2018, two weeks after he collapsed during a University of Maryland team workout.Photograph: Baltimore Sun/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJordan McNair, pictured in 2016 while at McDonogh School in Maryland, died in June 2018, two weeks after he collapsed during a University of Maryland team workout.Photograph: Baltimore Sun/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesCollege sportsMy son’s death during a college football workout was preventable. Lessons must be learnedMartin McNair with Simon FitzgeraldArizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich is fighting for his life after collapsing during practice. Tragedies like this can be avoidedFri 18 Sep 2026 10.10 EDTShareLate last month, Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayichcollapsed during a team workout. He is now fighting for his life after suffering from exertional heatstroke and, according to the Mayich family attorney, is unlikely to make a meaningful recovery. This young man was drafted by the St Louis Blues but will never get the opportunity to play in the NHL. While he is not the first young athlete severely harmed by heat-related illness in American sports, he should be the last.I have learned more about this preventable injury than I ever wanted to know. On 29 May 2018, my son Jordan McNair collapsed during a strenuous football practice at the University of Maryland. By the time he arrived at the hospital, he was dangerously overheatedand never recovered.For two weeks, as Jordan fought for his life through intensive care and an emergency liver transplant, one question kept coming: “What did we miss?”I think about the days before he signed with Maryland, when coaches sat at our kitchen table talking with our family about Jordan. I remember asking two questions:“Can Jordan get some playing time?”And, “What support do you have around mental health and substance abuse?”Those are the kind of questions many parents ask when they have never experienced a life-changing tragedy in collegiate sports. Jordan was going to play football at a Big Ten university. What could possibly go wrong?I didn’t ask:“If something happens to my son, what safety systems do you have in place?”“What is your emergency action plan?”“When was the last time you practiced it?”“Who has the authority to stop a workout when an athlete is in medical distress?”“What happens if my child suffers exertional heatstroke?”“Where is the equipment needed to save his life?”Those questions came in hindsight, as I walked toward the ICU every day while Jordan fought for his life. I kept asking myself:“What did I miss that night at the kitchen table?”Before Jordan collapsed, I thought heatstroke and heat exhaustion were one and the same. I thought if someone became overheated, you moved them into the shade, gave them water, let them cool down, and everything would be fine. I didn’t know a heat-related injury could kill my son. My education came through a baptism by fire.Suddenly, as the Mayich family may be learning now, I had to understand medical terms I had never heard before:rhabdomyolysis. Core body temperature. Multiorgan failure.Exertional heatstroke.View image in fullscreenJordan McNair during his time with the University of Maryland football team.Photograph: Courtesy of the Jordan McNair FoundationSince Jordan’s death, I’ve worked alongside medical professionals to cool athletes experiencing exertional heat illness at sporting events across the nation. I’ve seen first-hand how quickly proper recognition and response can change an outcome.One of the simplest explanations of exertional heatstroke has stayed with me. When your core body temperature rises above 104F (40C), it is like putting your body inside a microwave. Your organs begin to cook.There is a critical window of roughly 20 to 30 minutes to rapidly cool the athlete and avert catastrophe. Cold-water immersion can bring the body’s temperature down before the damage becomes irreversible.Time is everything.But what happened to Jordan wasn’t only about what went wrong on the football field on 29 May 2018. What happened to Mayich in Arizona isn’t only about what happened on 20 August 2026. The tragedy began long before.Every organization has layers of protection, and every layer can have weaknesses, the holes in the Swiss Cheese Model. One hole may not cause disaster because another layer can stop it. But when enough holes align, nothing remains between the athlete and tragedy.There was an emergency action plan in Jordan’s case. But having an emergency action plan on paper and being prepared to execute it are two very different things. Imagine having a fire evacuation plan nobody ever practices. Then one day the building catches fire. Who knows where to go, what to do, who calls 911 and who gets people out? The middle of the fire is the worst possible time to figure out the plan. Athletic emergencies are no different.Every time an athlete steps on to a field, court, track or practice facility, an emergency is possible. The systems designed to protect that athlete must be in place before it happens, and the people responsible for those systems must know exactly what to do.I used to say Murphy’s law was in full effect the day Jordan collapsed. While I wasn’t in Arizona for the team practice where Matthew Mayich collapsed, reports from that day reveal unsettling parallels to my son’s case.During a strenuous early-season workout, the athlete’s level of distress wasn’t properly recognized. The escalation from heat exhaustion to exertional heatstroke wasn’t appropriately addressed. The emergency action plan was not properly practiced or implemented. The lifesaving cooling response wasn’t initiated within that critical window. Necessary equipment wasn’t within immediate reach. Changes in the normal practice setting complicated the emergency response, and precious time was lost before treatment began.One hole.Then another.Then another.Until they aligned.By the time Jordan arrived at the emergency room, more than an hour and a half after he collapsed, his core body temperature was approximately 106F. My son never came home.Three days after Jordan died, on 16 June 2018, I began what would become my life’s work as a student-athlete safety advocate. There is a club of parents none of us ever asked to join. We are mothers and fathers who sent our children off to play the sports they loved and eventually had to bury them. We don’t need another member.View image in fullscreenMaryland players surround the No 79 painted on the field in honor of Jordan McNair before their game against Michigan State in College Park in November 2018.Photograph: Will Newton/Getty ImagesWe certainly don’t need another parent standing outside an ICU asking the same question I asked myself over and over:“What did I miss?”My prayers remain with Matthew Mayich and his family. I pray they receive the outcome every parent outside an ICU desperately hopes for.For years, I kept returning to the questions I asked at our kitchen table.Now, I know the question I should have asked. “Can my child play and will my child be safe?”Parents shouldn’t have to experience what my family has before they learn to ask that question. Medical professionals responsible for the health and safety of athletes shouldn’t wait until an athlete collapses to understand and practice their role in an emergency action plan.Schools and athletic programs shouldn’t discover holes in their safety systems while a child’s life hangs in the balance. Coaches need to understand their role in that system without being expected to diagnose or treat a medical emergency. Athletes should never wonder whether speaking up about how they feel will be interpreted as weakness.Theon-field cardiac arrestof Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin demonstrates that having a disciplined emergency action plan goes beyond heat-related injury. Hamlin’s full recovery after immediate CPR and emergent cardiac defibrillation is an excellent example of how lifesaving intervention should be available for athletes at risk. He not only made it to the hospital; he walked out on his own and eventually returned to the playing field.The NCAA, with over $1bn in revenue, owes its players that same level of emergency preparedness.This is an opportunity for youth sports organizations at every level to have mandatory emergency action plans in place for the life-threatening emergencies their athletes face. This includes heat-related injury as well as other serious sports-related emergencies such as cardiac events, traumatic head injuries and complications of sickle cell disease.Students, parents, coaches and administrators must hold athletic organizations accountable to have these resources in place because the next missed opportunity may be fatal.Martin McNair is the father of Jordan McNair and founder ofThe Jordan McNair Foundation.Dr Simon Fitzgerald is a trauma surgeon and surgical intensivist in Brooklyn, New York, and a medical advisory board member of The Jordan McNair Foundation.Explore more on these topicsCollege sportsCollege footballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: From ‘nappies at the ballpark’ to MLB: how Australia’s Travis Bazzana made baseball’s big leagues | MLB | The Guardian
description: The 24-year-old has taken his attention to detail from lining up bats and helmets as a toddler to helping the Cleveland Guardians towards the playoffs
Author: Joseph D'Hippolito
Headline: The 24-year-old has taken his attention to detail from lining up bats and helmets as a toddler to helping the Cleveland Guardians towards the playoffs
Content: Travis Bazzana became the first Australian top pick in Major League Baseball’s 2024 amateur draft, debuting for the Cleveland Guardians earlier this year.Photograph: Jason Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTravis Bazzana became the first Australian top pick in Major League Baseball’s 2024 amateur draft, debuting for the Cleveland Guardians earlier this year.Photograph: Jason Miller/Getty ImagesMLBFrom ‘nappies at the ballpark’ to MLB: how Australia’s Travis Bazzana made baseball’s big leaguesThe 24-year-old has taken his attention to detail from lining up bats and helmets as a toddler to helping the Cleveland Guardians towards the playoffsJoseph D'HippolitoFri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 20.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Sydney’s Travis Bazzana made his debut in Major LeagueBaseballon 28 April, it was the culmination of a journey that began when he was a toddler.“From the time he could stand, Travis was always wanting to throw or hit balls with any type of bat or racket available,” says Travis’s mother, Jenny. “Any visitors to the house, including his grandparents, were immediately invited to play or compete with him.”Mets fans celebrate home run against own team as returning hero Alonso goes yardRead moreTravis transformed his eagerness into a passionate discipline that enabled him to become the first Australian top selection in MLB’s amateur draft and the Cleveland Guardians’ All-Star second baseman.That discipline also defines his personality.“He’s an animal,” Guardians pitcher Parker Messick told the Cleveland Plain Dealer. “He loves the game of baseball. He takes it very serious every at-bat. Every time he’s on first base, every play in the infield, he’s locked in.”Despite being a rookie, the 24-year-old has excelled in the Guardians’ late surge for a spot in the MLB playoffs. In September, when Cleveland won seven of 10 games, Travis’s five home runs and safe hitting have helped put them into a strong position in the American League Central division alongside the Chicago White Sox.View image in fullscreenTravis has impressed in his rookie season, earning a call up to MLB’s All-Star team.Photograph: Aaron Josefczyk/UPI/ShutterstockTravis grew up in Wahroonga, in Sydney’s Upper North Shore, and began playing T-ball as a three-year-old for the Ku-Ring-Gai Stealers. His father, Gary, decided to register Travis after seeing his excitement at his brothers’ games.“Travis was in nappies at the ballpark,” Gary says. “Some of his first words were like ‘ball’, ‘hit’, ‘swing’, ‘catch’. He was buzzing around and really interested in everything that was going on. He had a little bat made from a cut-off broomstick, and he would put tennis balls on a tee and rifle them all around the park and annoy people all day long.”That enthusiasm wasn’t limited to the ballpark.“The fact that Gary was coaching youth teams meant there was generally a team kit bag in the house,” Jenny says. “At the age of three, Travis would empty the entire contents of the bag on to the floor in the lounge room. This was done with great attention to detail. All the bats and helmets were carefully lined up in a row as if getting them ready for a game.”View image in fullscreenTravis (in front on far right) at his brother’s birthday party which included a baseball clinic with Australian player Glenn Williams (centre back).Photograph: supplied by Glenn WilliamsTravis played other sports at school – but baseball was always No 1. When the internet became widely available, Travis used it to conduct extensive research.He would spend “hours each night looking up every hitting instruction video he could find and watching highlights of MLB and college baseball games”, Gary says. “He was writing his own ‘how to hit’ manual from 11 or 12 years old. He later would take this book to tournaments and tours, and record any tips that coaches gave him in the tournament exit meetings.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhereRead moreThat exposure included Baseball NSW clinics run by Glenn Williams, a former major-league player and two-time Olympian who noticed something different in Travis.“Like many athletes, Travis worked exceptionally hard,” says Williams, who is now the chief executive officer for Baseball Australia. “What set him apart, however, was that his effort was always purposeful. Every session, every drill and every extra rep was targeted at the specific areas he knew would have the greatest impact on his development.“That disciplined approach to continuous improvement – honest self-assessment, a willingness to learn, and focused execution – became one of the defining characteristics of his journey.”Travis honed his craft with the Stealers and the Sydney Blue Sox, before moving to the US in 2021 to join one of the country’s best college baseball programs at Oregon State University (OSU). He made an impression before ever taking the field.“He walked in the players’ lounge where all the career stat leaders are listed,” head coach Mitch Canham says. “He took a picture of it, and he’s like, ‘I’m going to break all these records.’ You don’t see that from a ton of people.”After three seasons, he owned Oregon State’s career records for hits (251), home runs (45), doubles (52), stolen bases (66), total bases (460) and walks (180). Those numbers ranked him among in the top college players.View image in fullscreenTravis quickly turned heads while playing US college baseball.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesIn 2024, Travis made the All-America first team for the second consecutive year, received the Pacific-12 Conference’s award as its player of the year and finished his career with a .360 average and 165 runs batted in. That performance motivated the Guardians to make him the first selection overall in MLB’s amateur draft that June.Travis extends his passion beyond himself. He once produced a PowerPoint presentation for his OSU teammates that analysed the breaking action of curveballs and sliders, and gave them tips on nutrition.“There wasn’t a guy that didn’t love ‘Bazz’,” Canham says. “His care level for other people was incredible. One time after a game, we sat on the bench for an hour and talked about how he can better help his teammates. I don’t think there was a guy that ever showed up in that clubhouse that didn’t want to spend time with him or learn a ton from him.”Travis’s commitment to the sport extends to the next generation of Australian players. During August’s Little League World Series in the US, he sent a video message of encouragement to the Ryde Hawks, his former team and Australia’s representative. The following week, Travis invited the Hawks squad to the Guardians’ clubhouse at Cleveland’s Progressive Field before a game. Nick Robson, who pitched and played second base for the Hawks, told ESPN what it means to see Travis succeed: “It shows that anyone from Sydney can be in the big league.”Explore more on these topicsMLBBaseballUS sportsAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Record-breaking ultrarunner has 500ml of pus drained from leg: ‘I just didn’t quite feel right’ | Australia sport | The Guardian
description: The 40-year-old Australian undergoes surgery to suck out fluid from his thigh following his 152-hour solo backyard marathon run
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: The 40-year-old Australian undergoes surgery to suck out fluid from his thigh following his 152-hour solo backyard marathon run
Content: Australian ultrarunner Phil Gore eats a meal and receives foot treatment while resting between ‘laps’ of his 152-hour solo back-yard marathon.Photograph: William BuckView image in fullscreenAustralian ultrarunner Phil Gore eats a meal and receives foot treatment while resting between ‘laps’ of his 152-hour solo back-yard marathon.Photograph: William BuckAustralia sportRecord-breaking ultrarunner has 500ml of pus drained from leg: ‘I just didn’t quite feel right’Australian Phil Gore in hospital after 152-hour solo runPersistent pain in thigh requires 12cm incision to suck fluid outJack SnapeThu 17 Sep 2026 21.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 21.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhil Gore’s legs have delivered extraordinary numbers, including running more than 1,000km last month in a solo attempt during a backyard ultra marathon. This week, they produced another: 500ml of pus, roughly the equivalent of a pint.The 40-year-old Australian saw a doctor earlier this week after a pain in his leg was not going away following his extraordinary, 152-hour solo ordealaided by Nerds, meat pies, Coco Pops and a cheeseburger.‘A cheeseburger worked really well’: the secrets behind a record-breaking 152-hour runRead moreIn his left thigh, what was initially thought to be a haematoma – a swelling of blood that usually disperses on its own – turned out to be something more serious.“I just didn’t quite feel right about it, so I wanted to get a second opinion,” Gore posted on Instagram.He went to a different sports doctor on Monday who went to aspirate, or suck out, the buildup.“He went to aspirate it and realised it wasn’t blood,” Gore said. “It was pus, which means that there’s an infection, more likely an abscess, and he suggested I go back to ER [emergency].”Gore checked in to the Fiona Stanley Hospital in Perth, and had the procedure.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“Surgery went well. I got a [roughly] 12cm incision in my thigh and about 500ml of fluid was cleared, and I’ve got a drain in now, still clearing more out. I have to stay in the hospital for 48 hours while it drains and I’m kept under observation.”He added he was grateful to the hospital staff because “it could have gotten a lot worse if left untreated” and apologised to supporters for not replying to their well wishes.Gore won last year’s Backyard Ultra World Championshipby covering 764km in Tennessee, USA.In backyard ultras, the winner only ever covers slightly more than the runner who finishes in second place.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUltrarunner Megan Eckert shatters US men’s and women’s records with 636 miles in six daysRead moreThe format drove Gore to test himself late last month in a solo bid, borrowing the backyard ultra format – running one 6.7km “lap” per hour for an entire week.He fell narrowly short of his goal, collapsing after six days and 15 hours, but still raised close to $300,000 to help fund medical research and health services for children in Western Australia. His 152 laps easily eclipsed his official world record of 119, set last year.Gore spent time this week working out the exact time during his effort – which was live streamed – his thigh began giving him trouble.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“Found the part where my leg started to hurt,” he said. “Lap 104. Still made it another 2 days.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia sportUltrarunningAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sydney Sweeney’s cartoonish provocation has sparked a culture war but let’s just admit sport can be sexy | Sport | The Guardian
description: Yes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appeal
Author: Emma John
Headline: Yes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appeal
Content: Sydney Sweeney’s advert for a sports betting site caused a storm of controversy this week.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney’s advert for a sports betting site caused a storm of controversy this week.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesSportSydney Sweeney’s cartoonish provocation has sparked a culture war but let’s just admit sport can be sexyEmma JohnYes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appealFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTShareHave you seen the 40-second video that will change the way you think about women’s sport, women’s bodies, just, you know, women? It’s been unavoidable on social media this week – brazen, unapologetic, dominating the algorithm like an AI kitten hacking a banana-bread recipe while lip-syncing to Cardi B. I for one have enjoyed it at least 50 times already.It starts with some carefully curated passive-aggression – “Dear Sydney”, “Hey Sydney”, “Respectfully Sydney” – and follows up with clips of what, in its own words, “a woman in sport actually looks like”. It shows its subject pounding the treadmill or powering down the back straight, flooring a rival with a tackle or a roundhouse kick, lifting weights or throwing herself through the air. It is, inevitably, soundtracked by Dua Lipa. Training Season is getting a serious bump this week.‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advertRead moreThealmighty backlashto the Novig advert that everyone would rather not have talked about at all has generated more montages than we’ve seen since Rocky IV. My own feed is swamped with inspo-insta reels from grassroots and elite athletes alike. Some might argue it’s the best thing to happen to women’s sport this week – unless, you know,they’re the European Solheim Cup team. Either way, a positively cartoonish piece of provocation lit the five-second fuse to the powder-keg stamped CULTURE WAR, and the resultant explosion has enveloped us all in its cloud of colourful outrage and content confetti.The noisy reaction to an actor posing almost naked with various items of sporting equipment demonstrates the power and importance of solidarity within women’s sport. For decades, being a woman in an incorrigibly sexist sector left you one of two responses. Either you ignored uncomfortable and demeaning situations so you could just get on with the thing you wanted to be doing, or you spoke out, braving either devastating indifference or a cacophony of scorn. These days, we’re privileged to have a far louder voice, and for it to be taken seriously.There is, however, a danger in taking every piece of deliberate provocation too seriously. And the danger is that it robs us of some of the delight of the thing we love in the first place. Instead of spending this week talking about Lottie Woad’s singles match in the Netherlands, or Chelsea’s 5-0 demolition of Manchester United in the WSL, we’ve surrendered billboards’ worth of brain space to an American celebrity who hasn’t even invested in a Premier League club yet.Personally I have also, as discussed, spent quite a lot of time scrolling other people’s highlights reels, and I won’t lie that they got me pretty pumped, but then that was very much their goal. From spiralling gymnastic tumbles to grunting deadlifts, all these women look fire. Even a unitedly earnest effort to remind us that sport is about effort and sweat and inclusivity can’t and shouldn’t hide the fact that it’s also, thrillingly, about human bodies and the gloriously impressive things they can be honed to do.View image in fullscreenAmy Hunt has led the backlash against Sydney Sweeney’s controversial betting advert by telling the US actress that ‘this is what women in sport look like’.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAHaving to argue that sportswomen aren’t sexual objects, on the other hand, feels as dated as the advert. Part of the problem of the ad is its almost comically regressive throwback to the era of Page 3 girls and 1980s erotica – the kind of aesthetic we now knowingly indulge within the safe confines of a Jilly Cooper TV adaptation. If we’re jumping this far back in the timeline, will we have to revisit, too, whether it’s appropriate to wear make-up on track, or skorts on court, or any other of the subsidiary arguments that determine how sexy or not a female athlete is required – or allowed – to be?Or can we unclench and leave them in the past where they belong? Might we even skip a bit further into a more confident future and say out loud the thing that we have always had to be extremely careful expressing? Which is that sport is a primarily physical pursuit that tends to turn the people at its apex into magnificent specimens of humanity. And that those aesthetics are a part of what makes it appealing in the first place.The bulging neck on the rugby pitch and the rock-hard calves on the marathon runner have a functional purpose, as opposed to the fantasy one that prompts today’s Hollywood actors to get superhero-buff. But that doesn’t mean we’re not allowed to admire them. Sport is an environment that invites us to witness and thrill to the power and grace of the human body. It’s not only our tribal allegiances and the dopamine hit of vicarious victory that we’re indulging when we marvel at our sporting heroes: it’s also our appreciation of their physical attributes, whether that’s Rafael Nadal’s arms or Jessica Ennis-Hill’s abs or Serena Williams’s everything.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd sometimes, when those attributes are in motion, sportcanbe sexy. Not in the ball-cradling way that Sydney Sweeney’s performance allows delusional men to believe. But in a way that nevertheless holds hostage to the eye and makes the pulse race. It’s rather absurd – and a little self-deluding – for sports fans to pretend either to ourselves or others that we don’t find some of our heroes pretty attractive.And no, as Amy Hunt so properly pointed out in her own clapback to the Sweeney ad, being an athlete is “not sexy all the time”. If anyone needed proof, the second most notorious viral video of this week was, in fact,a Hyrox competitor soiling herselfas she powered to victory. There has, in other words, been plenty of crap circulating on the internet this week. The sanest choice is to avert our eyes.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
