title: Somerset and Nottinghamshire title hopes hit by defeats: County Championship cricket, day four – as it happened | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Somerset and Nottinghamshire lost to Yorkshire and Sussex respectively in a big boost to Warwickshire
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Somerset and Nottinghamshire lost to Yorkshire and Sussex respectively in a big boost to Warwickshire
Content: 8h ago13.35 EDTSomerset and Notts stumble in title chaseTanya AldredWarwickshire will take an 11-point lead into the final round of the season after watching from the wings as their championship rivals Somerset andNottinghamshireboth fluffed their lines.Yorkshiretook only 82 minutes to rinse throughSomerseton an overcast Headingley morning, with bowlers on song and a helpful surface. Every run was agony as Toms Lammonby and Abell battled through the early overs until Lammonby nudged Ben Cliff behind and Abell was caught off a Ben Coad ball that shot off the bat shoulder and arced to point. A conveyor belt of wickets followed that not even Craig Overton could halt and, with Somerset all out for 101, Cliff led the players off with a career-best 11 wickets in the match.As the big, beautifulSomersetflag was folded away into a Sainsbury’s plastic bag, their head coach, Jason Kerr, said: “We knew the magnitude of the game but unfortunately Yorkshire played the better cricket.” The Leeds rain started at 2.50pm, but it was three hours too late. Had Somerset not jumped in their team coach so quickly, they would have seen the England and Wales Cricket Board’s pitch inspector Andy Mackay out in the middle. His arrival means that Yorkshire are in danger of a points penalty, little succour to Somerset who must entertain Surrey next week and hope, with the destination of the title no longer in their hands.Nottinghamshirehad to watch their dreams of successive titles wash almost out of sight as they were bowled out for 193 at Hove, beforeSussexknocked off a chase of 76 with barely a scare. Notts must entertain a resurgent Yorkshire next week and hopeWarwickshireslip up; while Sussex’s sixth win of a season that started with a 12-point penalty was bitter sweet – it was a last home game for a large handful of players the club can no longer afford.At Grace Road,Hampshirewere relegated afterLeicestershiredefied their points penalty to bounce back with a five-wicket win. They coasted to what could have been a difficult run chase thanks to the New Zealander Nick Kelly (86) and Ben Cox (75), who put on a merry 158.Leicestershirehave a mathematical chink of daylight between them and relegation – though they must beat Warwickshire while taking 20 more points than Essex can scrape together at Sophia Gardens. For Hampshire, who escaped relegation on the last day last year when Durham capitulated, reality bit.Meanwhile, in Division Two,Northamptonshirehad to be content with a draw after Ricardo Vasconcelos’s 132 took them to within 23 runs of beatingDerbyshire, with plenty of overs in the bank, before bad light intervened. They take 13 points which slots them four behind their promotion rivals Kent.ShareUpdated at14.06 EDT

title: Premier League action, Celtic v Rangers, T20 cricket and NFL – follow with us | Sport | The Guardian
description: Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports
Content: England batter Tom Banton hits out; Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers directs his teammates; Findlay Curtis of Rangers tussles with Colby Donovan of Celtic.Composite: Guardian Design; MI News/NurPhoto/Shutterstock; Zuma Press/Shutterstock; Rangers FC/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEngland batter Tom Banton hits out; Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers directs his teammates; Findlay Curtis of Rangers tussles with Colby Donovan of Celtic.Composite: Guardian Design; MI News/NurPhoto/Shutterstock; Zuma Press/Shutterstock; Rangers FC/ShutterstockYour Guardian sport weekendSportPremier League action, Celtic v Rangers, T20 cricket and NFL – follow with usHere’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reportsGuardian sportFri 18 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump toSaturdaySundaySaturdayFootball8am (all times BST)Matchday liveMichael Butlerrises early to barge open the door to Saturday’s football activity. He will be offering breaking news and updates from around the grounds in the buildup to five Premier League games, starting with the lunchtime meeting of the 17th and 19th clubs in the table, big names down on their uppers: Tottenham and Aston Villa, respectively. He won’t be forgetting the Championship, which braces for the renewal of two bitter feuds when the leaders, West Ham, travel to the Den on Saturday to face their London rivals Millwall for the first time in 14 years. Join the conversation by emailing your thoughts and queries tomatchday.live@theguardian.comPremier League12.30pmTottenham v Aston Villa liveAfter a summer spend in excess of £300m, things were supposed to be different this season ⁠after successive 17th-placed finishes. Instead, after four games, that is exactly where Tottenham find themselves again after no ​wins – and not a single goal – in their opening ​four games. Roberto De Zerbi remained confident after Tuesday’s League Cup ​loss at Liverpool that his side would “click” soon and the early kick-off at home to an Aston Villa side with ​only one point so far would ‌be an opportune moment for ​that to happen – for both teams.Daniel Gallanhelms the liveblog withPaul MacInnesour match reporter.Cricket2.30pmEngland v Sri Lanka liveJames Wallacehas over-by-over coverage of the third T20 after Harry Brook’s side overpowered Sri Lanka for the second time in three days, a six-wicket win in Cardiff being achieved with 7.5 overs to spare on Thursday. It gave England an insurmountable 2-0 lead in the three-match series, which has come on the back of beating India 4-0 earlier in the summer. In fact, England have won 22 of their past 25 matches in the short format of the game. Brook bludgeoned 114 not out from 49 balls in the opening win at Southampton, and this time Tom Banton got England over the line with an unbeaten 52 off 24 deliveries. Banton’s pivotal innings came after Jos Buttler became the first player to reach 15,000 runs in T20 cricket.Tanya Aldredwill report from Old Trafford.View image in fullscreenEngland’s six-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the second T20 clinched the three-match series with a game to spare.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersPremier League3pmClockwatchScott Murrayis at the controls with regular updates from the three Premier League mid-afternoon kick-offs. Front and centre will be the pacesetters and champions, Arsenal. They head to the south coast amid an ominous start to their Premier League defence after taking four victories from four but face the trickiest of trips, away to Brighton, whose tally of 13 goals from four games is the highest in the division. Monday’s 4-1 thrashing at Leeds was certainly a wake-up call for Matthias Jaissle. Defeat ended Newcastle’s unbeaten start this season and an injury-hit squad now face high-flying Hull at St James’ Park. Sergej Jakirovic’s side are fourth in the table with two wins and two draws, holding Chelsea 2-2 in their last outing.Women’s Super League5.30pmArsenal v Manchester United liveRenée Slegers’ Gunners stride out at the Emirates Stadium unbeaten, although they were frustrated in a scoreless draw with promoted Crystal Palace last weekend. Eva Olid’s Manchester United tenure has begun with defeats in both their opening games, and they have conceded seven goals, more than any other WSL team so far. Olid is expecting a response from their 5-0 trashing by Chelsea last weekend. “My main message is about being themselves,” she said. “I am not sure they are showing in the first two matches who they are and what they can do. For me it is so important that they show that to perform. We had a day to reflect and analyse the game, to see what we can do better and we know what we have to do.”Will Mageehas minute-by-minute coverage, andTom Garryreports.View image in fullscreenRenée Slegers will hope her side can find the target against Manchester United.Photograph: John Walton/PASundayFootball8amMatchday liveSunday brings four Premier League matches plus an Old Firm derby and a spicy clash at Molineux as Wolves host old foes West Brom.Emillia Hawkinsis on hand bright and early with all the breaking news at the helm of our essential football live blog. Join the conversation by emailing your thoughts and queries tomatchday.live@theguardian.comScottish Premiership12pmCeltic v Rangers liveCeltic have a 100% league record but are in something of a tailspin, having been thumped 3-0 in the League Cup by their Glasgow rivals at Ibrox on Sunday and then beaten 3-1 by Ferencvaros at Parkhead in the Europa League on Thursday. So it is less than an optimal moment to be going up against Rangers, who will be striving to make it six wins in succession across all competitions when they visit Celtic Park. Martin O’Neill certainly understands his side are a world away from last season’s uplift, calling their latest loss “a huge frustration” and “psychologically damning”. He admitted: “It’s not the start we wanted. Really need to concentrate now on Sunday [against Rangers] … Sunday’s a big game.”John Brewinhelms the blog withJonathan Liewreporting.Premier League2pmBournemouth v Liverpool liveLiverpool remain unbeaten under their new head coach, Andoni Iraola, in all competitions but managing three draws from four Premier League games has stifled any early-season momentum. Iraola will be back in familiar surroundings as his side travel to Bournemouth, the south coast club the Spaniard consistently had punching above their weight. Bournemouth are yet ‌to win in the league under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose, but three draws and a rather unlucky loss at Manchester City are scant return for some eye-catching football under the German.Daniel Harrishas the live blog, withBen Fisherreporting.Premier League4.30pmFulham v Manchester United liveOne month into the Premier League season, excuses about bedding-in processes and newly assembled squads needing time to gel are wearing thin and for Manchester United there is ⁠an acute sense of urgency as the international break looms. After so much pre-season optimism, the spotlight has turned on the ⁠manager, Michael Carrick. Only one ​win in four league games – at home to promoted Ipswich – has been compounded by Wednesday’s League Cup exit at home to Brighton, having led 2-0. Another setback at Craven Cottage against a ⁠Fulham side without a league win would increase the pressure on Carrick and deepen the sense that United’s season is in danger of drifting before it has properly begun. United will be buoyed by the fact they ‌have not lost at Fulham since 2009, but while the London club have made a slow start under Álvaro Arbeloa, a draw at Liverpool last week and a League Cup win at West Ham in midweek offered glimpses of better things to come.Taha Hashimbrings the noise in the live blog, withDavid HytnerandJacob Steinbergour reporting team at Craven Cottage.American football6pmNFL week two liveGraham Searlesis back for the best of week two’s action. He will be concentrating on Vikings v Bears and Steelers v Patriots from the eight 6pm fixtures. Minnesota opened their season with a comeback win over Green Bay, rallying from a 12-point deficit late in the third quarter to overwhelm the Packers. The Vikings’ defense will bid to shut down Caleb Williams in a battle of unbeaten teams after the Chicago quarterback inspired a record-breaking start to the season. Williams threw two touchdowns and ran for two more as the Bears pounded the Carolina Panthers 59-37 last weekend in the highest-scoring opener in NFL history. Pittsburgh, meanwhile, are coming off the successful debut of their new coach, Mike McCarthy, after the departure of Mike Tomlin, and a vintage effort from their 42-year-old quarterback Aaron Rodgers in their opening win over Atlanta. The Patriots will be entering their second home opener under Mike Vrabel, the architect of New England’s renaissance in the post-Tom Brady era, and with a third-year quarterback in Drake Maye whose post-Super Bowl run honeymoon appears to be over after one of the worst performances of his young career in last week’s 13-10 loss to Seattle.View image in fullscreenCaleb Williams led the Chicago Bears to a record-breaking start in the NFL’s opening weekend.Photograph: Scott Kinser/APExplore more on these topicsSportYour Guardian sport weekendUS sportsCricketfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Noahkai Banks, top dual-national prospect, chooses Germany in blow to USMNT | USA | The Guardian
description: The manager of Germany’s U-21 team confirmed the decision has been made for the 19-year-old, who had represented only the US at the youth level until now
Author: Alexander Abnos
Headline: The manager of Germany’s U-21 team confirmed the decision has been made for the 19-year-old, who had represented only the US at the youth level until now
Content: Noahkai Banks has chosen to represent Germany over the United States.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance Archive/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenNoahkai Banks has chosen to represent Germany over the United States.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance Archive/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.USANoahkai Banks, top dual-national prospect, chooses Germany in blow to USMNTGermany U-21 manager announces the decision19-year-old had represented only US at youth levelAlexander AbnosFri 18 Sep 2026 09.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States’ pursuit of dual-national defenderNoahkai Banksappears to be over.The 19-year-old was named in Germany’s U-21 squad for their upcoming U-21 European Championship qualifiers, with manager Antonio Di Salvo saying in an officialreleasethat Banks and Louey Ben Farhat, another dual national, have “chosen to represent Germany”.Born in Honolulu to an American father and German mother, Banks has until now only represented US youth national teams, including at the U-17 World Cup in 2023. Because that is an official Fifa competition, he would need to file a one-time switch to represent Germany.Teenager Noahkai Banks’ position and passing have him on the US’s World Cup radarRead more“We’ve been in contact with [Banks and Ben Farhat] for a while now and had focused our efforts on them,” Di Salvo said. “I’m very pleased that we have been able to lay out a future pathway with Germany for them and that they agreed with it.”The US and Germany have both recruited Banks, who rose to become one of the Bundesliga’s top young defenders last year with FC Augsburg. He played in 23 league matches for Augsburg last season, almost all of them starts, and has started and gone the full 90 in all four of their games so far this season.Mauricio Pochettino called Banks in to the senior US teams in September 2025 for friendlies against South Korea and Japan, but Banks did not get off the bench in either game – a loss to South Korea and a win over Japan, both by 2-0 scorelines.ESPNreportedthat Banks turned down a call-up to US camp in the March international window, the last before the 2026 World Cup.Even so, Banks was thought to stand an outside chance of making the Pochettino’s World Cup squad given the team’s lack of depth at center-back and relative lack of top-level young options coming through the system.“I told both [the US and Germany] that I just wanted to concentrate on the start of the season now,” Banks told Bild. “But I know that I have to decide by the next international break or at the latest by the international break after next.”Pochettino told reporters earlier this month that the federation had remained in touch with Banks along with other dual-nationals, saying that Bankswas “still in the same situation that [he] was before the World Cup when we talked”.Had Banks chosen the US, he probably would have been in thesquadfor the upcoming four-game international window. Pochettino leaned on youth in his selections, which include 18-year-old Philadelphia Union center-back Neil Pierre.Banks still has the USMNT tagged in the bio section of his official Instagram account. One would expect that to change soon.Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsMauricio PochettinonewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risks | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham’s focus on domestic problems leads some to fear issue has dropped off government’s radar
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Andy Burnham’s focus on domestic problems leads some to fear issue has dropped off government’s radar
Content: Protesters from Pause AI block the entrance to Downing Street on Wednesday.Photograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters from Pause AI block the entrance to Downing Street on Wednesday.Photograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockAI (artificial intelligence)‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risksAndy Burnham’s focus on immediate domestic problems leads some to fear issue has dropped off government’s radarKiran StaceyandDan MilmoFri 18 Sep 2026 10.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTowards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, his senior ministers, alarmed by the latest developments in artificial intelligence, began drawing up plans for a new AI safety law.They ordered a review of existing legislation to see what powers they already had, according to those briefed on the plans, and were exploring whether they could force the world’s most advanced technology companies to submit their products for safety testing before launching them.Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon call for curbs on AI at ‘pro-human’ summitRead moreIn the midst of the political chaos that engulfed the former prime minister as he fought to remain in office, however, the plans fell by the wayside.Now, after two weeks in which the worldhas been toldthere is a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans”, and King Charleshas warnedabout its potentially destructive capabilities, the government’s attention has turned again to what to do about AI.Andy Burnham, Starmer’s successor in Downing Street, has said relatively little about the technology in the past, and in one of his first acts in office he scrapped the department that had been leading the legislative work.The prime minister’s focus is on more immediate domestic problems. But as he grapples with balancing his first budget and bringing down the cost of living, some fear the threat posed by AI has dropped off the government’s radar.“The first duty of government is to keep people safe,” said Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the science and technology committee. “The government’s response to an existential threat cannot be to throw its hands up in the air and say there is nothing we can do.”View image in fullscreenChi Onwurah.Photograph: Mark Thomas/Rex/ShutterstockRisks v potentialBritain has been at the forefront of the debate on AI safety since Starmer’s predecessor, Rishi Sunak, decided to make it one of his top priorities in office.Amid worries about what super-intelligent tools could do without human involvement, Sunak convened a summit in the UK and persuaded the US, EU, Australia and Chinato cooperate on AI safety.Starmerwas more bullishabout AI’s potential “to increase productivity hugely, to do things differently, to provide a better economy that works in a different way in the future”.The Guardian has learned that in the former technology department, Emran Mian, the lead civil servant, had plans for AI to replace almost every civil servant in the department when they retired or moved on to a new job.But at the same time, some in government were keen to remain focused on the risks posed by the technology.Shortly before Starmer’s departure, Yvette Cooper, then the foreign secretary,told the Guardianshe believed AI posed a Hiroshima-style risk to humanity.AI isn’t going to end humanity ... right? – podcastRead moreStarmer’s government took steps to mitigate the risks Cooper and others had identified. His government allocated £115m in June to fund a response centre to deal with incidents when AI goes rogue and for a new AI biosecurity programme.Officials in the science department also began reviewing what powers ministers had to compel companies to cooperate with the UK safety regime, and what else they could legislate for.‘A critical moment’When Burnham took office earlier this summer, one of his first moves was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT).Kanishka Narayan, the junior minister in charge of AI, was given a promotion and placed in the Cabinet Office, where he continues to oversee the technology but without the logistical support of a dedicated department.The move alarmed some in the AI industry.Matt Clifford, the AI investor who had advised Starmer and Sunak,posted on X: “Right now is a critical moment for tech as an economic and national security issue. Tying up our most senior science and tech officials in a [reorganisation] wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance.”Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who chaired a UK government AI review in 2017, said: “The structure was a bit bloated in DSIT, but the fragmentation we have now has had a much worse impact.”‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot momentRead moreAI safety rose up the political agenda again over the summer.In July, OpenAI revealed one of its AI agentshad launchedan autonomous cyber-attack on Hugging Face, a real company, triggering alarm among technology experts around the world.Earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher, resigned from his job at Anthropic,claiming the companywas “gambling with our lives”. His comments were reposted online by one of his colleagues, Evan Hubinger, who added: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”Just as these warnings were being made,the Financial Times revealedthat Anthropic had launched the latest version of its Claude Mythos tool without submitting it to the UK safety institute first.Mounting concernsKing Charles intervened this week, convening a meeting of AI executives in Scotland, where he told them: “The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”View image in fullscreenKing Charles with the AI researcher Demis Hassabis and the Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, at Dumfries House in Cumnock, Scotland.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/ReutersPublic concern is also growing. YouGov said on Friday that just over a third of Britons see AI as the third potential cause of human extinction behind nuclear war and climate breakdown – a figure that more than doubled since last year. Two-thirds think AI has the potential to end human civilisation, a view shared by the Nobel-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, and one in six support a slowdown in AI development.In parliament, the Labour MP Liam Byrne has asked the head of the safety institute, Henry de Zoete, to testify in front of the business committee he chairs.De Zoete repliedearlier this week, explaining that no one outside the US had been allowed to see Anthropic’s latest product before it launched and insisting that his institute could still monitor such tools after they had been released.“We have teams of talented AI researchers working on research projects based on both pre-release and post-release testing that are fundamental to the UK’s understanding of AI risk, across chemical-biological, human influence and loss of control,” he said.Ministers have also begun to comment. Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister,told the TUC congressthis week there were “clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place”.In an article in the Times,Narayan wrote: “Nothing is off the table. Where further regulation, legislation, stronger protections or new powers are needed, we will act.”Wake-up callByrne believes ministers had a wake-up call.“I think the government is taking it seriously now,” he said. “It has become clear in the last two weeks that perhaps our safety advisers don’t have the power they need to keep us safe.”This still leaves the question unresolved by successive governments – what can the UK, as a middle-ranking power, do to curb the might of some of the world’s most advanced and fastest-growing technology companies?For some, the answer is straightforward: regulate and legislate, just as the government would do for any emerging threat.“The social media companies used to argue that the government is too powerless to act,” said Onwurah. “But there are things the government can do. We could say, for example, that if your frontier model has not gone through the safety institute, we are not going to allow you to sell your commercial models in our country.“Or, if your AI goes and attacks someone else like happened with Hugging Face, you are legally and financially responsible.”Many believe that action will only work if it is coordinated with other countries.“If the US and China do not figure this out, the UK is unlikely to deliver a safe environment on its own,” said Byrne. “But a safety regime which is set and enforced by the UK, Europe, India, Canada and Japan would be robust.”The former Cabinet Office minister Darren Jones has called on Burnham to put the issue at the top of the agenda when Britain hosts the G20 summit next year. “The AI safety conversation at the moment is around international collaboration on safety testing,” he said. “This is easier to do multilaterally, through treaties or agreements.”One former government official added: “If together we say we require you to pass your models through our safety institutes – if we did that at a large enough scale, we would be able to stand up to the US government.”Time to actWhatever the government decides to do, it may find that now is the best time to do it.Unusually, many in the industry are themselves calling for stricter regulation.OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon,said this week: “We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems.”One former government official said: “We have strengths in this country when it comes to AI. Our AI industry is third in the world behind the US and China, and we also have considerable convening power with other countries.“The question for me is whether the new prime minister is alive enough to this problem to take advantage of those strengths.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Technology policyComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins Palantir | Tom Watson | The Guardian
description: Peer takes full-time position at the controversial company as it fends off pressure from both Andy Burnham’s government and Sadiq Khan
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Peer takes full-time position at the controversial company as it fends off pressure from both Andy Burnham’s government and Sadiq Khan
Content: Part of Watson’s role at Palantir will be to ‘deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills’.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreenPart of Watson’s role at Palantir will be to ‘deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills’.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PATom WatsonFormer Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins PalantirPeer takes full-time position at the controversial company as it fends off pressure from both Andy Burnham’s government and Sadiq KhanRobert BoothUK technology editorFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnother former government minister has been hired by a controversial US AI company, this time Palantir, which has appointed Andy Burnham’s former ministerial colleagueTom Watson.The Labour peer and former deputy leader will operate alongside Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, as the company attempts to fend offpressure on Burnham’s government to axe its £330m NHS contract. It is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over theLabour London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. Palantir also wants to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annualturnoverof £427m.The company was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and providesAI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. Alex Karp, its chief executive, said: “This is just the latest chapter of Tom’s forty-year fight for better public services. We are fortunate to have him guide us as we help the British government to deliver for the British public.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNDIS data may have ended up in Palantir’s analytics platform as part of efforts to curb fraudRead moreHis job will be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”,Palantirsaid.Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, Watson has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir, including accompanying Mosley at Labour party conferences. He was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Palantir has a £240m contract with the Ministry of Defence.The move is just the latest example of a revolving door between British politics and big tech. After the former deputy prime minister Nick Cleggspent nearly seven years earning millions working for Mark Zuckerberg at Meta, the former prime minister Rishi Sunaklast year took jobs with Anthropic and Microsoftand the former chancellor George Osbornestarted working for OpenAI. Keir Starmer’s AI adviser, Matt Clifford,also joined Anthropic this month. He tried to retain the chair of a government science and tech research body, butquitunder pressure over conflicts of interest.‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health ministerRead more“The revolving door is proving very fruitful for big tech,” said Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group. “The only surefire way to stop tech companies benefiting from privileged information acquired by ministers or senior civil servants is to introduce an enforceable five-year ban on taking up industry posts.”Watson said he was “terrifically excited” by the new role as Palantir’s senior vice-president and highlighted two of the contracts that are in dispute when he said he wanted to help Palantir speed up NHS diagnosis, treatment and discharge from hospitals and enable “our police to crack crimes and root out corruption”. Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while working for Palantir in London.Explore more on these topicsTom WatsonPalantirnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate | Technology | The Guardian
description: Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear
Content: Christine Lagarde asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.Photograph: Bryan Meade/EPAView image in fullscreenChristine Lagarde asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.Photograph: Bryan Meade/EPATechnologyAnalysisWhy Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debateDan MilmoandAisha DownThough Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bearFri 18 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 17.19 EDTShareEurope’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank,Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear –and experts have differing views on this– then the technology will impact the continent regardless.Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’Read moreEurope has largely been absent from the highest levels of that debate, a result of the continent’slongstanding inabilityto produce a Silicon Valley-scale titan like Apple, Google or newcomer OpenAI. While it is a powerhouse in regulation, much to the White House’s chagrin, its lack of an Anthropic or Nvidia-sized frontrunner in the AI race has diminished its voice in the safety debate.Ursula von der Leyen, a powerful political figure on the continent as president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, addressed the issue this week by saying she will “invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.Her remarks gained nowhere as much traction as Donald Trump and China’s dismissal of a slowdown. Without the support of Washington or Beijing, any sort of pacing is impossible – with our without Europe’s input.Lagarde’s speech on Monday underlined the continent’s relative weakness. She asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force.” Self-sufficiency would also give Europe a chance to develop its own answer to the AI safety crisis.Margrethe Vestager, who clashed with the US tech industry as the EU’s former competition commissioner, co-authored a report this week – A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe – that echoed Lagarde’s warning. AI threatens to accelerate a development already affecting Europe, where citizens “are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere”, she says.Solutions to this, according to the report, include building more datacentres – the central nervous systems of AI – and also to ensure the continent is resilient enough to withstand “AI crises” like a powerful model slipping out of control.Vestager said that Europe does have a voice in the safety debate through its EU AI Act, the rare piece of AI legislation that sets out requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems to report safety incidents and address risks like a cutting-edge model evading control.But she adds: “Europe must … build its own AI to strengthen the ecosystem, retain talent, and inspire innovation.”Vestager acknowledges that if there is an existential threat, it requires a global solution; one that does not hand power to the US and China. And that requires a different kind of supranational body.“As for existential threats to humanity, we must first assess the actual level of threat – then act with urgency. The UN general assembly is an opportunity to address this. It is vital to move beyond the US-China rivalry narrative. There must be space for humanity between the egos of leaders like President Xi and President Trump.”Frederike Kaltheuner, an adviser to the AI Now Institute, a research body, says that Europe is dependent on US technology in ways that will be hard to undo, from search engines to chips to datacentres. But thenarrative that Europe is grievously behind in the racedepends on a particular view of artificial intelligence aggressively promoted by American tech bosses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBecause of their doomsday warnings, “we are exclusively talking about AI in a very narrow, specific kind of way – namely, the idea that there is such a thing as the AI frontier, which is getting better and better, and that access to the frontier is the most important thing that Europe needs for its security and economy.”The reality of the market points at something else, she says: many companies are not adopting so-called “frontier models” – like ChatGPT and Anthropic – because of high costs and fears over what might happen to their data.If this trend continues, Europe may not be so terribly positioned: the EU AI Act has a number of pragmatic measures which address how consumers might encounter AI on a day-to-day basis, legislating over matters such as labelling AI content, and the use of AI in medicine and hiring.“Europe has a competitiveness problem, that’s true,” says Itxaso Dominguez de Olazabal, a policy adviser at EDRI, a European digital rights organisation. But US tech boosters are “blaming it on laws and protections, and have promised that deregulation will make European companies more competitive … in a race to the bottom to see if we can catch big tech”.Nonetheless, the EU AI act is not viewed as model legislation for other countries or a vehicle for a global slowdown. Georgina Kon, a partner at law firm Linklaters, says the act is unlikely to be adopted as a global benchmark for several reasons, including criticisms of the heavy compliance burden, which has led to delays in parts of the act becoming active, and a narrow territorial focus on Europe. Those criticisms have also meant that lawmakers elsewhere have looked to differentiate their approach to AI legislation from the EU’s.“The EU AI Act is not something that everybody else in the world feels constrained by, although many tech companies will of course want to sell to the EU,” she says.Big tech still has a vast customer base in Europe. Kaltheuner worries that the doomsday narratives will push Europe towards dependency, encouraging it to adopt US AI models across the economy out of ill-defined fears over being left behind.“There’s a vision of the future where Europe’s economy, its public sector, its education system runs on models and on infrastructure that is controlled by a very small number of companies that happen to be also in the US. This would be a sovereignty problem.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)EuropeEuropean UnionChristine LagardenewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI ‘ethically hacked’ with help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: US cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: US cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’
Content: An OpenAI booth at the Dreamforce technology summit in San Francisco on Thursday.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn OpenAI booth at the Dreamforce technology summit in San Francisco on Thursday.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI ‘ethically hacked’ with help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbotUS cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorFri 18 Sep 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, in the latest example ofsecurity issuesat the company.A team at a US-based startup compromised a number of OpenAI employees’ChatGPTaccounts, starting a process that enabled them to access their target’s software cache – and potentially more.“The scope of what we could theoretically access was huge,”said researchers at Hacktron AI.Initially, the research team used Claude, which can generate code for hackers, to access ChatGPT accounts via anOpenAIstaff discussion forum hosted by the Discourse platform. They then made a harmless “pull request” – an attempt to change the code in a file – to OpenAI’s service on the GitHub software repository.Hacktron reported the hack to OpenAI, having carried out the operation under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers for testing its systems. The researchers stressed that they had access to, but did not download, the code from the GitHub repository.Despite initial use of Claude, the researchers said they were largely using OpenAI’s own cutting edge GPT-5.6 Sol model to carry out the hack, which wasfirst reportedby the Wall Street Journal.An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings”, adding that the company had addressed the vulnerabilities that had been exploited.Hacktron said AI tools had made a once-complex hacking task far easier and drastically shortened the time needed to plan and execute an attack. This is a common refrain from cybersecurity experts when discussing the impact of AI.“Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” said Hacktron, which received a $6,500 payment from OpenAI under the company’s bug bounty programme.The hack is the latest safety incident at OpenAI, which revealed in July that a “swarm” of agents – the term for AI tools capable of carrying out tasks autonomously – powered by its technologyhad hackedthe AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test.This week the San Francisco-based company revealed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” actions by its technology, and warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.Anthropic made a freshcall at the weekend for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. Anthropic also repeated warnings that unrestrained AI development posed an existential threat,concerns that some expertsare sceptical about.Donald Trump has rejected calls for a slowdown, citing a need to stay ahead of China’s AI industry and dismissing “negative forces … bringing up things that won’t happen”.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAnthropicChatbotsAI (artificial intelligence)ChatGPTHackingData and computer securitynewsShareReuse this content
