title: Australia claims it is a global pioneer in preventing online harm – should other countries follow suit? | Social media | The Guardian
description: As Anthony Albanese heads to the US to discuss social media reform, he has shown a level of leadership not always expected from a smaller country
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: As Anthony Albanese heads to the US to discuss social media reform, he has shown a level of leadership not always expected from a smaller country
Content: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and his communications minister, Anika Wells, want to strengthen the coalition of support for their fight against big tech.Composite: AAPView image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and his communications minister, Anika Wells, want to strengthen the coalition of support for their fight against big tech.Composite: AAPSocial mediaAustralia claims it is a global pioneer in preventing online harm – should other countries follow suit?As Anthony Albanese heads to the US to discuss social media reform, he has shown a level of leadership not always expected from a smaller countryGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandJosh TaylorFri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 20.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStatesmen, shysters, dictators. Over the years, the United Nations has seen all kinds of world leaders.But when he arrives in New York on Monday for the annual general assembly,Anthony Albanesewill be looking for collaborators.Determined to rein in the power of social media giants harming the lives of children, the Australian prime minister believes only a concerted effort by countries around the world will be enough to force change.Attending the UN leaders week in September last year, Albanese hosted a stylish event in a room overlooking the East River, talking up Australia’s world-leading moves to ban children under 16 from having social media accounts.That day, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the world was watching Australia. There to hear from families of children who had taken their own lives after online bullying, the leaders of Greece, Fiji, Tonga and Malta agreed it was time for change.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailA year later, the ban is responsible for the closure of as many as 5m accounts in Australia. And, as countries as diverse as France, Brazil and Indonesia follow suit, Albanese is taking the next step.Earlier this month he announced plans to legislate a digital duty of care, and rules to allow social media users to opt out of the powerful algorithms splintering communities, overheating political debates and targeting vulnerable people.“We took action because the community said ‘enough was enough’, and we would no longer let Australian kids be treated as commodities instead of children,” Albanese said, anticipating a fight domestically and on the world stage.Australia, a middle power and a long way from many of the world’s big diplomatic questions, is portraying itself as the leader in tackling big tech’s reach into all our lives.Albanese believes he is helping spur “a global movement” for change, using public pressure, big fines and diplomacy to correct harm playing out online, as well as in the real world.“Australia is working to prevent online harm, particularly for our children, and I am proud that Australia is setting the world standard for digital safety,” he said on Friday.‘Tech firms are losing the public’: social media age bans near tipping pointRead moreAs he flies to the US, where one of his first stops will be at Apple’s California headquarters for talks with its chair and former chief executive, Tim Cook, Albanese will be buoyed up by polling showing two-thirds of voters (66%) support opt out requirements for algorithms. A DemosAU poll this week found only 13% were opposed to the plan.The majority of respondents believed social media companies should be legally required to reduce foreseeable risks to users, even if it meant more restrictions on their business models.But the polling is set against a parallel, less positive conversation about AI and Australia’s datacentre boom, with growing disquiet among communities exposed to the country’s160-odd datacentresand about how they will be powered. To feed the AI that depend on those developments, Albanese appears open to negotiating trading Australiancopyright protectionsin order to do business with the same companies he has taken to task over social media.In the digital safety space, Tama Leaver, a professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth, says Australia has shown a level of leadership not always expected from a smaller country.“It is something that gives them a level of credibility, even if the world-leading nature of some of these plans might be slightly overstated,” he told Guardian Australia.Leaver points to the Netherlands, where a legal challenge found Meta was not compliant with the European Union’s Digital Services Act.A court ordered the company to add an easily accessible option for Facebook and Instagram users to block algorithmic recommendations, backed up by fines. Even by European standards, Dutch social media users have more power to shape their feeds.Similarly, last month, Meta agreed to a US$18bn settlement with state governments across America to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. Meta will also implement a suite of changes to better protect children online, including default daily time limits and night-time blocks.Labor sources describe the government’s online safety push as part of Albanese’s view of Australian leadership in an uncertain world. Acting with key partners, harnessing the concerns of parents and showing that even small countries can have an outsized voice when they’re prepared to lead.Albanese, and his communications minister, Anika Wells, want to strengthen the coalition of support.Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithmsRead moreWells says the wealthy owners of platforms including Google, Meta, TikTok and Snapchat have been “running real-time, unregulated product testing on Australians” for too long.“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she says.Under the next round of reforms, users over 16 will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with fines of more than A$100m for platforms breaking the rules. The rules have been dubbed “my feed, my way”.Children under 18 will be given new protections from specific harms, shielding them from pornography; posts promoting or encouraging eating disorders; misogynistic content; depictions of crime and dangerous stunts; and content likely to cause mental health problems, including abuse and bullying.Wells is also targeting so-called “nudify apps”, which create fake naked images. Regulators say this kind of abuse has grown more than fivefold since 2019.“We must move the burden of reporting online harm from the shoulders of victims and stop that harm at the source,” Wells says.“We must hold big tech accountable for the tools they are creating and putting out to market, including to children.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the draft legislation has had a difficult rollout.The Coalition says Labor is trying to give itself huge powers to censor conservative voices online, with insufficient checks and balances. The Greens, on whom Labor will rely to pass the laws through parliament, say the plan isn’t strong enough. Instead of opt-out ability, they want Australians to proactively opt in to algorithms.And political risk is waiting for Albanese in the US, too. The White House flagged possible pressure on Australia to stop targeting US-owned tech companies, saying Donald Trump’s administration wouldraise concerns with trading partners.Labor has pledged to take time to consult, with the legislation expected to be introduced before Christmas. Albanese will discuss the plans on a series of overseas trips planned before the end of the year: after the UN, he will attend meetings of Commonwealth leaders, as well as the Asean and Apec blocs and the G20 in December.While Australia’s social media ban has been watched around the world, in the 10 months since it came into effect, questions have been raised about its effectiveness.Research has found more than80% of teens under 16were still on social media following the ban. The government has passed laws to double the fines, and give the eSafety commissioner new powers to investigate compliance.Even if not completely effective, Greece, Britain and Denmark are advancing plans for similar bans, while restrictions already exist in countries including China, Indonesia and Malaysia.In a major speech this week, von der Leyen said it was time for Europe to follow Australia, proposing a new “EU Kids Act”.“I am aware that many perceive the power of big tech as overwhelming. And impossible to roll back,” she said. “I disagree.”The Australian eSafety commissioner’s office told a parliamentary committee last month that the ban “seeks to unwind more than 20 years of entrenched industry practice”.Wayne Holdsworth, father of Mac – a teen sextortion victim who took his own life – told the parliament that it would take three to five years to determine the ban’s success.“We have handed a poisoned chalice to our children that is dangerous and has had a significant negative impact on our kids – in some cases, fatal,” he said.“When seatbelts were introduced in the late 1970s, some adults didn’t wear them, because it creased their shirt as they threw their cigarette out the window whilst balancing their can of beer on their lap.”Jason Trethowan, chief executive of the youth mental health organisation Headspace, said: “You have to start somewhere.“You have to put a line in the sand and then work towards getting those percentages down. And it’ll be a positive.”double quotation markAustralia is best served by sharing the lead with other middle powers, even if we thought of it firstDr Rob NichollsDr Rob Nicholls, a senior researcher associate at the University of Sydney’s centre for AI, trust and governance, said the ban would probably work better over time – particularly as the 13 to 15-year-olds who had social media before the ban aged out of it.Nicholls said the Albanese government could help other countries follow in its footsteps.“It’s great to get on a plane to New York to skite about ‘leading’,” he said. “I think that the fast followers of the Australian lead will use the issues that have been found here to hone their legislative approaches.”And Australia need not seek to lead in all facets of social media regulation globally.“Australia is best served by sharing the lead with other middle powers, even if we thought of it first.”Trethowan believes if the changes work, Australia will empower other countries to demand similar features from platforms.“I think the technology companies are having to defend themselves or make changes to their algorithms and the way in which they design features to mitigate their potential fines,” he said.“Australia’s set it up for other countries to take on similar things.”Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaAnthony AlbaneseDigital mediaSocial media banfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My son’s death during a college football workout was preventable. Lessons must be learned | College sports | The Guardian
description: Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich is fighting for his life after collapsing during practice. Tragedies like this can be avoided
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich is fighting for his life after collapsing during practice. Tragedies like this can be avoided
Content: Jordan McNair, pictured in 2016 while at McDonogh School in Maryland, died in June 2018, two weeks after he collapsed during a University of Maryland team workout.Photograph: Baltimore Sun/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJordan McNair, pictured in 2016 while at McDonogh School in Maryland, died in June 2018, two weeks after he collapsed during a University of Maryland team workout.Photograph: Baltimore Sun/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesCollege sportsMy son’s death during a college football workout was preventable. Lessons must be learnedMartin McNair with Simon FitzgeraldArizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich is fighting for his life after collapsing during practice. Tragedies like this can be avoidedFri 18 Sep 2026 10.10 EDTShareLate last month, Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayichcollapsed during a team workout. He is now fighting for his life after suffering from exertional heatstroke and, according to the Mayich family attorney, is unlikely to make a meaningful recovery. This young man was drafted by the St Louis Blues but will never get the opportunity to play in the NHL. While he is not the first young athlete severely harmed by heat-related illness in American sports, he should be the last.I have learned more about this preventable injury than I ever wanted to know. On 29 May 2018, my son Jordan McNair collapsed during a strenuous football practice at the University of Maryland. By the time he arrived at the hospital, he was dangerously overheatedand never recovered.For two weeks, as Jordan fought for his life through intensive care and an emergency liver transplant, one question kept coming: “What did we miss?”I think about the days before he signed with Maryland, when coaches sat at our kitchen table talking with our family about Jordan. I remember asking two questions:“Can Jordan get some playing time?”And, “What support do you have around mental health and substance abuse?”Those are the kind of questions many parents ask when they have never experienced a life-changing tragedy in collegiate sports. Jordan was going to play football at a Big Ten university. What could possibly go wrong?I didn’t ask:“If something happens to my son, what safety systems do you have in place?”“What is your emergency action plan?”“When was the last time you practiced it?”“Who has the authority to stop a workout when an athlete is in medical distress?”“What happens if my child suffers exertional heatstroke?”“Where is the equipment needed to save his life?”Those questions came in hindsight, as I walked toward the ICU every day while Jordan fought for his life. I kept asking myself:“What did I miss that night at the kitchen table?”Before Jordan collapsed, I thought heatstroke and heat exhaustion were one and the same. I thought if someone became overheated, you moved them into the shade, gave them water, let them cool down, and everything would be fine. I didn’t know a heat-related injury could kill my son. My education came through a baptism by fire.Suddenly, as the Mayich family may be learning now, I had to understand medical terms I had never heard before:rhabdomyolysis. Core body temperature. Multiorgan failure.Exertional heatstroke.View image in fullscreenJordan McNair during his time with the University of Maryland football team.Photograph: Courtesy of the Jordan McNair FoundationSince Jordan’s death, I’ve worked alongside medical professionals to cool athletes experiencing exertional heat illness at sporting events across the nation. I’ve seen first-hand how quickly proper recognition and response can change an outcome.One of the simplest explanations of exertional heatstroke has stayed with me. When your core body temperature rises above 104F (40C), it is like putting your body inside a microwave. Your organs begin to cook.There is a critical window of roughly 20 to 30 minutes to rapidly cool the athlete and avert catastrophe. Cold-water immersion can bring the body’s temperature down before the damage becomes irreversible.Time is everything.But what happened to Jordan wasn’t only about what went wrong on the football field on 29 May 2018. What happened to Mayich in Arizona isn’t only about what happened on 20 August 2026. The tragedy began long before.Every organization has layers of protection, and every layer can have weaknesses, the holes in the Swiss Cheese Model. One hole may not cause disaster because another layer can stop it. But when enough holes align, nothing remains between the athlete and tragedy.There was an emergency action plan in Jordan’s case. But having an emergency action plan on paper and being prepared to execute it are two very different things. Imagine having a fire evacuation plan nobody ever practices. Then one day the building catches fire. Who knows where to go, what to do, who calls 911 and who gets people out? The middle of the fire is the worst possible time to figure out the plan. Athletic emergencies are no different.Every time an athlete steps on to a field, court, track or practice facility, an emergency is possible. The systems designed to protect that athlete must be in place before it happens, and the people responsible for those systems must know exactly what to do.I used to say Murphy’s law was in full effect the day Jordan collapsed. While I wasn’t in Arizona for the team practice where Matthew Mayich collapsed, reports from that day reveal unsettling parallels to my son’s case.During a strenuous early-season workout, the athlete’s level of distress wasn’t properly recognized. The escalation from heat exhaustion to exertional heatstroke wasn’t appropriately addressed. The emergency action plan was not properly practiced or implemented. The lifesaving cooling response wasn’t initiated within that critical window. Necessary equipment wasn’t within immediate reach. Changes in the normal practice setting complicated the emergency response, and precious time was lost before treatment began.One hole.Then another.Then another.Until they aligned.By the time Jordan arrived at the emergency room, more than an hour and a half after he collapsed, his core body temperature was approximately 106F. My son never came home.Three days after Jordan died, on 16 June 2018, I began what would become my life’s work as a student-athlete safety advocate. There is a club of parents none of us ever asked to join. We are mothers and fathers who sent our children off to play the sports they loved and eventually had to bury them. We don’t need another member.View image in fullscreenMaryland players surround the No 79 painted on the field in honor of Jordan McNair before their game against Michigan State in College Park in November 2018.Photograph: Will Newton/Getty ImagesWe certainly don’t need another parent standing outside an ICU asking the same question I asked myself over and over:“What did I miss?”My prayers remain with Matthew Mayich and his family. I pray they receive the outcome every parent outside an ICU desperately hopes for.For years, I kept returning to the questions I asked at our kitchen table.Now, I know the question I should have asked. “Can my child play and will my child be safe?”Parents shouldn’t have to experience what my family has before they learn to ask that question. Medical professionals responsible for the health and safety of athletes shouldn’t wait until an athlete collapses to understand and practice their role in an emergency action plan.Schools and athletic programs shouldn’t discover holes in their safety systems while a child’s life hangs in the balance. Coaches need to understand their role in that system without being expected to diagnose or treat a medical emergency. Athletes should never wonder whether speaking up about how they feel will be interpreted as weakness.Theon-field cardiac arrestof Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin demonstrates that having a disciplined emergency action plan goes beyond heat-related injury. Hamlin’s full recovery after immediate CPR and emergent cardiac defibrillation is an excellent example of how lifesaving intervention should be available for athletes at risk. He not only made it to the hospital; he walked out on his own and eventually returned to the playing field.The NCAA, with over $1bn in revenue, owes its players that same level of emergency preparedness.This is an opportunity for youth sports organizations at every level to have mandatory emergency action plans in place for the life-threatening emergencies their athletes face. This includes heat-related injury as well as other serious sports-related emergencies such as cardiac events, traumatic head injuries and complications of sickle cell disease.Students, parents, coaches and administrators must hold athletic organizations accountable to have these resources in place because the next missed opportunity may be fatal.Martin McNair is the father of Jordan McNair and founder ofThe Jordan McNair Foundation.Dr Simon Fitzgerald is a trauma surgeon and surgical intensivist in Brooklyn, New York, and a medical advisory board member of The Jordan McNair Foundation.Explore more on these topicsCollege sportsCollege footballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: To protect democracy, Democrats should talk about corruption – not authoritarianism | Jared Abbott and Joan C Williams | The Guardian
description: The party needs to thread the needle between college-educated and working-class voters. Our survey offers a way
Author: Jared Abbott
Headline: The party needs to thread the needle between college-educated and working-class voters. Our survey offers a way
Content: ‘One prominent Democrat provides the template for how to respond: Jon Ossoff, the US Senator up for re-election in Georgia.’Photograph: Bill Barrows/APView image in fullscreen‘One prominent Democrat provides the template for how to respond: Jon Ossoff, the US Senator up for re-election in Georgia.’Photograph: Bill Barrows/APOpinionDemocratsTo protect democracy, Democrats should talk about corruption – not authoritarianismJared AbbottandJoan C WilliamsThe party needs to thread the needle between college-educated and working-class voters. Our survey offers a wayFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.27 EDTShareResisting authoritarianism is the second-highest priority for Democrats’ college-educated base. But for working-class Americans, it’s only the 19th priority (out of 20), we found ina new survey. The gap between these two groups was larger than on any other issues: elites prioritized resisting authoritarianism an astonishing 33 percentage points more than non-elites did.Democrats’ dilemma is that their college-educated base insists they stand up to Donald Trump’s attacks on democracy, but they also need to win working-class votes. The way to thread that needle is to recognize that what’s needed to defend democracy in the short term is different from what’s needed to defend it in the long term.In the short term, Democrats’ base is right: immediate action is needed in the courts, exemplified by themore than 150 lawsuitsthat Democracy Forward has filed against the Trump administration and the82 filedby California attorney general Rob Bonta, contesting alleged corruption, funding cuts, election interference and more. Action in the streets is powerful, too, from the protests in Minnesota to the mobilization of more than 8 million people (chiefly highly-educated women) at No Kings rallies across the country. But while #resistance is necessary, it’s not enough. Democrats also need to take two additional steps.Democrats need to win. Here’s the message our research says worksRead moreThe first is to talk about defending democracy in ways that connect with working-class voters, which our survey defines as those without college degrees in the middle 50% of US income distribution. While “resisting authoritarianism” was a low priority for working-class voters of any race, “reducing corruption in government” was the third highest priority for white working-class respondents, fourth for working-class Latinos, and sixth for working-class African Americans, our survey found.In fact, reducing corruption was one of only two top working-class priorities we identified that wasn’t economic. Astudyout of the UK explains why. It found that working-class Britons use “corruption” not in a narrow legal sense but to express “deeply rooted feelings of injustice and unfairness”. “The whole system needs [to be] seriously looked at and reformed,” said one man, protesting MPs at the Parliament bar with their taxpayer-subsidized gin and tonics. “The government don’t care about me, they don’t care about my children,” said a working-class woman. Corruption talk is how working-class people protest against a political system that doesn’t seem to represent them – a political system that has become anti-democratic.This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert ReichRead moreOne prominent Democrat provides the template for how to respond: Jon Ossoff, the US Senator up for re-election in Georgia. “American politics is coin operated,”he said. “Money comes in, favors come out.” A former documentary film-maker, Ossoff knows how to communicate. First he adopts a catchy phrase–the “Mar-a-Lago mafia” – to describe the alliance of the Trump family and the ultra-rich that “has taken American corruption to spectacular new heights”. Then he ties corruption directly to negative impacts on ordinary people’s lives: “One point six billion of your tax dollars to fund and finance [Donald Trump’s sons’] mining project in Kazakhstan. All this, while you pay for more gas, for groceries, for healthcare.” Then, Ossoff pivots from political to economic elites: “Members of Congresslive in fear of these Super Pacs. And that corruption is why insurance companies get away with denying your claim for a procedure you needed to save your life … It’s why the ultra-rich get a tax break while you pay more for everything.” Republicans have been harnessing anger against economic elites and redirecting it against political elites for decades; with an approach like Ossoff’s, Democrats can reverse the process, redirecting anger against political elites on to economic elites benefitting from a corrupt system.If the first step for Democrats is to talk about corruption, not authoritarianism, the second step is to respect working-class priorities. Eight out of the top 10 working-class priorities are economic, our survey found, and while elites’ economic priorities focus tightly on prices, the working class also prioritizes higher wages and economic opportunity. Many working-class voters don’t rush to defend democracy because they feel it’s failed them for the last 40 years. American workers used to get 70% of GDP but today their share isonly 54%. That helps explain why virtually all Americans earned more than their parents in the decades immediately after second world war, butonly halfthose born in 1980 will. The only way to defend democracy in the long run is to prioritize creating an economy that delivers a stable, middle-class life for working-class Americans.Donald Trump is busyalienating the working-class voterswho swept him into office, butDemocratsare also unpopular. If they want to win elections consistently enough to build a progressive, democratic future, they first need to respect that working-class top priorities are economic – not Palestine, not ICE, not trans rights. Democrats also need to talk about “defending democracy” in ways that connect with working-class voters. Anger at corruption offers a powerful entry point when linked to the widely held view that the economic system is rigged. This approach has worked in countries as diverse asHungary, the Philippines, Guatemala and Malaysia. It can work here, too.Jared Abbott is the director of the Center for Working-Class PoliticsJoan C Williams is distinguished professor of law and Hastings Foundation chair (emerita) at University of California College of the Law San Francisco. She is the author of Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them BackExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicsJon OssoffUS midterm elections 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Robert Kraft’s attempts to silence Macklemore have backfired spectacularly | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The billionaire’s attempted crackdown on Ed Sheeran’s tour only amplified pro-Palestinian statements. It’s been a joy to watch
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The billionaire’s attempted crackdown on Ed Sheeran’s tour only amplified pro-Palestinian statements. It’s been a joy to watch
Content: ‘It seems he didn’t foresee that all of Sheeran’s opening acts and his live band would withdraw in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.’Photograph: Jack Plunkett/APView image in fullscreen‘It seems he didn’t foresee that all of Sheeran’s opening acts and his live band would withdraw in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.’Photograph: Jack Plunkett/APOpinionMacklemoreRobert Kraft’s attempts to silence Macklemore have backfired spectacularlyArwa MahdawiThe billionaire’s attempted crackdown on Ed Sheeran’s tour only amplified pro-Palestinian statements. It’s been a joy to watchFri 18 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTShareAfew weeks ago, the worst thing you could say about Ed Sheeran was that his music was a bit bland. A Guardian music writeronce comparedit to “aural wallpaper”. Which was a little bit rude to wallpaper: there are some very interesting designs out there!I don’t need to tell you what people are saying about Sheeran now, do I? The pop star has been in the news for days after he apparentlycrumbledwhen billionaire Robert Kraft demanded Macklemore be pulled from his tour because of the rapper’s pro-Palestine advocacy.As if he didn’t already look pathetic enough, Sheeran then released a statement throwing Macklemore under the bus. “After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting,” Sheeranwrote on Instagram. Macklemore, he said, had “asked to join my tour last year and I agreed, because I respect him as an artist”. (In other words: “I barely know the guy! Macklemore begged to be on my tour and I was kind enough to say yes!’)The pop star also gave the both-sides treatment to the ongoing genocide in Gaza and he said he didn’t like to be “political”. Except, of course, when it comes tocauses like Ukraine, which he knows he won’t get into any sort of trouble for supporting. I won’t rehash everything that’s been said about Sheeran’s cowardice, but please enjoy this viral TikTok where a woman called Erin Tatum cheekily welcomes Sheeran to the disability community. “My back is full of metal,”she says, “so I too know exactly what it feels like when your spine doesn’t work like it used to! Free Palestine.”Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutralityRead moreKraft isn’t the only billionaire trying to stifle criticism of Israel and stamp out speech: it’s a prevailing theme of our times. Pro-Israelbillionaireslike Kenneth Griffin have used their donation money topressure universitieslike Harvard to oppose students’ criticism of Israel. Meanwhile our billionaire president and his administration have aggressively cracked down on pro-Palestinian protesters, sanctionedlaw firmsperceived to be political enemies,restrictedhow news outlets cover the White House, andinterfered with academic freedomat higher education institutes.The Trump administration had also updated its immigration guidelines so foreigners could potentially bedenied a green cardfor expressing anti-American or anti-Israeli political opinions. As the ACLU attorneyJonathan Hafetzhas noted: “We are seeing the gravest assault on freedom of speech at least since the McCarthy era.”Normally news stories about billionaires trying to stamp out free speech are depressing. But watching Kraft’s intimidation attempts backfire on him and his little buddy Ed has been an absolute joy to watch. It seems Kraft didn’t realize that, for some people, morality is more important than money. It seems he didn’t foresee that all of Sheeran’s opening acts and his live band would withdraw in solidaritywith Macklemoreand Palestine, amplifying the pro-Palestinian statements that he was so desperate to quash. “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children,” the Irish singer Aaron Rowe said in astatementannouncing his departure from the tour.Kraft may have succeeded in removing Macklemore from Sheeran’s tour, but he hasn’t silenced him. Macklemore, to his credit, has kept trying to steer the conversation back to what is happening to Palestinians, rather than what is happening to Sheeran’s brand. On Wednesday, Macklemore said he’ddonate the entiretyof the $1m he has earned from Sheeran’s Loop tour to organizations supporting Palestinians and urged Kraft to match his donation. Kraftrespondedby saying Sheeran had “called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis”. He did not specify if he would do this or who he might donate to. Kraftalso insistedhe wasn’t trying to diminish the “suffering of innocent Palestinians”; he just didn’t want to “obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.There is only one person trying to obscure responsibility here, and that is Kraft. What is happening in Gaza and the West Bank cannot be glibly boiled down to a conflict against Hamas that has resulted in unfortunate suffering. It is, asmany expertsand human rights organizations, have said, a genocide that US taxpayers are helping to fund. There are no real plans for peace or Palestinian self-determination on the horizon: the goal seems to be cleansingall the Palestiniansfrom the territory so Trump can buildluxurybuildings.As Macklemore has stated, the focus of this story shouldn’t be on pop stars, it should be on what is happening to Palestinians. So let me recount just a few of the things that have happened recently. Starting with lastweekend, when a 27-year-old woman who was almost eight months pregnant was shot in the head in Gaza by Israeli forces, while she was sitting in her tent. Both Iman Shalouf and her unborn baby died a few hours later. At least nine other people were killed in the span of 48 hours during what the media still persists in calling a ceasefire (or sometimes, if they’re being daring, “a fragile ceasefire”.)Robert Kraft, once the NFL’s good guy, is just another billionaire silencing Macklemore | Howard BryantRead moreKids continue to be killed in Gaza at staggering rates. Earlier this week, Unicefdetailedattacks on multiple children over the past seven days including “sisters Bana, 6, and Lana, 12, [who] were killed alongside their parents in an airstrike in Beit Lahia while they slept”. And healthcare facilitiescontinue to be targets. On Tuesday, a Medical Aid for Palestinians-supported facility in northern Gazacame under firefrom Israeli quadcopters when a UN delegation was visiting the facility. A 65-year-old patient was killed.Meanwhile in the West Bank, violent settler attacks, encouraged and enabled bythe Israeli government, continue, as the economy is systematically being throttled. On Monday, the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem released a report calledThe Elimination Projectdetailing the “comprehensive mechanism of elimination that works to dismantle the conditions for continued Palestinian existence in the West Bank, while deepening Jewish control and supremacy in an irreversible manner”.It’s stories like this, I’d wager, that Kraft doesn’t want Macklemore drawing attention to. He hasn’t succeeded in his efforts on this particular occasion, but I can’t stress enough that this isn’t the end of it. The Trump administration and many of its billionaire backers remain intent on destroying our freedom of speech andrestricting criticismof Israel.Pretty soon people will stop talking aboutEd Sheeran. Attempts to control what we can talk about will continue.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMacklemoreOpinionEd SheeranPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaActivismcommentShareReuse this content

title: This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during a Likud party campaign rally in Tel Aviv on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during a Likud party campaign rally in Tel Aviv on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelThis Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myselfJonathan FreedlandSpend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alikeFri 18 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareCandidates always say it, but this time it’s true. When Israel goes to the pollson 27 October, it really will be the most important election in the country’s history – and not just for Israelis. I saw that for myself this last week, in a visit that served as a sharp reminder of both what is at stake – and the role of those watching from afar.More than one voter I spoke to voiced the fear that, if the coalition headed byBenjamin Netanyahuis returned to power next month, 27 October will not merely be Israel’s most important election: it will be its last. They were not referring to the absence of democracy in theoccupied territory of the West Bank – which we’ll come to – but rather to Israel’s internationally recognised, pre-1967 borders: what you might call Israel-proper. There, the last four years have seen a sustained assault on the machinery of liberaldemocracy by the most rightwing government since Israel’s establishment in 1948 – a committed, focused attempt to remove the checks and restraints on its own power, installing instead a kind of elective dictatorship.Democratic norms are breaking down all the time. While I was there, Netanyahu joined calls tostrip two Israeli film-makers of their citizenship, as a livid mob surrounded the home ofthe parents of one of the two directors. The film in question isNAZA, produced by the Guardian, which features interviews with two dozen Israeli military insiders, their identities disguised, and which is named for the acronym euphemistically used by the Israeli military when calculating the number of civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. Unlike everyone protesting against it, I have actually seen the film: I have some misgivings about specific choices it makes, but that is irrelevant. A country true to its self-designation as the only democracy in the Middle East would not threaten with expulsion or violence those who say what its rulers do not want to hear.But such egregious behaviour is becoming commonplace. Last month, Netanyahu’s wife, Sara,implied, without evidence, that Yair Golan, leader of the left-leaning Democrats party, had inside knowledge of the 7 October 2023 attacks that saw the massacre of 1,200 Israelis and the abduction of 251 hostages – the trauma of which still touches every aspect of Israeli life and looms over this election campaign. It’s part of a baseless conspiracy theory pushed by Netanyahu and his “poison machine” of acolytes and media allies to shift the blame for the PM’s own 7 October failures, but it’s especially despicable when directed against Golan. A former general, he leapt into his car on 7 October, drove south andpersonally rescued six of those who had come under fire. He is a hero of that dark day – and has threatened to sue Sara Netanyahu. As it happens, soon after her intervention, it was reported thatsomeone high upin Israel had indeed been explicitly warned before 7 October that a devastating Hamas attack was on the way. That someone was Benjamin Netanyahu and the warning came from the president of the United Arab Emirates. Netanyahu vehemently denied the allegation.It is a dirty campaign, filled with disinformation and lies, utterly in keeping with the degraded state of Israeli politics in the age of late-stage Netanyahu. Thanks to Israel’s unwritten constitution, there now remains only one serious obstacle in his way: the courts. He has had the judiciary in his sights since he returned to office nearly four years ago, not least because he wants to halt the ongoing corruption trial that could send him to jail. He tried to gut the supreme court once already,in early 2023, and, if he wins next month, most observers are clear: the court will be gone.That matters for Israelis, who will find themselves in a Turkey- or Russia-style autocracy poorly disguised as a democracy. But it also matters for Palestinians. Yehuda Shaul, an Israeli anti-occupation activist fully aware of the court’s inadequate record as a defender of Palestinian rights, told me thatIsraelhas been on the wrong road for a long time: “But so long as the courts and basic democratic institutions are standing, we can still turn back. If they’re gone, we’re heading off a cliff.”View image in fullscreenMahmoud Eshaq and his family prepare to leave their home in Ras ‘Ein al ‘Auja after continued harassment from Israeli rightwing settlers, 11 January 2026.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianI was with Shaul driving around the West Bank, seeing the changing reality there up close. I stood in the burnt-out and broken mosque of what had been the small Bedouin village of Mu’arrajat, its population chased out by settler terrorists – to use the formulationfavoured, remarkably, by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee. Through harassment and violence, they made the lives of the inhabitants there so unbearable that the villagers could hold on no longer. It was the same story inRas ‘Ein al ‘Auja, where I stood among similar ruins, including a small, abandoned school, and where a herd of settler-owned goats now grazes. Shaul points out the vast swathe of land, more than 100 sq miles, in the east of the West Bank, close enough to see Jordan, where now next to no Palestinians live. Small wonder that former Israeli prime ministerEhud Olmert speaks of ethnic cleansing, or that UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband does the same.I saw, too, in what the settlers call northern Samaria, the four settlements that Ariel Sharon dismantled in 2005, now returned and rebuilt along with 14 others either built or approved for construction. Their arrival sees roadside buildings demolished and olive trees uprooted, in the name of safety for settlers as they travel. And dotted, seemingly on every ridge and hilltop, the distinct, bright white caravans that mark a new officially “unauthorised” outpost, popping up with such frequency that Shaul can barely name them all – he estimates 250 new settlements and outposts have gone up since 2023 – and which are steadily encircling the major Palestinian cities, reducing them to isolated enclaves, thereby preventing the territorial contiguity that would be essential for a viable Palestinian state.Netanyahu’s coalition, with radical settler Bezalel Smotrich in de facto charge of theWest Bank, has directed this settlement expansion and turned a blind eye to the pogroms staged by the movement’s most aggressive wing. The best chance to stop it going farther and further comes on 27 October.Those outside the country appalled by what they see in Gaza or the West Bank sometimes struggle to know what they can do to help. The temptation is to rally around, say, the rapper Macklemore, calling out “Free Palestine” from Ed Sheeran’s stage – but that temptation fades a little when you see that the same Macklemore once performed dressed up as what looked unmistakably likean antisemitic caricature of a Jew, complete with a false, giant nose. He later apologised, saying a “Jewish stereotype” had never crossed his mind.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOr you might want to get fully behindMiliband’s sanctions package, which at long last signals that the settlement enterprise will not be allowed to continue with impunity – until you hear from those involved who say that the immediate impact will fall not on settlers but on Palestinians. That’s because the Netanyahu government’s predictable and predicted response – which includedthe closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem– has robbed Britain of its main mechanism to aid Palestinians through delivering development programmes and the like.The truth is that, for those desperate to see change, the best hope is the ejection from office of what has been a vile, cruel, bigoted and lethally dangerous government. Be under no illusion: even if Netanyahu is toppled, he will not be replaced by a peacenik who will instantly lead the country in the opposite direction. It doesn’t work like that. But there is a bloc, unofficially led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, which is defined by its opposition to the man who has ruled Israel on and off for much of the last 30 years and there are campaigners and activists, such as Shaul, who are fighting every hour of every day to avert further disaster. They are branded as traitors at home and shunned simply for being Israeli by too many supposed progressives abroad. They need allies and friends, because right now they are all that stands between this moment and the abyss.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Australia’s big polluters rely on carbon offsets for climate credibility. But the system looks like a house of cards | Adam Morton | The Guardian
description: Credits are treated as a straight alternative to emissions cuts, but carbon stored in nature is different to burning millennia-old fossil fuels
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: Credits are treated as a straight alternative to emissions cuts, but carbon stored in nature is different to burning millennia-old fossil fuels
Content: Data released by the Clean Energy Regulator shows fossil fuel companies bought about two-thirds of the offsets sold in Australia in the last reporting year.Photograph: redbrickstock.com/AlamyView image in fullscreenData released by the Clean Energy Regulator shows fossil fuel companies bought about two-thirds of the offsets sold in Australia in the last reporting year.Photograph: redbrickstock.com/AlamyClear airClimate crisisAustralia’s big polluters rely on carbon offsets for climate credibility. But the system looks like a house of cardsAdam MortonCredits are treated as a straight alternative to emissions cuts, but carbon stored in nature is different to burning millennia-old fossil fuelsFri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.48 EDTShareThe fight within the Greens that led senators to cross the floor last week overkoala protection in a national parkmay have finally put a spotlight on a bigger issue – one at the heart of much of Australia’s promise to act on the climate crisis. It’s this: the country and its polluting industries are too reliant on carbon offsets. The more reliance is placed on them, the more they look like a house of cards.Offsets can be a mind-deadening subject, but they matter. In Australia, they are known as Australian Carbon Credit Units. Each credit is said to represent one tonne of greenhouse gas that isn’t in the atmosphere and otherwise would have been. They are mostly generated from government-sanctioned projects that are meant to regenerate forests or capture and burn methane released from landfill sites.These type of projects have plenty to recommend them. With global heating moving into increasingly dangerous territory, the world needs to retain and regenerate all the forests it can, and create new ones. It also needs to sharply reduce how much methane and carbon dioxide is poured into the atmosphere.But we need to be realistic about what these carbon credits can and can’t do.double quotation markThe world’s biggest miner decided it was cheaper to buy new polluting trucks and paid for carbon offsetsAustralian carbon credits are treated as a like-for-like alternative for emissions cuts by fossil fuel producers, factories and other big polluting sites. Under the climate policy applied to big industrial facilities responsible for about a third of national pollution – the safeguard mechanism – there is no requirement that businesses make direct emissions cuts. They can just buy an unlimited number of offsets and claim them as their own reductions.This flexibility makes life easier for the owners of industrial sites that, under changes introduced by Labor three years ago, need to cut emissions intensity – the amount of pollution pumped out per unit of production – by between 1% and 4.9% a year. But it also creates problems.Geologically stored carbon that is dug up and used as coal, gas or oil has been underground for millennia. When it is brought to the surface and set on fire it releases heat-trapping gas that otherwise couldn’t escape. That gas can persist in the atmosphere for thousands of years.Sarah Hanson-Young on big tech’s ‘attack on democracy’ - podcastRead moreCarbon stored in nature operates on a much shorter timescale. It’s prone to fire and decay and destruction. There is no guarantee it can be kept out of the atmosphere.The extraordinary forest and peat fires burning on theIndonesian islands of Borneo and Sumatraare a case in point. They are estimated to have released nearly 20m tonnes of carbon dioxide in the first week of September alone.It echoes the vast amount of carbon released in Australian bushfires, particularly the black summer infernos of 2019-20. With arecord-breaking El Niñounder way, the odds of a version of that repeating in the next year or two are shortening.This is a significant problem in its own right, but not the biggest issue with relying on offsets.The Guardian has reported for years on the mountain of evidence that shows limiting the systemic damage from rising temperatures and accelerating extreme weather events requires immediate and sustained direct emissions cuts. AUN Environment Programme reportearlier this month that found global heating will reach 1.8C in a best-case scenario is just the latest example.We will also need strategies to draw CO2 from the atmosphere. But the latter is not a substitute for the former. It is an “and”, not an “or”.This is not a new problem, and the climate change minister, Chris Bowen, has acknowledged direct cuts are necessary. But this is largely not yet reflected in the design of the safeguard mechanism.It is easy enough to understand why this might be the case. Transformational change is hard, and climate policy has been a political killing field in Australia for most of this century. Fossil fuel interests dedicate huge resources to slowing climate action. No political leader wants to be the next victim of the climate wars victim. And the science-denying right is rising again.But those political considerations don’t change the problems with the system.Research in peer-reviewed journals has found the biggest Australian carbon credit methods have provided only a fraction of the emissions reductions that are claimed, while producing tens of millions of offsets. This is disputed, but there has been no project-level investigation to disprove it.The flood of carbon offsets being created means the price of credits is low (less than $40 a tonne of CO2). It gives polluters an incentive to meet their obligations under the safeguard mechanism by paying for credits representing cuts elsewhere rather than directly reducing their footprint.Albanese’s resources minister celebrating the Beetaloo carbon bomb is a hell of a choice. Labor can’t say it wasn’t warned | Clear AirRead moreThere was striking evidence of this earlier this year when the Guardian and ABC’s Four Corners revealed BHP hadscrapped and delayed projects to cut emissions, including stalling plans to replace diesel vehicles at iron ore mine sites with electric trucks. The world’s biggest minerdecided it was cheaper to buy new polluting trucksand pay for carbon offsets.The issue is even more acute with coalmines and fossil gas facilities. While they can take some steps to reduce onsite emissions, they ultimately need to be phased out to cut their pollution.Neither appears to be happening on a meaningful scale. Data from the Clean Energy Regulator, a government agency, shows about two-thirds of the offsets sold in Australia in the last reporting year were bought by fossil fuel companies. Meanwhile,direct pollution from coalmines increased.The government has a chance to address this. A review of the safeguard mechanism, required under law, is under way.There is a compelling argument that the best course would be to start again. Policy experts atNaru ResearchandClimate Analyticshave detailed flaws that go beyond those listed here. The Superpower Institute made a strong case the safeguard should be replaced with a“polluter pays levy”on companies that extract or import fossil fuels consumed in Australia.But assuming the safeguard survives, at least three things should happen.The emissions caps on big polluters, known as baselines, should be tightened to avoid ridiculous cases where some companies arerewardedfor pumping out more CO2than in the past. There should be a audit to remove any low-integrity offsets. And there should be limits on the number of offsets companies can buy.It might help if the government also acknowledges the safeguard should not just encourage industrial sites with a future to clean up their practice, but also push fossil fuel producers that can’t cut their pollution to close earlier than planned.If that doesn’t happen, the safeguard won’t have done its job.Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editorExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisClear airAustralian politicsCarbon offsettingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Earl Spencer SLATES the king. Charles DESTROYS Spencer. If only Diana were here to click on it | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: It’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeef, says the Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: It’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeef, says the Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Charles Spencer  on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, October 2024.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCharles Spencer  on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, October 2024.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockOpinionMonarchyEarl Spencer SLATES the king. Charles DESTROYS Spencer. If only Diana were here to click on itMarina HydeIt’s a battle for hearts and minds – and TikTok, and the ’Gram. Just as it should be. #royalbeefFri 18 Sep 2026 07.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareReading the extracts from Earl Spencer’s book about his sister Diana, and the king’s two-footedtakedown of it, it’s hard to escape the idea that Spencer and the Windsors are just elite content creators now. This entire thing is basically indistinguishable from a blockbuster influencer war, and I honestly won’t be happy till the king puts out a shade TikTok of him driving round the Sandringham estate in sunglasses captioned: “Threatening to release the receipts but never actually releasing the receipts … kinda chic.” Soundtrack: Mariah Carey’s Obsessed.Meanwhile, perhaps trying to disguise his full descent into the algorithm mines, Charles Spencer has started talking like one of those adverts for twee porcelain plates that you used to see in magazine supplements. You know the kind of thing – “these three little kittens are waiting to steal your heart”.Here is the earlon his Diana book, which he has called Swan Song: “At heart, this is a brother’s simple tribute to an extraordinary sister.” Mmm. And simply bound, very simply, into paginated form as a precious, simple keepsake that also functions as one of Penguin Random House’s lead titles for autumn and the run-in to Christmas. Favourite charming tribute from today’s serialisation in the Mail? Probably the bit when Diana drags Spencer for lunch in the London restaurant San Lorenzo to announce: “My husband is in love with his valet”. Nkay.View image in fullscreenKing Charles, then the Prince of Wales, with Charles Spencer, following a banquet in Cape Town not long after Princess Diana’s death in 1997.Photograph: John Stillwell/PABut the biggest tea-spill so far has been Spencer’s claim that Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after Diana’s death, then hissed: “Rest assured … we’ll forget about her soon enough.” Which definitely sounds like the kind of thing a father of two shockingly bereaved children would say if they were the future king character in a book written by someone quite bad at writing.By way of rejoinder,Buckingham Palace issued a statementthat began with the words “while we do not comment on books as a matter of principle”, and then – hilariously – went on to comment on the book. I mean, what principles? You always see these kinds of royal statements described as “highly unusual”, and yet in recent years their sheer frequency suggests they really aren’t. The royal family – and Spencer – do absolutely everything for the ’Gram. It’s all veryAlex Cooper v Alix Earle. I kept reading this week that Charles and William and Kate were “out in force” doing things likeplaying shinty on Buteand hosting AI summits. Yup, living for the timelines. Posting through it.And, indeed, posting about it, as that “we won’t comment on books” statement from the king continued in the more-in-sorrow-than-in-anger vein that is so particular to a contemporary social media drive-by. “His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”Wow. Apart from the pomposity, there is precisely nothing to distinguish this from the same kind of high-horse word salad you see farted out day after day by mid-tier creators involved in online beef about abortive podcast ventures or stolen brand deals. You know the kind of thing: “I’ve stayed quiet till now … But since you want to bring this to the internet, I have receipts. I’m done protecting people. The people who know, know.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Daily Star reports on Charles Spencer’s memoir Swan Song: Diana, My Sister.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty ImagesCharles Spencer has, of course, done a whole book of this stuff, probably making him the one the internet is less likely to side with. For just as it is possible to simply get up in the morning and decide not to post something on social media that makes you look like a complete shit, it is also possible to simply not do a whole book of this stuff. Why can’t Spencer just get a turret brand to sponsor his house upkeep like Molly-Mae would? “Loving our new #pediment and #pilasters! What’s one thing you love about your house? Tell me in the comments.”Instead, here is the earl on his Insta earlier this week: “A month ago I read ‘Swan Song’ out, over three days, for a recording so that it could be available on audiobook. When I finished the recording, I thought: ‘That is exactly what I wanted and needed to say – and she would, I reckon, have approved of every word.’” Oh for sure Diana would have approved. Nailed on.As we know, those who make money off Diana’s memory since she has died tend to do so with the absolute conviction that it’s what she would have wanted. Many of Diana’s indirect financial beneficiaries – her former psychics and energy healers,actors playing her in movies– give interviews announcing that her ghost has visited them to give the seal of approval to whichever commercial venture they’re involved in. Charles Spencer has yet to go down this route with Swan Song, though given the book isn’t actually published till next week – to permit the Mail the best run at the serial rights they paid him a fortune for – we definitely shouldn’t rule out the possibility that he’s keeping something spectral in the bag for the coming days.Ultimately, it’s increasingly impossible to escape the conviction that the royals and those familially connected with them behave as leading influencers – selling the absolute maddest form of lifestyle that you can still somehow pass off as a gift to your followers. The other day I rememberedan interview Prince Harry gavewhen his own book was out, where he said: “I genuinely believe, and I hope, that reconciliation between my family and us will have a ripple effect across the entire world. Maybe that’s lofty, maybe that’s naive.” Or maybe it’s just the lucrative way they all live now. Either way: #amazing.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com.
