title: An effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain? You read that right, and we will not settle for it | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: This scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability services, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: This scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability services, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: ‘Care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills.’Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreen‘Care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills.’Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFOpinionDisabilityAn effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain? You read that right, and we will not settle for itFrances RyanThis scandal shows there are many who don’t expect us to live rich lives – and that paternalism lives on in disability servicesDisabled people in UK need right to travel abroad, say MPs, after ‘ridiculous’ restrictionsFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.34 EDTShareDisabled people are being barred from leaving the country. This isn’t the first line of a dystopian novel but a scandal quietly happening across swathes of England. For the past six months, myself and my colleague Patrick Butler havespoken to disabled peoplewho have effectively been blocked from going abroad on a holiday or to a work event by their local care provider.There’s 38-year-old Lucy from Oxfordshire who needs to travel internationally as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. And Chelsea from Lancashire, a 25-year-old with cerebral palsy who dreams of swimming in Spain again. Then there’s 40-year-old Joel*, who has a muscle weakness and works for a global marketing brand but hasn’t been able to leave the UK for nine years.Some have live-in personal assistants (PAs) via NHS continuing healthcare, the non-means-tested home support for people with high needs. Others have 24/7 social care through their local authority. But when they try to leave the country, all hit the same wall: they are told they are not allowed to use their care package abroad, sometimes even if they pay any extra costs themselves.Here’s the plot twist. Some areas of the country are permitting care users to go on holiday or travel for work – while disabled people just a few miles down the road can be stopped. Others are told they can travel but have to pay any extra expenses – effectively still barring them financially from going – while some care boards offer to cover the cost. As there is limited to no national guidance on the issue, disabled people’s right to travel depends on a postcode lottery, with local care officials inspecting their plans for a trip away and having the power to rule “go” or “stay”.This week,MPs and peers called for national guidelinesto end this injustice. Figures such as the work and pensions select committee chair, Debbie Abrahams, the crossbench peer Jane Campbell and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn told the Guardian that the government must guarantee the rights of disabled people to travel and ensure they have the support they need to do so.You can practically hear the right preparing to oppose the move with a cry of “Free holidays on the NHS!” But care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills. Disabled people who need 24/7 support for everyday activities already have care funding in place, and in many cases use their own money to pay PAs’ travel expenses, such as accommodation and plane tickets (on top of the already extortionate price of accessible travel). When Lucy was told by her care board she couldn’t take her PAs to a spinal cord conference in Germany this spring, her employer had already offered to pay any additional costs.View image in fullscreenBlocked from travel: Lucy, who needs to travel as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe question, then, is why would authorities want to stop disabled people going abroad? If it’s not just about tight budgets, why should it matter to them how an adult chooses to use their care package? You could say that it’s about practicalities: it’s easier not to worry about insurance or visas (disabled people largely sort this themselves for their PAs anyway). But it seems naive not to think there’s some prejudice lurking under the bureaucracy. Blocking disabled people from going on holiday or working abroad goes to the heart of cultural assumptions about disability: that we don’t have careers or families or friends like other, “normal” people.Sixty years afterdisabled people left institutionsand were able to live independently, alongside the vast gains, the stain of paternalistic control still lurks in disability services. It’s the social worker who suggests you get a commode next to your sofa because it’s cheaper than an accessible bathroom. It’s the care worker who speaks very slowly to you and picks your clothes out on your behalf. It’s the occupational therapist who suggests you get a hospital-style bed that your husband can’t fit in (and is visibly surprised you have a husband).We’re not supposed to talk about this stuff. There’s an unwritten rule that says disabled people should be just grateful for what they’re given by the state, lest we appear to be scroungers or burdens. I say “unwritten”. It’s written in some newspapers most weeks.It is uncomfortable, I suppose, in part because it is so ordinary. This isn’t the sort of prejudice that comes with an ableist slur or a violent push. It is the gentle, everyday belief that certain kinds of lives – certain kinds of people – come with low expectations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI had an amazing experience as a disabled person at school in the 70s. Since then, discrimination has got far worse | Mik ScarletRead moreJust look at the way much of the political and media class discuss social care. In the rare instances that younger disabled people are mentioned alongside elderly people, social care is still solely spoken about in terms of personal care – say, help to wash or prepare a meal. As Andy Burnham has put reform of the care sector on the agenda in recent months, it’s notable there has been little talk of its role in supporting a disabled person’s family role or career: whether that’s help to drop the kids off at school on the way to the office or to get to the pub to celebrate a friend’s birthday.That’s understandable. Underthe current system, as many as 1.5 million disabled people in England are left without access to even the most basic help. If you are suffering the indignity of sitting in soiled clothes because a care worker hasn’t arrived to assist you to the bathroom, it can feel pointless – delusional, even – to mention you’ve not seen the sea in years.But to settle for this state of affairs forces disabled people to accept a half-life, to be relieved to at least be clean and fed, and to try to forget the colour that defines being human. It diminishes not only our humanity but the principle that disability campaigners fought for decades for and underpins the modern care system: for disabled people to have choice and independence over our lives, just like everyone else.When I recently spoke to Campbell, who has 24/7 PAs herself, about the care abroad scandal, she said something telling: “It’s as if those controlling [these decisions] believe disabled people don’t deserve the same experiences they enjoy.”As pressure for national guidelines mounts, I can’t help but think that is a wise litmus test. Would you expect a non-disabled person to live like this? And if not, why do you think it’s OK for disabled people?*Name has been changedFrances Ryan is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDisabilityOpinionSocial careCare workersEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big response, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big response, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionDevolutionSlowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UKSimon JenkinsIt’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big responseFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.19 EDTShareMonday must have been a historical first. Never before have three of the four “nations” of the United Kingdom jointlydemanded freedomto vote for its dissolution. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have lost confidence in England. They declared in Cardiff that the unionist government at Westminster is “coming to an end”.There was no such Celtic alliance against the Normans, Edward I or Cromwell. Celtic MPs have never formed a voting coalition in parliament. The Victorian Liberal party advanced “home rule for all”, but that was not independence and it got nowhere.Irelandrebelled, but it did so alone. When this eventually succeeded, Britain said good riddance, kept hold of Belfast and continued to centralise power in London.So this is serious stuff. Yet London politics this week treated the declaration as on a par with the Oxfordshire village of Piddingtonvoting to go it aloneto ward off the possibility of asylum seekers being housed nearby.The UK’s only serious geographical devolution came in 1999. It was half-hearted, mostly decentralising the running of the welfare state. But it surged the vote for Scottish and Welsh separatism and fed rather than abated the cause of independence. We can only imagine if ruling parties in Bavaria or Provence or Sicily had opted for independence from Germany, France or Italy – or if California said it had enough of Donald Trump’s US. The result would be political eruption.What does theCardiff “memorandum of understanding”actually mean? The answer is not much in detail. There was advocacy of policy collaboration, as on childcare and economic growth. There were hints of moves towards further devolution, of the sort promised by Andy Burnham. But there was no suggestion of a new Celtic state, a British Celtica. The talks seemed to concentrate on self-determination, which Burnham had described as “off limits”, at least in the case of Scotland. Yet this was a man who declared self-determination for the Falklands would be defended even at the cost of tens of millions of pounds a year.The reality is that these three nations of the union have markedly different relations with England. Northern Ireland’s bipartisan government, a legacy of civil war and the Good Friday agreement, is clearly dysfunctional.As Donald Trump remarked last week, it really should advance toward Irish union.As interfaith relations slowly improve, a possible majority in favour of reunion also becomes more plausible. Support for union in Northern Irelandis now around one-third, with a majority among the young. Self-determination is not in Burnham’s gift but is written into Northern Ireland’s constitution. Observers accept that it must and will happen one day.Wales may also have a majority of its under-35sin favourof independence. But only a bare Welsh majorityvoted foreven mild devolution in 1997 and support for independencehovers at 32%. The poor performance of the Welsh health and education services makes self-government ever more alarming, and the generosity of the London Exchequer ever more essential. Perhaps the novelty of the new Plaid Cymru government can transform things, but Welsh independence is at best a distant fantasy.This leavesScotland. Here independence is an active issue. The population of 5.5 million puts the country in the 5-10 million band of Europe’s medium-sized states, such as Denmark, Norway, Finland, Austria and Switzerland. “Small is beautiful” appears to suit Europe’s distinctive welfare economies and keeps them ahead of their larger neighbours.Scottish unionists keep pointing toScotland’s £25bn fiscal deficit, financed by London’s Treasury and sustaining the country’s struggling health service. But independence is a dynamic not static state. In 1922 Ireland wasamong the poorest countries in Europe, far behind Scotland. Its economic self-sufficiency seemed hopeless, and for some 30 years it was indeed in desperate straits. Yet by the 1990s Irish membership of the EU and the adoption of a fierce fiscal autonomy had utterly transformed it into the celebrated “Celtic Tiger”. From limping behind Scotland and other poorer European regions, Dublin raced ahead. It has become one of Europe’s richest nations per capita, albeit partly thanks to its status as a base for corporate tax avoidance.Ireland’s burst of economic vitality in the late 20th century could never have taken place had it remained an adjunct of Britain. Income per head is now ahead of Scotland’s, having once lagged far behind. It grew between 2012 and 2022by 9%on average, against Scotland’s 1%. Whether Ireland is richer than Denmark is much debated, but the performance of an autonomous Ireland cannot be gainsaid. It is a lighthouse for the macro-economics of smallness.There is every reason why Scotland could feel held back by longstanding English dominance. Its economy, like the rest of Britain’s, has always been down the queue from London and the south-east. It has long felt cheated of its maritime oil and gas reserves. Trade has been crippled by Brexit. Unionists argue that theBarnett formula subsidy of £50bn a yearis fair compensation. But Ireland’s experience suggests that dependence on foreign subsidy is a curse, not a blessing. The most glaring comparative statistic is that health outcomes in both Ireland and Denmarkare now well ahead of Scotland’s. The scale of Glasgow’s drug deaths are a horror story.British loyalist though I may be, if I were a Scot I would have no hesitation. This is a real nation, and has been throughout history. Scotland has a personality and a culture recognised worldwide. Its capital, Edinburgh, is among Europe’s finest cities. Its “Silicon Glen” should be leading Europe’s AI revolution. Tourism is an obvious attraction. That the country should stumble behind its Nordic neighbours is absurd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland would have a tough transition to self-reliance, as did Ireland. But experience everywhere suggests that small autonomous democracies fare well, witness other relative newcomers such as Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the Baltics. Their governments can concentrate on their own priorities and promote their own virtues.An independent Scotland would be bespoke. It could retain its royal figurehead and Commonwealth membership. It could even honour a “united kingdom” and the king could stay in Balmoral. Relations with other states, EU and non-EU, would be complicated, as they are at borders across the continent. That is for diplomacy to resolve. The issue is self-determination, not convenience.Burnham is the first British prime minister to appear sincere in decentralising political power. How far he understands its significance is moot. His beloved “metro mayors” are accountable regionally, not representatives of truly local loyalties. They appear as his agents, enacting his policies and enforcing his planning quotas on subordinate councils. He has shown he will stamp the Piddingtons of England into the ground.That is why Burnham should welcome any Scottish desire for “independence”. It would be the most exciting constitutional reform of the UK in centuries and one that, on current figures, would save the Treasury around £25bn a year – the cost of the Scottish fiscal deficit. It would also release the Tartan Tiger.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDevolutionOpinionScotlandNorthern IrelandIrelandWalesScottish independenceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Think it’s time for gen Z to ‘grow up’? You’re even more out of touch than the British state | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: We can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching on, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: We can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching on, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Young people at the London job show in Westfield White City shopping centre, May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYoung people at the London job show in Westfield White City shopping centre, May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianOpinionYoung peopleThink it’s time for gen Z to ‘grow up’? You’re even more out of touch than the British stateGaby HinsliffWe can’t expect young people to make a seamless transition from childhood to adulthood in this chilly economic climate. Finally, Westminster is catching onFri 18 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTShareWhen did you realise you had finally grown up? It’s a trick question, obviously: maturity is just realising that life is full of things you don’t feel old enough for but somehow manage anyway, while getting better at pretending to know what you’re doing. But the question is worth asking nonetheless, because for gen Z the goalposts of grownup life are clearly shifting.It’s a truism that adulting now comes later than it did to generations who still don’t consider adulting a verb, with43% of 25-year-olds still living at homeand plenty more jobless university graduatesboomeranging back there this summer, thanks to a grim labour market. Since they’ll probably be working longer into what were once retirement years, perhaps it’s only natural that they’re taking longer to get started. But there’s a fine line between choosing to grow up more slowly and becoming trapped into a kind of limbo between childhood and adulthood, with nobody to pull you out of the morass beyond parents who aren’t sure how to handle this new life stage either.If your unemployed 22-year-old is getting rejection after rejection, should you rewrite their job applications for them, or let them figure it out for themselves? What do you do with an 18-year-old too depressed to leave their bedroom, now they’re old enough to make their own GP appointments but not mature enough to know they need one? Kidulthood can be a minefield.The idea that the state should recognise the years roughly between 18 and 25 as a phase distinct from either childhood or full adulthood, which needs its own tailored policies, is catching on around Westminster.The Nuffield Foundationcharitable trust, which has spent two years researching changing journeys to adulthood, held a seminar this week drawing together threads from academia to Alan Milburn’s genuinely thoughtful review of what is causing so many young people to be Neet (not in education, employment or training). As Milburn put it to theNuffield Foundation’s Carey Oppenheim, councils have to ensure that teenagers are studying or training up to 18, but what happens after that is not their problem. Yet in the Netherlands, the state’s responsibilities extend up to 24 or, in some cases, 27. Guess which country has fewer Neets.More broadly, he suggested, the British state may be too quick to shrug off responsibility for young people struggling with the transition to adulthood. “We haven’t aligned now with the reality of the transitions that young people are going through in their lives,” he said.In Australia, Oppenheim points out, the equivalent of Britain’s children and adolescent mental health services runs from age 12 right up to age 25, recognising a growing argument within medicine that adolescence doesn’t end neatly at 19. But in Britain, teenagers still hit a cliff edge, tumbling abruptly out of children’s mental health services into adult ones where the threshold for intervention can be far higher. Even the new social media ban for under-16s assumes teenagers are mature enough at 17 to handle what they couldn’t the day before.Meanwhile theIPPR thinktank’s State of A Generationproject, another deep dive into the coming of age process, warns of a society where “transitions to adulthood are blocked” and young people are increasingly nihilistic about their future.There’s much we still don’t understand about this evolving life stage, including how far to accept it and how far to push back. If a quarter of 18- to 34-year-olds living with their parents say they’re genuinelyhappy at home or not ready to leave, rather than feeling stuck, does that imply a worrying failure to launch? Or, asthe demographer Prof Ann Berringtonargues, a new form of “privileged dependence”, where some young people enjoy a financial and emotional security that ultimately boosts them into adult life, and it’s the young people who can’t go home in a crisis we should worry about?There’s an obvious danger here of over-babying young people, potentially making them even more anxious in the process, or of the state intruding too far into the lives of twentysomethings who are coping fine. As the parent of a 19-year-old, I’m well aware that gen Z are often far more resilient and competent than they get credit for.But a significant minority do seem to be falling into a gap between childhood and adulthood, and in a chilly economic climate they look increasingly exposed. Maybe the real mark of having finally grown up is feeling ready to help someone else do the same.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis article was amended on 18 September 2026. An earlier version described the Nuffield Foundation as a “thinktank”. In fact it is constituted as a charitable trust.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsYoung peopleOpinionYouth unemploymentGenerational inequalityInequalityUnemploymentcommentShareReuse this content

title: The spectre of ‘remigration’ is haunting Europe. Slovenia in 1992 gives us a blueprint for this state terror | Miha Mazzini | The Guardian
description: In February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrants, says writer and film-maker Miha Mazzini
Author: Miha Mazzini
Headline: In February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrants, says writer and film-maker Miha Mazzini
Content: Pedestrians crossing a bridge in Ljubljana, Slovenia.Photograph: DavorLovincic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPedestrians crossing a bridge in Ljubljana, Slovenia.Photograph: DavorLovincic/Getty ImagesOpinionSloveniaThe spectre of ‘remigration’ is haunting Europe. Slovenia in 1992 gives us a blueprint for this state terrorMiha MazziniIn February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrantsFri 18 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.48 EDTShareSo much of your daily life – your job, your health, your home – hinges on the fact that your name is in a government database. Are you a legal citizen of your country, with everything that entails? You are, until an anonymous bureaucrat hits a key one night and strips it all away, turning you into an illegal immigrant. It happened inSloveniain 1992.“I took my son to register for secondary school. The clerk rifled through the papers, then stared at me as if refusing to see the boy standing right next to me. Finally, she said: ‘But you don’t have a son. He doesn’t exist.’” I can’t forget the look on the face of the woman who was telling me this story. It was a mixture of deep hurt and bewilderment, with a pause after every sentence, as if she were walking through a minefield. During the research for my book Erased, I compiled countless stories like this: stories I once would have thought impossible.On 26 February 1992, the Slovenian government quietly deleted 1.3% of its citizenry overnight. The criterion was frighteningly simple: anyone born in another part of the former Yugoslavia who was a permanent resident of Slovenia (regardless of whether they considered themselves naturalised) suddenly lost their citizenship, their right to reside, their healthcare, their pension: everything. They were transformed into illegal immigrants overnight, without prior notification, and with no right to appeal. The goal was to cleanse Slovenia of a Balkan “fifth column” and pivot closer toEurope.I have long felt this dark piece of Slovenian history to be an ugly stain on the conscience of my nation; but its spirit is spreading across Europe and beyond. The horrors of migrant deaths in the Mediterranean and the English Channel are regularly witnessed and documented, the victims dying at the very gates of “fortress Europe”. But even if you are already inside the fortress, even if you consider yourself fully naturalised, you are perhaps no longer safe. In an age of constant video surveillance, there is nothing fantastical about an official refusing to renew a permit, or unearthing a minor “offence” committed decades earlier, to strip away your citizenship.The spectre of “remigration” is haunting Europe, and its shadow looms ever larger. What Slovenia did in 1992 has become a blueprint for a quiet, bureaucratic form of state terror.The woman who told me about her son lived in a village equidistant between two towns. During her pregnancy, she had to choose between two maternity hospitals. After the collapse of Yugoslavia, the town she had picked was across the new border in Croatia, while her village remained in Slovenia. And so, on that fateful day in 1992, her son ceased to exist. His story had a happy ending: Slovenia is a very small country, and if you have a wide enough network, you’ll eventually find someone who knows someone. So the boy emerged from the ranks of the disappeared and was able to attend school. But for those without friends in high places, things rarely ended happily.View image in fullscreenA 2015 exhibition in Ljubljana showing passports belonging to the erased.Photograph: Jure Makovec/AFP/Getty ImagesOne man was rushing to work, speeding, when he was pulled over by the police. Unable to find him in the registry, they took him to an asylum centre. He had been born in Serbia, but Slovenia’s only border with the former Yugoslavia is with Croatia. So they deported him there instead. Croatia was at war with Serbia at the time, and the man was treated as a prisoner of war. He was lucky: had he been born in Croatia, he would have been conscripted and sent straight to the frontlines.For six years, 1.3% of the population hid and survived however they could. They worked illegally for subsistence wages, at the mercy of bosses and landlords. One man locked himself in his flat, eating old canned food, refusing to open the door to anyone. It was a wise strategy. There were cases of the erased returning home to find their locks changed: someone had simply claimed and occupied their flat, realising the victim would have no recourse to call the police.There were also stories of profound kindness: a citizen who officially contracted every disease imaginable because he kept lending his healthcare card to the erased; a waitress who walked out of her shift with a first aid kit to treat an injured, erased man who had just been thrown out of the hospital. Relying on the kindness of strangers, however, is a lottery I wouldn’t wish on anyone.In 1998, the Slovenian constitutional court ruled the erasure unconstitutional, and the immediate threat subsided. But thelong road to restoring rightsand securing measly compensation for the victims turned into agruelling odysseythat, for some, continues to this day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA monument has sincebeen erectedfor the erased in Ljubljana, and a park named after them. But it is always easier to build a monument than to issue an apology, let alone settle dues. The UK has its own unresolved equivalent in the Windrush generation – andtheir monument is standing, too.Many of the erased never doubted their status because they considered themselves Slovenians. Overnight, they were expected to deport themselves to countries they had no meaningful connection to. I was reminded of their fate when reading about the US administration’s “operation second look”, which entails ICE agents scavenging decades-old files for minor administrative discrepancies in the hope of stripping people of their citizenship.As it so often does, Europe follows America’s lead.Gregory Bovino,the former US Border Patrol “commander-at-large”, was recently in Europe and treated like a rock star. At arightwing gatheringin Portugal he noted that he and the Austrianethnonationalist Martin Sellnerare “on the same sheet of music”. Perhaps the original Slovenian experiment in “remigration” was indeed exactly what it was claimed to be back then: a step closer to Europe, but a meaner and more sinister version of Europe.Miha Mazzini is a writer, film-maker and anthropologistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treason | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Politicians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidence
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Politicians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidence
Content: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham face being stripped of their citizenship for treason.Photograph: Maria Laura Antonelli/AGF/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham face being stripped of their citizenship for treason.Photograph: Maria Laura Antonelli/AGF/ShutterstockOpinionNAZAThe Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treasonEditorialPoliticians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidenceFri 18 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTShareAcross Israel, politicians, military leaders and much of the media are trying to discredit a documentary that almost none of them have seen. Produced by the Guardian, NAZA examines theAI-powered targeting systemsused by the Israel Defense Forces to bombard Gaza after Hamas’s brutal 7 October 2023 attacks. Named after the Israeli military acronym euphemistically usedfor “collateral damage”, NAZA features interviews with 24 anonymous insiders who reflect on their role in the death-dealing. Israeli leaders have branded the film a “blood libel” and “fiction”. Its Oscar-winning directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, face beingstrippedof their citizenship for treason.This is absurd. NAZAshowshow bureaucratic distance and routine can turn extreme violence into ordinary work. More than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 20,000 children, have been killed in the campaign by Israel’s military. A democracy that values life would at least investigate the film’s claims. Instead Israel’s government, which says it is committed to democratic accountability, is attacking journalists.The allegations in NAZA come from military insiders. For many, it does not appear to be remorse that drives them to speak out. Some are proud of what they have done. One recalls the“insane fun”of planning airstrikes in Gaza. Crucially, Israeli soldiers describe the military accepting large numbers of Palestinian casualties as the price for killing a single Hamas operative. When civilian fatalities rise to as many as hundreds for one enemy combatant, proportionality looks less like a military assessment and more like a licence for mass death.NAZA’sstoryis not only about death and destruction but also some of the people behind it: polite, educated members of Israel’s liberal middle class, much like the directors themselves. They built and operated a system that told them women and children would die in large numbers. Yet they told themselves that responsibility for the deaths of innocent Palestinians lay elsewhere. The acronym, NAZA, turns possible fatalities into a number per target. By the time an operator approves a strike, morality has disappeared up the chain of command.An election campaign has seen Israeli politicians shamefully weaponise controversy to outflank each other on the right. If such leaders are saying that the conduct of the Israeli military is beyond independent review, that can hardly be consistent with the commitment to the rule of law. Israel’s government might invoke national security to defend its actions. But the film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Ominously, Israel’s domestic intelligence service may be involved in a leak investigation. By turning the army on the documentary’s directors, Israel is making anexampleof them. Far-right activists target their families by making threats. If the filmmakers were to return to Israel now, their lives might well be indanger.TheCommittee to Protect Journalistsand 10 other press-freedom groups have warned that Israel must protect its journalists and filmmakers – not brand them traitors and paint targets on their backs. Yet the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has seized on the controversy to threaten anyone who “defames” Israeli soldiers with loss of citizenship. Rather than investigate alleged crimes, he would punish those who expose them. Israel’s leaders ought to be protecting those who scrutinise power, not pointing a mob towards them.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Eating is my superpower’: Nigella turns up the heat on Bake Off | The Great British Bake Off | The Guardian
description: The domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty Gang
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: The domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty Gang
Content: Sweet and sour … Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood in the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Patch Dolan / Channel 4View image in fullscreenSweet and sour … Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood in the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Patch Dolan / Channel 4The Great British Bake OffInterview‘Eating is my superpower’: Nigella turns up the heat on Bake OffMichael HoganThe domestic goddess is about to be let loose in the Bake Off tent. Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood spill the beans about bonding over dirty martinis, ‘Professor Precision’ – and why they call themselves the Salty GangFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike the Cleopatra of cake, new Great British Bake Off judge Nigella Lawson reclines on a chaise longue throughout our interview, gently fanning herself. Fellow judgePaul Hollywoodchuckles from a nearby armchair. “She’d sit like this between takes in the tent,” he says indulgently. “Reading a book and sipping a coffee while someone fed her grapes.” “Peeled grapes,” specifies Lawson with a grin.After Prue Leith stepped down from soggy bottom-spotting duties in January – on the unarguable basis that “I’m 86, for goodness sake!” – there was widespread jubilation when Lawson was announced as her replacement. The arrival of the domestic goddess has created serious buzz around Bake Off’s upcoming series. A contest that was at risk of growing stale has become essential viewing again, thanks to the velvet-voiced, spatula-licking doyenne of culinary TV.“It was lovely to see Nigella come into the tent,” says Hollywood. “We’ve only had two changes to the judging team in 16 years but it’s worked really well. I’ve always been a big fan and she fitted in beautifully – not just with me but with the whole team. She picked up the Bake Off vibe straight away. It was pretty seamless, actually.”View image in fullscreen‘Even Paul got the giggles!’ … Paul Hollywood and Nigella Lawson in the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch DolanHer TV career was launched with Nigella Bites way back in 1999. Why Bake Off, and why now? “I wanted to do something a bit different,” says Lawson. “I’ve written many books, which I adore, but it means spending a lot of time alone. I was keen to be part of something bigger, part of a team. When I was approached about Bake Off, I instinctively thought: ‘That would be lovely.’ It almost feels too good to be true that you can enjoy something this much and call it work.”Predictably, there have been tabloid rumours that the judgely duo have been butting heads. Lawson allegedly said that Hollywood arriving on set at Welford Park in a helicopter was “cringe”, which is all the evidence gossipmongers need. Yet there’s no sign of tension on screen, let alone today. Their conversation is full of good-natured ribbing and punctuated by peals of laughter. Hollywood seems enchanted by his new partner-in-cake, while Lawson is endearingly self-effacing, all too aware that she’s joining a long-running hit and simply doesn’t want to “stuff it up”.Before her appointment was confirmed, the pair had an unofficial chemistry test at a Channel 4 event. “We chatted for 10 minutes and had a great time, didn’t we?” recalls Lawson. “I knew instantly it was going to work. It surprised even us, I think, how well we hit it off. It was lucky that we did get on. Can you imagine if we didn’t? I bet Paul would have said so!”What does she like about the marquee’s resident master baker? “One of the many lovely things about Paul is that he’s good at being teased. I called him ‘Professor Precision’, then he teased me back and suddenly it all relaxed. He’s much more playful than he looks on camera. He often acts bad cop and does that laser stare but he’s always himself, which encourages other people to be themselves, too. We complement each other. He gets straight to the point and, as you can tell, I’m a witterer. I love talking about food and sometimes can’t stop. When I wittered on in the tent, I did see him go like this once …” She mimes pretending to nod off. He shrugs unrepentantly.Once she was officially onboard, Lawson hosted separate bonding sessions with her co-stars. “I decided to meet everyone properly before we started,” she says. “I didn’t want the first time we hung out together to be on set.” Hollywood came first. “I went for drinks at Nigella’s house,” he remembers. Oh, to be a fly on the wall. Was there food? “Salami, olives, that kind of thing,” says Lawson. “I wasn’t going to bake for him. That would be madness.” “I was disappointed,” deadpans Hollywood. “I was hoping for a cake on a gingham altar.”View image in fullscreenOven ready … (from left) Paul Hollywood, Alison Hammond, Nigella Lawson and Noel FieldingPhotograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4“Play your cards right and you never know,” she shoots back. “No, I wanted it to be as relaxed as possible. Paul brought a bottle of red wine and said: ‘Do you want a glass?’ I said, ‘You’ll have to open it yourself. I’m wearing a white suit!’ And we went from there.” Next came co-hosts Noel Fielding andAlison Hammond. “Noel came round for tea and I did make him a cake,” Lawson confesses. “Oh, thanks very much,” says Hollywood.“I love Noel,” she continues. “He and I look like two ghouls first thing in the morning.” “Two goths, climbing out of your coffins,” laughs Hollywood. Lawson puts her pale forearm next to his teak-tanned one. “Look! I have to be painted a bit brown, otherwise it’d cause issues for the camera.” And Hammond? “I met Alison at This Morning and we went out to lunch. I hitched a ride to the restaurant in her car and we were practically married by the time we arrived. We have a real laugh together and talked about everything.”The love affair seems to be mutual. Fielding has compared her to “an Italian film star”, while Hammond says: “We’re obsessed.” As they pose for photos, Hammond whispers: “Doesn’t Nigella look beautiful? She’s a vision!” “Stop it,” scoffs Lawson modestly.When the casting call came, it wasn’t an immediate yes. “I was apprehensive at first,” she admits. “I wasn’t sure whether I was even qualified and mindful that it was a risk, both for me and the show. So I had a big meeting with the producers and said: ‘Look, these are the things I can’t do.’ They said: ‘That’s OK, that’s what Paul does.’ I didn’t want them to go to the wrong shop, as it were. I’m not a scientist, a technician or a professional baker but what I can do is talk about food, its taste, texture and why I like it. I said: ‘If you now decide you don’t want me after all, I promise I won’t be offended.’ Happily they still did.”Hollywood previously formed partnerships with Dame Mary Berry and Dame Prue Leith. He refers to their successor in regal terms: “I’ve gone dame, dame, queen. I loved working with Mary. She’s got a lot of bantz, has Bez. We made a good team with Mel and Sue. We’d watch Eurovision, all sitting on the bed in dressing gowns. Prue and I would open a bottle of wine and put the world to rights. Nigella and I have done a very similar thing – not with wine but with a couple of dirty martinis or spicy margaritas.”Lawson describes her judging style as “pretty direct”. “I assumed I was going to be good cop but realised I just have to be honest. I can’t pretend if I don’t like something. Honesty can feel a bit brutal but you’re not critiquing the person, you’re critiquing the bake. It’s not personal. We’ve all got our own palate and can only speak subjectively.” This double act have their own areas of expertise. “I talk about flavour because eating is my superpower. I’m learning from Paul, though. I’ll start stealing all his lines, going: ‘This needs another three minutes, turn the oven up 20 degrees.’ But on the whole, I talk taste and he talks technique. You’ve got to play to your strengths.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs an avowed Bake Off superfan – she reels off a list of her favourite alumni, from series one winner Edd Kimber through to last year’s Jasmine Mitchell – how was walking into the fabled tent for the first time? “Oh god, a bit overwhelming,” she confesses. “But I held hands with Alison, which helped. It felt daunting but became cosy within about two minutes.”This year, the climate crisis came for Bake Off. We’re meeting on one of summer’s most sweltering days, with temperatures hitting 35 degrees. Was it this hot in the tent during filming? “Hotter, like a greenhouse” grimaces Lawson. “Plus you’ve got a mic pack on, which is like wearing a mini radiator. The bakers coped well, considering.” Were there melting chocolate disasters? “It was more caramel that was the issue,” says Hollywood. “There were some sticky moments.” “And that was just Paul,” quips Lawson.Don’t expect mention of microwaves. Lawsonwent viralin 2020 when she jokingly referred to her “meecro-wah-vay” – a clip shortlisted as one of Bafta’s TV moments of the year. It was a family in-joke and she’s determined to resist saying it again, instead calling it “the you-know-what”. Bake Off viewers, however, should listen out for a reference to “desecrated coconut”.View image in fullscreenLine-up … (from left) Gabe, Nikki, Shannon, Danni, Mo, Clara, Tom, Molly, Yannis, Gary, Moyin, and Connie are the new contestants on the Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Love Productions/Channel 4Her predecessor Leith had a penchant for boozy bakes. Does Lawson have a similar sweet spot? “It’s not a sweet one, actually,” says Hollywood. “Nigella loves salt.” “I don’t mean over-salty,” she says. “Just that a pinch of salt can balance the sweetness. Similarly, I love anything citrus. A tang of sharp and bitter, rather than unadulterated sweetness. That’s why having raspberries in a vanilla cake is nice. They all tease me, saying: ‘Just add a tablespoon of salt and she’ll like it.’ I’m landed with that now.” “So much so that our WhatsApp group is called Salty Gang,” says Hollywood. Who’s the most active? “Not us,” says Lawson. “It’s mostly Noel and Alison sending funny stuff. We just reply with laughing emojis, like old people.”The Nigella factor is likely to give Britain’s biggest cookery show a ratings boost. “She’s a breath of fresh air, for sure,” says Hollywood. “Certainly for my male mates. They’ve told me they’ll be tuning in for the first time in 16 bloody years!”Lawson demurs. “Not trying to be humble but it’s not about me. I’m joining a long-established, deeply loved show. Bake Off is a national treasure with a fabulous audience. It’s been part of people’s lives over many years. I wouldn’t blame them if they thought: ‘Oi, why is she coming on my programme?’ As long as I don’t actively drive people away, I’ll be happy.” Will the viewing figures include the new judge herself? “I don’t like watching myself but I do want to see it because there’s an awful lot of action that we’re not around for. I’ll fast-forward through my bits and watch the bakers.”During her first time in the tent, the new recruit had a hoot. “We sometimes did a bit too much rabbiting and got told to shush,” says Lawson. “We had so much fun. Even Paul got the giggles. Alison once sent us out of the tent in disgrace. Paul’s very good at remaining poker-faced and then when nobody else is looking, he makes faces at you.” Has Hammond succeeded in her mission to get them all dancing? “I cannot dance on camera, I told her that,” says Lawson. “As judges, we need to retain a modicum of decorum and dignity … we try, anyway.”Salty and sassy, it sounds like La Lawson is in the tent to stay. “Bake Off’s like Hotel California,” says Hollywood. “You can check out any time you like but you can never leave. And I think Nigella’s here for good.”The Great British Bake Off returns on Tuesday22 Septemberat 8pm on Channel 4.Explore more on these topicsThe Great British Bake OffTelevisionReality TVNigella LawsonPaul HollywoodAlison HammondNoel FieldingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The man’s a psychopath when it comes to hedgerows’: Derek vs Derek, the unexpectedly heartwarming doc about farmers at war | Movies | The Guardian
description: One Devon farmer, called Derek, is committed to rewilding his land. His neighbour, also a Derek, tends cattle and crops. What happened when a film-maker decided to follow the bickering pair?
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: One Devon farmer, called Derek, is committed to rewilding his land. His neighbour, also a Derek, tends cattle and crops. What happened when a film-maker decided to follow the bickering pair?
Content: At loggerheads … Derek Gow and Derek Banbury.Photograph: Joss BarrattView image in fullscreenAt loggerheads … Derek Gow and Derek Banbury.Photograph: Joss BarrattMoviesInterview‘The man’s a psychopath when it comes to hedgerows’: Derek vs Derek, the unexpectedly heartwarming doc about farmers at warPatrick BarkhamOne Devon farmer, called Derek, is committed to rewilding his land. His neighbour, also a Derek, tends cattle and crops. What happened when a film-maker decided to follow the bickering pair?Fri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerek Gow and Derek Banbury should hate each other. Gow is an outspoken rewilder widely credited with bringing back the beaver in England. As he returns his Devon sheep farm to wild nature, he is also breeding storks, wildcats, red-backed shrikes, glowworms and even adders to return to the countryside. Over the hedge, Banbury, his neighbour, is proud to be an intensive farmer, producing milk and beef cattle behind tightly clipped hedges.“It’s like he’s just gone mad,” says Banbury of Gow at the start ofDerek vs Derek, an illuminating and unexpectedly funny new documentary that follows the pair over three years. “And the madness is now crossing the road on to my land.”What begins as a portrait of neighbours at war, with no hope of bridging the chasm between modern chemical farmers and idealistic rewilders, or between the needs of food production and the worsening extinction crisis, is slowly and subtly upended, as the two Dereks learn to live alongside each other and hopeful seeds of common ground are sown.Documentary-maker James Dawson started following Gow as he sold the last of his sheep, planning a film about the dramatic changes brought about by rewilding his farm. Then, when Dawson first visited Gow, he was put up at the Banburys, where wife Linda has turned former pigsties and old sheds into holiday cottages. As soon as Dawson met Derek Banbury over breakfast in the farmhouse kitchen, he knew he had to make a rather different film.As well as a boundary, both Dereks share a certain charisma, bloody-mindedness, business acumen and, actually, a love of animals. Gow is an imposing, fast-talking, sweary Scot who criticises “showers of morons” in conservation for convening endless committees while species plummet towards extinction. He’s equally disdainful of farmers “spaffing” public money on Land Rovers and sticking sheep on overgrazed pastures and feeding them fish-meal from the Gambia, “raping what’s left of a disastrous environment to produce something that nobody wants”.Meanwhile, Banbury, who has an impish grin and quick wit, is unrepentant about agribusiness. “I love farming,” he declares in the film. “Intensive farming, that’s supplying the world with food. The population’s getting bigger. It’s not getting smaller, and everyone is going to be happy if they’ve got full bellies. I’ve done it for 50 years and I won’t change. I won’t change.” Or will he?double quotation markThe auctioneer called out: ‘Derek, hair and makeup’s waiting,’ right in front of everyone, and they all started laughingDerek BanburyI find both Dereks in the Banburys’ kitchen, where Linda is doling out tea and cake and Banbury’s four grownup children (three daughters and one son) and dogs are bustling around. They are preparing to welcome an audience of farmers, neighbours and friends to a special preview of Derek vs Derek, which is being shown on a temporary screen erected in the Banburys’ biggest, newest barn.Banbury is laughing, but he is also raging: the production company was duty-bound to bring in a health and safety officer, and he’s been instructed to reduce the number of chairs in the barn. “It’s my farm! Nobody tells me what to do!” he says. “I’ve done what I wanted for 50 years.”“It’s in case there’s a fire,” reasons his eldest daughter, Katie.“Oh, for God’s sake! It’s a steel building and concrete walls. If there’s a fire, people will run out quickly.”“My Derek doesn’t get cross often,” says Linda. “But he’s cross now.”It takes all four Banbury children to calm Derek down. A few chairs are shuffled around to enable a swift evacuation. Meanwhile, Banbury admits he was “a little bit” reluctant to appear in a film where he assumed Gow would be the hero. “Then James [Dawson] started going outside and filming some of my animals. Then they came up with a little payment, and it started from there.”View image in fullscreenField of dreams … Farmer and rewilding advocate Derek Gow.Photograph: Joss BarrattWhen Dawson’s cameras followed Banbury to the local cattle market, the farmer got some stick. The auctioneer called out “‘Oh Derek you’re needed, hair and makeup’s waiting for you,’ right in front of everyone, and everyone started laughing.” When Banbury told a spraying contractor that he and Gow would soon be on The One Show, the contractor replied: “What, as the Teletubbies?”Banbury doesn’t mind because, in a way, he is the hero of the film. As well as documenting the transformation of Gow’s land from grim mudbath to natural paradise, the film follows Banbury’s journey from feeling a visceral dislike of wild boar, storks and beavers to acknowledging the losses brought about by intensive farming. Linda, his perceptive wife, who preaches tolerance and an acceptance of beavers, is a second breakout star.The Banburys and Gow received a standing ovation at film festivals in Thessaloniki, Greece, and in Sheffield. Banbury, who has never before visited Mayfair in central London, thinks he might have to buy a new suit for the film’s UK premiere there. How does he feel he comes across? “I’ve got more confident as I’ve got older and I know what I’m talking about. I’m proud to be a farmer and I’ve tried to do the best I can. We’re tied a bit by the price of milk, but we just keep going, we keep struggling on and we love what we do.”His father started out with just 14 cows, and in those days he could support his family with a small farm of less than 150 acres. Like most farmers, Banbury has had to expand – and intensify production – to survive. His farm has become a small village of barns housing 200 milking cows, with 600 in total. While sparrows still chirrup on the farm and swallows dip over the pond, Banbury has noticed the loss of nature as he fertilises, sprays and takes three or four cuts of silage each year. “I wish there was more insects and birds and bees but I don’t study that. I study my crops,” he says in the film.Dawson documents the tensions when rewilding and intensive farming share the same corner of north-west Devon. Gow’s wild boar escape and rootle up Banbury’s pasture. Banbury has the boar shot. Banbury “hates” storks, and don’t talk to him about beavers, which are acclaimed by conservationists for creating new wetlands that become havens for wildlife: “I can’t see that they do any good at all. They just do vicious damage,” he thunders. When Gow writes a book about the history of wolves in Britain and hosts a conference considering their reintroduction, Banbury and other local farmers are apoplectic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd yet, Banbury is taken to see Gow’s meadows, which after unpromising beginnings, are today burgeoning with rare birds, wildflowers and butterflies, and admits “we’ve got to have areas like this for the wildlife”. Gow does not want to rewild the world, but suggests if every farmer set aside 10% of their least productive land for wildlife, it could reverse the extinction crisis. “I hate to say it but sometimes he’s right,” nods Banbury on film.View image in fullscreenBattle fields … Dereks Banbury and Gow.Photograph: Joss Barratt“The man’s a psychopath when it comes to hedgerows,” Gow initially says of Banbury, but as the film progresses, there is talk of Banbury allowing hedges to grow wild and create corridors for nature to move through his neat green fields. So will he? “It depends on the land. It depends if we’re paid for it,” he tells me. Banbury is due to re-fence his fields this autumn; Gow hopes he will make a bit more space for nature.For all Gow’s bristle, Linda recognises him as a “big Scottish softie at heart”. Has Gow’s view of farmers softened as well? “I do have great sympathy for them, especially the older men,” he says. “Some of them are just bastards. They are hard, hard farmers but they know what has happened. They know of the loss of nature. These inflexible and difficult old men are the last generation who understand that.”Today, Gow gives rewilding talks with illustrations from the Ladybird books of the 1950s and 60s that recall a lost British countryside – “pictures of the redshanks with chicks and hedgehogs and bats in these beautiful woodlands under a full moon at night. And you look and think: that’s attainable. It’s not alarming. It’s not scary. It’s actually something that’s quite alluring.”’double quotation markMost conservationists have to understand farming and farmers better and, despite all the rhetoric, I’m not sure they doDerek GowGow’s latest big idea is that farmers could be paid to do what he does: breed rare wild animals in captivity and release them. They would then be invested in seeing local populations of “their” wild animals thrive. “They’re the guys that are sitting in the pubs at night, they’re talking to their neighbours. If there are issues, it’s much easier to resolve them amongst themselves,” he says. “As a farmer, you become part of the solution. You’d feel good. But most conservationists have to understand farming and farmers better and, despite all the rhetoric, I’m not sure they do.”Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to GazaRead moreMore than 300 farmers and neighbours turn up for the Banburys’ special screening, where they are served local cider, pasties and ice-cream. They laugh loudest at Banbury’s put-downs of rewilding. But, as Gow says afterwards, “when the film finished, no one was arguing” against the facts of nature loss. As well as a cinematic release, Derek vs Derek will be shown at special on-farm screenings across the country. Its makers hope it might forge new conversations and even new working relationships between farmers, conservationists and rewilders.Has the two Dereks’ relationship been strengthened by the film? Gow took the Banburys to see flamingoes when they visited the film festival in Thessaloniki together. He also ensured Derek and Linda found a cab after the show in Sheffield. The first thing Gow asks when he pops into the Banburys’ kitchen the morning after the screening – after ribbing them about their St George’s flags flying from their farm buildings – is whether he can borrow their trailer. While he’s there, Linda serves him another of her generous cooked breakfasts.Are Derek and Derek friends? I ask Banbury. “Yeah!” he beams. A big sincere smile. “You can’t be no other can you, when you’re neighbours? He’d do anything for me. And I’d do anything for him.”Derek vs Derekisin UK cinemasfrom 2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFarmingWildlifeConservationinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a mess. I had to do something’: the personal struggle that inspired rap star Giggs to start a special needs school | Giggs | The Guardian
description: After a battle to get his autistic children properly assessed, the London MC has co-founded a specialist centre in Kent to help neurodivergent kids realise their potential
Author: Ian Gittins
Headline: After a battle to get his autistic children properly assessed, the London MC has co-founded a specialist centre in Kent to help neurodivergent kids realise their potential
Content: A remarkable venture … Giggs pictured at St James House, the new Send school he has co-founded in Kent.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianView image in fullscreenA remarkable venture … Giggs pictured at St James House, the new Send school he has co-founded in Kent.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianGiggs‘It was a mess. I had to do something’: the personal struggle that inspired rap star Giggs to start a special needs schoolAfter a battle to get his autistic children properly assessed, the London MC has co-founded a specialist centre in Kent to help neurodivergent kids realise their potentialIan GittinsFri 18 Sep 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been a busy few weeks for the London rapperGiggs. Two weeks ago, he was in New Jersey with his fiancee Valerie as she gave birth to the couple’s daughter, Noa. The next day, he flew home and went straight to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium to guest on stage with Jay-Z. “Yeah, it’s been crazy,” he smiles.Remarkably, as soon as Noa was delivered, he also found time to livestream from the US hospital to the launch event for his latest project: not an album, but a specialist school and assessment centre for neurodivergent children.Giggs, 45, has teamed up with education charity the OMG Foundation, to launch St James House, a secondary school for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) and those in alternative provision, in Gravesend, Kent. It’s a project with extremely personal origins.“I’ve been fighting for my seven-year-old son, Israel,” Giggs says when we meet at the school on his return to the UK. “He’s autistic but the system was failing him. We couldn’t get him diagnosed and he wasn’t getting the support and assessments he needed. It was a mess. I thought, well, I’ve got to do something.”If Giggs is tired, you can’t tell from the way he bounds around the former business offices now being converted into a 75-pupil school.View image in fullscreenGiggs (right) and OMG Education CEO Jamal Miah.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianThe Peckham-born musician has four children including his newborn; all three older kids are autistic. His eldest son, the rapper ML, was diagnosed more than a decade ago, in his early teens. Last year, the father-and-son duo made a joint track about living with autism, Own Motion. “When I was young, I was ashamed, now I just own it,” ML raps.“At the time, I read ML’s diagnosis and thought, this is me as well,” recalls Giggs. “So, I went to get assessed. It was just a man and woman in a room with a notepad and I thought, this is bullshit. How the fuck are they going to know if I’m autistic or not? After five minutes, I walked out. I didn’t hear anything, but then 10 years later I was in the doctor’s and he looked at my notes and said, ‘It says here that you’re autistic. I was, like, ‘Is it?’ Because I didn’t even know.”View image in fullscreenThe under-construction St James House school in Gravesend.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianGiggs belatedly learning his own diagnosis coincided with his battle to obtain diagnoses and education, health and care plans (EHCPs) for Israel and his daughter, Isla. Last year, he went on Newsnight to rail against the flaws and inadequacies in the Send educational system. Israel was given his EHCP the next day.Yet this clearly isn’t an avenue for most parents struggling with the difficult, opaque Send system. Prime minister Andy Burnham recently acknowledged that the overladen system is “broken” and pledged greater assistance for the parents of special needs children attempting to navigate it.The difficulties Giggs had getting these crucial assessments for his children was a primary motivation when he decided to launch St James House. He and his co-founder, OMG Foundation CEO Jamal Miah, have long been acquainted.“I’ve known Giggs since he used to record in a south London music studio that I ran 20 years ago,” says Miah, when we meet on an earlier visit to the school. “We kept in touch then coincidentally we found that we had both moved out to Kent. We saw a lot of disadvantaged kids around Gravesend and decided to do something for them.”OMG Foundation already runs one school in east London. When Miah and Giggs decided to start one in Kent, Giggs insisted it needed an assessment centre built in. “Because a lot of parents don’t know how to get EHCPs,” says Miah. “Until their kids have got those, it’s hard to do anything for them.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘What Giggs is doing with this project is tremendous’ … Frances Akinde, executive head teacher at St James House.Photograph: Peter Flude/the GuardianThe school and assessment centre will be overseen by executive head Frances Akinde, a specialist in neurodivergent education who praises the value of art and music therapy. “I also used to do parental advocacy work, and one of the parents I advised was Giggs,” she explains. “What he is doing with the St James House project is tremendous.”The assessment centre, employing educational psychologists, occupational therapists and speech-and-language specialists, opened this month. The school is due to follow suit in January. Miah reports that OMG Foundation are well on the way to raising the £930,000 they need to begin operations, spurred by Giggs pulling in big names for a recent charity auction.“I reached out to people that I know,” he says. “Damien Hirst gave us seven artworks. Dynamo agreed to do two private shows. Stephen Fry gave us stuff, and Ed Sheeran and Robbie Williams. They all wanted to be get involved. They’re all proper, man.”It’s a remarkable venture, and when St James House opens in the new year, Giggs knows exactly what he wants it to do for the autistic and ADHD children thronging through its doors.“I want us to be Professor Xavier for the neurodivergent universe,” he concludes, referring to the founder-educator figure in the X-Men comic books. “The X-Men started as a school before they all became superheroes. We can help autistic children to realise that they are geniuses and show them how to use their superpowers.”Explore more on these topicsGiggsSpecial educational needsAutismNeurodiversitySchoolsParents and parentingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Quentin Bell and Olivia Sterling review – two artists with a magic touch | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Bell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and power
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Bell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and power
Content: A brilliant young painter … Olivia Sterling, Our General Aims, 2022.Photograph: Hendrik Zeitler/Olivia SterlingView image in fullscreenA brilliant young painter … Olivia Sterling, Our General Aims, 2022.Photograph: Hendrik Zeitler/Olivia SterlingArt and designReviewQuentin Bell and Olivia Sterling review – two artists with a magic touchCharleston, LewesBell’s strange and charming ceramics celebrate a life dedicated to creativity, while next door Sterling’s bawdier, weirder paintings form a critique of race and powerEddy FrankelFri 18 Sep 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQuentin Bell was not a great artist, but that didn’t stop him. He saw the world as a magical place. The ceramicist (son of the Bloomsbury group’sVanessa Bell; biographer of his auntVirginia Woolf) spent his life lost in a world of magic, myth, newts in ponds, levitating women and knights on horseback. He died in 1996, leaving behind decades of pots, plates, figurines and drawings filled with wonder and amazement.It all started when Bell was nine years old. Taken to a magic show by some relatives, he saw a jaw-dropping spectacle: a beautiful woman seeming to float in the air. It stayed with him throughout his life.Five sculptures here show bodies caught in mid-air, raised off the ground, stiff as a board. There are rough messy works in wire and wood and plaster from the 1960s, bronze from the 80s and painted ceramics from the 90s; from modern and stark to gaudy and bright, it’s levitation that set him on his creative path and never left his side.View image in fullscreenA spectacle he couldn’t forget … Quentin Bell with Levitating Figure at Cobbe House, Sussex.Photograph: The Charleston TrustMost of the work hereis ceramic: plates, pots and figurines. They’re humorous, brightly coloured, shiny objects. They’re like messy, rough takes on chintzy 18th-century European decorative art, rococo porcelain with its depictions of reclining ladies in voluminous dresses. The figurines aren’t great: they’re basic and poorly rendered, often malformed and pretty unremarkable, if quite funny in places.View image in fullscreenNo minimalism … Quentin Bell, Platter: Playing Card.Photograph: Lee RobbinsHis plates and teapots fare better, especially the later cups and jugs, which are colourful and decorative. But his drawings and illustrations are where it really falls apart. He paints Greek myths and biblical scenes, he illustrates the story of Cinderella and his own imagined history of Sussex, but none of it is well executed or particularly interesting. They feel like fun creative projects meant to entertain his kids, which some of them were.What makes it compelling is that everything here is at odds with the aesthetic trends of his era. There’s none of the austere minimalism of influential contemporary potters such as the amazing Bernard Leach, none of the abstraction or surrealism that was coursing through Europe, none of the grim interwar realism that defined so much English modernism. Instead, there’s something way more anachronistic. This is strange, charming, incredibly English, totally eccentric creativity being expressed on its own terms.The main takeaway from this exhibition isn’t that Quentin Bell is good at art; he’s not even the best Bell. The main takeaway is that there’s something powerful, even beautiful about dedicating your life to creativity.Way better is thedisplay of new works next doorby the brilliant young English painter Olivia Sterling. She’s taken the magical obsessions of Bell and pushed them to bawdier, weirder, funnier, more critical extremes. Her whole shtick is about using the language of old cartoons and comics, the symbolism of food, the representation of the human body, and twisting it all into biting critiques of race and power dynamics. This is her at her strangest, darkest and filthiest.View image in fullscreenMenacing … Olivia Sterling, Emotionally True, 2026.Photograph: Olivia SterlingYou walk into a room-sized painting of vast bodies squeezed into corsets and girdles or flopping about in dressing gowns, like you’ve stumbled into the backstage of some burlesque show. And then the performance starts. A woman has become a dirty dining table in one menacingly red painting, plates of half-eaten cake and glasses of milk strewn across her body. In another work, a pink corpse is littered with ice-creams, a magician’s rabbit scampers over her belly and milk spurts from her nipple. Smaller works show white liquid being squeezed and pulled out of teats and orifices. A huge triptych depicts a white body lying in a magician’s sword box, one black woman pressing down on top of it, another plunging a sword in.Sterling is drawing a line between magic and power; she’s saying they’re both fundamentally the same thing: an illusion, a world maintained through artifice. It’s clever, political, incisive narrative painting. But, crucially, it’s also fun, ridiculously colourful and totally overblown. If it was miserable, serious and dour, you’d feel like you were getting lectured. Instead, you feel like you’re watching a Tom and Jerry episode about greed and racism, with all the violence and slapstick intact. Now that’s a good magic trick.AtCharleston, Lewes, until 7 MarchExplore more on these topicsArt and designBloomsbury groupPaintingArtCeramicsDrawingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The damage was much worse than I had imagined’: the shocking inside story of Salman Rushdie’s survival | Movies | The Guardian
description: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life
Author: Claire Armitstead
Headline: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life
Content: Eliza Griffiths, Salman Rushdie and Alex Gibney.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEliza Griffiths, Salman Rushdie and Alex Gibney.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘The damage was much worse than I had imagined’: the shocking inside story of Salman Rushdie’s survivalClaire ArmitsteadAfter ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous lifeFri 18 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic friend, who told her the man she had married just a year earlier, and who had set off the previous night for a speaking engagement nearly 400 miles away, had been hurt. “What kind of hurt?” she panicked. Turning on the television, she was assaulted by blurry images of chaos on stage as audience members surged to the rescue. Her husband, SirSalman Rushdie, had been stabbed multiple times and was fighting for his life.Within days of desperately chartering a plane to fly her to Rushdie’s hospital bedside, not knowing if he was alive or dead, Griffiths – a poet and photographer who works under her full name Rachel Eliza Griffiths – had begun to make a video diary recording his treatment and recovery. “When it had become likely that I was going to survive,” says Rushdie drily, “I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this. By which I meant something very modest: maybe she would take a picture of me on her iPhone every couple of days just to document the recovery, but Eliza had bigger ideas.”One of her first ideas was that it needed to be shot not on a phone but with a proper camera. “I explicitly remember when the box arrived with my camera,” Griffiths says. “I cried because it was reconnecting me to my identity as an artist. The person I used to be, even just 24 hours ago, was being returned to me. It was giving both of us this permission to continue to be artists and tell our stories together.”The couple are sitting in separate rooms of their New York home to tell their shared story over video link. Griffiths is warm and animated, as the memories rush out. Rushdie is more reserved and sardonic, smartly turned out, with only a black lens over his right eye to attest to the horrific injuries he suffered.Both have already published memoirs about the experience: Rushdie’sKnife, in 2024 and Griffiths’The Flower Bearersearlier this year. Now they are the subjects of an unflinching film, Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, which combines Griffiths’ video diary with archive footage from the period following the fateful day in 1989 when a fatwa was issued against Rushdie for the offence allegedly caused to Islam by the supposed blasphemy of his fourth novel, The Satanic Verses. Iran’s then supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini called for the execution of the 41-year-old author and his publishers, forcing him into hiding, where he remained, under armed guard, for nine years.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a very intimate point of view from love between two people in a new marriage’ … Griffiths and Rushdie.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIt is hard to say which time zone of the film is more viscerally shocking: the grisly footage of Rushdie being stitched and stapled back together in 2022, or the murderous hatred that roars out from news headlines in the months and years following the fatwa. In the US, the office of the Riverdale Press newspaper is firebombed after it runs an editorial about the book defending free expression; in Pakistan, six people are killed in riots; in Japan, a translator is stabbed to death; in Italy, another translator is stabbed in his home, while, in London, an effigy of a mutilated Rushdie is paraded through the streets by a furious crowd, some of whom declare on camera that nothing less than hanging will satisfy them.Incorporating the archive footage was the idea ofAlex Gibney, an Oscar-winning documentary maker (his newest film is a four-hour study of Elon Musk) who was invited by Rushdie and Griffiths to direct – or, as he describes it, “curate” – the film. Rushdie was initially opposed to dredging up the past, reasoning that his attacker – known simply as “A” in both his memoir and the film – was “just one crazy kid”. “I don’t see it as being representative of a larger matter,” he insists. “I think I was unfortunate in that this person was motivated by who knows what influences, and at this venue where he came to attack me, there was absolutely no security protection at all.”The venue he was speaking at was at the heart of an idealistic community at Chautauqua in upstate New York, whose naivety in not having a single security guard in the hall Rushdie now sharply questions. Yet just three years before the attack, at a talk hosted by the Guardian at the Sheldonian in Oxford for his Booker-shortlisted novel Quichotte, he was tetchy to find plainclothes police at the entrances, complaining that only in the UK was such security still deemed necessary. “Well the thing is,” he says now, “in the preceding 20 years, I’d done hundreds of public events all over the world with no trouble, and it didn’t seem necessary to surround the Sheldonian with armed men.”double quotation markThere was absolutely no security protection at allAs the film reveals, not everyone shared his confidence. The Palestinian-American historian Edward Said predicted that the main threat Rushdie faced would not be soon from a religious fanatic, but at some time in the future from a random individual. The film’s power lies in the connection it forges between the two time frames: it demonstrates that the body in the bed in 2022, with a destroyed eye bulging from its socket, is what happens if the right to free speech is violently and publicly opposed.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to understand this story as a kind of healing film’ … Alex Gibney.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianGriffiths, who is Rushdie’s fifth wife, was an 11-year-old growing up in Delaware when the fatwa was issued.
