Gibney was “a wayward film-maker in search of a career” who had made a few TV documentaries and was trying to write some scripts. “I was doing a lot of reading because I didn’t get much work, so I was well aware of Salman as a novelist and an essayist,” he says. “But I think we [he and his editor] had forgotten, too, how vast it was. You know, you go through a process, starting by saying, OK, let’s see what kind of clips there are about the fatwa, and we were stunned.”He concedes that Rushdie would have preferred less of the footage. “Salman doesn’t want to be defined by this. He bristles, and I understand it. You want to be defined by your artistic work, not by the political opportunism of a down-on-his-luck tyrant. But at the same time, I think it was hugely important for the audience to understand just how global it was.”Gibney’s original idea was to model the film on Dennis Potter’s hit 1980s TV series The Singing Detective, based on Potter’s experience of struggling with the chronic skin disease psoriasis. “The simple story is that he comes in, in terrible shape, and over the course of the series, he recovers physically. But in the meantime, his life passes before his eyes. He thinks about his childhood. He hallucinates … and he imagines bits and pieces of his life through his own detective fiction. Salman was on his own path with Knife, and in some ways, they kind of coalesced. But ultimately, I did the smart thing with a writer of Salman’s stature, which is just to use enormous portions of Knife as the narration for the film.”Though Rushdie wryly complains that he is the only one of the trio to receive no production credits, apart from “based on the book by …” (Griffiths has two, as cinematographer and executive producer), it gives full range to his “free-associating” mind, flitting from literary citation to animation and movie excerpts.View image in fullscreen‘The film becomes a third perspective’ … Rushdie.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn one scene, he recalls a famous image from Georges Méliès’ classic short of 1902, Le Voyage dans La Lune, of a spacecraft crashing into the eye of the moon. “This is the literary device known as foreshadowing,” he wrote in the memoir. The night before the attack, happy because he was in love and had just signed off the proofs for his next novel (2023’s Victory City), he sent Griffiths a photograph of the moon seen from his hotel balcony. “Here’s a man in the dark, ignorant of the danger that’s already very close … the future rushes at him while he sleeps … Except strangely it’s really the past returning, my own past rushing at me … a masked man with a knife seeking to carry out a death order from three decades ago.”Seeing the image reproduced for reference in a printed text is nothing like experiencing it on the big screen, juxtaposed with Griffiths’ unstinting footage of what Rushdie described as “my bulging boiled-egg eye [hanging] out of my face, the iris improbably perched on the swollen white …”Why did Griffiths – and by extension the film – put so much emphasis on the horror of Rushdie’s damaged eye? “I think for me, the camera is part of how unbearable it was, and the shock for anyone to see their loved one being so wounded, so damaged, so violently attacked by another human being,” she replies. “And so I feel that, though the camera could be a sort of screen, also it was so open and you can’t look away.”She continues: “It’s a very intimate point of view from love between two people in a new marriage, and this is where we’re at. It was just I’m moved to pick up the camera, or I can’t believe we’re in this situation. The camera is real, and I’m not. This can’t be happening to us. But then I’m like: ‘Well, it’s real because I can see it in the camera.’”In the early days, when Griffiths was filming by day and camping out in Rushdie’s hospital room by night, she knew she could not show him what he looked like, any more than she could reveal her own fear and distress, which spill out in a tearful selfie monologue. It was only after he was finally allowed home that she asked if he’d like to see it. “I hadn’t really sat by myself and looked at much of it either,” she says. “When we finally did look at it, we did it together, and then it kind of became: ‘Oh, this is bigger than us, and maybe other people need to see it.’”For Rushdie, the viewing was a rollercoaster. “First of all, I thought I looked really much worse than I thought I looked – the damage was much worse than I had imagined it to be. And then I felt quite pleased because I thought I don’t look like that any more. I look like this. So it actually dramatised the recovery.”View image in fullscreen‘I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this’ … Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie.Photograph: Altitude FilmThe final minutes of the film show the couple revisiting the scene of the attack, and laying to rest some of the misrememberings. Early on, Rushdie berates himself for submitting to his attacker. “I ask myself: why didn’t I do anything? Why did I just stand there? Well, in the film, you see that I didn’t just stand there. I tried to get away from him. So memory and reality are sometimes at odds with each other, and the film becomes a third perspective.”Gibney tried, and failed, to get an interview in jail with “A”, the destroyer, who was wrestled to the floor and whose motives remain a mystery. “I wanted to understand this story as a kind of healing film, which I think we all of us need, and also about their investment in their love for each other,” he says. “So while it’s gruesome in parts and difficult and deals with the dark places of the human psyche, nevertheless, it finds a way out to a really good place.”Rushdie and Griffiths had been together for five years when the attack happened, having met at the opening night of a festival that he had co-founded and chaired for the writers’ charity PEN. Though they didn’t hide their relationship, they did not flaunt it either, so that at the time of the attack, few people beyond their immediate friends and family knew they were married. “Being private is part of my personality,” says Griffiths. While the attack shoved Rushdie back into the spotlight, it forced her into it for the first time. She recalls looking out on this new reality as the plane carrying her to her husband’s bedside landed on an airstrip packed with law enforcement troops and realising she was just going to have to deal with it, “which is another part of my personality”. In an epigraph to his memoir, Rushdie quoted Samuel Beckett: “We are other, no longer what we were before the calamity of yesterday.” How much do they feel they have been changed by what’s happened? “Well,” he says, “I’m better than maybe I have any business to be. And Eliza, too.”He still travels back and forth to see his sons and grandchildren in the UK, and the couple will be with them for the film’s London premiere. Has the attack ever tempted them to leave Trump’s US, where the forces against free speech and human rights seem ever more entrenched and dangerous? “What, for Farage’s Britain?” scoffs Rushdie. I take it that’s a no, then.Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie is released in the UK on 30 September. It was released in the US on 17 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSalman RushdieAlex GibneyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I toured with a hole in my brain. I don’t regret a thing’: punk duo Lambrini Girls on fighting extreme times with extreme measures | Music | The Guardian
description: Their debut stormed the charts and wowed Iggy Pop, but health crises threatened to derail the Brighton duo. Now they’re back, taking aim at the manosphere, fascism and the ruling class
Author: Kate Hutchinson
Headline: Their debut stormed the charts and wowed Iggy Pop, but health crises threatened to derail the Brighton duo. Now they’re back, taking aim at the manosphere, fascism and the ruling class
Content: ‘Do we get branded misandrists? Of course we fucking do’ … Phoebe Lunny (left) and Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Jessie MorganView image in fullscreen‘Do we get branded misandrists? Of course we fucking do’ … Phoebe Lunny (left) and Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Jessie MorganMusic‘I toured with a hole in my brain. I don’t regret a thing’: punk duo Lambrini Girls on fighting extreme times with extreme measuresTheir debut stormed the charts and wowed Iggy Pop, but health crises threatened to derail the Brighton duo. Now they’re back, taking aim at the manosphere, fascism and the ruling classKate HutchinsonFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt a last-minute surprise show in London, the British punk duo Lambrini Girls are sharing their stage with a continuous tide of crowd surfers. They move almost as one, a jumble of limbs rippling over a sea of bodies – emboldened, perhaps, by the band’s vow to double up as security guards. “If you don’t feel safe, tell us and we’ll punch them in the dick!” shouts Phoebe Lunny, the lead vocalist and guitarist.She also requests that people pick up anyone who falls over in the moshpit and goes around with the mic asking fans to introduce themselves if they are “queer legends” (there are many). “This show is as much yours as it is ours,” Lunny announces, before she and the bassist Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez pummel everyone with shouty rants, furious beats and sludgy grunge.Backstage, before the gig, the two Lambrini Girls are sitting on a battered sofa. Lunny, 29, is the chattier of the two, with bleached-blond waves and broken Mary Janes. Macieira-Boşgelmez is a year older, with red hair and a quiet poise, that seems at odds with her headbanging stage presence. They’re not long back from a European tour where their visuals made their politics plain. In France, the screen read “Fuck Marine Le Pen”. For London, it’s “Fuck Nigel Farage”.“The issues we address are not specific to the UK,” says Macieira-Boşgelmez. “Oppression is growing. People’s anger is growing.”View image in fullscreen‘The system is so unfair’ … Phoebe Lunny and Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez on stage in London last year.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsTheir second album, No Refunds, was announced this week, capping a successful few years for the band who formed in Brighton in 2019. There have been magazine covers, support slots with Iggy Pop, Idles andAmyl and the Sniffersand a remix by the queer idol Peaches. In January 2025, their debut albumWho Let the Dogs Outcharted at No 16 – not bad, given that it contains a song called Cuntology 101. Recently, they’ve been able to pack in their 9-to-5s, although they feel a little ashamed about it. “The guilt is extremely prevalent,” says Macieira-Boşgelmez. “It is on my mind every single day. You watch your friends work so fucking hard …” Lunny agrees: “The system is so unfair.”The band has a sense of humour – their debut EP featured a cover illustration of a giant flaming turd and one early song is effectively just a call-and-response of “Craig David” – but they’re serious about confronting that unfair system. At the London show, their touring drummer, Misha Phillips, delivers an impassioned speech about transgender liberation before they unleash one of their most popular songs, Terf Wars. These biting calls for social justice mean they’re often compared to riot grrrl bands such as Bikini Kill (for whom Lambrini Girls will be opening next week in Brooklyn). As the duo have evolved, so has their mission to represent “the disenfranchised, disaffected and disillusioned”, Lunny says.Lunny was raised in Sussex by a single mother, a primary school teacher and socialist, who politicised her. Lunny did a music BTec: “I didn’t pass and went to the University of Burger King.” Macieira-Boşgelmez, who is of Turkish and Portuguese heritage, moved to the UK to become a musician and says she has always had “a really strong sense of justice” from growing up “financially privileged. My parents made sure that I knew that.”In September 2025, just as Lambrini Girls were really popping off, Macieira-Boşgelmez took time out from touring (a friend stepped in to cover her). She had been diagnosed with autism and bipolar disorder four years prior andwrote a candid, moving social media postabout the distressing effect of touring on her health. “It was slowly accumulating and gradually getting worse and that was influencing my behaviour and me not being aware of my limits,” she says now.When Macieira-Boşgelmez returned in February 2026, the duo went to play Australia for the first time. During one gig, Lunny leapt from a balcony and injured herself. She was told it was “just whiplash”. It was six weeks before she discovered what was up. “It was only when I was in a hotel at 2am, fitting and passing out on the floor, that it was obvious that something was really wrong,” she says.Lunny had a small bone fracture in her neck, which had punctured a hole in her brain membrane. Fluid had been draining out. “So now I have a lopsided brain,” she says, matter-of-factly.She was forced to rest for nearly four months, but being laid up in bed wasn’t her style. “So then I started touring with a hole in my brain. It was the hardest thing I’ve ever had to do.” She took flights in a wheelchair. “I had to lay side of stage, force myself up with willpower and rely on adrenaline to carry me. As soon as I was off stage, the pain would disorient me to the point where I didn’t know where I was. The thing is, I insisted on touring as it offered me 40 minutes of feeling like myself again. I don’t regret a thing.”View image in fullscreen‘The world is a far darker place than it was two years ago’ … Lunny (left) and Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Jessie MorganShe had two rounds of surgery in July this year and feels as if she is finally recovering, but says: “I’d kill to have a body that was capable of what it was able to do before.” The new album includes an acoustic track, Spilt, an unwavering look at her booze-fuelled party era. “I feel very fortunate that I can’t really relate to that song any more and that’s testament to growing up a bit,” she says. “I’ve had so many health scares. I’m very restricted with my drinking.”But, for the most part, No Refunds is bigger and beefier, railing against fascism and “the ruling class”, Lunny says. “We’re trying to shake people and say fucking get off your asses. The world is a far darker place now than it was two years ago. Even though we thought it couldn’t get any worse, it has.”Musically, it strikes a balance between corrosive grunge low-end, bristling punk intensity and the arch delivery of Britpop, with some of their peppiest songs yet – although a suggestion of Elastica, a female-fronted band, elicits the subtlest of shared sideways glances. “The majority of my influences from that era, because it was so male-dominated, are men,” says Lunny. “I’m a huge fan of Blur.”There is some classic Lambrini Girls sarcasm, such as Is This AI?, Don’t Talk to Me Till I’ve Had My Abortion and the lead single Cult of Celebrity, which references the Epstein files (“Oh, how the other half live / … on Lolita island”). But the fun-poking has largely been replaced by fury; the lyrics are less direct, more conceptual. “I don’t want to go through a list of societal ills and be like: right, we’ve done that,” Lunny says, mimicking ticking off a list. “Because I feel like that trivialises it.” A lot of the last album was “I don’t like this and here is why”, but No Refunds is more about “trying to build a world”.View image in fullscreenStrength and secuirty … Lunny (left) and Macieira-Boşgelmez.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/RedfernsRegarding another new song, Gaza Beach, Lunny says she “wanted to write a song about Palestine for years, but I couldn’t do it. Obviously, to encapsulate a genocide is incredibly difficult to do in a way which doesn’t sensationalise the suffering of hundreds of thousands of people”. But seeing an AI-generated video of how a glitzy new resort in the territory might look gave her the idea. “I started thinking: well, what would that actually look like? I felt like I was able to convey the moroseness and the insidiousness of this genocide [but also] encapsulate the imperialist settlement, which was really important to do.” She is encouraged to see more artists speaking out about it, too. “You don’t have to write a song about it, but you have to use your voice.”Macieira-Boşgelmez cites Macklemore being criticised by Pink forhis pro-Palestine commentson Ed Sheeran’s tour (we spoke before Macklemore was kicked off the tour and Sheeran faceda retaliation of his own). “Even though there are some artists that are speaking out about this, the backlash you face is still incredibly disproportionate,” she says.In April, Lunny revealed that she was oncearrested for harassmentand faced a possible six-month jail sentence after she emailed promoters to warn them about booking an allegedly “dodgy” male musician. The case was dropped, although Lunny was made to write a letter of apology to the man. “It was a long time ago; I can’t say specifics,” she says now.Abusive men and abuses of power are recurrent themes on No Refunds, including one track that is specifically about the manosphere (The Basement).Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutralityRead more“We talk about male violence a lot, we talk about the oppression of women a lot,” she says. “Do we get branded misandrists? Of course we fucking do. The people that brand us that are ‘incels’. We are not misandrists. We both have a lot of male friends that we adore.” It’s more, they say, about taking aim at the “capitalist patriarchy”.It’s a grim world, but Lambrini Girls aren’t without optimism. “There is still a lot of value to be found in community,” Lunny says. “When I feel hopeless about the rise of the far right and us edging towards a new iteration of techno feudalism and that AI might kill us all, I have strength and security in my friends around me. I look at Selin and she gives a real fuck.Thatgives me hope.”The community at Lambrini Girls’ shows is just as strong. Towards the end of the London gig, a fan scales a large circular rig in the centre of the space. For a moment, their legs dangle down precariously, hovering above the pit. There is a collective sharp intake of breath. But soon hands are thrust aloft, fingers clasp around their ankles and the lone ranger drops into a throng of arms.“Solidarity will prevail in times like these through listening to each other, uplifting each other, supporting each other,” says Macieira-Boşgelmez. “As much as you might feel it, you are not alone.”No Refunds is released via City Slang on 15 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockBrightonPunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Susan Calman: Tall Tales review – comic’s first tour in 10 years is raw and riotous | Comedy | The Guardian
description: Faux truculent and palpably adorable, the standup is in her element exposing her supposed flaws and the unseen idiocies of her TV career
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Faux truculent and palpably adorable, the standup is in her element exposing her supposed flaws and the unseen idiocies of her TV career
Content: Peachy and bulletproof set pieces … Susan Calman.Photograph: Steve UllathorneView image in fullscreenPeachy and bulletproof set pieces … Susan Calman.Photograph: Steve UllathorneComedyReviewSusan Calman: Tall Tales review – comic’s first tour in 10 years is raw and riotousPerth Concert HallFaux truculent and palpably adorable, the standup is in her element exposing her supposed flaws and the unseen idiocies of her TV careerBrian LoganFri 18 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTall Tales isSusan Calman’s first new standup set for 10 years, designed to show us the real Susan behind the cuddly personality we see on TV. Given that was the premise ofher 2016 touring showtoo, it’s clear that a decade away has done little to develop – but also nothing to diminish – the Glaswegian’s onstage shtick. This is a compelling return, stuffed with experiences and insights gleaned from that standup downtime, and which undergirds familiar tales of cat fancying, being small and entering menopause with a heartfelt reckoning with recent bereavement and rocky mental health.That last material feels raw, as she tells us she only returned to standup (the thing she feared the most, she says) to shock herself out of a bad depression. That would be hard to credit based on her show alone, which finds Calman in her element: faux truculent but palpably adorable, fulminating at the indignities of short, lesbian, middle-aged womanhood, revealing to us the unseen idiocies of her gilded TV career. Her supposed flaws are arrayed for our pleasure: her catastrophising (cue a fun anecdote about being trapped on a hotel balcony), her addictive personality, and – in the peachy set-piece that closes act one – her hormonal lust for righteous revenge.Tilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumnRead moreThat number, about her newfound love for golf, finds Calman at her best, when the occasionally generic midlife patter becomes uniquely, idiosyncratically her. See her story about her granny’s recipe for “Italian mince”, her penchant for the80s TV show Hart to Hart, or the tale of terrorising her neighbour with the Weeping Angel (from Doctor Who) she keeps in her back garden. The behind-the-scenes stories culled from her work on daytime telly are homelier, although she does derive fromher Strictly Come Dancing stinta bulletproof standup set-piece about, ahem, personal grooming.All of this is given emotional heft by the recent parental loss and experience of depression, which – while the point isn’t laboured – clearly knocked Calman for six. This may, she says, be her last standup show. If so, this pint-sized tall tales teller goes out with her head held high.Touring until 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsComedySusan CalmanTelevisionStrictly Come DancingDoctor WhoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Zack Snyder is angling to make another Batman movie. Stranger things have happened | Movies | The Guardian
description: Two Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Two Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns
Content: Anyone? … Ben Affleck in Batman v Superman, 2016.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures/Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenAnyone? … Ben Affleck in Batman v Superman, 2016.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures/Warner Bros./AllstarWeek in geekMoviesZack Snyder is angling to make another Batman movie. Stranger things have happenedBen ChildTwo Batman projects are already in the making at DC Studios, but Snyder has set his sights on the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight ReturnsFri 18 Sep 2026 07.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTShareThere cannot be too many film-makers who have spent quite so long being told that their version of a superhero universe is over, asZack Snyderhas. His Batman is gone, his Superman has been dismantled and the studio that once handed him the keys to DC is now run by James Gunn and Peter Safran, two men whose first order of business was to build something completely different. And yet here he is, determined not to give up, telling anyone who will listen about his proposal to bring the classic Frank Miller graphic novel The Dark Knight Returns to multiplexes.In an interview with Varietyto promote his forthcoming film The Last Photograph, Snyder returned to an idea he has been talking about for years: adapting Miller’s famously grim 1986 vision of an ageing Batman coming out of retirement in a dystopian Gotham. “The reason why it’s The Dark Knight Returns, if anyone would ever let me do it outside of the DC Universe since it’s a novel that just happens to have superheroes in it, is if I could do Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, those two books next to each other, to me, represent the complete cycle of the superhero comic book medium,” the film-maker said.“You can do no more than those two books. Watchmen came at the beginning of the superhero movie phase, so it would be super fitting to have The Dark Knight Returns come now, at what I would say is possibly – I don’t want to call it the twilight, but – we’re down the road of the superhero movie genre, and I think audiences would understand the why of it.”View image in fullscreenA return with interest? Ben Affleck as Batman in 2016.Photograph: Clay Enos/Warner Bros./AllstarWhat’s this, you may ask? Isn’t this the guy who was in charge of the caped crusader and man of steel back when they were played by Ben Affleck and Henry Cavill, and didn’t he already spend a significant chunk ofBatmanv Superman recreating Miller’s seminal comic with the serial numbers only lightly filed off? It all seems pretty unlikely. For starters, comic book studios rarely make straight-up adaptations of iconic graphic novels – at least outside the animated sphere. Then there’s the small matter of the two existing Batman projects already running concurrently under DC Studios: Robert Pattinson’s grungy doom-laden version, about to embark on a second outing under the auspices of Matt Reeves (The Batman Part II), and a second dark knight who’s due to turn up in the forthcoming The Brave and the Bold, this time with It director Andy Muschietti attached.Wouldn’t a third caped crusader be taking things too far, even in a genre where multiversal alternates have increasingly become commonplace? Then again, stranger things have happened. Nobody expected Snyder’s four-hour version of Justice League to ever get made, either. The “release the Snyder cut” campaign remains one of the most bizarre examples of fan power to have emerged. Yes, Snyder’s early DC films, Man of Steel and Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice did well at the box office, especially given the studio’s later struggles, but the idea that Warner Bros would one day hand Snyder $70m to exhume Justice League, perform emergency franchise surgery on it and release two four-hour versions on TV (one entirely in monochrome) still feels closer to an AI fever dream than reality. Did Snyder really have the huge and dedicated following to justify it?There may be one glimmer of hope on the horizon for those who long to see a greying Batfleck battle Cavill’s Superman once again. Paramount Skydance’s planned takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, which could yet struggle to get over the line, might signal another shake-up of the Gunn-led DC Studios. There are even murkiercorners of the blogospherethat suggest Paramount boss David Ellison could bring Snyder back once Gunn’s contract (allegedly) expires next year.In the meantime, Snyder will keep on keeping on with his backdoor campaign to get The Dark Knight Returns into cinemas. This may not be “release the Snyder cut” just yet, but somewhere in the darker reaches of the internet, a hashtag is warming up.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekSuperhero moviesDC ComicsZack SnyderBatmanComics and graphic novelscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with culture | Arts Council England | The Guardian
description: In first interview since starting job – and after visiting school where arts are central – Dawn Airey says she wants to fix ‘shocking’ lack of access
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: In first interview since starting job – and after visiting school where arts are central – Dawn Airey says she wants to fix ‘shocking’ lack of access
Content: ‘When I was at school you went on cultural trips. It was just accepted,’ Airey said.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘When I was at school you went on cultural trips. It was just accepted,’ Airey said.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianArts Council England‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with cultureIn first interview since starting job – and after visiting school where arts are central – Dawn Airey says she wants to fix ‘shocking’ lack of accessMark BrownNorth of England correspondentFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly half of children in England have been to a museum or the theatre in the past year, while three-quarters have not been to an art gallery, research shows.Dawn Airey, the new chair ofArts Council England, said the figures were “shocking” but also “an amazing opportunity to ensure they do have that experience to enrich their lives”.In her first interview since taking up the job six weeks ago, Airey said experience of arts and culture “should almost be a human right”.“When I was at school you went on cultural trips. It was just accepted that you would go to your local gallery. You can have great art but if there is no access it might as well not be there. That is the challenge,” she said.Airey, a TV industry veteran and former Channel 5 boss, spoke to the Guardian while on a whistlestop tour of arts projects in Barrow-in-Furness, Cumbria.View image in fullscreenPrimary school pupils in a music session led by musicians and conductors from Liverpool Philharmonic at the Barrow Youth Hub.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianShe succeeds Nicholas Serota as chair of an organisation that has had a bumpy few years, beginning with huge cuts imposed by the Conservatives.Anindependent review of ACEby Margaret Hodge this year levelled a number of criticisms, including that it had overly complicated application processes, which “stifled creativity and innovation”.Arts organisations were also last year put through the wringer when ACE’s grant processing platform, Grantium, crashed,causing widespread funding limbo.Airey recalled that on her first visit as chair to ACE’s London office, “it felt quiet, a little bit subdued. I didn’t expect that.”She said she wanted ACE to get its “swagger” back. “I want the Arts Council to be open, I want it to be confident, I want it to be leading conversations, I want it to have a sense of fun, a sense of energy.“We’ve been quite process-driven and it doesn’t need to be. We’ve got to relax. I want us to be loud.”Airey was speaking as ACE published its first Creative Young Lives survey, one of the biggest of its type undertaken. It looks at how children and young people engage – or don’t – with arts and culture.View image in fullscreenAirey meeting pupils at Dowdales secondary school in Dalton-in-Furness.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThefigures showedthat in the past year 51.79% of young people had been to a museum, 48.56% to the theatre or a show, 26.31% to an art gallery or exhibition, and 22.25% to a music event.In the survey, 74% of children said being creative was important to them, and 60% said they would definitely like to do more creative and cultural activities.Cost is one of the biggest barriers, with 32% of respondents saying it prevented them from making more visits to cultural places. More than half (55%) said making creative activities more affordable would help them increase their participation.ACE said the detailed survey provided “robust data”, with previous studies “not conducted a scale to allow such granular analysis”.On her visit this week, Airey saw first-hand the value of giving young people easy access to culture, at the arts-madDowdales schoolin Dalton-in-Furness.Its headteacher, Emma Aubrey, has fostered close links with the Royal Shakespeare Company, Birmingham Royal Ballet and the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra,which performs in Barrowand has a youth hub.Aubrey said it had been a battle to ensure arts education was “front and centre” at her school while watching it being marginalised nationally.“It has been tough to say: no, we will continue to do that, and we teach drama and dance as well as music to every child in key stage 3 every week.”View image in fullscreenPupils taking part in a dance class at Dowdales school.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianOn the day the Guardian visited, 12- and 13-year-olds were rehearsing Romeo and Juliet – and also considering their town centre. It was “rough”, said one child. “There’s nothing good going on,” said another. It was “run down”. People “feel there’s not much they can do about it, it’s already happened”.The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school | EditorialRead moreThey were talking about Barrow, but it could be almost any English town centre: the nation’s problems summed up in seconds by children rehearsing Shakespeare.Aubrey is clearly proud of the school’s arts focus, and not necessarily because it is going to create lots of artists. “It’s about opening up a world that can be very insular and isolated and very industry-driven. It’s about making them believe they can be anybody,” she said.ACE distributesmore than £650m a year of public and lottery moneyto arts organisations and individuals, and will next week publish new, “simpler” guidance for the next national portfolio funding round.In Barrow, Airey met a number of organisations that had benefited from Arts Council money.View image in fullscreenAirey at a roundtable session with arts leaders in Barrow-in-Furness.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianAt one roundtable she told participants: “The Arts Council has been through a bit of a tough time … I want us to get our swagger back.”Airey said ACE would be actively involved in the government’s ambition to “rewire the nation”, adding: “We have been doing that a long, long time.”The idea of ACE getting its swagger back was enthusiastically received by panellists, who spoke of the challenges of getting everyone on board when arguing for embedding art and culture in places such as Barrow, a town dominated by its shipyard building nuclear submarines.Jo Reilly, the deputy directorof Art Gene, said: “We need you to be an advocate for us at all levels.”Explore more on these topicsArts Council EnglandDawn AireyArts in schoolsArts fundingArts policyMuseums (Education)Creativity in the classroomnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to answer for its ‘dismal record’ in Eurovision before committee of MPs | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Digital, culture, media and sport committee expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses and music industry experts
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Digital, culture, media and sport committee expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses and music industry experts
Content: The UK finished last this year with Eins, Zwei, Drei by Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UK finished last this year with Eins, Zwei, Drei by Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesEurovisionUK to answer for its ‘dismal record’ in Eurovision before committee of MPsDigital, culture, media and sport committee expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses and music industry expertsJamie GriersonFri 18 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe and Jake. Daz Sampson. Electro Velvet. Who could forget them?Most people, probably. They are some of the many acts who represented the UK at theEurovisionsong contest in the last 20 years that have failed to find a place in the country’s cultural pantheon.Now, the chair of an influential parliamentary committee has decided to interrogate exactly why the UK has been performing so poorly.Dame Caroline Dinenage, who heads the digital, culture, media and sport committee,told the BBC: “We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years is the result of bad song choice, weak performance … or something else.”Prior to 2000, the UK could be proud of its efforts: it finished in the top 10 every year except 1978, 1987 and 1999, and won with Love Shine a Light by Katrina and the Waves in 1997.View image in fullscreenKatrina and the Waves after winning Eurovision in Dublin in May 1997.Photograph: John Giles/APBut since then it has reached the top 10 only three times and finished in last place six times – in2003,2008,2010,2019,2021and2026– with Jemini and James Newman scoring nul points in 2003 and 2021 respectively. The exception was Sam Ryder’s Space Man in 2022,which came second.The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC with support from a record label or music management company.The Commons committee is reportedly expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses as well as music industry experts over the coming months.In 2026, Bulgaria won the contest when Dara swept to victory with the songBangaranga. The 27-year-old singer’s triumph was the first victory for Bulgaria, which joined Eurovision in 2005 and had sat out the past three editions.View image in fullscreenDara in Vienna in May.Photograph: Lisa Leutner/ReutersThe UK finished last with Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle. The YouTuber, who makes his own synthesisers, failed to win over neutral voters with the song Eins, Zwei, Drei. The song received zero points in the public vote, meaning it did not make it into the top 10 in any of the voting countries.The contest has become increasingly political, primarily over the inclusion of Israel, which has been participating since 1973. Ireland is to boycott the contest for the second year running over the Gaza war. It wasone of five countries, along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.Explore more on these topicsEurovisionArts policySam RydernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers | Books | The Guardian
description: More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki
Content: From top to bottom, left to right: Temesgen Ghebreyesus, Dawit Isaak, Dawit Habtemichael, Seyoum Tsehaye, Fessehaye ‘Joshua’ Yohannes, Medhanie Haile, Amanuel Asrat, Said Abdelkadir, Sahle ‘Wedi-Itay’ Tsegazeab, Idris Said ‘Aba Arre’, Yousif Mohammed Ali, Matheos Habteab.Photograph: PEN InternationalView image in fullscreenFrom top to bottom, left to right: Temesgen Ghebreyesus, Dawit Isaak, Dawit Habtemichael, Seyoum Tsehaye, Fessehaye ‘Joshua’ Yohannes, Medhanie Haile, Amanuel Asrat, Said Abdelkadir, Sahle ‘Wedi-Itay’ Tsegazeab, Idris Said ‘Aba Arre’, Yousif Mohammed Ali, Matheos Habteab.Photograph: PEN InternationalBooks‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writersMore than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias AfwerkiElla CreamerFri 18 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.Nobel laureatesOlga Tokarczukand JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiledin the Guardianin 2015.The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.Earlier this year, PEN Internationallaunched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president ofPENInternational. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”Explore more on these topicsBooksEritreaPENAfricaJM CoetzeeOlga TokarczuknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was making history, not copying it’: the greatest Gordon Parks photographs | Gordon Parks | The Guardian
description: As a new exhibition celebrates the 20th anniversary of the Gordon Parks Foundation, those who knew him discuss his most powerful images
Author: Briana Ellis-Gibbs
Headline: As a new exhibition celebrates the 20th anniversary of the Gordon Parks Foundation, those who knew him discuss his most powerful images
Content: Untitled, 1941.Photograph: Gordon ParksView image in fullscreenUntitled, 1941.Photograph: Gordon ParksGordon Parks‘He was making history, not copying it’: the greatest Gordon Parks photographsAs a new exhibition celebrates the 20th anniversary of the Gordon Parks Foundation, those who knew him discuss his most powerful imagesBriana Ellis-GibbsFri 18 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTShareGordon Parks was not only a renowned photographer but also a poet, composer, director and mentor to so many, past and present, a Renaissance man whose talent spanned disciplines. Born in Fort Scott, Kansas, Parks used his craft to illuminate the lives, worlds and humanity of people.He created the Gordon Parks Foundation with Life magazine editor Philip B Kunhardt Jr in 2006 to promote and support artistic and educational initiatives that advance his legacy and vision. In celebration of the foundation’s 20th anniversary, the Jack Shainman Gallery inNew Yorkwill present the exhibit Gordon Parks: Voices in the Mirror.It’s an opportunity for people to see how his work transcends time as he used his lens to connect people. In the exhibit, the families of Muhammad Ali and Malcolm X, Alice and Rebecca Walker, Bryan Stevenson, Ava DuVernay, Hank Willis Thomas and others remember the importance of Parks’s legacy and the impact of his work.The Guardian spoke with some of these dignitaries on the impact of Parks’s legacy and the images taken by him that resonate with them the most.View image in fullscreenLonnie Ali.Photograph: Stephanie Augello/Getty ImagesLonnie AliLonnie Ali is the wife of Muhammad Ali, and theinterimpresident and CEO of theMuhammad Ali Center.View image in fullscreenUntitled, London, England, 1966.Photograph: Courtesy of the Gordon Parks Foundation and the Jack Shainman GalleryMy favorite Gordon Parks photo is the one where he followed Muhammad to London in 1966. It’s a young [Ali] in a very pensive or reflective mood, leaning against a staircase with a suit. The world was beginning to open up for him, and it was that pensive look of reflection on where he had been and where he was going.Gordon was so good at capturing the moment, and I don’t even think it was something Muhammad could stand there and pose for. Park’s photos of him are one of the more intimate portrayals of [Ali].The article that Gordon did on him did a lot to make people see the human side, the charismatic, charming, witty, little childish side of Muhammad, that endeared him to so many.His images can still connect you to his subjects and what he photographed. That power of his artistry in capturing the moment still draws people in, even generations who never met him.Muhammad and Parks carved out the life they wanted, and they were not to be denied. They were trailblazing men. Resilient. Warriors in their own way. Muhammad, on a canvas with his fist, but also with his heart, and Gordon with his camera, and with his heart and wit of how he made that picture come alive.View image in fullscreenKyle Johnson.Photograph: Frank Micelotta/ABC/Getty ImagesKyle JohnsonKyle Johnson starred in Gordon Parks’s film The Learning Tree, released in 1969 and based onParks’s 1963 autobiographical novel. The film was the first major Hollywood studio film directed, producedandscored by a Black director. Johnson portrayed Parks through the fictional character Newt in the movie.View image in fullscreenA Memory, 1993.Photograph: Courtesy of the Gordon Parks FoundationWorking with Gordon was quite relaxed, quite comfortable, and he made everyone else feel that way. When we began shooting, he said to us: “This is going to be our chance to tell our story, cause my story is the story of so many Black people in America. It’s our story, and our history.”This was really the first time that Black people could see themselves as they understood themselves on screen. Almost everyone who approached me after seeing the movie was speaking about how uplifting it was and how they’ve been waiting their lives to see this portrayal of themselves as fully fledged human beings appearing on the screen.His painting appears in the photo from [Parks’s photo book Arias in Silence] as the background, and the thing that is in the foreground is hard to believe, but that is a leaf. He’d go out on a walk and see something interesting and bring it back, and he shot the things in his living room with the available light. The leaf seems animate, like an expression of a human being. Even the shape of it. You can almost see the person inside.It’s like the great impressionistic painters. Maybe you don’t see the woman the painter was seeing; maybe you don’t see it the first time, the second time or the 10th time. But if you come back to the impressionistic work, you see something that you didn’t see before. That’s the thing: now it jumps out at you, whereas before you couldn’t recognize it. I think it was just this sense of life or afterlife that it has. There’s something about it that just says, this is not an object. This is not a leaf. This is an expression of an actual person of a spirit and a soul. It has enough to suggest its previous existence as a human, and yet something of that remains here.Gordon very much had a sense of [the decisive moment], which is instilled in all of his work. If you look at his work, whether it’s portraiture, fashion or things in the natural world, if the photo was taken two seconds before or after, it just wouldn’t be his photo.View image in fullscreenRebecca Walker.Photograph: Tibrina Hobson/Getty ImagesRebecca WalkerRebecca Walkeris a writer, teacherand co-founder ofthe Third Wave, a non-profit organization that advocates for young women to get involved in activism and leadership roles. She is the daughter of novelist Alice Walker.View image in fullscreenUntitled, Shady Grove, Alabama, 1956.Photograph: Courtesy of the Gordon Parks Foundation and the Jack Shainman GalleryAt first glance, the image looks like a beautifully outfitted, middle-class Black father and his children going to get some ice cream, and it feels very contemporary because of the colors. I am happy to see a Black middle-class father and his children in this way because so often Black men and their children are portrayed as victims and, generally, in a kind of degraded way.Then, if you look again, you see the sign that says “White” and “Colored”. It dawns on you that, in fact, this exchange is being delineated and shaped by a deeply painful, integrating system of segregation. This beautiful family is meant to feel less than, and the white person inside bustling to serve them, even though she’s in a service position, is made to feel superior, just based on their race. Then the weight of the Jim Crow South settles, and then the disturbance is there, just lurking, and it begins to haunt you.I think what was so moving to me was this brother’s dignity. They’re going up to get their ice cream, and he’s not going to let this sign or this system keep him from it. They’re not going to be made to feel inferior in any way. It’s a real portrait of something that we need to pay more attention to, which is the ways in which our hard-earned dollars are propping up a system that is not necessarily benefiting Black people. It’s also very moving to me because my mother grew up in the Jim Crow South, and in many ways it’s a representation of a scene that I imagine could come from her life.I felt like Gordon was seeing us and we didn’t even know he was looking. He was just walking around in a seemingly very ordinary way. We could see in the photographs that he was really seeing so much more deeply, seeing beyond what we were presenting and seeing into our deepest beings, not just in the present, but how we were connected to the past and the future in those moments and how we transcended time. He really understood the historical importance at the moment.I’m proud of Mr Parks for taking that image, understanding its importance and how beautiful we are, and doing it so beautifully with such care. As opposed to leading with the brutality, he’s leading with the humanity.View image in fullscreenHank Willis Thomas.Photograph: Paul Bruinooge/Patrick McMullan/Getty ImagesHank Willis ThomasHank Willis Thomas isa conceptual artist known for his work focused on themes of culture and identity.View image in fullscreenAmerican Gothic, Washington DC, 1942.Photograph: Courtesy of the Gordon Parks Foundation and the Jack Shainman GalleryGordon Parks is definitely the definition of a Renaissance man. He was a person who had lived many lives. Parks led by the way he lived his life, the quality in which he lived, and the way he carried himself, which was deeply inspiring. It seemed as if the rules of the world that were fed out to confine him did not actually limit him at all, but he actually excelled past and transcended any boundary that society put in his place.He was so committed to not being confined to a box that I’m always more compelled by the sensibilities and the revelations I have when learning about the stories behind the photographs. This idea that we’re looking at a picture, literally standing in someone’s shoes, looking through someone else’s eyes, and the fact that he chose that specific second to capture, I think, is fascinating. It’s a time-travel for me.He took the image American Gothic while working for the US government during a time when the government thought that documenting the stories and sometimes the struggles of the American people could be a way to bond and inspire us and create empathy and compassion. I think that he probably learned through that early assignment that those lessons were something he could carry on to his career, and so when I think about his other work, I can’t help but think that he was still, in some ways, continuing that project.I think the story [in his photos] is about empathy, bearing witness, courage, perseverance and seizing the moment. I hope that he wouldn’t just try to tell us something, but would try to encourage us to think, invite us to look more closely at the things we take for granted, or don’t even see or bear witness to. Every story he found and every person he found, he was making history, not copying it.Gordon Parks: Voices in the Mirror is on display at the Jack Shainman Gallery until 6 November

title: TV tonight: more zombies get an ass-kicking in The Walking Dead spin-off | Television | The Guardian
description: Maggie and Negan renew bitter rivalries as Dead City returns for a third series. Plus: the Lycett Arms is open for merriment and mayhem. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Maggie and Negan renew bitter rivalries as Dead City returns for a third series. Plus: the Lycett Arms is open for merriment and mayhem. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Refusing to die … Jeffrey Dean Morgan and Lauren Cohan in The Walking Dead: Dead City.Photograph: Robert Clark/© 2026 AMC Global. All Rights Reserved.View image in fullscreenRefusing to die … Jeffrey Dean Morgan and Lauren Cohan in The Walking Dead: Dead City.Photograph: Robert Clark/© 2026 AMC Global. All Rights Reserved.TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: more zombies get an ass-kicking in The Walking Dead spin-offMaggie and Negan renew bitter rivalries as Dead City returns for a third series. Plus: the Lycett Arms is open for merriment and mayhem. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme VirtueandAli CatterallFri 18 Sep 2026 05.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 05.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneThe spin-off from the zombie franchise that refuses to die is back for a third series – and immediately gets back to what it does best: kicking infected ass in apocalyptic New York. Bitter enemies Maggie (Lauren Cohan) and Negan (Jeffrey Dean Morgan) are at the point where Negan is literally about to stab Maggie in the back – but an interruption brings a change in events …Hollie RichardsonGeorge Clarke’s Amazing Spaces: First Home8pm, Channel 4This new series focuses on affordable, nontraditional homes. Even if it does accept the impossibility of the housing market as a fait accompli, it offers intriguing ideas. This time: Kat, whose bespoke tiny home will cost her £50k; Sean, who is building his own; and a Dutch experiment in regulatory relaxation around construction.Phil HarrisonYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaView image in fullscreenPoking holes … Brooke Shields and Amalia Williamson in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVThere are shades of Murder, She Wrote to this cosy, Maine-set whodunnit, as sleuthing novelist Allie (Brooke Shields) and her gen Z sidekick Andi (Amalia Williamson) casually unmask killers. Their latest case involves the suspicious suicide of a smarmy podcaster’s wife. Can the duo poke holes in his airtight alibi?Graeme VirtueLive from the Lycett Arms10pm, Channel 4More boozy merriment as Joe Lycett’s pop-up pub opens its doors once again. This time, landlord Lycett will be delegating his least favourite tasks to temp manager Mel Giedroyc, while special guest Sophie Willan lounges on a barstool and has a natter. As subliminal chatshow formats go, there have been many worse.PHNew Zealand Spy10pm, Sky OneThe 1970s-set espionage spoof created by Kiwi comic Paul Williams wraps up its first season with a deadpan double bill. With one hapless agent missing and the actually competent Sue (Rose Matafeo) ready to quit, it’s left to Michael (Williams) to don scuba gear and two wristwatches to foil a toxic sabotage plot.GVThe Rainmaker10.45pm, ITV1“I guess you’re right about being an acquired taste.” Uh-oh. Is Rudy and Sarah’s romance heading for the rocks? Certainly, last week’s expensive suit gift went down like a cup of cold sick, and episode four puts their relationship under more pressure, when Sarah accidentally lets slip the existence of the hospital’s secret committee.Ali CatterallExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightJoe LycettfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No Land to Stand On by Mahmoud Khalil review – a searing account of political imprisonment | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury
Author: Houman Barekat
Headline: The Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury
Content: Mahmoud Khalil at a news conference in New York.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APView image in fullscreenMahmoud Khalil at a news conference in New York.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewNo Land to Stand On by Mahmoud Khalil review – a searing account of political imprisonmentThe Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet furyHouman BarekatFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMahmoud Khalil was completing a master’s degree at Columbia University when, in March 2025, plain-clothed officers from the Department of Homeland Security snatched him from his home in New York and took him to an immigration detention centre; he was then transferred to another facility in Louisiana, more than 1,000 miles away. As a green card holder, Khalil has permanent US residency, but secretary of state Marco Rubio had determined that his continued presence in the country would have “adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States”, and sought his deportation under a legal provision dating back to the McCarthy era. Khalil was released on bail in June 2024 after a federal judge ruled his detention unconstitutional, but the Trump administration is still trying to have him removed.Khalil – who was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria – had been targeted because of his advocacy on behalf of pro-Palestinian protesters during campus protests over Columbia University’s links to Israel. They were calling for Columbia to cut its ties with Israeli academic institutions and companies profiting from Israel’s onslaught on Gaza; in response, the universitycalled in the NYPD.There was no suggestion that Khalil had done anything unlawful, and no criminal charges were brought against him; the government had simply identified him as an influential pro-Palestinian voice on campus, and for that reason alone they wanted him gone. He spent a total of 104 days in detention, missing the birth of his son.Khalil recounts this Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury in his memoir, No Land to Stand On. The episode is a damning snapshot of the Trump administration’s creeping authoritarianism and the cruelty of its immigration enforcement policy. Khalil was a high-profile detainee whose case drew considerable public scrutiny; he had access to lawyers, and was eventually able to extricate himself. Many of his fellow prisoners at the facility, hailing from places as diverse as Georgia, Romania, Senegal, Nepal, El Salvador and Chechnya, were less fortunate. They languish in detention for months on end, at the mercy of an opaque and glacially slow legal bureaucracy, “forgotten in a system designed to forget them”.Khalil notes that the private ownership of the detention centre produced a perverse incentive structure. It “was not operated by the government, it was operated by shareholders. By people who made money when beds were filled and lost money when they were empty … Every man in this facility was a line item on a balance sheet. Every day we spent here was revenue.” This might explain why, whenever an asylum claim is successful, the state appeals the decision as a matter of course, needlessly extending the applicant’s detention by many more months. So much for the land of liberty.At Columbia, too, the prerogatives of the private sector impinge on the public interest. The university, Khalil quips, “turned out to be a real estate empire with a campus attached”; its board of trustees is “not so much a neutral administrative body as a deeply ideological one … drawn overwhelmingly from finance, real estate, corporate law, and weapons manufacturers”. So when students called out the university’s entanglement with a state credibly accused of committing war crimes, the college administration treated it “as a crisis to be managed rather than a grievance to be heard”.In the meantime, a broad coalition characterised by reading groups, fundraising bake-sales and solidarity with anti-Zionist Jewish groups was smeared as an antisemitic hate movement. There was much hand-wringing about student safety, at least some of which was in bad faith: “When pro-Israel students showed up at our events to film and harass us, the administration called it a legitimate expression of campus discourse. When we held a silent vigil, they described it as a security risk.” People may quibble over who is harassing whom in any given flashpoint, but one thing is undeniable: only those on one side of this argument are at risk of being spirited away by unidentified agents of the state on spurious pretexts.Khalil dislikes being referred to as an activist because the term implies some degree of volition, when in reality he had no choice: “From the moment I was born Palestinian, my existence was political.” His personal backstory, told here in parallel with the account of his arrest and detention, is indeed shaped by political turmoil. As a teenager he was shot in the leg by Bashar al-Assad’s security forces; in 2013, aged 18, he fled Syria for Lebanon, where eventually he ended up working for the British embassy in Beirut. It was there that he met his future wife, a US citizen, before moving to New York in 2022.What happened next is a warped travesty of the American dream: having grown up under a brutal dictatorship, Khalil settles in the US and exercises its much-vaunted political liberties, only to be locked up without charge alnd threatened with deportation. Palestinians, he concludes, “are the exception to every rule the supposed free world claims to hold sacred”. Given the horrors of the past three years, it’s hard to disagree.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
