title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels | Teen books | The Guardian
description: A tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and more
Author: Imogen Russell Williams
Headline: A tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and more
Content: Making a splash … a detail from Once Upon a Tiger by Sarah Massini.Illustration: Simon and SchusterView image in fullscreenMaking a splash … a detail from Once Upon a Tiger by Sarah Massini.Illustration: Simon and SchusterChildren's book roundupTeen booksReviewChildren’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novelsA tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and moreImogen Russell WilliamsFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnce Upon a Tigerby Sarah Massini, S&S, £14.99Tiger is irate to find three cheeky human cubs climbing on his back – but when they refuse to be scared off, he becomes increasingly attached to them. A sweet, classic-feeling picture book fable, heightened by tender, expressive illustrations.View image in fullscreenMama’s Weddingby Circle Yuen, Lantana, £12.99Mama is getting married, but Ruby has mixed emotions – how will Daddy Albert feel on the day? A gorgeous, nuanced picture book about blended families and new milestones.I Am a Squirrelby Scott Rothman, illustrated by Tom Tinn-Dinsbury,Happy Yak, £7.99Big brother won’t believe that little brother’s a squirrel, even though he loves gathering nuts and leaping from tree to tree. But wait – is it time for a hawk to join the game? A funny, acutely observed picture book about sibling dynamics and imaginary play.View image in fullscreenThe Mole Construction Companyby Shingo Nagasaki, translated by Lisa Wilcut, Do Re Mi, £12.99Oh no, the Squirrels’ treehouse is tipping over! Enter the Moles with cranes and diggers to rebuild in this hugely engaging 4+ read-aloud story, translated from Japanese and perfect for vehicle-loving preschoolers.Three Brides for the Devilby Sally Nicholls, illustrated by John Broadley, Andersen, £12.99Charismatic and wealthy, the Devil rides into town in search of an obedient wife. Will one of the widow’s three daughters fit the bill? This elegant, subversive revisiting of Bluebeard, fascinatingly illustrated in intricate pen and ink, will grip 7+ readers as well as older children.View image in fullscreenGhost and Toastby Phil Corbett,Piccadilly, £8.99Trying to remember how he arrived in a haunted mansion, Ghost is surprised to find a cheery companion in Toast, a perfectly ordinary sentient slice of browned bread. Surreal jokes abound as the unlikely duo attempt to thwart the nefarious Croissant in this daft, delicious 7+ graphic novel.Henry Tudor: The Incredible Diaries of Me!by Danny Wallace, illustrated by Tor Freeman,Simon & Schuster, £7.99Eight-year-old Henry Tudor is the best at everything - especially making rude and obnoxious demands. When he’s challenged by a mysterious opponent, however, he’s forced to acknowledge that he might not be completely infallible in this highly illustrated, laugh-a-minute, subversively “historical” 7+ diary.View image in fullscreenHow the Rivermaid Grew Her Tail and Other West African and Caribbean Mythsby Jessica Wilson, illustrated by Sophie Bass,words & pictures, £12.99Weaving together the storytelling traditions of West Africa and the Caribbean, this lush, joyful 8+ collection offers tales ranging from the trickster Anansi to the Jamaican rivermaid of the title, describing the origins of each story with enticing details of food, culture and landscape. Wilson’s ornate text is enhanced by Bass’s boldly coloured, swirling illustrations.The Haunting of Old Splinterby Jack Mackay,Rock the Boat, £8.99When he makes a grisly discovery in his uncle’s sinister mansion, Peter wonders if the old stories are true. Can Old Splinter’s mysterious Wishing Claw actually grant wishes - and if so, at what cost? A superlatively creepy revisiting of The Monkey’s Paw for 8+, from a brilliant new horror writer.View image in fullscreenTackling Racism Togetherby AM Dassu, illustrated by Mia Saine,words & pictures, £10.99Informative and timely, this straightforward little book, produced in partnership with Show Racism the Red Card, provides a broad understanding of racism and its impacts, looking at systemic inequality, how our views are formed and how we can challenge racism in all its forms. A classroom must for 8+ readers.Impossible Creatures: The Neverfearby Katherine Rundell, Bloomsbury, £16.99When a dear friend is kidnapped from the Glimt Midsummer Feast, Christopher and Anya must undertake a desperate series of tasks to win her release. Funny, bloody, and richly underpinned with classical mythology, Rundell’s return to the world of Glimourie is layered with powerful themes of conservation, love, sacrifice and hope for readers of 9+.View image in fullscreenAnd Then We Screamedby Holly Bourne, Usborne, £9.99In the small town of Maple Lakes, everything is perfect – until cheerleader Abigail starts screaming in the middle of an exam. As more girls follow suit, student journalists Clover and Brody investigate the cause, only to discover the sad, terrible secrets beneath the town’s tranquil exterior. A fiercely feminist, gripping and emotionally resonant thriller from a much-loved YA author.Dead Girlsby Beck Kubrick,Simon & Schuster, £12.99When five teenage girls are found murdered in Clossdale, suspicion falls on 17-year-old Ash, daughter of notorious serial killer “Evil Evelyn”. Determined to clear herself, Ash devises a plan to stop the killings, teaming up with her foster sister and best friend. But the girls aren’t expecting to discover a dark conspiracy dating back through generations of power. This blackly comic, splendidly camp graphic novel is a must for YA slasher-film fans.View image in fullscreenThen We’ll Be HappybyAlan Carrigan, Chicken House, £8.99Seventeen-year-old Sam, who has cerebral palsy, just wants some control over his life. When an inaccessible bus bars him from a school trip, he decides to campaign for change – but soon finds himself well out of his comfort zone, confronting his own internalised ableism as he investigates what happiness might look like for him now, rather than in a remote future. Carrigan’s YA debut is a humorous, sometimes painful, deeply engaging account of coming of age as a disabled teenager.Between Ghosts and Godsby Ann Sei Lin, Walker, £16.99As a mortal, Kasu sold her soul to a demon; now she works in a lower-world gambling den, exchanging ghosts’ treasures for gambling tiles, and living virtuously in the hope of reincarnation. When Arun, a mortal prince, arrives in the underworld looking for his mother, Kasu wants nothing to do with him - but as she and Arun are drawn closer, she may risk all her hopes to help his quest. A lush, delectable dark YA fantasy, rooted in Chinese mythology.Explore more on these topicsTeen booksChildren's book roundupChildren and teenagersChildren's books: 7 and underChildren's books: 8-12 yearsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Letter to Brezhnev review – terrific return for Merseysiders’ romance with Russian sailors | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Ellie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, passionate yet still tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 film
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Ellie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, passionate yet still tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 film
Content: Hello, sailor! … Thomas Cotran and Ellie Clayton in Letter to Brezhnev.Photograph: AB PhotographyView image in fullscreenHello, sailor! … Thomas Cotran and Ellie Clayton in Letter to Brezhnev.Photograph: AB PhotographyTheatreReviewLetter to Brezhnev review – terrific return for Merseysiders’ romance with Russian sailorsRoyal Court, LiverpoolEllie Clayton and Angela Simms are superb in a funny, tender adaptation that hugs close to the 1985 filmMark FisherFri 18 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy some quirk of marketing,Letter to Brezhnevis always associated with Margi Clarke. In the 1985 movie, she was the actor who played Teresa, the sharp-talking chicken-factory worker out for a good time in post-industrial Liverpool. The film, though, rightly belongs to Alexandra Pigg as Elaine, Teresa’s best friend, who trades a dead-end life of unemployment for a fantasy fling with a Russian sailor.A few years before the collapse of the Soviet Union – and a year before Willy Russell’s similarly themedShirley Valentine– Elaine dared to believe in escape and in border-defying love. On stage, she is played just as winningly by Ellie Clayton and with much the same combination of wit and wonder. She is the Kirkby girl who has a night on the town with a wallet of stolen cash and finds the world unexpectedly opening up to her. Elaine can be naive, petulant and cynical, but she never lets you stop rooting for her.As Teresa, Angela Simms is the necessary corrective to Elaine’s dreamy romanticism: she lives for the moment and gives as good as she gets. Only in her quieter moments will she admit her rebelliousness is skin deep. They make a terrific pair.View image in fullscreenOut for a good time … Leona Sinama-Pongolle, Angela Sims and Ellie Clayton in Letter to Brezhnev.Photograph: AB PhotographyFrank Clarke’s if-it-ain’t-broke adaptation hugs closely to his original screenplay, adding the odd joke but sticking to the same sequence of taxi rides, club nights and ferry crossings. You might expect that to constrain the director – but no, Nicole Behan injects her production with tremendous energy, exchanging the movie’s subtle charm for ribald theatrical flair, drawing out the humour and the passion without diminishing the tender emotional heart.Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaRead moreThe show takes shape around a multi-level set by Mark Walters, inventively lit by Ian Scott, with gangplanks, bedrooms and barbed wire neatly emerging from a towering frontage of wooden cupboards. In lesser hands it could dwarf the performers, but it is too cleverly conceived for that: something also true of Rob Green’s musical direction. At choice moments, he elevates the soundtrack of 70s and 80s hits by mixing in live vocals, whether it’s You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real) orLips Like Sugar, showcasing an excellent ensemble.Say what you like about movie adaptations, but with cast members from the film in the first-night audience, this one is joyfully at home on the stage.AtRoyal Court theatre, Liverpool, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreLiverpoolreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison drama | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Rona Munro’s understated untangling of a fractured relationship is revived with Christine and Lois Mackie
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Rona Munro’s understated untangling of a fractured relationship is revived with Christine and Lois Mackie
Content: Estranged and unalike … Christine and Lois Mackie in Iron.Photograph: Shay RowanView image in fullscreenEstranged and unalike … Christine and Lois Mackie in Iron.Photograph: Shay RowanTheatreReviewIron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaHome, ManchesterRona Munro’s understated untangling of a fractured relationship is revived with Christine and Lois MackieMark FisherFri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can see why they cast real-life mother and daughter Christine and Lois Mackie in the central roles ofRona Munro’s 2002 prison drama. With Christine playing Fay, a lifer who is inside for murder, and Lois as Josie, her daughter and only visitor, it is no stretch to believe they are related.The irony, though, in this probing, slippery play, is not just that they are estranged but they have become quite unlike each other. It has been 15 years since Josie saw her mother and, having been raised by a grandmother, has grown into a sensible career woman, all suits, business parties and international travel.Mackie junior plays her with an air of detachment: you can imagine her drifting frictionlessly through the world of personnel just as you can see her struggling for definition in her private life. Whatever happened in her childhood has stripped her of an identity. She comes to the visiting room to be coloured in.Compared with such middle-class smoothness, Fay is all sharp edges. Mackie senior plays her like a captive bird, her eyes forever searching for danger, her body contained but ready for flight. It is a superb performance, inconsolable one moment, manipulative the next, hungry for trust but untrustable. Is her “erratic impulse control” a consequence of being locked up or a character flaw? She leaves us guessing.Fences review – August Wilson’s classic family drama is as smart as paintRead moreAs they meet, month by month, they only seem less alike. That is part of Munro’s point: in other circumstances, someone like Josie could forget that people like Fay exist, still less consider the purpose of prison, its effects on mental health and the degree to which women, in particular, can be incarcerated less because of malice than because of a bad roll of the dice. Whether Fay is guilty or innocent, the women’s trauma starts with a man.Sam Holland-Bunyan’s bare-bones production forBest Girlis quiet and subdued, the better to untangle the psychological knots in the women’s relationship as they are watched over by the seen-it-all prison guards (Ellaney Hayden and Jamie Smelt). The low-key approach mutes Munro’s humour and makes a long play seem longer, even as it renders a fractured relationship compelling and sad.AtHome, Manchester, until 19 September. Then atThe Dukes, Lancaster, 30 September–3 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreRona MunroHome in ManchesterPrisons and probationUK criminal justicereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Baka Beyond: Sing the World Awake review – powerful Cameroonian vocals burst through fussy arrangements | Music | The Guardian
description: This fusion of western folk and the traditional music of the Baka people is an uneven patchwork of sound – but there is remarkable power in its yearning ululations
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: This fusion of western folk and the traditional music of the Baka people is an uneven patchwork of sound – but there is remarkable power in its yearning ululations
Content: A distinct fusion … Baka Beyond.Photograph: Carla WordenView image in fullscreenA distinct fusion … Baka Beyond.Photograph: Carla WordenGlobal album of the monthMusicReviewBaka Beyond: Sing the World Awake review – powerful Cameroonian vocals burst through fussy arrangements(March Hare Music)This fusion of western folk and the traditional music of the Baka people creates an uneven patchwork of sound – but it astonishes when their vocals are placed front and centreAmmar KaliaFri 18 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the past 30 years, British folk musicians Su Hart and Martin Cradick have been developing a distinct fusion of traditional Cameroonian vocal music with western instrumentation. Their 1993 debut record Spirits of the Forest, released on Joe Boyd’s Hannibal Records, focused on the female singers of the Baka people, who use a polyphonic style of yodelling to evoke dawn spirits. Hart and Cradick have maintained the relationship over the decades, splitting royalties equally and supporting the community through their Global Music Exchange charity. Sing the World Awake, their first album in 12 years, centres field recordings made with a new Baka generation and deepens their exploration into an ancient oral tradition.View image in fullscreenBaka Beyond: Sing the World Awake album coverCradick’s instrumental arrangements are expansive and wide-ranging. Topé Malangui Kpode features sprightly, Ghanaian highlife-inspired guitar melodies and percussive polyrhythms. Fair Molly (Mál Bhán Ní Chuilleanáin) features Gaelic vocals from guest singer Irene O’Meara, and The Swift harnesses the intricate folk sound of Ben Moneypenny’s violin playing. Each song alights on snatches of Baka vocals, although the overall effect of splicing these unique melodies into different genres creates an uneven patchwork of sound.The album reveals its remarkable power when the Baka ensemble are front and centre. Dance the Dawn beautifully interweaves Mbakolo Elaine’s yearning ululations with finger-picked acoustic guitar and a soft bed of synth melody, gently embellishing her piercing song, while the powerful group vocals of Nahwia Hélène, Loni Julienne, Barma Thérése and Mayo Jacqui ricochet like dub echo on the reggae-inspired We Miss You! The title track is a highlight, featuring a large ensemble of Baka singers who each respond to the soaring yodelling of lead vocalist Loni Julienne to produce an enveloping soundscape of undulating voices. Deeply skilful and strangely moving, when the Baka voices are presented unadorned in full force they are unlike anything else you are likely to find on record.Also out this monthTurkish psychedelic innovatorsBaba Zulamark 30 years as a band withXXX (Glitterbeat). Delving into murky, dub-influenced territory, the record blends droning bass with twanging saz melody and sparse darbuka rhythm to produce a charmingly ambient odyssey. A gem of a find, the rerelease of a rare album of 1980s Ethiopian synth experiments byTeodros Makonnen,Teodros Makonnen With His Organ (Muzikawi), is a wistful exploration of Ethio-jazz melodies and early electronic dancefloor sounds. Syrian composerKhaled Kurbeh’s latest albumIthā Sajā (Research)is a profoundly tender collection of solo piano pieces that weave dextrous Iraqi folk rhythms with soothing neoclassical melodies, each inspired by recording at dawn and dusk.Explore more on these topicsMusicGlobal album of the monthCameroonFolk musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the euphoric ‘Bollywood electronic’ of the Twins and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Omar and Jamal Ikram, 21-year-old brothers, are making lo-fi glitchy dance-pop with the melodic sensibilities of Bollywood music
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Omar and Jamal Ikram, 21-year-old brothers, are making lo-fi glitchy dance-pop with the melodic sensibilities of Bollywood music
Content: ‘We don’t want brown kids to feel like they have to fit into anything’ … the Twins.Photograph: Arran Ashan/PR imageView image in fullscreen‘We don’t want brown kids to feel like they have to fit into anything’ … the Twins.Photograph: Arran Ashan/PR imageAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the euphoric ‘Bollywood electronic’ of the Twins and the week’s best new tracksOmar and Jamal Ikram, 21-year-old brothers, are making lo-fi glitchy dance-pop with the melodic sensibilities of Bollywood musicShaad D'Souza,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 18 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromAldershot, HampshireRecommended if you like2hollis, the Hellp, Jai PaulUp nextNew single Wish U out nowYou, like me, may be growing tired of the 2020s’ so-called “indie sleaze” revival, which has so far yielded a few good parties and not that much good music. But the music of the Twins – Aldershot-born brothers Omar and Jamal Ikram – is made of sturdier stuff. The 21-year-olds are progenitors of a sound they call “Bollywood electronic” – a strain of loud, lo-fi, ultra-glitchy dance-pop that sounds like 2hollis if his songs were heavy with screwy samples of south Asian pop. Their debut album, last year’s Turmeric, captures the still-potent appeal of Jai Paul’s classic Str8 Outta Mumbai – which fused the lackadaisical sheen of 2010s electronic pop with the shining rhythmic and melodic sensibilities of Bollywood music – and, as is de rigueur for the contemporary era, makes it bolshie and frenetic, taking in the euphoric aggression of early Skrillex and unnerving noise of Aphex Twin.Turmeric was a minor hit, thanks in part to Fuckersby, a collaboration with on-the-rise British rapper Fakemink, as well as the Twins’ monthly NTS show,also called Turmeric, which turns one this month. (Its combination of classic British pop stars such as Lily Allen, Punjabi artists such as Sukshinder Shinda, and contemporary electronic acts the Hellp and Sophia Stel gives it the feeling of a late-night pirate radio station totally out of time and place.) The duo’s follow-up EP There&Back, released in May, polishes up the Twins’ sound a little, but not that much – if anything, their collaborations with Rada and Varg2TM on There&Back are even louder and wilder than anything on Turmeric. The duo’s future plans aren’t clear, but their mission is: “We don’t want brown kids to feel like they have to fit into anything,” Jamal said in an interview. “People are always gonna try to label what you’re doing, but you don’t have to move like that.”Shaad D’SouzaThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenPleasingly candid … Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul.Photograph: Courtesy of Paul KooikerCharlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul – Googoo GagaOnly this puckish Belgian duo could make a gorgeous choral refrain from “poo and pee and poo and pee”, which is the prelude to their pleasingly candid, dark electropop account of new parenthood.LS​Voice Actor – High-RiseWith a stunning beat by Lukid, like a house track heard throbbing across a wind-buffeted body of water, Noa Kurzweil ruminates about the psychological damage of apartment block living.BBTSex Week – Life Is a CircleWhat starts as prettily precious folk-pop à la Big Thief or@wilds out into thrilling hyperpop that keeps one foot on the ground (including whinnying horse samples) while spiralling ecstatically skywards. Rare to hear music so surprising.LSJGrrey – BelieveConversational verses slam into a spirited chorus with gospel overtones – appropriate for the London neo-soul singer’s search for something to have faith in as the world goes asunder.BBTOR – Nokik MessiahJohn Talabot pivots to his actual initials (Oriol Riverola) for an album of “the most euphoric possible variant of ambient”. The first taste sounds ready to blow, with piercing synth shards colliding into an unbroken crescendo.LSOscar Later – The Moon Belongs to YouFrom the Londoner’s awesomely accomplished new EP of big-room rollers, this track has an inspired conceit: old-time comical folk song Yon Yonson is turned into Ibiza-grade techno with hard-rock guitar detailing.BBTDana Margolin​ – Big Beautiful SoundThe frontperson of UK indie band Porridge Radio strikes out solo, and the squall of that band has abated to leave bright, clear air on this timeless folk song. Lovely Mike Mills-directed video, too.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Empress Of: Dream House review – a tender and openhearted rebirth after wildfires razed her house | Music | The Guardian
description: Lorely Rodriguez contemplates the meaning of home – both physical and emotional – on a gorgeously humid, hopeful album that makes a virtue of her searching nature
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Lorely Rodriguez contemplates the meaning of home – both physical and emotional – on a gorgeously humid, hopeful album that makes a virtue of her searching nature
Content: Feeling right at home … Lorely Rodriguez AKA Empress Of.Photograph: Courtesy of Luca MastroView image in fullscreenFeeling right at home … Lorely Rodriguez AKA Empress Of.Photograph: Courtesy of Luca MastroMusicReviewEmpress Of: Dream House review – a tender and openhearted rebirth after wildfires razed her house(Major Arcana/Giant Music)Lorely Rodriguez contemplates the meaning of home – both physical and emotional – on a gorgeously humid, hopeful album that makes a virtue of her searching natureLaura SnapesFri 18 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince the early 2010s Lorely Rodriguez has cut a restless, inventive figure. She’s slipped from raucous pop to silkier sounds, explored her Honduran-American heritage and, on her last album, flipped the staple awards season phrase “for your consideration” into a full-frontal club-pop meditation on uneven relationships. Her gorgeous fifth album makes a feature of this searching nature. Written after her family home burned down in the 2025 California wildfires, Dream House is about the rebuilding of that home – birdsong-dappled field recordings of its construction keep popping up – but also contemplates what it means to feel at home in yourself and with others.View image in fullscreenThe album artwork for Dream House by Empress Of.Photograph: PRFor all the violent loss behind the record, it sounds amazingly airy, free and open-hearted. The directness of For Your Consideration softens to a humid atmosphere that’s bright with hope, Rodriguez’s undulating synth lines bubbling with impatience and ecstasy as they cushion her soaring arrow of a voice. The bangers leap above the fray: SYW, featuring Cecile Believe, elegantly twists EDM to evoke an uncontainable desire; the equally yearning HandsOn sparks with glassy chimes and battering percussion. I Pray 4 U evokes the frisky joy of Jayda G, and Machete, dwelling on defiant post-breakup rebirth, slices like a laser through the night sky.Impressively, the calmer moments are no less arresting. Blue Light taps Dev Hynes for a slinky trawl through alienation and the title track wipes away trip-hop’s murk to expose its sweetness, more than fulfilling Rodriguez’s promise that “good things are coming”.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockDance musicElectronic musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Exaudi: Pocket Universe album review – virtuoso vocals with a joyfully bonkers bent | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Four substantial, eclectic works written for James Weeks’ ensemble are brought together here, encompassing swooping folk phrasing, delicate harmonising and exuberant stylistic skill
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Four substantial, eclectic works written for James Weeks’ ensemble are brought together here, encompassing swooping folk phrasing, delicate harmonising and exuberant stylistic skill
Content: Irrepressible … vocal ensemble Exaudi.Photograph: Courtesy of Jon CartwrightView image in fullscreenIrrepressible … vocal ensemble Exaudi.Photograph: Courtesy of Jon CartwrightClassical musicReviewExaudi: Pocket Universe album review – virtuoso vocals with a joyfully bonkers bentExaudi/Weeks(NMC)Four substantial, eclectic works written for James Weeks’ ensemble are brought together here, encompassing swooping folk phrasing, delicate harmonising and exuberant stylistic skillErica JealFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a lot of joy in this release fromExaudiand their conductor, James Weeks, bringing together four substantial, eclectic works written for the vocal group during the 2010s. The first is Guide byCassandra Miller. Based on a devotional song as recorded in 1968 by the folk singer Maria Muldaur, phrases of which are repeated freely by the singers in imitation of Muldaur’s swooping, full-voiced style, it builds quickly into a kind of controlled cacophony.View image in fullscreenExaudi: Pocket Universe.Andrew Hamilton’s Proclamation of the Republic imagines Patrick Pearse outside the Dublin General Post Office at Easter 1916, reading the historic text to a largely confused or oblivious public; little by little, pairing syllables on a quietly but insistently repeating two-note figure, the music blooms into something that seems to unite the crowd as they walk away, humming.The slow movement of this vocal symphony, if you like, isLeo Chadburn’s Affix Stamp Here, the most immediately accessible of the pieces. Placenames and years are spoken, before solo voices sing lines written on old postcards; the rest pick out and harmonise single words as if illuminating them. The yearning harmonic palette and deadpan wit of the piece belies a bigger impact: these tiny windows into the lives of others conjure a feeling of being a small speck in a big universe.Finally, there is the title track, byGeoff Hannan, in which Latin passages of astrophysical discourse by Galileo and Newton tap-dance their way past the ear in irrepressible style: an exuberant end to a virtuosic, slightly bonkers recording.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. Author: Jonathan Jones

A woman has passed out with her white clay pipe in her hand, its stem leading the eye towards what amounts to a still life arrangement beside her: there is a richly decorated cup for spirits, presumably gin, beside a fanned out deck of cards, a mirror, another pipe and a jug of booze. title: ‘Like a Bond villain’s lair’: I climbed the Dolomites to the world’s most spectacular mountain hut | Dolomites holidays | The Guardian
description: Perched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisine
Author: Andrew Gilchrist
Headline: Perched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisine
Content: ‘Santnerpass Hut is perched on a sheer cliff and resembles a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eye-popping hit of modernity and innovation’.Photograph: Andrew GilchristView image in fullscreen‘Santnerpass Hut is perched on a sheer cliff and resembles a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eye-popping hit of modernity and innovation’.Photograph: Andrew GilchristDolomites holidays‘Like a Bond villain’s lair’: I climbed the Dolomites to the world’s most spectacular mountain hutPerched above the clouds in northern Italy, Santnerpass refuge doesn’t just look stunning. It’s a marvel of eco-building – and vegetarian cuisineAndrew GilchristFri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ithink my boots are falling apart!” shouts Nigel just as we hit the pinnacles, a whole range of them jutting up and out from the mountainside, all thrillingly tall, spiky and knobbled. Through them we painstakingly step, fingers aching in gloves, heads sweating in helmets – squashing up narrow chimneys, squeezing through mighty boulders and inching along slender ledges on a twisting path that’s only just discernible through swathes of sharp white scree.I know how Nigel’s boots are feeling: the going is far harder than I was expecting. This is only the first day of our annual trip to the Dolomites, a vast range of breathtaking sawtooth peaks in northern Italy, but my head’s already full of the thought I have every year as we start out: “If only you’d got fitter.”View image in fullscreenBut it should be worth all the scrapes, bumps, scares and sweat. Somewhere up ahead, hopefully not too far, is Rifugio Passo Santner, or Santnerpass Hut, a spectacular mountain refuge that, as everyone who sits near my desk at work knows, has been obsessing me ever since I first saw a picture of it eight months ago.Allowing you to stay deep in the mountains for days on end, the high-altitude Dolomites huts we overnight at all have their charms, from hearty food to giddying views to a generous way with the grappa. But in terms of appearance, they tend to fall into two not particularly pulse-quickening camps: stone block or cuckoo clock. Although you’re almost always overjoyed to see them, none could ever pass for a Bond villain’s lair, however much grappa you’ve had.double quotation markHuts tend to fall into two not particularly pulse-quickening camps: stone block or cuckoo clockYet that is exactly what Santnerpass Hut resembles. Perched on top of a sheer cliff, this elongated triangle encased in a gleaming wrapper of galvanised steel looks like a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eyepopping hit of modernity, originality and innovation in a place where tradition usually dictates more of the same.After one final push, the five of us scramble up on to the summit and there it is just ahead, side on and glowing silver in the late afternoon sun, like a star that has touched down on Earth to enjoy the stunning views of the surrounding peaks with the rest of us, up at the bracing height of 2,734m.“Welcome!” says the bartender as we enter. “You made it. Well done!” With the customary relief – if not actual jubilation – that follows a tough climb finally ending, we ease off our backpacks, gloves and boots then look around, slowly realising that Santnerpass Hut isn’t just a treat for the eyes from the outside.Inside, what you first notice is the unbroken parade of huge windows wrapping around the refuge’s front and flanks. This doesn’t just turn every spot of the roomy ground floor into a light-filled observation point. It also means the hut achieves passive heating since it’s effectively one big solar collector. So there’s no need for log-devouring stoves. That’s quite an achievement at ground level; at more than 2km up, with no road access, it’s verging on miraculous.View image in fullscreen‘Santnerpass Hut was built in 1956 but was taken over, closed and rebuilt, finally opening to the eager climbing public in the summer of 2023.’Photograph: Andrew GilchristThen there’s the wood. It’s blond and everywhere. Guests are basically cocooned within a spellbinding timber tapestry that casts everything in a warm yellow glow, quite a novelty to anyone used to the dingy two-watt corridors and bedrooms of most refuges.The flooring is larch, the restaurant furnishings maple and the load-bearing A-frame spruce, its hefty angular joists exposed on the sundeck, where we soon find ourselves sinking well-earned ice-cold drinks and marvelling at this beacon of sustainable architecture.There are other things to marvel at. Off in the distance, piercing up through an immense blanket of cloud, the lofty peaks of the Latemar group are catching the last rays of the sun, turning pink, orange and purple in a ravishing Dolomites phenomenon known as theenrosadira, triggered by calcium and magnesium in the rock. “This place is incredible,” says Donnie, sipping an Aperol spritz. “I’ve never been anywhere like it in my life.”double quotation markGuests are basically cocooned within a spellbinding timber tapestry that casts everything in a warm yellow glowSantnerpass Hut was built in 1956 but in the last decade or so was taken over, closed and rebuilt, finally opening its generous glass doors in 2023. Designed by alpine specialistsSenoner Tammerle Architects, the new refuge is not just meant to please the eye: the shape lets it shed thick snow and deflect howling winds.There are more surprises when we take our pre-dinner showers. Not only does the wood here give way to zesty yellow laminated panels that wouldn’t look out of place in a chic nightclub, the showerheads also actually stay pointing at your body for the full three minutes of hot water a token gets you.Dinner, however, may have been the biggest surprise of all. It was completely vegetarian – a shock for all of us and a treat for veggies Sam and Nigel. No goulash, no ragu, no pork chops. Instead, out of the kitchen came herb-sprinkled lentils with asparagus, radish and onion, pea and mint soup, then beetroot dumplings on a rich bean, tomato and yellow pepper broth, washed down with superb local wine in actual wine glasses and finished off with creme brulee.“A delicious and nutritious meal,” said Sam, running his spoon round his plate. “What an eye-opener. A win-win for hiker and planet.”Curfew was at 10pm but the restaurant was clearing out anyway. This may have been due to the fact that, in high spirits after our action-packed day, we had taken the hut’s guitar off the wall and treated everyone to that Proclaimers Alpine classic Sunshine on Leith, managing to get a singalong going with the very up-for-it, very international audience.View image in fullscreen‘Made it’ … the writer on the summit, nearing the refuge.Photograph: Donald LivingstoneThe refuge sleeps 4o in 16 rooms. Ours was a spacious affair with bunkbeds, a dainty dormer window and two large cubbyholes each, one for your bag, the other for your stuff – so much more useful than the usual pointless wardrobes and drawers that no one ever unpacks into, since you’ll be gone in a hurry at the crack of dawn.We reached Santnerpass Hut via the König Laurin cable car, 22 miles (35km) from Bolzano, gateway to the Dolomites. After that, it’s a rising, fairly straight line to the refuge, a two-to-three-hour hike through loose scree, then boulders and pinnacles. But be warned: the last section is a via ferrata, meaning there’s a metal cable for you to clip your harness to, and grab hold of as you reach trickier, more treacherous passages. It’s not for beginners.I’d heard, though, that there was another route and, keen to take it back down to the cable car, asked at reception. “Yes, there’s another way,” said Romina Huber, who co-owns and runs the hut with her husband (and chef) Michel Perathoner. “It’s not a via ferrata and it’s super beautiful.”Truly, madly, steeply: a via ferrata tour of the DolomitesRead moreShe wasn’t kidding. First it took us past the Vajolet towers, dramatic spires that lure climbers from all over the world. Then we swung right on to a winding path of fine white scree that rises sharply through meadows full of edelweiss, saxifrage, dwarf pine and boulders, leading to bulging cliffs and eventually the Coronelle Pass, an astonishing vantage point at 2,360m.“Well, that was a walk and a half,” said Mac as we descended in the cable car 30 minutes later, exhausted after the final knee-popping trudge down from the pass on timber-pinned switchbacks. “My boots,” said Nigel, lifting his feet to let us see a rip in one and a sole flapping off the other, “have completely had it.”Santnerpass Hutstarts at€105pp per night, including breakfast and four-course vegetarian dinnerHutiquette: the mountain hut codeMountain huts may occasionally be rather luxurious these days, but their original function, still relevant, is survival. There are, as you might expect, several very sensible codes that make great use of words like “respect”, “other users”, and “environment”. My own code is no less worthy and comes from hard-won experience.No complainingHuts are not hotels. If there’s a problem, go sort it out. Certainly, never complain about snoring, even when you are convinced it is about to trigger an avalanche. I once did, only to be informed, rather too forcefully, that is was me doing the snoring, an outrageous lie that triggered grunts of approval from other grumpy insomniacs. Gel ear plugs work well.ShareIt’s sometimes hard to drop the urban habit of self-assertion to ensure survival. One night in a Corsican hut with a shared sleeping platform, an obnoxious Brit in a down bag shoved all the other sleepers into a pile at one end of the bench, claiming later that he was “dreaming of being pushed”. I pray never to run into him again.Clean up after yourself… and take your rubbish home. TheBritish Mountain Bothy Codehas a good reminder on this point. I’d go even further and say, try to leave absolutely no trace at all. Visiting one treasured wild swimming spot recently, I found the scorch mark of a campfire. Whoever it was had not left any rubbish, and there was nothing to mark their visit, except that dreaded black spot, as if Blind Pew had delivered a death sentence.The hut is for everyoneI once cycled to a remote Icelandic hut and found it blissfully empty of people. Lighting the fire, I prepared my simple meal, and apart from wishing I had packed a beer, looked forward to a night of splendid isolation. Then a large group of locals arrived. I felt my heart sink. My solitary bliss was gone. They sat down, gave me a beer, and two hours later, after helping to eat their huge delicious feast, I felt like I’d joined a tribe. When a hut generates that kind of gang conviviality, it’s uplifting.Look after othersIn Scandinavia, this is a social habit that is deeply embedded. You turn up in a hut in winter and there are logs because the last visitors left them for you. You cut your finger and they all have the plaster that you forgot to bring. TheNorwegian Mountain Codehas a list of essential reminders.Kevin RushbyExplore more on these topicsDolomites holidaysItaly holidaysClimbing holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysArchitectureAdventure travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Buster’s stout punch, from The Prince Bar – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A velvety, Guinness-based, punch-style pick-me-up
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A velvety, Guinness-based, punch-style pick-me-up
Content: ‘Warm the cockles’: Buster’s stout punch.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Jack Hall.View image in fullscreen‘Warm the cockles’: Buster’s stout punch.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Jack Hall.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Buster’s stout punch, from The Prince Bar – recipeA velvety, Guinness-based, punch-style pick-me-upWill HawesFri 18 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePunch isn’t just for summer parties, and this Caribbean-inflected one, featuring rum, brandy, stout, lemon and nutmeg, will warm the cockles of a crowd on any autumn evening. It’s named afterPrince Buster, the Jamaican ska legend and inspiration for our bar’s name.Buster’s stout punchServes20250g demerara sugar, or cane sugar4 large unwaxed lemons900ml Jamaican dark rum, ideally a well-aged one –Myers’sorPlanteray Original Darkfor preference400ml VSOP cognac– we useMartell300ml Guinness– we useGuinness Foreign Extra StoutorGuinness West Indies PorterFreshly grated nutmeg, to garnish and to taste (optional)Put the sugar in a large bowl, then finely grate in the zest of all four lemons(use a Microplane, if you have one); save the rest of the fruit for later. Gently massage the lemon zest into the sugar, to release the oils, then pour in a litre of hot water from the kettle and stir to dissolve the sugar. Strain the sugar water through a fine sieve and into a punch bowl, to sift out the spent zest.Measure in the rum, cognac and stout, squeeze in the juice of all four lemons, stir and put in the fridge to chill until your guests arrive.To serve, stir a good couple of handfuls of ice into the punch, grate over the nutmeg to taste, then ladle into glasses of your choosing. Top each serving with a light dusting of grated nutmeg, if you like.Will Hawes, co-founder,The Prince Bar, London EC1Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodCaribbean food and drinkBeerFruitHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns | Baking | The Guardian
description: Everyone loves an iced finger bun, but these light and moist bakes with a blackcurrant fondant topping might be your new favourite afternoon treat
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: Everyone loves an iced finger bun, but these light and moist bakes with a blackcurrant fondant topping might be your new favourite afternoon treat
Content: Helen Goh’s blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotBakingHelen Goh’s recipe for blackcurrant and vanilla finger bunsEveryone loves an iced finger bun, but these light and moist bakes with a blackcurrant fondant topping might be your new favourite afternoon treatHelen GohFri 18 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoft, feather-light and topped with a thick strip of icing: few things are as irresistible to me as an iced finger bun. Here, I’ve flavoured the fondant with blackcurrant jam, which lends a gentle tartness to balance the sweetness, though almost any good-quality jam will work. A simpletanzhong(a cooked flour-and-milk paste) gives the buns their wonderfully fluffy crumb and keeps them soft for longer. For a more indulgent version, split the buns along the top and fill with whipped cream and a spoonful of jam instead. They’re best assembled just before serving, and make a particularly lovely afternoon treat.Blackcurrant and vanilla finger bunsPrep10 minProve2 hr+Cook1 hr 15 minMakes12For the dough270ml whole milk7g dried instant yeast400g strong white bread flour,plus extra for dusting50g caster sugar1 large egg, lightly whisked¾tsp fine sea salt1 tsp vanilla paste60g unsalted butter, cut into small cubes and softened, plus a little extra for greasingFor the blackcurrant fondant70g blackcurrant (or other) jam180g icing sugar, sifted2 tsp lemon juice1 tiny pinch fine sea salt1-2 tsp hot water, as neededPour the milk into a small saucepan and heat gently until just lukewarm. Measure 140ml into the bowl of a stand mixer, stir in the yeast and leave until bubbly.Meanwhile, whisk the remaining milk in the pan with 25g of the flour, then cook, whisking constantly, on a medium heat for about five minutes, until it thickens into a smooth paste. Set aside to cool until just warm.Whisk the milk and yeast mix, then add the remaining 375g flour, the sugar, egg, salt, vanilla and the cooled milk/flour mix. Attach the dough hook and mix on low speed for about three minutes, until it turns into a rough dough. Turn up the speed to medium, add the butter a few cubes at a time and mix for eight to 10 minutes in total, scraping the base and sides of the bowl occasionally, until the dough is smooth and elastic. The dough should start to pull away from the sides of the bowl while still feeling soft and slightly tacky. Transfer the dough to a large, lightly greased bowl, cover and leave in a warm place for one to two hours, until doubled in size.Line a large baking tray with baking paper. Turn out the dough on to a lightly floured work surface and weigh it. Divide the total by 12, then cut the dough into 12 equal 60g pieces. Shape each one into a tight ball by pulling the edges into the centre and pinching to seal underneath. Put the balls seam-side down on your worktop and, using lightly cupped hands, roll until smooth. Gently roll each ball back and forth to form neat, 12cm-long logs; if you like, taper the ends slightly.Arrange the buns on the lined tray, leaving about 3cm between them (they’ll expand and just meet as they bake, which helps keep the sides soft). Cover loosely and leave to prove for an hour, until risen and puffy.Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, then bake the buns for 15 minutes, rotating the tray once halfway, until lightly golden. Transfer to a rack to cool completely.Meanwhile, make the fondant. Warm the jam gently until loosened, then pass it through a fine sieve – you should have about 50g. Whisk in the sifted icing sugar, lemon juice and salt, until smooth, then add just enough water to make a thick, spreadable fondant. Transfer to a shallow bowl wide enough to dip the buns into.Dip the top of each cooled bun into the fondant, allowing any excess to drip back into the bowl, then put on a rack for the icing to set before serving.Explore more on these topicsBakingThe sweet spotFoodSnacksCakeFruitrecipesShareReuse this content
